title: מבנה הסוגיות – Gittin
note: חלוקה לסוגיות ולשלבי הדיון שנוצרה בבינה מלאכותית באתר talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).
note_de: KI-erzeugte Einteilung in Sugjot und Argumentationsschritte von talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum); englisch, hebräisch wo dort vorhanden.
note_en: AI-generated sugya sections and argument steps from talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: rule for a get from outside Israel
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: rule for a get from outside Israel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who brings a get from outside Israel must say 'it was written before me and signed before me'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that one who brings a get from outside Israel must testify that it was written and signed in his presence.

items.text: Disputes about the boundaries of outside Israel
items.text_en: Disputes about the boundaries of outside Israel
items.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel extends the rule to Rekem and Hager, Rabbi Eliezer even to Kfar Ludim to Lud, while the Sages limit it to those bringing from outside Israel or taking out. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds even from hegmonia to hegmonia. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir debate the status of specific coastal towns.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel extends the requirement to say 'in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed' to those bringing a get from Rekem and Hager.
Rabbi Eliezer extends the requirement even to one bringing a get from Kfar Ludim to Lud.
The Sages limit the requirement to one who brings a get from outside Israel or takes one out.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that the requirement applies even from one hegmonia to another within outside Israel.
Rabbi Yehuda defines the boundaries of outside Israel for gittin: Rekem is like the east, Ashkelon like the south, and Akko like the north.
Rabbi Meir states that Akko is considered like outside Israel for gittin.

items.text: Mishnah: get within Israel does not require the declaration
items.text_en: Mishnah: get within Israel does not require the declaration
items.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes that one who brings a get within Israel does not need to say 'written and signed before me', but if there are challengers, it must be validated by its signatories.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who brings a get within the Land of Israel does not need to declare 'written and signed before me', but if there are challengers, it must be validated by its signatories.

items.text: Gemara's opening question and Raba's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question and Raba's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the reason (for the Mishnah's rule)? Raba begins to answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asking what is the reason for the Mishnah's rule that one who brings a get from overseas must testify that it was written and signed in his presence.
Raba begins to answer the Gemara's question, though his full answer is not yet given in this segment.

items.text: Rava's reason for requiring two witnesses
items.text_en: Rava's reason for requiring two witnesses
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the requirement for two witnesses is because witnesses to the delivery are not readily available to authenticate the get.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the requirement for two witnesses is because witnesses to the delivery are not readily available to authenticate the get.

items.text: Gemara's question on the difference between the two reasons
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the difference between the two reasons
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rabbah's reason (scribes not proficient in writing for her sake) and Rava's reason (lack of witnesses to authenticate).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rabbah's reason (scribes not proficient in writing for her sake) and Rava's reason (lack of witnesses to authenticate).

items.text: Gemara's answer: practical differences
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: practical differences
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the difference arises in cases where two witnesses bring the get, or when it is sent from one city to another within Eretz Yisrael, or within the same country overseas.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the practical difference between the two reasons is in cases where two witnesses bring the get, or when it is sent from one city to another within Eretz Yisrael, or within the same country overseas.

items.text: Objection to Rabbah from the principle of one witness in prohibitions
items.text_en: Objection to Rabbah from the principle of one witness in prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rabbah: if the concern is lack of proficiency, why require two witnesses? One witness is normally believed in prohibitions. It answers that here there is a חזקת איסור of a married woman, making it a matter of ערוה requiring two witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rabbah: if the concern is lack of proficiency in writing for her name, why require two witnesses? One witness is normally believed in prohibitions.
The Gemara begins to answer: one witness is believed only where no חזקת איסור (presumption of prohibition) exists, such as a doubtful piece of forbidden fat.
The Gemara resolves: here there is a חזקת איסור (presumption of prohibition) of a married woman, making it a matter of ערוה (forbidden relations) requiring two witnesses.

items.text: Resolution: most scribes are proficient
items.text_en: Resolution: most scribes are proficient
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that most scribes are proficient, and even Rabbi Meir who is concerned for a minority would agree that court scribes are well-trained; the rabbis merely required a get for stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that most scribes are proficient, and even Rabbi Meir, who is concerned for a minority, would agree that court scribes are well-trained; the rabbis merely required a get for stringency.

items.text: Opening statement: leniency due to agunah
items.text_en: Opening statement: leniency due to agunah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Rabbis were lenient with a get because of the concern for the wife's agunah (being chained to the marriage).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Rabbis were lenient with a get (bill of divorce) because of the concern for the wife's agunah (being chained to the marriage).

items.text: Objection: This is a stringency, not a leniency
items.text_en: Objection: This is a stringency, not a leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that allowing a single witness is actually a stringency, because with two witnesses the husband would not dare to challenge the get, but with one he might.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that allowing a single witness is actually a stringency (חוּמְרָא), because with two witnesses the husband would not dare to challenge the get, but with one he might.

items.text: Resolution: The witness is precise
items.text_en: Resolution: The witness is precise
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that since the Sages debated how many witnesses are needed (two or three), the single witness will be precise and not cause the husband to challenge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that since the Sages debated whether the delivery requires two or three witnesses, the single witness will be precise and not cause the husband to challenge.

items.text: Rava's view and the objection from ervah
items.text_en: Rava's view and the objection from ervah
items.desc_en: Rava says the leniency is because witnesses are not available for kiyyum. The Gemara objects that a single witness is not trusted for matters of ervah, which require two witnesses.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the leniency of a single witness for kiyyum (validation) is because witnesses are not readily available, and a single witness is generally trusted in matters of איסורין (ritual prohibitions).

The Gemara objects that the principle of a single witness being trusted in איסורין applies only where no prior prohibition is established, but here the woman is already established as an אשת איש (married woman), making it a matter of ערוה (forbidden relations), which requires two witnesses.

items.text: Rejection of objection and return to earlier argument
items.text_en: Rejection of objection and return to earlier argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the objection by citing Resh Lakish that witnesses on a document are like their testimony was investigated in court, and the Rabbis required kiyyum only as a stringency. The earlier objection about leniency vs. stringency is repeated and resolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that, in principle, document validation (קיום שטרות) should not be required at all, citing Resh Lakish's principle that witnesses on a document are considered as if their testimony was investigated in court, and the Rabbis only required it as a stringency.
The Gemara objects that requiring two witnesses is actually a stringency (חומרא), not a leniency (קולא), because with two witnesses the husband cannot disqualify the get, but with one he can.

The Gemara resolves the objection by noting that since the master (מר) already stated the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina about how many witnesses are needed, the husband will initially scrutinize the get and will not come to challenge it.

items.text: Rava's reason for not adopting Rabbah's view
items.text_en: Rava's reason for not adopting Rabbah's view
items.desc_en: Rava explains why he does not hold like Rabbah: the Mishnah does not say 'in my presence it was written for her sake', implying that lishmah is not required. Rabbah responds that the Mishnah could have said that, but it was shortened to avoid the scribe cutting the get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rava does not adopt Rabbah's view that the Mishnah's wording implies the requirement of לִשְׁמָהּ (for her sake).
Rava argues that the Mishnah does not explicitly state 'in my presence it was written for her sake, in my presence it was signed for her sake,' implying that לִשְׁמָהּ (for her sake) is not required.

sub.text: Gemara's objection on behalf of Rabbah
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection on behalf of Rabbah
sub.desc_en: Rabbah responds that the Mishnah could have stated that phrase, but it was shortened to prevent the scribe from cutting the document.
The Gemara rejects Rabbah's concern, arguing that even now the scribe might cut the document, but he is more likely to cut one out of three words than one out of two.

items.text: Rabbah's reason for not adopting Rava's view
items.text_en: Rabbah's reason for not adopting Rava's view
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains why he does not hold like Rava: the Mishnah mentions both writing and signing, implying lishmah is needed. Rava responds that the Mishnah could have been shorter, but it was expanded to avoid confusion with regular kiyyum. Rabbah counters that the cases are different (e.g., a woman is trusted here but not there). Rava retorts that since they are trusted when they say 'we know', confusion could arise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbah does not adopt Rava's view that the declaration is needed because witnesses are unavailable to ratify the document.

Rabbah argues that if the reason were merely ratification, the Mishnah would only require 'in my presence it was signed'; the inclusion of 'in my presence it was written' proves that writing for her sake (lishmah) is required.

Rava responds that by right the Mishnah could have been shorter, but it was expanded to prevent people from confusing this with ordinary ratification of documents, which would then be done via a single witness.

Rabbah objects that the cases are incomparable: there witnesses say 'we know', here they say 'in my presence'; there a woman is not trusted, here she is; there an interested party is not trusted, here he is.

Rava rejects the objection, arguing that even in the case of a bill of divorce, if witnesses say 'we know' they are trusted, so confusion with ordinary ratification via a single witness could still arise.

items.text: Question about the Tanna who requires lishmah
items.text_en: Question about the Tanna who requires lishmah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna that requires both writing lishmah and signing lishmah, according to Rabbah's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks, according to Rabbah who attributes the requirement to lack of expertise in writing לִשְׁמָהּ (for her sake), who is the Tanna who requires both writing and signing לִשְׁמָהּ?

items.text: Gemara's first question: Whose view is the Mishnah?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Whose view is the Mishnah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's requirement of writing for her sake fits Rabbi Meir (who requires signature for her sake but not writing) or Rabbi Elazar (who requires writing but not signature). It cites a baraita showing that Rabbi Meir requires signature for her sake but not writing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's requirement of writing for her sake aligns with Rabbi Meir, who requires signature for her sake but not writing.

The Gemara cites a baraita that one may not write a get on something attached to the ground, but if written, detached, signed, and given to her, it is valid, supporting Rabbi Meir's view that writing need not be for her sake.

items.text: Attempt to attribute to Rabbi Elazar and rejection
items.text_en: Attempt to attribute to Rabbi Elazar and rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers that the Mishnah might be Rabbi Elazar, who requires writing for her sake biblically but not signature. However, it rejects this because the Mishnah's three invalid gett are rabbinic, and Rabbi Elazar does not require signature for her sake even rabbinically.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah might follow Rabbi Elazar, who requires writing for her sake (לשמה) but not signature for her sake.
The Gemara raises the counterargument that perhaps Rabbi Elazar requires signature for her sake only rabbinically (מדרבנן), not biblically (מדאורייתא).
The Gemara rejects the attribution because the Mishnah's three invalid gett are rabbinic (דרבנן), yet Rabbi Elazar does not require signature for her sake even rabbinically.

items.text: Citation of the Mishnah of three invalid gett
items.text_en: Citation of the Mishnah of three invalid gett
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah listing three rabbinically invalid gett: written in his own hand without witnesses, with witnesses but no date, or with only one witness. Rabbi Elazar adds that even without witnesses, if given before witnesses, it is valid and collects from encumbered property, because witnesses sign only for the sake of tikun olam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah listing three rabbinically invalid gett: written in his own hand without witnesses, with witnesses but no date, or with only one witness.
Rabbi Elazar adds that even without witnesses, if given before witnesses, it is valid and collects from encumbered property, because witnesses sign only for the sake of tikun olam.

items.text: Attribution to Rabbi Meir and resolution
items.text_en: Attribution to Rabbi Meir and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must be Rabbi Meir, who requires writing for her sake only rabbinically. It cites Rav Nachman that Rabbi Meir said even if one finds a get in the garbage, it is valid, implying that writing for her sake is not biblically required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah must be Rabbi Meir, who requires writing for her sake only rabbinically (מדרבנן), not biblically (מדאורייתא).
Rav Nachman cites Rabbi Meir's statement that even if one finds a get in the garbage, it is valid, implying that writing for her sake is not biblically required.

items.text: Rejection of the initial attempt to attribute the Mishnah to Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Rejection of the initial attempt to attribute the Mishnah to Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier suggestion that the Mishnah reflects Rabbi Meir's view that a get requires witnesses only at delivery, not at signing. It argues that if the Mishnah were following Rabbi Meir's Torah-based reasoning, it should have said 'Rabbi Meir would say it is a Torah law' rather than the actual language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the attribution of the Mishnah to Rabbi Meir, arguing that if it were based on Torah law, the Mishnah should have explicitly said 'Rabbi Meir would say it is a Torah law'.

items.text: Attribution to Rabbi Elazar with a distinction
items.text_en: Attribution to Rabbi Elazar with a distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara instead attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Elazar, who requires witnesses only when there are witnesses present at the signing; if there are no witnesses at all, he does not require signing. This is supported by Rabbi Abba's statement that Rabbi Elazar invalidates a get that is forged from within.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar, who requires witnesses only when there are no witnesses at all, but when witnesses exist, he requires them, citing Rabbi Abba's statement that Rabbi Elazar agrees a forged-from-within document is invalid.

items.text: Alternative attribution to Rabbi Yehuda and explanation of initial avoidance
items.text_en: Alternative attribution to Rabbi Yehuda and explanation of initial avoidance
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who requires both writing and signing on detached material. The Gemara then explains why it initially avoided attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda: it first sought to attribute it to Rabbi Meir, as the anonymous Mishnah follows him, and then to Rabbi Elazar, since the halakha follows him in gittin.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda, who requires both writing and signing on detached material (בְּתָלוּשׁ).
Cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda invalidates a get unless both writing and signing are on detached material.
The Gemara asks why it initially avoided attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara explains it first sought to attribute the Mishnah to Rabbi Meir (since anonymous Mishnahs follow him) and then to Rabbi Elazar (since the halakha follows him in gittin).

items.text: Introduction of the Mishnah about Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Introduction of the Mishnah about Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabban Gamliel requires an agent from Rekem and Cheger to declare, and Rabbi Eliezer even requires it from Kfar Ludim to Lud. Abaye explains they are discussing towns adjacent to and absorbed within the Land of Israel's border, and Rabbah bar bar Chanah testifies that he saw such a place, comparing its distance to that between Bei Kubei and Pumbedita.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: Rabban Gamliel requires the agent from Rekem and Cheger to declare, and Rabbi Eliezer even requires it from Kfar Ludim to Lud.
Abaye explains that the Mishnah deals with towns adjacent to and absorbed within the border of the Land of Israel.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah testifies that he saw such a place, comparing its distance to that between Bei Kubei and Pumbedita.

items.text: Initial attempt to define the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Initial attempt to define the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the Tanna Kamma holds these places do not require the declaration, and suggests the dispute is about the reason: one holds it is because they are not expert in writing for her sake, while the other holds it is because witnesses are not readily available to validate the get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the first Tanna holds these places do not require a declaration, and asks whether the dispute is about the reason: one holds because people are not proficient in writing for her sake, and the other because witnesses are not readily available to authenticate the get.

items.text: Rabbah's resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbah's resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the dispute by asserting that everyone agrees the reason is lack of expertise in writing for her sake. The Tanna Kamma holds that adjacent towns are expert, Rabban Gamliel adds that absorbed towns are expert but adjacent are not, and Rabbi Eliezer adds that even absorbed towns are not, to avoid a distinction within the diaspora.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous assumption and introduces that both Rabbah and Rava each resolve the dispute according to their own reasoning.

Rabbah resolves that all agree the reason is lack of expertise in writing for her sake (לִשְׁמָהּ), and the dispute is only about which towns are considered expert: Tanna Kamma says adjacent towns are expert, Rabban Gamliel adds absorbed towns but not adjacent, and Rabbi Eliezer adds even absorbed towns are not, to avoid a distinction within the diaspora.

items.text: Rava's alternative resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's alternative resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the dispute differently: everyone agrees the reason is lack of available witnesses. The Tanna Kamma holds that witnesses are found in adjacent towns, Rabban Gamliel adds that they are found in absorbed towns but not adjacent ones, and Rabbi Eliezer adds that even absorbed towns lack witnesses, to avoid a distinction within the diaspora.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the dispute by asserting that all agree the reason is lack of available witnesses, and the Tanna Kamma holds that witnesses are found in adjacent towns.

Rava continues: Rabban Gamliel adds that witnesses are found in absorbed towns but not adjacent ones, and Rabbi Eliezer adds that even absorbed towns lack witnesses, to avoid a distinction within the diaspora.

items.text: Introduction of a new Mishnah and initial inference about the dispute
items.text_en: Introduction of a new Mishnah and initial inference about the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where the Sages say an agent from the diaspora does not need to declare, implying the Tanna Kamma holds that one who brings a get does need to declare. The Gemara then asks whether the dispute is about the same two reasons as before.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where the Sages say a messenger does not need to say 'in my presence it was written and signed', and infers that the first Tanna holds a messenger does not need it, asking whether the dispute is about the reason of lack of proficiency.
The Gemara infers that the Tanna Kamma holds that one who takes a get out does not need to declare, and asks whether the dispute is about the same two reasons as before.

The Gemara proposes that the dispute is whether the reason is that people are not expert in writing for the sake of the woman (לשמה), or that witnesses are not readily available to authenticate the get.

items.text: Rabbah and Rava resolve the dispute over the reason for the requirement
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rava resolve the dispute over the reason for the requirement
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rava each explain the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and the later Rabbis according to their own views. Rabbah holds the reason is because people are not expert in writing for her sake, and the dispute is about whether we decree a carrier from one place to another on account of a carrier from abroad. Rava holds the reason is because witnesses are not readily available to authenticate the get, and the later Rabbis merely clarify the Tanna Kamma's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbah and Rava each resolve the dispute according to their own reasoning, with Rabbah holding that everyone agrees the reason is lack of expertise in writing for her sake, and the dispute is about whether we decree a carrier from one place to another on account of a carrier from abroad.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Tanna Kamma's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Tanna Kamma's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna Kamma holds we do not decree a carrier from one place to another on account of a carrier from abroad.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the later Rabbis' position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the later Rabbis' position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the later Rabbis hold we do decree a carrier from one place to another on account of a carrier from abroad.

Rava resolves according to his own reasoning: everyone agrees the reason is that witnesses are not readily available to authenticate the get, and the later Rabbis merely come to clarify the Tanna Kamma's position.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbah from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbah from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who brings a get from one province to another in a Medinat HaYam must say 'in my presence it was written and signed', implying that within the same province in a Medinat HaYam it is not required. This is difficult for Rabbah but not for Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah requiring one who brings a get from one province to another in a Medinat HaYam to say 'in my presence it was written and signed', implying that within the same province in a Medinat HaYam it is not required, which is difficult for Rabbah but not for Rava.

items.text: Reinterpretation of the Mishnah to defend Rabbah
items.text_en: Reinterpretation of the Mishnah to defend Rabbah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests reinterpreting the Mishnah: it does not mean within the same province in a Medinat HaYam, but rather from one province to another in Eretz Yisrael. This is supported by a separate Mishnah that explicitly states that one who brings a get in Eretz Yisrael does not need to say the formula, but the new Mishnah teaches that even initially it is not required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes reinterpreting the Mishnah: the phrase 'from one province to another in Medinat HaYam' actually means 'from one province to another in Eretz Yisrael'.
The Gemara objects: the Mishnah already explicitly states that one who brings a get in Eretz Yisrael does not need to say the formula.
The Gemara resolves: the earlier Mishnah might have been understood as applying only בדיעבד (after the fact), so the new Mishnah teaches that even לכתחילה (the ideal standard) it is not required.

items.text: Alternative challenge to Rava from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Alternative challenge to Rava from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Some pose the challenge differently: the Mishnah implies that from one province to another in Eretz Yisrael it is not required, which is difficult for Rava but not for Rabbah. The Gemara then reinterprets to mean within the same province in a Medinat HaYam.

sub.desc_en: Some pose the challenge differently: the Mishnah implies that from one province to another in Eretz Yisrael it is not required, which is difficult for Rava but not for Rabbah.
The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah to mean that within the same province in a Medinat HaYam it is not required, resolving the difficulty for Rava.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if from one province to another in Eretz Yisrael is not required, then the Mishnah should have stated 'one who brings from one province to another' without qualification. The Gemara answers that in Eretz Yisrael it is indeed not required because pilgrims are commonly found to authenticate the get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if from one province to another in Eretz Yisrael is not required, then the Mishnah should have stated 'one who brings from one province to another' without qualification.
The Gemara answers that in Eretz Yisrael it is indeed not required because pilgrims are commonly found to authenticate the get.

items.text: Question about the time without the Temple
items.text_en: Question about the time without the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this answer works when the Temple exists, but when it does not, what can be said? It answers that since courts are permanently established, witnesses are commonly found.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this answer works when the Temple exists, but when it does not, what can be said?
The Gemara answers: since courts are permanently established, witnesses are commonly found.

items.text: Challenge from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says even from one hegmonia to another (in Eretz Yisrael) requires the formula. Rabbi Yitzchak explains this was due to a specific case. This is difficult for Rabbah, but the Gemara says Rabbah accepts Rava's view. The difference between them is whether two witnesses who bring the get are sufficient, or whether it applies within the same province in a Medinat HaYam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that even from one hegmonia to another in Eretz Yisrael requires the formula 'בפני נכתב ובפני נחתם'.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that this was a specific case of a city named Asasyot with two hostile hegmonias, so the requirement was exceptional.
The Gemara notes that this baraita is consistent with Rava's view but difficult for Rabbah's view.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbah actually accepts Rava's view, so the difficulty is removed.
The Gemara asks what practical difference remains between Rabbah and Rava if Rabbah accepts Rava's view.
The Gemara answers that the difference is whether two witnesses who bring the get are sufficient, or whether the requirement applies within the same province in a מדינת הים (overseas land).

items.text: Introduction of a new Mishnah and question
items.text_en: Introduction of a new Mishnah and question
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about one who brings a get from a Medinat HaYam and cannot say the formula, and asks what 'cannot say' means.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about one who brings a get from a Medinat HaYam and cannot say the formula, and that if there are witnesses it can be validated by its signatures.
The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'cannot say' — what specific inability is being described.

items.text: Opening objection: a deaf person cannot deliver a get
items.text_en: Opening objection: a deaf person cannot deliver a get
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a deaf person cannot bring a get, citing the Mishnah that excludes a deaf person, an imbecile, and a minor from being valid messengers to deliver a get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a deaf person cannot deliver a get, citing the Mishnah that excludes a deaf person, an imbecile, and a minor from being valid messengers.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution: the case of a deaf person who was initially competent
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution: the case of a deaf person who was initially competent
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the case involves a messenger who was competent when he received the get but became deaf before he could recite the required declaration. This resolution works for Rava but is difficult for Rabbah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a messenger who was competent (פקח) when he received the get but became deaf before he could recite the required declaration.
The Gemara notes that this resolution works smoothly for Rava but remains difficult for Rabbah.

items.text: Rabbah's difficulty and the Gemara's attempted resolution
items.text_en: Rabbah's difficulty and the Gemara's attempted resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the case is after the deaf person learned, but then he could still recite the declaration. The Gemara proposes a decree lest the matter revert to its flawed state, but then objects that this is an uncommon case and the Sages do not decree for uncommon cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case we are dealing with, suggesting it is after the deaf person learned to speak.
The Gemara objects that if so, the deaf person could still recite the declaration, so the mishnah's ruling is problematic.
The Gemara proposes a decree lest the matter revert to its flawed state, as a reason for the mishnah's ruling.
The Gemara objects that if so, the deaf person could still recite the declaration, so the decree is unnecessary.
The Gemara rejects the decree because a deaf person who became deaf after being competent is an uncommon case, and the Sages do not decree for uncommon cases.

items.text: Counterexample from a woman bringing her own get
items.text_en: Counterexample from a woman bringing her own get
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that a woman bringing her own get is also uncommon, yet she must recite the declaration to avoid a difference in agency. The Gemara then asks why a husband does not need to recite it, and explains that the declaration is needed only to prevent the husband from challenging the get, but when he holds it himself, he cannot challenge it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a woman bringing her own get is also uncommon, yet the Mishnah requires her to recite the declaration to avoid a difference in agency.
The Gemara asks why a husband who brings his own get does not also need to recite the declaration.
The Gemara answers that the declaration is needed only to prevent the husband from challenging the get, but when he holds it himself, he cannot challenge it.

items.text: Shmuel's inquiry about two messengers
items.text_en: Shmuel's inquiry about two messengers
items.desc_en: Shmuel asks Rav Huna whether two messengers who bring a get from overseas need to recite the declaration. Rav Huna answers that they do not, reasoning that if they could testify that they witnessed the divorce, they would be believed.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel asks Rav Huna whether two messengers who bring a get from overseas need to recite the declaration.
Rav Huna answers that they do not need to recite the declaration.
Rav Huna supports his answer by reasoning that if the messengers said they witnessed the divorce itself, they would be believed.

items.text: Applying the same reasoning to two messengers
items.text_en: Applying the same reasoning to two messengers
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this resolution works for Rava but is difficult for Rabbah, and then repeats the same pattern of argument: the case is after they learned, a decree is proposed, but it is uncommon, and the counterexample of a woman is raised, leading to the same conclusion about the husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the resolution works for Rava but is difficult for Rabbah.
The Gemara answers that the case is after they learned (the halacha).
The Gemara questions: if so, even one messenger should be sufficient.
The Gemara objects with a decree: lest the matter revert to its flawed state.
The Gemara questions: if so, even two messengers should be required.
The Gemara rejects this: two messengers bringing a get is uncommon, and the Sages did not decree for uncommon cases.
The Gemara objects with the case of a woman, which is uncommon yet she may bring her own get, with a condition.
The Gemara questions: if so, the husband himself should also need to say the formula, but a baraita exempts him, because he holds the get and cannot challenge it.

items.text: Final resolution: the declaration is a leniency
items.text_en: Final resolution: the declaration is a leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that if the get is validated by its signatures, it is valid even without the declaration, showing that the requirement is a leniency for the woman. The Gemara resolves Rabbah's difficulty by explaining that the case is after she married, and the declaration is a leniency to avoid uprooting her marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: an agent who brought a גט (bill of divorce) from overseas and gave it without the declaration is valid if the signatures are ratified, showing the declaration is a leniency, not a stringency.
The Gemara objects: this works for Rava but is difficult for Rabbah; it answers that the case is after they learned the law.
The Gemara asks: but you said there is a decree lest the matter return to corruption; the answer is that she already married, so the leniency applies.
The Gemara resolves: the baraita means that if you think to be stringent and remove her, the declaration was instituted as a leniency, not a stringency.

items.text: Gemara's question on the rationale for the declaration
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the rationale for the declaration
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages instituted the requirement for the messenger to say 'in my presence it was written and signed'. It suggests it is because the husband might later contest the get, and the messenger's declaration preempts that. The Gemara then questions why we should initiate a challenge if the husband does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages instituted the messenger's declaration, suggesting it is to preempt the husband's potential challenge, then questions why the court should initiate a challenge if the husband does not.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on the reason
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on the reason
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: one says the declaration is needed because people are not expert in writing for her sake, and the other says it is because witnesses to authenticate the get are not readily available.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: one says the declaration is because people are not expert in writing the get for her sake, the other says because witnesses are not readily available to authenticate it.

items.text: Proof that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds the reason of lack of expertise
items.text_en: Proof that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds the reason of lack of expertise
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a story: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba brought a get before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and asked if he needed to say the declaration. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi replied that it is only required for earlier generations who were not expert, but later generations who are expert do not need it. This confirms his position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proves that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds the reason 'because people are not expert in writing for her sake' by citing a story where Rabbi Shimon bar Abba brought a get before him and he ruled that the declaration is only needed for earlier generations who were not expert.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answered that the declaration was only required for earlier generations who were not expert, but later generations who are expert do not need it, confirming his position.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the story
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the story
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: how can Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi say later generations do not need the declaration, given that Rabba (or Rava) holds a different view? Also, we already said the concern is that the matter might become corrupted. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon bar Abba had another person with him, but he was not mentioned out of respect for Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: how can Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling stand, given that Rabba (or Rava) holds a different view, and we already said the concern is that the matter might become corrupted?
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon bar Abba had another person with him, but he was not mentioned out of respect for Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Dispute on how many witnesses are needed for delivery
items.text_en: Dispute on how many witnesses are needed for delivery
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina: one says the get must be given in front of two witnesses, the other says in front of three. It then proves that Rabbi Yochanan holds two, citing a story where he instructed a messenger to give it in front of two and say the declaration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina regarding how many witnesses are required for the delivery of a get (bill of divorce).
The Gemara proves that Rabbi Yochanan holds the opinion of two witnesses by citing a story where he instructed Ravin bar Rav Chisda to give the get in front of two and recite the declaration.

items.text: Attempt to link the dispute to the earlier reasons
items.text_en: Attempt to link the dispute to the earlier reasons
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute about two or three witnesses corresponds to the earlier reasons: one who says two holds the reason of lack of expertise, and one who says three holds the reason of lack of witnesses. But it objects: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds lack of expertise, yet Rabbi Yochanan holds lack of witnesses, and here Rabbi Yochanan says two. Also, Rabba (or Rava) holds a different view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute about two or three witnesses corresponds to the earlier reasons: one who says two holds the reason of lack of expertise, and one who says three holds the reason of lack of witnesses.

The Gemara objects: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds the reason of lack of expertise, yet Rabbi Yochanan holds the reason of lack of witnesses, and here Rabbi Yochanan says two witnesses, contradicting the suggested alignment.
The Gemara adds another objection: Rabba (or Rava) holds a different view, further undermining the suggested alignment.

items.text: Alternative explanations for the dispute
items.text_en: Alternative explanations for the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara first suggests the dispute is about whether a messenger can become a witness and a witness can become a judge. Then it rejects that because we hold that a witness can become a judge by rabbinic law. Finally, it suggests the dispute is about whether a woman is considered reliable to bring the get: one holds that since a woman is eligible, people might rely on her, so we need three; the other holds that people know not to rely on a woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether a messenger can become a witness and a witness can become a judge.
The Gemara objects that we already hold by rabbinic law that a witness can become a judge.
The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether a woman is reliable to bring the get, with one opinion holding that people might rely on her.
The other opinion holds that people know not to rely on a woman, so only two are needed.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Meir's stringency
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Meir's stringency
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan: if one brings a get from abroad and gives it without the declaration, Rabbi Meir says the child is a mamzer, while the Sages say the child is not a mamzer but the get must be given again in front of two. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir's view is consistent with his principle that any deviation from the formula established by the Sages renders the get invalid and the child a mamzer.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited supporting Rabbi Yochanan: if one brings a get from abroad and gives it without the declaration, Rabbi Meir rules that the child is a mamzer.
The Sages in the baraita disagree: the child is not a mamzer, and the agent must take the get back and give it again in front of two with the declaration.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Meir's extreme stringency: is the omission of the declaration alone enough to invalidate the get and make the child a mamzer?

sub.text: Gemara's answer citing Rav Hamnuna in the name of Ulla
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing Rav Hamnuna in the name of Ulla
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Meir follows his own principle, as stated by Rav Hamnuna in the name of Ulla: anyone who deviates from the formula established by the Sages regarding gittin must divorce and the child is a mamzer.

items.text: Stories about strictness and leniency in get writing
items.text_en: Stories about strictness and leniency in get writing
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates two stories: Bar Hedya came before Rabbi Achai who required him to examine every letter, but Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi said it is not necessary, and if one is strict, it casts aspersions on earlier gittin. Then Rabba bar bar Chanah brought a get that was only partially written in his presence, and Rabbi Elazar ruled that even one line written for her sake suffices. Rava says something else.

sub.desc_en: Bar Hedya comes before Rabbi Achai, who requires him to examine every letter of the get.
Bar Hedya then comes before Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, who tell him he does not need to examine every letter.
The Gemara objects that if one were to be strict, it would cast aspersions on earlier gittin.
Rabba bar bar Chanah brings a get partially written in his presence, and Rabbi Elazar rules that even one line written for her sake suffices.
Rav Ashi begins to say something, but the text cuts off at the section boundary.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Ashi's ruling on hearing the scribe's quill
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Ashi's ruling on hearing the scribe's quill
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Ashi's view: even if the messenger is in the house and the scribe in the attic, or vice versa, or even if the messenger goes in and out all day, the get is valid. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to a case where the messenger hears the sound of the quill and the scroll, and addresses a potential objection about the messenger going out to the market.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited supporting Rav Ashi's ruling: a get brought from overseas is valid even if the messenger is in the house and the scribe in the attic, or vice versa, or even if the messenger goes in and out all day.

The Gemara objects: if the messenger is in the house and the scribe in the attic, the messenger does not see the writing; rather, the case must be where he hears the sound of the quill and the scroll.

The Gemara questions the baraita's statement about the messenger going in and out all day: if the messenger is valid even without seeing the scribe, why mention the case of going in and out? And if it refers to the scribe, it is obvious that the scribe's going out does not invalidate the get.

The Gemara resolves: the baraita is necessary for a case where the scribe went out to the market and returned, lest one think another person found him and told him to write; the baraita teaches that it is still valid.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the status of Babylonia for gittin
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the status of Babylonia for gittin
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel disagree: Rav considers Babylonia like Eretz Yisrael for gittin, while Shmuel considers it like outside the land. The Gemara initially suggests they argue over the reason for the leniency (lack of expertise in writing for her sake vs. lack of witnesses for authentication), but rejects this because Rabba holds like Rava. Instead, both agree that authentication is needed; Rav says witnesses are available due to the yeshivot, while Shmuel says the yeshiva scholars are busy with their studies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rav considers Babylonia like Eretz Yisrael for gittin, while Shmuel considers it like outside the land.

The Gemara suggests that the dispute hinges on the reason for the leniency: Rav holds it is due to lack of expertise in writing for her sake (and Babylonians are expert), while Shmuel holds it is due to lack of witnesses for authentication (and witnesses are not available).
The Gemara objects: Rabba holds like Rava, so the initial suggestion is inconsistent.
The Gemara resolves: both agree authentication is needed; Rav says witnesses are available due to the yeshivot, while Shmuel says the yeshiva scholars are busy with their studies.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's statement and Rabbi Yirmeya's objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's statement and Rabbi Yirmeya's objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba reports that Rav Huna said they considered themselves in Babylonia like Eretz Yisrael for gittin after Rav came. Rabbi Yirmeya objects from a Mishnah that limits the leniency to places near the border, and Babylonia is far north. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yirmeya himself resolves the objection by excluding Babylonia from the Mishnah's rule.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba reports that Rav Huna said they considered themselves in Babylonia like Eretz Yisrael for gittin after Rav came.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects from a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda defines the northern border of Eretz Yisrael as Acco, and Babylonia lies far north of that.
The Gemara notes that even Rabbi Meir, who is lenient, only extends the leniency to nearby Acco, not distant Babylonia.
Rabbi Yirmeya himself resolves the objection by excluding Babylonia from the Mishnah's rule.

items.text: Defining the boundaries of Babylonia for gittin
items.text_en: Defining the boundaries of Babylonia for gittin
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Yosef discuss the geographical extent of Babylonia for the purpose of gittin, comparing it to the dispute about lineage. Rav Yosef states that for gittin, everyone agrees the boundary extends to the second bridge of the Arba.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What are the boundaries of Babylonia for the purpose of gittin?
Rav Pappa answers that the dispute about boundaries for lineage applies equally to gittin.
Rav Yosef resolves that for gittin, all agree the boundary extends to the second bridge of the Arba.

items.text: Rav Chisda's practice and its rationale
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's practice and its rationale
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda required authentication for a get from Aktispon to Bei Ardashir but not vice versa. The Gemara initially suggests he holds the reason is lack of expertise in writing for her sake, but rejects this. Instead, both agree authentication is needed; the difference is that people from Aktispon go to the market in Bei Ardashir and know the signatures there, but not vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports Rav Chisda's practice: he required authentication for a get from Aktispon to Bei Ardashir but not vice versa, and proposes that he holds the reason for requiring authentication is lack of expertise in writing for her sake, and those from Bei Ardashir are learned.
The Gemara objects: how can you think Rav Chisda holds that reason, given that Rabba (who is earlier) already holds the view of Rava (that the reason is lack of witnesses)?

The Gemara resolves: everyone agrees authentication is needed; the difference is that people from Aktispon go to the market in Bei Ardashir and know the signatures there, but those from Bei Ardashir are busy in their own market and do not know the signatures from Aktispon.

items.text: Practices of Rabba bar Avuha, Rav Sheshet, and Rava regarding authentication
items.text_en: Practices of Rabba bar Avuha, Rav Sheshet, and Rava regarding authentication
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Avuha required authentication from one town to another, Rav Sheshet from one neighborhood to another, and Rava even within the same neighborhood. The Gemara notes that Rava himself said the reason is lack of witnesses, but the people of Mechoza are different because they are itinerant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports three varying practices: Rabba bar Avuha required authentication from one town to another, Rav Sheshet from one neighborhood to another, and Rava even within the same neighborhood.
The Gemara questions Rava's practice, noting that he himself stated the reason for requiring authentication is that witnesses are not readily available to validate the signatures.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the people of Mechoza are different because they are itinerant, so witnesses are not found even within the same neighborhood.

items.text: Rav Kahana's get and Rav's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's get and Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana brought a get, and Rav ruled that he did not need to say 'in my presence it was written and signed' because the distance between Sura and Nehardea is not considered a distant place.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanin reports that Rav Kahana brought a get from Sura to Nehardea or vice versa, and Rav ruled that he did not need to say 'in my presence it was written and signed' because the distance is not considered a distant place.

items.text: Explanation of the phrase 'if you did, you benefited'
items.text_en: Explanation of the phrase 'if you did, you benefited'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the meaning of the phrase 'if you did, you benefited' from the previous Mishnah: if a husband comes to contest the get, we do not pay attention to him. This introduces the need for the declaration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'if you did, you benefited' means.
The Gemara explains that the phrase means: if a husband comes to contest the get, we do not pay attention to him.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yishmael and the man from Kfar Sisai
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yishmael and the man from Kfar Sisai
items.desc_en: A man brings a get before Rabbi Yishmael, who instructs him to say 'written and signed in my presence' to avoid needing witnesses. Rabbi Il'ai later objects that Kfar Sisai is within Eretz Yisrael, but Rabbi Yishmael silences him, saying the ruling was issued permissively.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts a story where a man from Kfar Sisai brings a get before Rabbi Yishmael, who instructs him to say 'written and signed in my presence' to avoid needing witnesses.
Rabbi Il'ai objects that Kfar Sisai is within Eretz Yisrael, citing the Mishnah that even the Sages only dispute Rabbi Meir regarding distant Akko, not nearby Kfar Sisai.
Rabbi Yishmael silences Rabbi Il'ai, ruling that since the matter was issued permissively, it stands.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yishmael's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yishmael's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yishmael told the man to say the declaration to avoid witnesses, since the man was from Kfar Sisai which is close. It answers that the full reasoning was not presented to him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: But Rabbi Yishmael himself told the man to say the declaration 'so that you will not need witnesses' — so why did Rabbi Il'ai object?
The Gemara answers: The full reasoning (that Kfar Sisai is close and does not require witnesses) was not presented to Rabbi Yishmael at the time he gave his ruling.

items.text: Rabbi Avyatar's ruling on gittin from outside Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Rabbi Avyatar's ruling on gittin from outside Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avyatar sends a message to Rav Chisda that gittin coming from there to here do not require the declaration. The Gemara considers whether this is because they are not proficient in writing for her sake, but objects that those from there are learned. It concludes that the reason is that witnesses are available due to many travelers.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avyatar sends a message to Rav Chisda that gittin coming from there (outside Eretz Yisrael) to here (Eretz Yisrael) do not require the declaration 'in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed'.
The Gemara asks: Does Rabbi Avyatar hold that the reason is because those from there are not proficient in writing for her sake, but these (from Eretz Yisrael) are learned?
The Gemara objects: How can you think that? Rabba has the ruling of Rava (that even those from there are learned).
The Gemara concludes: Rather, everyone requires the document to be ratified (by witnesses), and since there are many travelers who go up and down, witnesses are readily available.

items.text: Rav Yosef's challenge to Rabbi Avyatar's authority
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's challenge to Rabbi Avyatar's authority
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef questions Rabbi Avyatar's authority, citing a letter he sent to Rav Yehuda about people who fulfilled a verse without ruling lines. Abaye defends Rabbi Avyatar, arguing that not knowing a tradition does not make one unqualified.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef questions Rabbi Avyatar's authority, citing a letter he sent to Rav Yehuda about people who fulfilled a verse without ruling lines.
Rabbi Yitzchak and a baraita give conflicting rulings on how many lines may be written without ruling.
Abaye defends Rabbi Avyatar, arguing that not knowing a tradition does not make one unqualified, as it is a matter of received tradition (גמרא) not reasoning.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Avyatar and Elijah about the concubine in Gibeah
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Avyatar and Elijah about the concubine in Gibeah
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Avyatar and Rabbi Yonatan disagreed about whether the concubine found a fly or a hair. Elijah confirmed that both are words of the living God, and Rav Yehuda explains the difference: a fly is disgusting, a hair is dangerous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rabbi Avyatar and Rabbi Yonatan about whether the concubine in Gibeah found a fly or a hair.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Avyatar and Elijah
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Avyatar and Elijah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avyatar encounters Elijah and asks what God is studying; Elijah reports that God is engaged with the concubine of Gibeah and cites both opinions.
Rabbi Avyatar objects that there can be no doubt before Heaven.
Elijah explains that both opinions are words of the living God: a fly is disgusting but not dangerous, a hair is dangerous and causes anger.

Rav Yehuda explains the practical difference: a fly in the bowl is disgusting, a hair in that place is dangerous; an alternative version says both are in the bowl, but a fly is an unavoidable accident while a hair is negligence.

items.text: Teachings on excessive fear in the home
items.text_en: Teachings on excessive fear in the home
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda warns against excessive fear in the home, citing the concubine in Gibeah. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav lists three sins that result from it: forbidden relations, bloodshed, and Shabbat desecration. Rabba bar bar Chana lists three things one must say on Shabbat eve.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda warns against excessive fear in the home, citing the tragic case of the concubine in Gibeah.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav lists three sins that result from excessive fear in the home: forbidden relations, bloodshed, and Shabbat desecration.
Rabba bar bar Chana lists three things one must say on Shabbat eve: 'Have you tithed? Have you prepared the עירוב (Shabbat boundary)? Light the lamp!'

items.text: Excessive fear in the home and the incident with Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Excessive fear in the home and the incident with Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that he independently derived the principle of teaching with ease. Rabbi Abahu warns against excessive fear in the home, citing the case of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, whose household attempted to feed him a limb from a living animal due to the fear he instilled. The Gemara clarifies that they only sought to feed him, but did not actually do so.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that he independently derived the principle of teaching with ease, not having heard it from Rabbah bar bar Chanah.
Rabbi Abahu warns against excessive fear in the home, citing the case of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel whose household attempted to feed him a limb from a living animal.
The Gemara objects that it is impossible that they actually fed him, given that God does not bring calamity through the animals of the righteous, let alone the righteous themselves.
The Gemara clarifies that they only sought to feed him a limb from a living animal, but did not actually do so.

items.text: Informing against oppressors
items.text_en: Informing against oppressors
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva asks Rabbi Elazar whether it is permitted to hand over those who oppress him to the government. Rabbi Elazar responds with a verse from Psalms, advising silence and trust in God. When Mar Ukva persists, Rabbi Elazar advises him to frequent the study hall, and the oppressors will be punished. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Elazar's ruling was later used against him.

sub.desc_en: Mar Ukva asks Rabbi Elazar whether it is permitted to hand over those who oppress him to the government.
Rabbi Elazar cites a verse from Psalms, advising silence even when a wicked person is before him.
Mar Ukva persists, saying the oppressors greatly distress him and he cannot bear it.
Rabbi Elazar advises Mar Ukva to be silent before God and frequent the study hall, and the oppressors will perish on their own.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Elazar's own ruling was later used against him when he was handed over to the government.

items.text: Prohibition of music
items.text_en: Prohibition of music
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva is asked about the source for the prohibition of music. He cites the verse 'Al tismach Yisrael el gil ba'amim'. The Gemara questions why he did not cite another verse, and explains that the cited verse teaches that even vocal music is prohibited, not just instrumental.

sub.desc_en: The sages ask Mar Ukva for the source of the prohibition of music.
Mar Ukva cites the verse 'אַל תִּשְׂמַח יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶל גִּיל בְּעַמִּים' (Do not rejoice, Israel, with joy like the nations) as the source.
The Gemara objects that Mar Ukva could have cited the verse 'בַּשִּׁיר לֹא יִשְׁתּוּ יָיִן' (They will not drink wine with song) instead.
The Gemara explains that the other verse would only prohibit instrumental music (זִמְרָא דְמָנָא), but Mar Ukva's verse teaches that even vocal music (דְּפוּמָּא) is forbidden.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse 'Kinah and Dimonah and Ad'adah'
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse 'Kinah and Dimonah and Ad'adah'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Natan asks Rav Ashi about the meaning of the verse listing city names. Rav Ashi initially says they are cities in Eretz Yisrael. Rav Huna objects, and then cites an interpretation from Rav Geviha of Argiza: anyone who has jealousy against another and remains silent, God will judge. Rav Ashi questions this with another verse, and Rav Acha from Bei Choza'a offers a similar interpretation regarding one who has a grievance.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Natan asks Rav Ashi about the meaning of the verse listing the cities 'קִינָה וְדִימוֹנָה וְעַדְעָדָה', and Rav Ashi initially answers that they are simply cities in Eretz Yisrael.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Natan's objection and citation
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Natan's objection and citation
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Natan objects that he already knows they are cities, and cites Rav Geviha of Argiza's interpretation: anyone who has jealousy (קנאה) against another and remains silent (דומם), the Eternal One (שוכן עדי עד) will judge him.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's challenge and Rav Acha's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge and Rav Acha's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges with a similar verse about other cities, and Rav Acha from Bei Choza'a offers a parallel interpretation: anyone who has a grievance (צעקת לגימא) against another and remains silent, the One who dwells in the bush (שוכן בסנה) will judge him.

items.text: Prohibition of crowns and the discussion with the Exilarch
items.text_en: Prohibition of crowns and the discussion with the Exilarch
items.desc_en: The Exilarch asks Rav Huna about the prohibition of crowns. Rav Huna cites a rabbinic decree from the war of Vespasian. Rav Chisda adds a verse from Ezekiel linking the removal of the priestly mitznefet to the removal of crowns. Rav Huna returns and praises Rav Chisda. Later, Ravina finds Mar bar Rav Ashi making a crown for his daughter, and Mar bar Rav Ashi distinguishes between men and women.

sub.desc_en: The Exilarch asks Rav Huna for the source of the prohibition against wearing crowns.
Rav Huna answers that the prohibition is rabbinic, citing the Mishnah that during the war of Vespasian they decreed against wedding crowns and the אירוס (a type of wreath).
Rav Chisda adds a verse from Ezekiel linking the removal of the priestly mitznefet (turban) to the removal of the crown, providing a biblical basis for the prohibition.

sub.text: Rav Huna's praise of Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Huna's praise of Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna returns, finds Rav Chisda sitting, and praises him, saying his name 'Chisda' (kindness) matches his kind words.

sub.text: Ravina's challenge and Mar bar Rav Ashi's distinction
sub.text_en: Ravina's challenge and Mar bar Rav Ashi's distinction
sub.desc_en: Ravina finds Mar bar Rav Ashi making a crown for his daughter and challenges him with the verse; Mar bar Rav Ashi distinguishes between men, who are analogous to the High Priest, and women, who are not.

items.text: Interpretation of 'Zot lo Zot' regarding the golden calf
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Zot lo Zot' regarding the golden calf
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avira, citing Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, explains the verse 'Zot lo Zot' as a dialogue between God and the ministering angels. The angels argued that Israel deserved mercy because they accepted the Torah, but God responded that they forfeited it by worshipping the golden calf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the meaning of the phrase 'Zot lo Zot' in the verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Avira citing Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avira citing Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avira, citing Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, explains that the verse describes a dialogue: the angels argued that Israel deserved mercy for accepting the Torah, but God responded that they forfeited it by worshipping the golden calf.

items.text: Charity from limited resources and the parable of the sheep
items.text_en: Charity from limited resources and the parable of the sheep
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avira, citing Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, teaches that if one's sustenance is limited, he should give charity from it. The school of Rabbi Yishmael adds that one who gives charity from his assets is saved from Gehinnom, illustrated by a parable of two sheep crossing water.

sub.text: Rabbi Avira citing Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avira citing Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avira, citing Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, teaches that if one's sustenance is limited, he should give charity from it.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael adds that one who gives charity from his assets is saved from Gehinnom, illustrated by a parable of two sheep crossing water.

items.text: Opening statements on charity and poverty signs
items.text_en: Opening statements on charity and poverty signs
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra derives from the verse that even a poor person supported by charity must give charity. Rav Yosef teaches that such a person will no longer be shown signs of poverty.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra derives from the verse 'וְעִנִּתִךְ' that even a poor person supported by charity must give charity.
Rav Yosef teaches from the verse 'לֹא אַעֲנֵּךְ עוֹד' that such a person will no longer be shown signs of poverty.

items.text: Contradiction regarding the northern boundary of Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding the northern boundary of Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's statement that Akko is north of Eretz Yisrael, citing a baraita that distinguishes between land to the east and west of the road from Akko to Keziv regarding impurity and tithes. The baraita defines the boundary up to Keziv, with Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei adding up to Lavlav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's statement that Akko is north of Eretz Yisrael is correct, citing a contradictory baraita.
The baraita describes the halachic status of land to the east and west of the road from Akko to Keziv regarding impurity and tithes.
The baraita continues, stating that land to the west of the road is pure and obligated in tithes and the Sabbatical year.
The baraita defines the boundary up to Keziv, with Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei adding up to Lavlav.

items.text: Abaye's explanation of the geographical sign
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation of the geographical sign
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the baraita provides a geographical sign, and supports this with a verse where the Tanna similarly gives a sign, as explained by Rav Pappa.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that a strip of land extends eastward, and the Tanna provides a geographical sign for it.
The Gemara questions whether the Tanna would give a geographical sign in this manner.
Abaye answers affirmatively, citing a verse where the Tanna gives a sign, as explained by Rav Pappa that the sign refers to the east of the road.

items.text: Contradiction regarding a get brought by ship
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding a get brought by ship
items.desc_en: Two contradictory baraitot are presented: one states that bringing a get by ship is like bringing it within Eretz Yisrael, the other states it is like bringing it from outside the land.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that bringing a get by ship is like bringing it within Eretz Yisrael.
A second baraita contradicts the first, stating that bringing a get by ship is like bringing it from outside the land.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution: dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution: dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the contradiction by attributing the baraitot to different opinions: one follows the Rabbis, the other follows Rabbi Yehuda, who distinguishes based on whether the ship is touching the ground.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the contradiction between the two baraitot by attributing one to the Rabbis and the other to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yirmeya cites a Mishnah that dirt from outside the Land brought by ship is liable for tithes and Sabbatical year laws, supporting the Rabbis' position.
Rabbi Yehuda qualifies the Mishnah: the liability applies only when the ship is touching the ground (גוששת), but if not, the dirt is exempt.

items.text: Abaye's alternative resolution: both are Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative resolution: both are Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that both baraitot follow Rabbi Yehuda, and the difference is whether the ship is touching the ground or not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction between the two baraitot by asserting that both follow Rabbi Yehuda, distinguishing between when the ship is touching the ground (גוששת) and when it is not.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's analogy and Rava's challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's analogy and Rava's challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira compares the case of a perforated pot placed on pegs to the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis. Rava challenges this, suggesting that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about a ship may not apply to a pot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira proposes an analogy: a perforated pot placed on pegs corresponds to the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis regarding the status of a ship.
Rava challenges the analogy, suggesting that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about a ship may not apply to a pot, as the ship's unique context might be the basis for his position.

items.text: שתי אפשרויות להבנת מחלוקת התנאים
items.text_en: Gemara's initial analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on a ship vs. a flowerpot
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's leniency for a ship is because it is made to flee, unlike a flowerpot. Alternatively, the Sages only permitted a ship because the water does not interrupt the airspace, unlike a flowerpot.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה שתי אפשרויות להבנת מחלוקת התנאים: האחת מתייחסת לעציץ שאינו עשוי לברוח, והשנייה מבחינה בין ספינה לעציץ בשל הפסק האוויר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah permits a ship because it is made to flee, unlike a flowerpot which is not.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציעה אפשרות ראשונה להבנת מחלוקת התנאים: ההבדל בין ספינה לעציץ הוא שספינה עשויה לברוח ואילו עציץ אינו עשוי לברוח.

sub.desc_en: Alternatively, the Gemara explains that the Sages permitted a ship because the water does not interrupt the airspace, unlike a flowerpot where the airspace is interrupted.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציעה אפשרות שנייה: ההבדל הוא שמי הים נחשבים כקרקע סמוכה ואינם מפסיקים את האוויר, אך עציץ מפסיק את האוויר.

items.text: בירור מקום המחלוקת על ידי רב נחמן בר יצחק
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's distinction: rivers vs. the Great Sea
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asserts that regarding rivers of Eretz Yisrael, there is no dispute; the dispute is only about the Great Sea.
items.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק מבהיר שהמחלוקת היא רק בים הגדול, ולא בנהרות של ארץ ישראל שכולם מודים בהם.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asserts that regarding rivers of Eretz Yisrael there is no dispute; the dispute is only about the Great Sea.
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק מבהיר שהמחלוקת היא רק בים הגדול, ולא בנהרות של ארץ ישראל שכולם מודים בהם.

items.text: Baraita defining Eretz Yisrael's boundaries and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Baraita defining Eretz Yisrael's boundaries and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: A baraita defines Eretz Yisrael as from the mountains of Amnon inward, and islands are considered by a string from those mountains to Nachal Mitzrayim. Rabbi Yehuda holds that whatever is opposite Eretz Yisrael is like Eretz Yisrael, citing a verse. The Rabbis use that verse for islands, while Rabbi Yehuda says islands need no verse.

sub.desc_en: A baraita defines Eretz Yisrael's boundaries: from the mountains of Amnon inward is Eretz Yisrael; islands are measured by a string from those mountains to Nachal Mitzrayim.
Rabbi Yehuda states that whatever is opposite Eretz Yisrael is like Eretz Yisrael, citing the verse 'וּגְבוּל יָם' (the boundary of the sea).
Rabbi Yehuda adds that for islands on the sides, a string is drawn from Kapluria to the Ocean and from Nachal Mitzrayim to the Ocean to determine their status.
The Gemara asks: what do the Rabbis do with the verse 'וּגְבוּל' (and the boundary)? They need it for the islands.
The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yehuda holds that islands do not require a verse (they are included by the general rule).

items.text: דין עכו לגיטין והשוואת סוריא
items.text_en: Question about selling a slave to Syria and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether selling a slave to Syria is like selling to chutz la'aretz. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba answers from the Mishnah: Rabbi Meir says Akko is like Eretz Yisrael only for gittin, not for slaves, and certainly Syria which is farther.
items.desc: רבי מאיר קובע שעכו כארץ ישראל לגיטין, ורבי חייא בר אבא מסיק מכאן שסוריא רחוקה יותר אינה נחשבת כארץ ישראל לעבדים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba whether selling a slave to Syria is considered like selling to חוצה לארץ (outside the Land) or not.
sub.desc: רבי מאיר קובע שעכו נחשבת כארץ ישראל לעניין גיטין.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba answers from the Mishnah: Rabbi Meir says Akko is like Eretz Yisrael only for גיטין (bills of divorce), not for slaves, and certainly Syria which is farther away.
sub.desc: רבי חייא בר אבא משיב: כבר שניתם – רבי מאיר אומר שעכו כארץ ישראל לגיטין, אבל לא לעבדים, וכל שכן סוריא הרחוקה יותר.

items.text: ברייתא על דיני סוריא
items.text_en: Baraita: Three ways Syria is like chutz la'aretz and three like Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: A baraita lists three similarities to chutz la'aretz: its earth is impure, selling a slave there is like selling to chutz la'aretz, and bringing a get from Syria requires a messenger. Three similarities to Eretz Yisrael: it is obligated in tithes and shemitta, one may enter it in purity, and buying a field there...
items.desc: ברייתא מונה שלושה דרכים שבהן סוריא שווה לחוצה לארץ (טומאת עפר, מכירת עבד, הבאת גט) ושלושה שבהן שווה לארץ ישראל (מעשר, שביעית, טהרה וקניית שדה).

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that Syria is like chutz la'aretz in three ways, listing them: its earth is impure, selling a slave there is like selling to chutz la'aretz, and bringing a get from Syria requires a messenger.
sub.desc: ברייתא מונה שלושה דרכים שבהן סוריא שווה לחוצה לארץ (טומאת עפר, מכירת עבד, הבאת גט) ושלושה שבהן שווה לארץ ישראל (מעשר, שביעית, טהרה וקניית שדה).

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three ways Syria is like Eretz Yisrael: it is obligated in tithes and shemitta, one may enter it in purity, and buying a field there has a certain status (the text is cut off).

items.text: דין קניין בסוריא כקניין בפרוורי ירושלים
items.text_en: Opening statement on Syria's status
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that buying land in Syria is like buying in the outskirts of Jerusalem, making it liable for tithes and Sabbatical year laws, based on the view that individual conquest is considered conquest.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת את דין הקונה שדה בסוריא, שנחשב כקונה בפרוורי ירושלים, ומסבירה שהטעם הוא משום שכיבוש יחיד נחשב כיבוש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that buying land in Syria is like buying in the outskirts of Jerusalem, making it liable for tithes and Sabbatical year laws, based on the view that individual conquest is considered conquest.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בקביעה שהקונה שדה בסוריא דינו כקונה בפרוורי ירושלים.

items.text: קושיית טומאת עפר סוריא ותירוצה
items.text_en: Clarification on impurity in Syria
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can enter Syria in purity if its soil is impure, and answers that entry is via a sealed container. It cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda debate impurity in the land of the nations, concluding that in Syria only the soil is impure, not the air.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: כיצד ניתן להיכנס לסוריא בטהרה אם עפרה טמא? ומתרצת שהכניסה היא בשידה, תיבה ומגדל, כפי ששנינו בברייתא המבחינה בין ארץ העמים לסוריא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can enter Syria in purity if its soil is considered impure.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: כיצד נאמר שניתן להיכנס לסוריא בטהרה, והרי אמרת שעפרה טמא?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that one enters via a chest, box, or cabinet, which protects from the soil's impurity.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהכניסה היא בשידה, תיבה ומגדל, שאינם נוגעים בעפר.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who enters the land of the nations in a sealed container — Rabbi Meir declares impure, Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda declares pure.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהכניסה היא בשידה, תיבה ומגדל, שאינם נוגעים בעפר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that even Rabbi Meir only decrees impurity for the land of the nations (both soil and air), but in Syria only the soil is impure, not the air.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהכניסה היא בשידה, תיבה ומגדל, שאינם נוגעים בעפר.

items.text: הלכה למעשה בקניין שדה בסוריא
items.text_en: Practical halakha of buying land in Syria
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that buying land in Syria allows writing a deed of acquisition even on Shabbat, by telling a non-Jew to do so, as the rabbis did not decree against this due to the importance of settling the Land of Israel.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת את ההלכה הנובעת מכך: שכותבים אונו (שטר קניין) על השדה, ואפילו בשבת, על ידי אמירה לגוי, משום ישוב ארץ ישראל.
