sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical halakhic implication arises from the statement that buying a field in Syria is like buying in the outskirts of Jerusalem.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: לאיזו הלכה נלמד מכך שקונה שדה בסוריא כקונה בפרוורי ירושלים?

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet answers that the implication is that one may write a deed of acquisition (אונו) for the field, even on Shabbat.
sub.desc: רב ששת עונה: שכותבים עליו אונו (שטר קניין), ואפילו בשבת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: how could writing a deed on Shabbat even enter one's mind, since it is a prohibited labor?
sub.desc: רב ששת עונה: שכותבים עליו אונו (שטר קניין), ואפילו בשבת.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the objection by explaining that one tells a non-Jew to write the deed, and since the rabbis did not decree against this indirect instruction due to the importance of settling the Land of Israel, it is permitted.
sub.desc: רב ששת עונה: שכותבים עליו אונו (שטר קניין), ואפילו בשבת.

items.text: ברייתא: עבד המביא גטו
items.text_en: Baraita on a slave bringing a get
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a slave brings a get that says 'yourself and my property are acquired to you,' the slave acquires himself but not the property.
items.desc: תנו רבנן: עבד שהביא גטו וכתוב בו 'עצמך ונכסיי קנויין לך' – עצמו קנה, נכסים לא קנה.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states: if a slave brings his bill of manumission written 'yourself and my property are acquired by you,' the slave acquires himself but not the property.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בדין עבד המביא גטו, ומבדילה בין קניין עצמו לקניין נכסים.

items.text: מחלוקת אביי ורבא בקניין עבד ונכסים
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava debate 'all my property'
items.desc_en: Abaye initially argues that if the get says 'all my property is acquired to you,' the slave acquires both himself and the property. Rava objects that property acquisition is like a regular document, not a get. Abaye then reverses, saying if property is not acquired, the slave does not acquire himself either, but Rava counters that self-acquisition is like a woman's get.
items.desc: איבעיא להו: 'כל נכסיי קנויין לך' מהו? אביי ורבא נחלקו: אביי סבר שקניין עצמו מושך קניין נכסים, ורבא חולק. לאחר מכן אביי חוזר בו, ורבא מקשה על חזרתו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if the bill of manumission states 'all my property is acquired to you,' what is the halakha?
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה בעיה: מה דין לשון 'כל נכסיי קנויין לך' – האם היא מקנה גם את העבד עצמו?

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that since the slave acquires himself, he also acquires the property.
Rava objects that while self-acquisition is like a woman's get, property acquisition requires ratification like other documents.
sub.desc: רבא מקשה: אפשר להבין שהעבד קונה את עצמו, שכן דומה לגט אשה, אבל הנכסים – מדוע יקנה? הרי דינם כקיום שטרות בעלמא.

sub.desc_en: Abaye reverses his position, arguing that since the property is not acquired, the slave does not acquire himself either.
Rava rejects Abaye's reversal, reiterating that self-acquisition is like a woman's get and should be valid.

items.text: פסק רבא וזיהויו עם רבי שמעון
items.text_en: Rava's final ruling and Rabbi Shimon's support
items.desc_en: Rava concludes that in both cases, the slave acquires himself but not the property. Rav Adda bar Mattana asks if this follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a statement can be split, citing a Mishnah where a slave who receives all property goes free, but if any land is left out, he does not.
items.desc: רבא פוסק: אחד זה ואחד זה – עצמו קנה, נכסים לא קנה. רב אדא בר מתנה מקשה על רבא שזה כשיטת רבי שמעון הסובר 'פלגינן דיבורא', ומביא משנה התומכת בכך.

sub.desc_en: Rava concludes that in both cases, the slave acquires himself but not the property.
sub.desc: רבא פוסק: גם בגט שחרור וגם בגט אשה, העבד קנה את עצמו אך לא קנה נכסים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Mattana asks Rava if his ruling follows רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon), who holds that a statement can be divided.
sub.desc: רבא פוסק: גם בגט שחרור וגם בגט אשה, העבד קנה את עצמו אך לא קנה נכסים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where a slave who receives all property goes free, but if any land is left out, he does not, supporting Rabbi Shimon's view.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא כראיה: הכותב כל נכסיו לעבדו – יצא בן חורין, ואם שייר קרקע – לא יצא, ורבי שמעון חולק.

items.text: The slave's freedom and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: The slave's freedom and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that a slave is free unless the master explicitly excludes one ten-thousandth of his property. It cites Rav Nachman's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Meir, and then notes a contradiction: Rav Nachman also said that a deathly ill person who writes all his property to his slave and recovers can retract the property but not the slave's freedom. The Gemara resolves that the slave is free because he has acquired a reputation as a free man.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a slave is forever free unless the master explicitly excludes one ten-thousandth of his property.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Nachman's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Meir, as Rabbi Yosei praised Rabbi Shimon with a verse.
The Gemara objects by citing a contradictory ruling from Rav Nachman: a deathly ill person who writes all his property to his slave and recovers can retract the property but not the slave's freedom.
The Gemara resolves that the slave is free because he has acquired a reputation as a free man, even though the property gift is retractable as a gift of a deathly ill person.

items.text: תירוץ רב אשי: טעם הגט שאינו כרות
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi offers a different reason for the Mishnah's ruling: the document is not a valid get because it is not cut (i.e., it lacks the proper form of a divorce document).
items.desc: רב אשי מתרץ את הסתירה באופן אחר: הטעם שהעבד משתחרר הוא משום שהגט אינו כרות, כלומר שהעבד לא נכלל במתנה, ולכן הוא נשאר בן חורין.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the reason the slave is free is that the document is not a valid severed get (גט כרות) because the master did not explicitly exclude the slave from the property.
sub.desc: רב אשי מתרץ את הסתירה באופן אחר: הטעם שהעבד משתחרר הוא משום שהגט אינו כרות, כלומר שהעבד לא נכלל במתנה, ולכן הוא נשאר בן חורין.

items.text: בירור המונח 'עוררין' במשנה
items.text_en: The meaning of 'protesters' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's phrase 'if there are protesters, it is validated by its signatures.' It questions how many protesters are needed: one is insufficient because Rabbi Yochanan said a protest requires at least two. Two protesters would create a tie, so the Gemara concludes it refers to the husband's protest.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במשנה הבאה: 'אם יש עליו עוררין' – מה פירוש 'עוררין'? הגמרא שוללת אפשרות של עורר אחד או שניים, ומסיקה שמדובר בעורר של הבעל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how many protesters are needed to invalidate a get validated by its signatures.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מהו מספר העוררין במשנה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one protester is insufficient because Rabbi Yochanan ruled that a protest requires at least two.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מהו מספר העוררין במשנה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that two protesters would create a tie, making it impossible to decide which side to rely on.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: האם עוררין הם שניים? ומקשה: הרי שניים ושניים הם, מדוע להכריע?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers specifically to the husband's protest, which is effective even alone.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: האם עוררין הם שניים? ומקשה: הרי שניים ושניים הם, מדוע להכריע?

items.text: משנת המביא גט ממדינת הים
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bringing a get from overseas and similarities to manumission
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who brings a get from overseas and cannot say 'it was written and signed in my presence' may validate it by its signatures if there are witnesses. It then notes that divorce documents and manumission documents are equal in the laws of the bringer and the sender, and this is one of the ways they are alike.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שהמביא גט ממדינת הים ואינו יכול לומר 'בפני נכתב ובפני נחתם', אם יש עדים – יתקיים בחותמיו. וכן גיטי נשים ושחרורי עבדים שווים בדינים אלו.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who brings a get from overseas and cannot say 'it was written and signed in my presence' may validate it by its signatures if there are witnesses.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין המביא גט ממדינת הים שאינו יכול לומר 'בפני נכתב ובפני נחתם', ומציעה חלופה של קיום בחותמיו אם יש עדים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah adds that divorce documents and manumission documents are equal in the laws of the bringer and the sender, and this is one of the ways they are alike.
sub.desc: המשנה מוסיפה שגיטי נשים ושחרורי עבדים שווים בדיני המוליך והמביא, וזו אחת הדרכים שהם שווים.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על 'אינו יכול לומר' ותירוץ רב יוסף
items.text_en: Gemara: The case of a deaf messenger
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'cannot say' means, suggesting it refers to a deaf person. But a deaf person is invalid to bring a get, as taught in a Mishnah. Rav Yosef explains: the case is where the messenger was healthy when he gave the get but became deaf before he could say the required declaration.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מה פירוש 'אינו יכול לומר'? אם הכוונה לחירש, הרי חירש אינו כשר להביא גט. רב יוסף מתרץ: מדובר באדם שהיה פקח כשנתן את הגט, אך נתחרש לפני שאמר 'בפני נכתב ובפני נחתם'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'cannot say' means, suggesting it refers to a deaf person, but objects that a deaf person is invalid to bring a get as taught in a Mishnah.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הכוונה לחירש שאינו יכול לומר 'בפני נכתב ובפני נחתם', הרי חירש פסול מלהביא גט מעיקרו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the case is where the messenger was healthy (פיקֵּחַ) when he gave the get but became deaf before he could say the required declaration.
sub.desc: רב יוסף מתרץ: מדובר באדם שהיה פקח כשנתן את הגט, אך נתחרש לפני שאמר את דבריו.

items.text: ברייתא: שלושה דרכים ששווים גיטי נשים לשחרורי עבדים
items.text_en: Baraita: Three ways divorce and manumission are alike
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Baraita that lists three ways divorce documents and manumission documents are equal: in the laws of the bringer and sender, that a get with a Samaritan witness is invalid except for these, and that all documents... (the text is cut off).
items.desc: הברייתא מונה שלושה דרכים שבהם גיטי נשים ושחרורי עבדים שווים: לעניין המוליך והמביא, פסלות עד כותי, ועוד. הגמרא מביאה את תחילת הברייתא.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists three ways in which bills of divorce for women and emancipation documents for slaves are equal: in the laws of the agent who brings or takes them, in the invalidity of a get with a Kutim witness, and in all other documents.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המונה שלושה דרכים שבהם גיטי נשים ושחרורי עבדים שווים.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: כשרות שטרות בערכאות גויים
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that documents authenticated in gentile courts are valid, except for bills of divorce and manumission. It also cites Rabbi Meir's opinion that in the case of a man who says 'Give this get to my wife and this manumission document to my slave,' he may retract both.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת בקביעה ששטרות העולים בערכאות של גויים כשרים, למעט גיטי נשים ושחרורי עבדים. ומביאה את דברי רבי מאיר האומר שאם אמר 'תן גט זה לאשתי' יכול לחזור בשניהם.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that documents authenticated in gentile courts are valid except for bills of divorce and manumission, and cites Rabbi Meir's opinion that one who says 'Give this get to my wife and this manumission document to my slave' may retract both.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בקביעה ששטרות העולים בערכאות של גויים כשרים, למעט גיטי נשים ושחרורי עבדים.

items.text: Gemara's question on the exclusion
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to the Rabbis, the Mishnah's exclusion of Rabbi Meir's case is understandable, but according to Rabbi Meir himself, what does the Mishnah exclude?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to the Rabbis, the Mishnah's exclusion of Rabbi Meir's case is understandable, but according to Rabbi Meir himself, what does the Mishnah exclude?

items.text: Answer: Exclusion of the baraita about illiterate witnesses
items.text_en: Answer: Exclusion of the baraita about illiterate witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah excludes the case of witnesses who cannot sign, where they tear a blank paper and fill the tears with ink. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies this: it applies only to bills of divorce, but for manumission and other documents, if they can read and sign, they sign; otherwise, they do not. The Gemara then corrects the baraita to include reading as a requirement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah excludes the case of witnesses who cannot sign, where one tears a blank paper and fills the tears with ink.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies that the leniency applies only to bills of divorce, but for manumission and other documents, witnesses must know how to read and sign.
The Gemara corrects the baraita to include reading as a requirement: witnesses who cannot read have the document read to them, and those who cannot sign use the tearing method.

items.text: קושיית 'ועוד' ותירוץ: מילתא דליתיה בשטרות
items.text_en: Challenge: Other excluded cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Are there no other cases? There is the case of one who says 'Give this get to my wife' and dies, where they do not give after death, versus 'Give a maneh to so-and-so' where they do give after death. The Gemara answers that the Mishnah only teaches matters not applicable to regular documents, not those that are applicable.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: ועוד יש ברייתא האומרת 'תנו גט זה לאשתי ומת לא יתנו לאחר מיתה', ומתרצת: כי קתני מילתא דליתיה בשטרות, אבל מילתא דאיתיה בשטרות לא קתני.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Are there no other cases? It cites the case of one who says 'Give this get to my wife' and dies, where they do not give after death, versus 'Give a maneh to so-and-so' where they do give after death.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: ועוד יש ברייתא האומרת 'תנו גט זה לאשתי ומת לא יתנו לאחר מיתה', ומביאה את הברייתא במלואה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah only teaches matters not applicable to regular documents, not those that are applicable.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: כי קתני מילתא דליתיה בשטרות, אבל מילתא דאיתיה בשטרות לא קתני.

items.text: שליחות רבין: דין שכיב מרע
items.text_en: Supporting tradition from Rabbi Abahu
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition from Ravin in the name of Rabbi Abahu: Rabbi Elazar sent to the diaspora that a shekhiv me'ra who says 'Write and give a maneh to so-and-so' and dies, they do not write and give, lest he only intended to transfer ownership via a document, and a document is ineffective after death.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה את שליחות רבין בשם רבי אבהו: רבי אלעזר שלח לגולה ששכיב מרע שאמר 'כתבו ותנו מנה לפלוני' ומת, אין כותבים ונותנים, שמא לא גמר להקנותו אלא בשטר ואין שטר לאחר מיתה.

sub.text_en: Gemara citing a tradition from Ravin in the name of Rabbi Abahu
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition from Ravin in the name of Rabbi Abahu that Rabbi Elazar sent to the diaspora: a shekhiv me'ra (a person on his deathbed) who says 'Write and give a maneh to so-and-so' and dies, they do not write and give, lest he only intended to transfer ownership via a document, and a document is ineffective after death.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את שליחות רבין בשם רבי אבהו, הכוללת את דברי רבי אלעזר ששלח לגולה: שכיב מרע שאמר 'כתבו ותנו מנה לפלוני' ומת – אין כותבים ונותנים, שמא לא גמר להקנותו אלא בשטר ואין שטר לאחר מיתה.

items.text: קושיית לשמה ומחובר ותירוץ: פסולא דרבנן
items.text_en: Challenge: The requirement of lishmah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What about the requirement of lishmah (intent)? According to Rabbah, it is the case of molikh umevi (the messenger who brings and brings back), but according to Rava, it is difficult. Additionally, both Rabbah and Rava have the case of mechubar (attached). The Gemara answers that the Mishnah only teaches rabbinic invalidations, not Torah-level ones.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והא איכא לשמה? ומתרצת: לרבא קשיא, ועוד בין לרבא בין לרבה הא איכא מחובר. ומתרצת: כי קתני פסולא דרבנן, דאורייתא לא קתני.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What about the requirement of לִשְׁמָהּ (intent for the sake of the act), which is a Torah-level invalidation not listed in the Mishnah?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והא איכא לשמה? – הרי יש במשנתנו דין 'לשמה' שהוא פסול דאורייתא, ומדוע לא נשנה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes: According to Rabbah, the case of מוֹלִיךְ וּמֵבִיא (the messenger who brings and brings back) already covers לִשְׁמָהּ, but according to Rava, this is difficult.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבררת: בשלמא לרבה היינו מוליך ומביא, אלא לרבא קשיא – שהרי לרבא 'לשמה' אינו נכלל במוליך ומביא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds: Moreover, both according to Rabbah and Rava, there is also the case of מְחוּבָּר (attached), which is a Torah-level invalidation not listed.
sub.desc: הגמרא מוסיפה קושיה: ועוד, בין לרבה בין לרבא, הא איכא מחובר – הרי יש דין מחובר שהוא פסול דאורייתא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: The Mishnah only teaches rabbinic invalidations (פְּסוּלָא דְרַבָּנַן), not Torah-level ones (דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא), so לִשְׁמָהּ and מְחוּבָּר are excluded.
sub.desc: הגמרא מוסיפה קושיה: ועוד, בין לרבה בין לרבא, הא איכא מחובר – הרי יש דין מחובר שהוא פסול דאורייתא.

items.text: קושיית ערכאות גויים ותירוץ בעדי מסירה
items.text_en: Resolution: Gentile courts and the principle of witnesses of delivery
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Gentile courts are a Torah-level invalidation, yet the Mishnah teaches them! It answers that the Mishnah deals with witnesses of delivery, following Rabbi Elazar who says witnesses of delivery effect the divorce. The Gemara supports this from the latter clause where Rabbi Shimon says these are valid, and Rabbi Zeira explains that Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Elazar's view, implying the first tanna disagrees.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והא ערכאות של גויים פסולא דאורייתא הוא? ומתרצת: בעדי מסירה וכרבי אלעזר. ומקשה עוד: מכלל דתנא קמא סבר לא? ומתרצת שרבי שמעון ירד לשיטת רבי אלעזר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that gentile courts are a Torah-level invalidation (פסולא דאורייתא), yet the Mishnah teaches them as valid.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והא ערכאות של גויים פסולא דאורייתא הוא, ומדוע שנינו במשנה שהן כשרות?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with witnesses of delivery (עדי מסירה), following Rabbi Elazar who holds that witnesses of delivery effect the divorce.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והא ערכאות של גויים פסולא דאורייתא הוא, ומדוע שנינו במשנה שהן כשרות?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports this from the latter clause where Rabbi Shimon says these are valid, and Rabbi Zeira explains that Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Elazar's view, implying the first tanna (תנא קמא) disagrees.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מכלל שהסיפא אומרת שרבי שמעון ירד לשיטת רבי אלעזר, משמע שתנא קמא סבר לא?

items.text: Gemara's question on the previous Mishnah's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the previous Mishnah's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the previous Mishnah's distinction between 'names of certainty' and other cases, noting that the concept of 'return' (חזרה) is Torah-based and yet taught. It resolves that the Mishnah only teaches matters not found in Kiddushin, but then objects that 'return' itself is found in Kiddushin, and distinguishes by the case of agency against her will (בשליחות בעל כרחה), which exists in Gittin but not in Kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the Mishnah's categories, suggesting 'names of certainty' (שֵׁמוֹת מוּבְהָקִין) as a possible distinction.
The Gemara objects that the concept of 'return' (חזרה) is Torah-based, yet the Mishnah teaches it, undermining the proposed distinction.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah only teaches matters not found in Kiddushin, excluding those already taught there.
The Gemara objects that 'return' itself is found in Kiddushin, and resolves by distinguishing the case of agency against her will (בשליחות בעל כרחה), which exists in Gittin but not in Kiddushin.

items.text: Mishnah: Get with a Kutim witness is valid only for Gittin and Shichrurim
items.text_en: Mishnah: Get with a Kutim witness is valid only for Gittin and Shichrurim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any document with a Kutim witness is invalid, except for bills of divorce and emancipation of slaves. A case is cited where Rabban Gamliel validated a get with Kutim witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any get (גט) with a Kutite witness is invalid except for bills of divorce and manumission, citing a case where Rabban Gamliel validated such a get.

items.text: Gemara's question: Whose opinion is the Mishnah?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Whose opinion is the Mishnah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the Mishnah, suggesting it is neither the first Tanna, nor Rabbi Elazar, nor Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the Mishnah, suggesting it is neither the first Tanna, nor Rabbi Elazar, nor Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

items.text: Supporting Baraisa: Dispute about Kutim matzah
items.text_en: Supporting Baraisa: Dispute about Kutim matzah
items.desc_en: A Baraisa is cited: Kutim matzah is permitted and one fulfills his obligation with it on Pesach. Rabbi Elazar forbids it because they are not meticulous in mitzvah details. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that any mitzvah Kutim have adopted, they are more meticulous than Israel.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the dispute about Kutim matzah: the Tanna Kamma permits it and allows fulfilling the obligation on Pesach, Rabbi Elazar forbids it because Kutim are not meticulous in mitzvah details, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that any mitzvah they have adopted they are more meticulous than Israel.

items.text: Analysis: Why each Tanna fails to match the Mishnah
items.text_en: Analysis: Why each Tanna fails to match the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains: If the Mishnah follows the first Tanna, even other documents would be valid; if Rabbi Elazar, even a get would be invalid; if Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, if they are established in the practice, even other documents would be valid, and if not, even a get would be invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion is in the Mishnah and rejects the first tanna and Rabbi Elazar: the first tanna would validate even other documents, Rabbi Elazar would invalidate even a bill of divorce.
The Gemara also rejects Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: if the Samaritans are established in the practice, even other documents would be valid; if not, even a bill of divorce would be invalid.

items.text: Rejection of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and introduction of Rabbi Elazar's view
items.text_en: Rejection of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and introduction of Rabbi Elazar's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that the Mishnah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel with a distinction between established and non-established practices, because then why mention only one witness? It could be two. It then cites Rabbi Elazar who said they only validated one Kutim witness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) with a distinction between established and non-established practices, then why mention only one witness? Even two should be valid.
The Gemara cites רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) who explicitly said they only validated one Kutim witness, supporting the rejection of the previous suggestion.

items.text: Resolution: The Mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar with an Israelite witness at the end
items.text_en: Resolution: The Mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar with an Israelite witness at the end
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah always follows Rabbi Elazar, and the case is where an Israelite signed at the end (alongside the Kutim witness).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah always follows Rabbi Elazar, and the case is where an Israelite signed at the end alongside the Kutim witness.

items.text: Gemara's defense of the earlier ruling about a Kutim witness
items.text_en: Gemara's defense of the earlier ruling about a Kutim witness
items.desc_en: The Gemara defends the earlier ruling that a single Kutim witness is valid for a get by arguing that if the Kutim were not trustworthy, the court would not have allowed him to sign. It then addresses the objection that this reasoning would apply to all documents, and resolves it by saying that in the case of a get, the court leaves a gap for an older witness, just as in other documents.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara defends the validity of a single Kutim witness by arguing that the court would not have allowed him to sign if he were not trustworthy.
The Gemara objects that if this reasoning were applied universally, it would validate Kutim witnesses for all documents, not just a get.
The Gemara resolves by stating that in a get, the court leaves a gap for an older witness, just as in other documents, so the reasoning is specific to a get.

items.text: Rav Pappa's inference and Rav Ashi's explanation
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's inference and Rav Ashi's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa infers from the previous discussion that witnesses of a get do not sign one without the other. Rav Ashi explains the reason: a decree due to the requirement that all witnesses sign together (כולכם).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa deduces from the earlier discussion that witnesses of a get do not sign without each other.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rav Pappa's statement.
Rav Ashi explains that the rule is a decree due to the requirement that all witnesses sign together (as in 'כולכם').

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines Rabbi Elazar's statement that only a single Kutim witness was validated for a get. It questions what he adds to the Mishnah, and explains that without his statement, one might have thought that even two Kutim witnesses are valid, but he teaches that only one is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Elazar's statement that only a single Kutim witness was validated for a get.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Elazar adds to the Mishnah, which already states that a get with a Kutim witness is invalid.
The Gemara explains that without Rabbi Elazar's statement, one might have thought that even two Kutim witnesses are valid, but he teaches that only one is valid.

items.text: Objection from the incident with Rabban Gamliel and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the incident with Rabban Gamliel and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a case was brought before Rabban Gamliel with two Kutim witnesses and he validated the get. Abaye resolves by saying the text should read 'its witness' (singular). Rava says that Rabban Gamliel actually disagrees and validates with two, and the Mishnah is missing that detail.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a case was brought before רבן גמליאל (Rabban Gamliel) with two Kutim witnesses and he validated the גט (bill of divorce).
Abaye resolves by saying the text should read 'its witness' (singular), implying only one Kutim witness was involved.
Rava says that Rabban Gamliel actually disagrees and validates with two Kutim witnesses, and the Mishnah is missing that detail.

items.text: Mishnah: Documents from gentile courts
items.text_en: Mishnah: Documents from gentile courts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all documents that come up in gentile courts are valid, even if signed by gentiles, except for divorce documents and emancipation documents. Rabbi Shimon says even these are valid, and they were only mentioned in the context of when they were made by a layperson.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that documents from gentile courts are valid except for divorce and emancipation documents; Rabbi Shimon permits even those when made by a layperson.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on sale and gift documents
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on sale and gift documents
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah rules categorically, distinguishing between sale and gift. For a sale, the document is merely evidence because the buyer acquires by paying money before the gentiles. For a gift, the document itself is the means of acquisition, so it would seem invalid, but Shmuel says the law of the land is the law, making it valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that the Mishnah rules categorically, not distinguishing between sale and gift documents.
The Gemara explains that for a sale, the document is merely evidence because the buyer acquires by paying money before the gentiles.
The Gemara questions how a gift is acquired if not by the document itself, which would be worthless coming from gentiles.
Shmuel resolves that the law of the land is the law, making gentile gift documents valid.

items.text: Alternative explanation and discussion of Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Alternative explanation and discussion of Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: the Mishnah's exception is only for divorce documents. The Gemara then questions how Rabbi Shimon can validate divorce documents from gentile courts, since gentiles are not capable of effecting divorce. Rabbi Zeira says Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Elazar's view that witnesses of delivery effect the divorce. Rabbi Abba objects that Rabbi Elazar invalidates a forged document, and the Gemara begins to resolve this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the Mishnah's exception is only for divorce documents (גיטי נשים), not for all documents.
The Gemara questions how Rabbi Shimon can validate divorce documents from gentile courts, since gentiles are not capable of effecting divorce (בני כריתות).
Rabbi Zeira explains that Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Elazar's view that witnesses of delivery (עדי מסירה) effect the divorce, not the court's authority.
Rabbi Abba objects that Rabbi Elazar himself invalidates a forged document (מזויף מתוכו), which would apply to a gentile-written document.
The Gemara begins to resolve the objection by clarifying the specific case under discussion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that documents are invalid if signed by non-Jews, except for well-known names.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that documents are invalid if signed by non-Jews, except for well-known names.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of well-known names
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of well-known names
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa defines well-known names. The Gemara questions why the Mishnah didn't explicitly distinguish between well-known and non-well-known names, and offers two answers: first, that non-well-known names are treated like those made by a layperson, and second, that the Mishnah's latter clause refers specifically to monetary documents.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes unambiguous gentile names, and Rav Pappa provides examples.
The Gemara objects that if only unambiguous names are valid, the Mishnah should have explicitly distinguished between unambiguous and ambiguous names rather than referring to laypersons.
The Gemara offers the first answer: the Mishnah implicitly means that ambiguous names render the document like one made by a layperson and thus invalid.
The Gemara offers a second answer: the latter clause of the Mishnah refers specifically to monetary documents, not to bills of divorce.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei's tradition
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei's tradition
items.desc_en: A baraita reports that Rabbi Shimon told the Sages in Tzaydan that Rabbi Akiva and the Sages agree that documents from non-Jewish courts are valid, even for divorces and slave manumissions; they only dispute when documents are made by a layperson.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that Rabbi Shimon told the Sages in Tzaydan that Rabbi Akiva and the Sages agree that documents from non-Jewish courts are valid, even for divorces and slave manumissions; they only dispute when documents are made by a layperson.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion and Gemara's challenge
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion and Gemara's challenge
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that these documents are valid only where no Jews sign, but the Gemara questions why we don't decree due to places where Jews do sign. The Gemara answers that locations are not confused with each other.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that these documents are valid only where no Jews sign, but invalid where Jews sign.
The Gemara challenges: why not decree a prohibition even in places without Jewish signatories, lest one confuse them with places where Jews do sign?
The Gemara answers: while a name might be confused, one location is not confused with another, so no decree is needed.

items.text: Ravina and Rafram on non-Jewish courts
items.text_en: Ravina and Rafram on non-Jewish courts
items.desc_en: Ravina considered validating documents from non-Jewish gatherings, but Rafram objected, citing the Mishnah's term 'courts' (ערכאות).

sub.desc_en: Ravina considered validating documents from gentile assemblies, but Rafram objected that the Mishnah only permits those from courts (ערכאות).
Rafram objected, citing the Mishnah's term 'ערכאות' (courts), implying that only formal courts, not mere gatherings, are valid.

items.text: Rava's ruling on Persian documents
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on Persian documents
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a Persian document given in front of Jewish witnesses can be used to collect from free property, provided the witnesses can read it, the writing is common (not easily forged), and the document has a return line. The Gemara questions why it cannot collect from liened property, and answers that it lacks publicity (קלא).

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a Persian document delivered before Jewish witnesses can be used to collect from free property.
The Gemara objects that the witnesses cannot read the Persian document, and Rava answers that they do know how to read it.

The Gemara objects that the document lacks forgery-proof script and the requirement that the last line repeat the document's content, and Rava answers that the script is widely used and the last line does repeat the content.
The Gemara objects that if so, the document should also collect from encumbered property, but Rava answers that it lacks public notoriety (קלא).

items.text: Resh Lakish's inquiry to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's inquiry to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan a question, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks a question of Rabbi Yochanan, introducing a new sugya.

items.text: Question about witnesses with non-Jewish names
items.text_en: Question about witnesses with non-Jewish names
items.desc_en: A question is raised about witnesses on a get whose names are like non-Jewish names. The answer is that only the specific names Lokus and Lus were encountered and validated, but other names that Jews commonly use are not valid.

sub.desc_en: A question is raised about witnesses on a get whose names are like non-Jewish names.
The answer states that only the names Lokus and Lus were encountered and validated.
The answer clarifies that only Lokus and Lus are valid, but other names that Jews commonly use are not.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita that says gittin from overseas with witnesses whose names are like non-Jewish names are valid because most Jews abroad have such names. The response is that the baraita itself gives the reason, so it is not a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish raises an objection from a baraita that bills of divorce from overseas with witnesses whose names are like gentile names are valid because most Jews abroad have such names.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita itself gives the reason, so it is not a contradiction to the earlier ruling.

items.text: Alternative version of the initial exchange
items.text_en: Alternative version of the initial exchange
items.desc_en: Some say that the question was asked about the Mishnah itself, and the answer was derived from the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports that the question was asked about the Mishnah itself, and the answer was derived from the Mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: Revoking delivery of a get or manumission document
items.text_en: Mishnah: Revoking delivery of a get or manumission document
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: One who says 'Give this get to my wife' or 'this manumission document to my slave' may retract both, according to Rabbi Meir. The Sages say: He may retract the get but not the manumission, because one can benefit a person in his absence but not harm him. Rabbi Meir objects that the master disqualifies his slave from terumah just as he disqualifies his wife; the Sages respond that it is because the slave is his property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of one who says 'Give this get to my wife or this manumission document to my slave,' and Rabbi Meir rules that he may retract both.
The Sages respond that he may retract the get but not the manumission, because one can benefit a person in his absence but not harm him.
The Sages support their position by noting that a master may choose not to feed his slave but is obligated to feed his wife.
Rabbi Meir objects that the master disqualifies his slave from תרומה (priestly portion) just as he disqualifies his wife, implying a parallel harm.
The Sages reject the objection, explaining that the slave is the master's property (קנינו), so the disqualification is not a harm but an exercise of ownership.

items.text: Gemara: Debate about seizing property for a creditor where it harms others
items.text_en: Gemara: Debate about seizing property for a creditor where it harms others
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef sit before Rabbi Yirmeya, who is dozing. Rav Huna says: Learn from the Sages that one who seizes property for a creditor acquires it. Rav Yitzchak asks: Even where it harms others? Rav Huna says yes. Rabbi Yirmeya awakens and rebukes them, citing Rabbi Yochanan that one does not acquire in such a case, and explains that the Mishnah's ruling is because 'all who say

sub.desc_en: The gemara sets the scene: Rav Huna and Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef sit before Rabbi Yirmeya, who is dozing.
Rav Huna asserts that one can infer from the Sages that one who seizes property for a creditor acquires it.
Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef objects: even where it harms others? Rav Huna answers yes.
Rabbi Yirmeya awakens and rebukes them, citing Rabbi Yochanan that one who seizes property for a creditor where it harms others does not acquire it.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that if one objects from our Mishnah, the principle is that anyone who says 'give' is considered to say 'acquire on behalf of'.

items.text: Rav Chisda links the dispute to a Tannaitic debate
items.text_en: Rav Chisda links the dispute to a Tannaitic debate
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says that the issue of seizing for a creditor where it harms others is a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding gleanings. Amemar or Rav Pappa adds a further statement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the case of seizing property for a creditor where it harms others is a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding gleanings, citing the Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer says the poor person acquires it and the Sages say it goes to the first poor person found.
Amemar or Rav Pappa adds a further statement, though the text is cut off and the content is not provided in the source.

items.text: Distinguishing the Mishnah from the gleaning case
items.text_en: Distinguishing the Mishnah from the gleaning case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning in the gleaning case does not apply here, and similarly why the Rabbis' reasoning there does not apply here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer's opinion in the gleaning case does not apply here because there he could have acquired the produce for himself, but here he cannot seize property for himself.

The Gemara explains that the Rabbis' opinion in the gleaning case does not apply here because there the verse 'לֹא תְלַקֵּט לְעָנִי' (you shall not gather for the poor) restricts acquisition for the poor, but here no such verse applies.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer interprets the verse 'do not glean for the poor', and answers that it is a warning to the poor about his own property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer interprets the verse 'לֹא תְלַקֵּט (do not glean)'.
The Gemara answers that the verse is needed to warn a poor person about his own field.

items.text: Inference from the Mishnah and attempted refutation
items.text_en: Inference from the Mishnah and attempted refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a master can say 'work for me and I will not support you', but then limits the case to where the master said 'use your earnings for your food'. It questions why a wife is different and answers that she cannot support herself, but then objects that a slave also cannot support himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a master can tell his slave 'work for me and I will not support you'.
The Gemara limits the case to where the master said 'use your earnings for your food'.
The Gemara questions why a wife is different, since the same logic could apply to her.
The Gemara answers that a wife cannot support herself, so the husband must provide.
The Gemara objects that a slave also cannot support himself, so why is he different?

items.text: Proof from the law of a slave who fled to a city of refuge
items.text_en: Proof from the law of a slave who fled to a city of refuge
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that a slave who fled to a city of refuge is not supported by his master, and his earnings go to the master. This seems to prove the master can say 'work for me and I will not support you', but the Gemara limits it to where the master said 'use your earnings for your food', and explains the surplus and the special case of a city of refuge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a slave exiled to a city of refuge, whose master is not required to sustain him and whose earnings belong to the master, concluding that the master can say 'work for me and I will not sustain you'.
The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with a case where the master told the slave to use his earnings for his own sustenance.
The Gemara asks: if the master said that, why do the slave's earnings belong to the master?
The Gemara answers: the earnings belong to the master only for the surplus beyond the slave's sustenance.
The Gemara asks: isn't it obvious that the surplus belongs to the master?
The Gemara explains that the baraita teaches that even though the master does not give the slave his full sustenance when the slave earns little, he still takes the surplus when the slave earns more.
The Gemara asks: what is special about a city of refuge that the baraita specifically mentions it?
The Gemara answers that one might think the verse 'and he shall live' requires providing extra sustenance in the city of refuge, so the baraita teaches that this is not required.

items.text: Contradiction from the wife's case in the baraita
items.text_en: Contradiction from the wife's case in the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita says a husband must support his wife who fled to a city of refuge, implying he did not tell her to use her earnings. This would contradict the earlier limitation, but the Gemara resolves by saying the wife cannot support herself, and the case where she can is permissible due to modesty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: from the baraita's latter clause that a husband must support his wife who fled to a city of refuge, it implies he did not tell her to use her earnings, contradicting the earlier limitation.
The Gemara argues: since the latter clause is about a case where he did not say this to her, the first clause about the slave must also be a case where he did not say it.
The Gemara rejects the inference: actually the master did say it to the slave, but the wife's case is different because her earnings are insufficient.
The Gemara objects again: from the baraita's last clause that if he said 'use your earnings' he is permitted, it implies the first half of that clause was a case where he did not say it.
The Gemara resolves: the baraita means that if her earnings suffice and he said 'use your earnings', he is permitted.
The Gemara asks: if her earnings suffice, what is the point of stating this halakha specifically regarding a city of refuge?
The Gemara answers: lest you think modesty concerns prevent her from working outside, the baraita teaches that it is permitted.

items.text: Debate between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages
items.text_en: Debate between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute might be between Tannaim, but then rejects that reading and reinterprets the baraita as dealing with a case where the master said 'use your earnings for your food' and the slave cannot support himself in a famine. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the slave can demand support or freedom so people will pity him, while the Sages say people pity free men too.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute might be between Tannaim, citing the positions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages.
The Gemara asks whether the Tannaim are disputing the very principle of whether the master can refuse to support the slave.
The Gemara objects that the language of the baraita (demanding freedom, not earnings) and its limitation to famine years show the dispute is not about the general principle.
The Gemara reinterprets the baraita as dealing with a case where the master said 'use your earnings for your food' and the slave cannot support himself in a famine.
The Gemara explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the slave can demand support or freedom so people will pity him, while the Sages say people pity free men too.

items.text: Proof from Rav's statement about consecrated hands
items.text_en: Proof from Rav's statement about consecrated hands
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings Rav's statement that a slave whose hands were consecrated can borrow and eat, implying the master can say 'work for me and I will not support you', but the Gemara limits it to where the master provides food, and then the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings Rav's statement that a slave whose hands were consecrated borrows and eats, and infers that the master can say 'work for me and I will not support you'.
The Gemara rejects the proof by limiting the case to where the master provides food, and then the text cuts off.

items.text: Question about the consecrated slave's earnings
items.text_en: Question about the consecrated slave's earnings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a slave who consecrates his hands can borrow and eat, and suggests that the consecration applies only to surplus. It then raises an objection: the Temple could say the slave sufficed without surplus before, so why now? The Gemara answers that the Temple wants the slave to improve.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a consecrated slave can borrow and eat, and suggests that the consecration applies only to surplus earnings.
The Temple objects that the slave sufficed without surplus before, so why should he now borrow?
The Gemara answers that the Temple itself wants the slave to improve, and the consecration applies only to amounts less than a perutah.

items.text: Rav's statement and its implication
items.text_en: Rav's statement and its implication
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav's ruling that a slave who consecrates his hands works and eats, because otherwise who would serve him? It then analyzes whether this implies the master can say 'work with me and I will not feed you' or not, concluding that the slave cannot support himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rav's ruling that a slave who consecrates his hands works and eats, because otherwise who would serve him.
The Gemara analyzes whether Rav's case implies the master can say 'work with me and I will not feed you' or not, considering the slave's ability to support himself.
The Gemara concludes that the slave cannot support himself, so the master cannot say 'work with me and I will not feed you'.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the injured slave
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the injured slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one who cuts off another's slave's hand pays the master for lost work and medical costs, but the slave is supported by charity. This seems to prove the master can say 'work with me and I will not feed you', but the Gemara deflects by saying the master provides food, and the charity is for surplus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one who cuts off another's slave's hand pays the master for lost work and medical costs, but the slave is supported by charity, and infers that the master can say 'work with me and I will not feed you'.
The Gemara deflects by saying the master provides food, and the charity is for surplus.
The Gemara objects that the term 'sustained' is imprecise for surplus, and concludes that the master can indeed say 'work with me and I will not feed you'.
The Gemara affirms the conclusion that the master can say 'work with me and I will not feed you'.

items.text: Clarification of the payment components
items.text_en: Clarification of the payment components
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah specifies 'his lost work and his medical costs' – the lost work is obvious, but medical costs might be considered the slave's own benefit, so it teaches that if the slave heals faster due to strong medicine, the extra payment goes to the master.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's statement that the injurer pays compensation for lost work and medical costs to the master, and notes that lost work is obvious but medical costs require explanation.
The Gemara questions why medical costs go to the master, since the slave needs healing for himself.

The Gemara answers that the ruling is necessary in a case where doctors estimated five days of healing but strong medicine healed in three, lest one think the saved cost belongs to the slave due to his pain; it teaches that the extra goes to the master.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar on freedom's benefit
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar on freedom's benefit
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Elazar saying to Rabbi Meir that freedom is a benefit for a slave, but Rabbi Meir counters that for a priest-slave it is a detriment because it disqualifies him from terumah. The Gemara analyzes their arguments: Rabbi Elazar notes the master can refuse to feed him, and Rabbi Meir responds that even a runaway priest-slave eats terumah, but this one does not. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir's point is that even if you answer the food issue, you cannot answer the terumah issue, and if you suggest the master could divorce him, the slave might run away.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar reports that he and his colleagues told Rabbi Meir that freedom is a benefit for a slave.
Rabbi Meir counters that freedom is a detriment for a priest-slave because it disqualifies him from eating תרומה (priestly portion).
Rabbi Elazar argues that the master can refuse to feed the slave, so freedom is still beneficial.
Rabbi Meir responds that even a runaway priest-slave still eats תרומה, but a freed priest-slave does not.
The baraita adds that for a woman, divorce is a detriment because it disqualifies her from תרומה and loses her sustenance.
The Gemara asks what the disputants meant and explains that Rabbi Meir said: 'You answered me about sustenance, what will you answer about תרומה?'
The Gemara resolves that if one suggests the master could divorce the slave to disqualify him from תרומה, the slave might run away instead.

items.text: Continuation of the previous argument about the slave and terumah
items.text_en: Continuation of the previous argument about the slave and terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara quotes a statement that a slave who fled or a wife who rebelled still eats terumah, but this slave does not. This is the basis for the previous discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that a priest's slave who fled or a priest's wife who rebelled still eat terumah, but this slave does not, establishing the basis for the previous discussion.

items.text: Rava's explanation of the Mishnah's reasoning
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the Mishnah's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's answer 'because he is his acquisition' is correct, as the master can take four zuz from an Israelite and disqualify the slave from terumah wherever he is.

sub.desc_en: Rava affirms the Mishnah's reasoning that the master can take four zuz from an Israelite and disqualify the slave from terumah wherever he is, because the slave is his acquisition.

items.text: Question for Rabbi Meir and answer about a Jewish slave
items.text_en: Question for Rabbi Meir and answer about a Jewish slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that a slave can be disqualified from terumah, what about a Jewish slave? Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers: because the master causes him to lose a Canaanite maidservant. The Gemara objects that he gains a free woman, but the slave prefers a maidservant because she is available and less modest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Meir, the case of a priest's slave is settled, but what about a Jewish slave?

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers: because the master causes him to lose a Canaanite maidservant.
The Gemara objects: on the contrary, the master permits him a free woman, but the slave prefers a maidservant because she is available and less modest.

items.text: New Mishnah: giving a get or shichrur after death
items.text_en: New Mishnah: giving a get or shichrur after death
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if one says 'Give this get to my wife' or 'this shichrur to my slave' and dies, they are not given after death. But if he says 'Give a maneh to so-and-so' and dies, they are given after death.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: if one says 'Give this get to my wife' or 'this shichrur to my slave' and dies, they are not given after death, but if he says 'Give a maneh to so-and-so' and dies, they are given after death.

items.text: Rav Yitzchak's condition: the maneh must be set aside
items.text_en: Rav Yitzchak's condition: the maneh must be set aside
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav says: the ruling applies only when the maneh is piled up and placed in a corner.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav limits the Mishnah's ruling to when the maneh is piled up and placed in a corner.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: is the case a healthy person or a dying one?
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: is the case a healthy person or a dying one?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: are we dealing with a healthy person? If so, even if the maneh is set aside, he hasn't performed a kinyan. If a dying person, why require it to be set aside? For a dying person's words are like written and delivered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's case involves a healthy person (בריא) or a dying person (שכיב מרע), and objects that either way the requirement of the coins being set aside is problematic.
Rav Zevid answers that the case is always a healthy person, and the ruling follows Rav Huna's principle that a transfer in the presence of all three parties effects acquisition.
Rav Pappa answers that the case is always a dying person, and the requirement of the coins being set aside is to avoid suspicion that the dying person meant a buried coin.
The Gemara rules that we do not suspect a buried coin, and then asks why Rav Pappa did not adopt Rav Zevid's explanation.

items.text: Rav Zevid's answer: a healthy person with a kinyan
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's answer: a healthy person with a kinyan
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid says: it is always a healthy person, and it follows Rav Huna's ruling that if one says 'I have a maneh in your hand, give it to so-and-so' in the presence of all three, he acquires it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid answers that the case always involves a healthy person (בריא), and it follows Rav Huna's ruling that if one says 'I have a maneh in your hand, give it to so-and-so' in the presence of all three, the recipient acquires it.

items.text: Rav Pappa's answer: a dying person with a specific maneh
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer: a dying person with a specific maneh
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says: it is always a dying person, and it follows another ruling of Rav: if a dying person says 'Give this maneh to so-and-so from my property', they give it; if he says 'maneh' without specification, they do not give it, because we suspect he meant a buried maneh.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asserts that the case always involves a dying person (שכיב מרע), and invokes another ruling of Rav: if a dying person says 'give this maneh to so-and-so from my property' they give it, but if he says 'maneh' without specification they do not give it.
Rav Pappa concludes that the reason for not giving an unspecified maneh is the suspicion that the dying person meant a buried maneh (מנה קבור).

items.text: Halakhic conclusion and question about Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Halakhic conclusion and question about Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha: we do not suspect a buried maneh. Then it asks: why didn't Rav Pappa say like Rav Zevid?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that we do not suspect a buried maneh (מנה קבור).
The Gemara asks why Rav Pappa did not adopt Rav Zevid's position.

items.text: Rav Papa's position on Rav's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Papa's position on Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Papa holds that Rav's ruling applies equally to loans and deposits.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa holds that Rav's ruling applies equally to loans and deposits.

items.text: Rav Zevid's objection and support from the mishna
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's objection and support from the mishna
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid rejects Rav Papa's view, arguing that the mishna deals with a dying person (שכיב מרע) who does not need to say 'give', as shown by the baraita about one going out in a chain gang.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Zevid rejects Rav Papa's view, and explains that Rav Zevid holds the mishna deals with a dying person (שכיב מרע).
The Gemara infers from the mishna that only if the person dies do they not give, but while alive they do give, and only if he said 'give'.

sub.text: Supporting baraita about one going out in a chain gang
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita about one going out in a chain gang
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one going out in a chain gang who says 'write a get for my wife' — they write and give, and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri adds even a dangerously ill person, showing that a dying person does not need to say 'give'.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge to Rav Zevid
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge to Rav Zevid
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions whether the mishna follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri or the Rabbis, undermining Rav Zevid's proof.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: who says the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri? Perhaps it follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Rav's ruling on transfer in the presence of all three
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on transfer in the presence of all three
items.desc_en: Rav Huna citing Rav rules that if one says 'I have a maneh in your hand, give it to so-and-so' in the presence of all three, the recipient acquires it. Rava limits this to deposits, but Rav holds it applies even to loans, and Levi agrees.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna citing Rav rules that if one says 'I have a maneh in your hand, give it to so-and-so' in the presence of all three, the recipient acquires it.
Rava limits Rav's ruling to deposits, not loans.
Rava retracts, affirming that Rav's ruling applies even to loans.
Shmuel in Levi's name supports that the ruling applies even to loans.

items.text: Amemar's explanation for the ruling
items.text_en: Amemar's explanation for the ruling
items.desc_en: Amemar explains that the transfer works because the debtor is considered to have said at the time of the loan: 'I obligate myself to you and to anyone who comes on your behalf.'

sub.desc_en: Amemar explains that the transfer works because the debtor is considered to have said at the time of the loan: 'I obligate myself to you and to anyone who comes on your behalf.'

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection to Amemar
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection to Amemar
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that if the reasoning is based on the time of the loan, then one could not transfer to future-born children, even according to Rabbi Meir who allows transferring something not yet in existence.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects to Amemar's reasoning: if the acquisition is based on the time of the loan, then transferring to future-born children (who did not exist at that time) would be invalid, contradicting the accepted rule.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's supporting argument from Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's supporting argument from Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi supports his objection by citing Rabbi Meir's position: even Rabbi Meir, who allows transferring something not yet in existence (דבר שלא בא לעולם), only permits it for something that will eventually come into existence, not for something that never existed at the time of the transaction.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi offers a different explanation for the ruling, though the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states his own conclusion (the continuation is implied but not fully given in the text).

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in the Mishnah's case, the debtor's benefit from the distinction between old and new loans motivates him to commit himself to the transaction, even without a formal kinyan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the debtor's benefit from the distinction between old and new loans motivates him to commit himself to the transaction, even without a formal kinyan.

items.text: Objection from the Bar Elyashiv case
items.text_en: Objection from the Bar Elyashiv case
items.desc_en: Huna Mar bar Rav Nechemya objects to Rav Ashi: if the Mishnah's reasoning is based on benefit, then in cases like the Bar Elyashiv family, where they immediately take the money, would they also not acquire? The Gemara rejects this, saying it would lead to arbitrary distinctions.

sub.text: Huna Mar bar Rav Nechemya's objection
sub.text_en: Huna Mar bar Rav Nechemya's objection
sub.desc_en: Huna Mar bar Rav Nechemya objects to Rav Ashi: if the Mishnah's reasoning is based on benefit, then in cases like the Bar Elyashiv family, where they immediately take the money, would they also not acquire?
The Gemara rejects the objection, saying that accepting it would lead to arbitrary distinctions (נתת דבריך לשיעורין).

items.text: Mar Zutra's principle of three halakhot without reason
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's principle of three halakhot without reason
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra states that the Sages established three matters as halakha without a stated reason: the Mishnah's case, Rav Yehuda's ruling about a husband writing all his property to his wife, and Rav Chananya's ruling about a father marrying off his adult son in the house.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra declares that the Sages established three matters as הלכה (binding law) without a stated reason.

Mar Zutra lists the first matter: the Mishnah's case (the one just discussed), and the second: Rav Yehuda's ruling that a husband who writes all his property to his wife only makes her an אפוטרופיא (guardian).
Mar Zutra lists the third matter: Rav Chananya's ruling that a father who marries off his adult son in the house acquires the son's property.

items.text: Rav's case of a verbal instruction in the presence of all parties
items.text_en: Rav's case of a verbal instruction in the presence of all parties
items.desc_en: Rav tells Rav Acha Bardela to give a kav of morika to Ploni in his presence, stating he cannot retract. The Gemara clarifies that this teaches that even for a small gift, the presence of all parties is required, supplementing Rav's earlier ruling about a large gift.

sub.desc_en: Rav instructs Rav Acha Bardela to give a kav of morika to Ploni in his presence, stating he cannot retract.
The Gemara questions whether Rav's statement implies he could retract if he wished.
The Gemara explains that Rav meant these matters are not subject to retraction.
The Gemara objects that Rav already taught this rule elsewhere regarding a gift in the presence of all three parties.
The Gemara resolves that the earlier ruling applied to a large gift, but Rav's new case teaches that even a small gift requires the presence of all parties.

items.text: Case of the gardeners and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Case of the gardeners and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: Gardeners who owed money to a landowner instructed one of them to give the debt in the landowner's presence with a kinyan. Later, the debtor claimed he had nothing. Rav Nachman ruled he must pay because of Rav Huna's ruling and the kinyan. Rava objected that the debtor claimed lack of funds, not refusal, making the kinyan a mistaken one that can be retracted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: gardeners settled accounts, one owed five isteri, and they instructed him to give it to the landowner in his presence with a kinyan.
The debtor later found he had nothing; Rav Nachman ruled he must pay because of Rav Huna's ruling and the kinyan.
Rava objects that the debtor claimed lack of funds, not refusal, making the kinyan a mistaken one that can be retracted.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on 'holekh'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on 'holekh'
items.desc_en: An amoraic dispute: if one says 'Take a maneh to Ploni whom I owe', Rav says the agent is liable for loss and cannot retract; Shmuel says since he is liable, he can retract. The Gemara suggests they argue whether 'holekh' is like 'z'khi', but concludes both agree it is like 'z'khi'; the real dispute is whether we apply the principle of 'miggo'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an amoraic dispute: Rav says the agent is liable for loss and cannot retract; Shmuel says since he is liable, he can retract.
The Gemara suggests the dispute is whether 'holekh' (go) is like 'z'khi' (acquire for him) in effecting acquisition.

The Gemara rejects the suggestion and concludes both agree 'holekh' is like 'z'khi'; the real dispute is whether we apply the principle of 'miggo' (since he could have claimed otherwise, his claim is believed).

items.text: Supporting baraita for Rav and discussion on a deposit
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rav and discussion on a deposit
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav: whether one says 'holekh' or 'ten' for a debt or deposit, the agent is liable and cannot retract. The Gemara questions why a deposit case is different, as the owner may not want his deposit with another. Rabbi Zeira answers that it refers to a confirmed denier.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav's position: whether one says 'holekh' or 'ten' for a debt or deposit, the agent is liable and cannot retract.
The Gemara questions why a deposit case is different, as the owner may not want his deposit with another person.
Rabbi Zeira answers that the baraita refers to a confirmed denier, so the owner would prefer the deposit to be transferred.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's case and the principle of not becoming a borrower's slave
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's case and the principle of not becoming a borrower's slave
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet had garments in Mechoza and asked Rav Yosef bar Chama to bring them. Rav Yosef gave them to him with a kinyan but later evaded. Rav Sheshet praised him for not making himself a 'slave to the lender'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet had garments in Mechoza and asked Rav Yosef bar Chama to bring them; Rav Yosef gave them and agreed to a kinyan.
Rav Yosef later evaded the kinyan, and Rav Sheshet praised him for not making himself a 'slave to the lender'.

items.text: Introduction of Rabbi Achai's case
items.text_en: Introduction of Rabbi Achai's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of Rabbi Achai bar Rabbi Yoshiya who had a silver ingot in Nehardea, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case where Rabbi Achai bar Rabbi Yoshiya had a silver ingot in Nehardea, setting up the next discussion.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Dostai and Rabbi Yosei's gift
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Dostai and Rabbi Yosei's gift
items.desc_en: Rabbi Dostai and Rabbi Yosei are sent to deliver a gift to a powerful person. They are pressured to give it, and Rabbi Dostai agrees while Rabbi Yosei refuses. When they return, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi criticizes Rabbi Dostai for not only failing to assist but also telling them to throw it. Rabbi Dostai explains that the recipients are dangerous officials who would kill without hesitation, and Rabbi Yehuda accepts the justification.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sends Rabbi Dostai and Rabbi Yosei to deliver a gift, but the recipients demand a formal acquisition and then return the gift.
Rabbi Dostai agrees to the acquisition while Rabbi Yosei refuses, and when pressured, Rabbi Dostai tells them to throw the gift.
Upon their return, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rebukes Rabbi Dostai for not only failing to assist but also telling them to throw the gift.
Rabbi Dostai explains that the recipients are dangerous officials who would kill without hesitation, so he acted to save his life.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi confirms the officials' power and proximity to the kingdom, then accepts Rabbi Dostai's action as proper.

items.text: Two conflicting baraitot on returning a lost gift
items.text_en: Two conflicting baraitot on returning a lost gift
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two baraitot that conflict: one says that if a messenger goes to deliver a gift and cannot find the recipient, the money returns to the sender; the other says it goes to the heirs of the intended recipient.

sub.text: Gemara's presentation of two conflicting baraitot
sub.text_en: Gemara's presentation of two conflicting baraitot
sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents two conflicting baraitot: one says the money returns to the sender, the other says it goes to the heirs of the intended recipient.

items.text: Initial suggestion: dispute over 'holekh ke-zakhi'
items.text_en: Initial suggestion: dispute over 'holekh ke-zakhi'
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the baraitot disagree about whether the term 'holekh' (go) is equivalent to 'zakhi' (acquire) for the recipient, meaning the messenger acquires on behalf of the recipient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the two baraitot disagree about whether 'הולך' (go) is equivalent to 'זכי' (acquire) for the recipient.

items.text: Three Amoraim resolve the contradiction
items.text_en: Three Amoraim resolve the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel says everyone agrees 'holekh' is not like 'zakhi', but the baraitot differ based on whether the sender is healthy or a dying person (shekhiv mera). Rav Zevid says both cases are shekhiv mera, differing on whether the recipient was alive at the time of delivery. Rav Pappa says both are healthy, differing on who died first.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel resolves the contradiction by asserting that everyone agrees 'holekh' is not like 'zakhi', and the baraitot differ based on whether the sender is healthy (baria) or a dying person (shekhiv mera).
Rav Zevid offers an alternative resolution: both cases involve a shekhiv mera, but they differ on whether the recipient was alive at the time of the money delivery.
Rav Pappa gives a third resolution: both cases involve a healthy sender, and the difference is whether the recipient died before the giver or the giver died before the recipient.

items.text: Extended baraita with multiple opinions
items.text_en: Extended baraita with multiple opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a longer baraita with more opinions: Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yaakov say the money returns to the sender's heirs; Yesh Omrim say it goes to the recipient's heirs; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi cites Rabbi Meir that 'mitzvah le-kayem divrei ha-met' applies; Chachamim say they divide; and elsewhere they said the agent may do as he wishes. Rabbi Shimon HaNasi reports a precedent that it returns to the sender's heirs. The Gemara analyzes whether these opinions reflect a dispute about 'holekh ke-zakhi'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute about 'הולך (the agent's delivery) being equivalent to זכי (the recipient's acquisition)' is a dispute between Tanna'im, citing the first baraita that the money returns to the sender.

sub.text: Baraita citation: Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yaakov
sub.text_en: Baraita citation: Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The baraita records that Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yaakov say the money returns to the sender's heirs, while Yesh Omrim say it goes to the recipient's heirs.

sub.text: Baraita citation: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi citing Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Baraita citation: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi citing Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, citing Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Meir, invokes the principle of 'מצוה לקיים דברי המת (it is a mitzvah to fulfill the words of the deceased)'.

sub.text: Baraita citation: Chachamim and the anonymous statement
sub.text_en: Baraita citation: Chachamim and the anonymous statement
sub.desc_en: The Chachamim say they divide the money, and elsewhere they said the agent may do as he wishes.

sub.text: Baraita citation: Rabbi Shimon HaNasi's precedent
sub.text_en: Baraita citation: Rabbi Shimon HaNasi's precedent
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon HaNasi reports a precedent that the money returns to the sender's heirs.

The Gemara proposes that the Tanna Kamma holds 'הולך' is not like 'זכי', Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yaakov also hold it is not like 'זכי' and do not apply 'מצוה לקיים דברי המת', while Yesh Omrim hold 'הולך' is like 'זכי'.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds 'הולך' is not like 'זכי', but when the sender dies, the principle of 'מצוה לקיים דברי המת' applies.
The Gemara explains that the Chachamim are uncertain and say they divide, the anonymous statement prefers 'שודא (judicial discretion)', and Rabbi Shimon HaNasi merely reports a precedent.

The Gemara rejects the previous analysis, stating that in the case of a healthy person (בריא) everyone agrees, and the dispute here is about a dying person (שכיב מרע) and reflects the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Elazar requires formal acquisition for a dying person's gift, while the Rabbis hold that mere speech suffices.

items.text: Rejection and alternative resolution via Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Rejection and alternative resolution via Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous analysis, stating that in the case of a healthy person all agree. Instead, the dispute is about a shekhiv mera and hinges on the Tannaic dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis regarding whether a dying person's verbal gift is effective without a formal kinyan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous analysis, stating that in the case of a healthy person all agree, and the dispute is actually about a shekhiv mera (שכיב מרע, dying person) and hinges on the Tannaic dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis.

The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Elazar holds that a dying person's gift requires a formal kinyan (קניין, acquisition act) for property with אחריות (lien liability), while the Rabbis hold that mere verbal declaration suffices.

The Gemara continues the Mishnah citation, recounting the story of the sick mother of the sons of Rochel who said 'תינתן' (let it be given), illustrating the Rabbis' position that verbal declaration suffices for a shekhiv mera.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's case and the dispute about fulfilling the words of the deceased
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's case and the dispute about fulfilling the words of the deceased
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's case of a dying person who allocated gifts, and the Sages upheld her words. It identifies the Tanna Kamma as Rabbi Elazar, and explains that Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yaakov also follow Rabbi Elazar, holding that we do not fulfill the words of the deceased. The 'Yesh Omrim' opinion follows the Rabbis. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, citing Rabbi Meir, also follows Rabbi Elazar but holds that when the person dies, we do fulfill the words of the deceased. The Sages are uncertain, and here they said that the court's decision is preferable. Rabbi Shimon HaNasi came to teach a precedent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case where a dying woman allocated a gift to her daughter and the Sages upheld her words, citing the harsh response of the son.

The Gemara identifies the Tanna Kamma as following Rabbi Elazar, and notes that Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yaakov also follow Rabbi Elazar, holding that we do not fulfill the words of the deceased, while the 'Yesh Omrim' opinion follows the Rabbis.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi citing Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Elazar but holds that when the person dies we do fulfill the words of the deceased; the Sages are uncertain and here said the court's decision is preferable; and Rabbi Shimon HaNasi came to teach a precedent.

items.text: Inquiry about Rabbi Shimon HaNasi's title
items.text_en: Inquiry about Rabbi Shimon HaNasi's title
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: Is Rabbi Shimon HaNasi himself the Nasi, or is he speaking in the name of the Nasi? It attempts to resolve this from Rav Yosef's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon HaNasi, but the question remains unresolved, concluding with 'Teiku'.
