sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about Rabbi Shimon HaNasi: is he himself the Nasi, or does he speak in the name of the Nasi?
Rav Yosef rules that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon HaNasi, but the question remains unresolved (תיקו).
The Gemara concludes that the question remains unresolved, leaving it with 'Teiku'.

items.text: Reconciling Rav Yosef's ruling with the principle of fulfilling the words of the deceased
items.text_en: Reconciling Rav Yosef's ruling with the principle of fulfilling the words of the deceased
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Yosef ruled that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon HaNasi, but we already know that the words of a dying person are considered as written and delivered. Rav Yosef establishes the case as involving a healthy person. The Gemara then objects that the case involves sending to heirs, and we have a principle to fulfill the words of the deceased. The answer is that the items should return to the sender.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Yosef's ruling, noting the established principle that the words of a dying person (שכיב מרע) are considered as written and delivered.
Rav Yosef explains that the case involves a healthy person (בריא), and the rule of fulfilling the words of the deceased applies only to a dying person, so the gifts revert to the sender.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the phrase 'Hadran alach HaMevi Kama'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion and transitions to the next Mishnah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah of the new chapter
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah of the new chapter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a get brought from overseas is invalid: if the agent says it was written in his presence but not signed, or signed but not written, or half written and all signed, or all written and half signed. It also discusses cases of conflicting testimony from one or two witnesses, with Rabbi Yehuda validating some cases.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a messenger who brings a get from overseas fails to properly testify about its writing or signing, and rules on their validity.
The Mishnah presents cases of conflicting testimony from one or two witnesses, with Rabbi Yehuda validating some cases.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's redundancy
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's redundancy
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the case of an agent who says it was written and signed in his presence, since it was already taught earlier. It explains that without this repetition, one might think it is only a requirement but not invalidating if omitted, so the Mishnah teaches that it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the requirement for the messenger to say 'in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed' when it was already stated in the first Mishnah.
The Gemara explains that without the repetition, one might think the requirement is only ideal (לכתחילה) but not disqualifying (בדיעבד), so the Mishnah teaches that it is indeed required.

items.text: Clarifying 'half written' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Clarifying 'half written' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which half of the get is meant when it says 'half written'. If it means the first half, that contradicts Rabbi Elazar's ruling that even one line written for its sake suffices. Rav Ashi explains that it means the second half.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which half of the get is meant when the Mishnah says 'half was written in my presence' — if it is the first half, it contradicts Rabbi Elazar's ruling that even one line written for its own sake suffices.
Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah refers to the second half of the get, which must be written in the messenger's presence.
Rav Ashi resolves the question by explaining that 'half written' refers to the second half of the get.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling on the case of all written and half signed
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling on the case of all written and half signed
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that even if two witnesses testify to the signature of the second witness, the get is invalid. The reason is that either the entire get must be validated through the witnesses' testimony, or the entire get must be validated through the Sages' enactment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that even if two witnesses testify about the second signature, the get is invalid, and asks for the reason.
The Gemara explains that the get must be either entirely validated through proper testimony or entirely through the rabbinic enactment.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rav Chisda's ruling.
Rav Chisda explains that the get must be validated either entirely through witness testimony (קיום הגט) or entirely through the Sages' enactment (תקנת חכמים), not a mix of both.

items.text: Rava's objection to Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Rava's objection to Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: Rava objects: Is there anything that if one witness testifies it is valid, but with two witnesses it is invalid? Rava offers an alternative explanation, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects: if one witness would make the get valid, why would two witnesses make it invalid?
Rava provides his own explanation, beginning to state that even in such a case the get is valid.

items.text: Opening ruling and reason
items.text_en: Opening ruling and reason
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one witness and another testify about the signature of the second witness, it is invalid. The Gemara explains the reason: it might be confused with general document validation, and money would be lost based on one witness.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one witness and another testify about the signature of the second witness, it is invalid, and the Gemara explains the reason: it might be confused with general document validation, leading to monetary loss based on one witness.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge and new explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge and new explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: if one witness testified to the entire statement it would be valid, so why is it invalid when there is another with him? He then offers a new explanation: even if one says 'I am the second witness' it is invalid, because the entire validation must be either all in the get's validation or all in the rabbinic enactment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: if one witness had testified to the entire statement it would be valid, so why is it invalid when there is another with him?
Rav Ashi explains: even if one says 'I am the second witness' it is invalid, because the entire validation must be either all in the get's validation or all in the rabbinic enactment.

items.text: Gemara's question from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the Mishnah's case: 'In my presence it was written entirely, in my presence half was signed' is invalid. It questions what the other half is, and argues that if one testifies to writing and one to signing, it should be invalid, so why mention 'half'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case: if one witness testifies to the entire writing and another to the entire signing, it is invalid, so why mention 'half'?

items.text: Resolution: either like Rava or Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Resolution: either like Rava or Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's case is either like Rava's or Rav Ashi's explanation, and it excludes Rav Chisda's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's case follows either Rava's or Rav Ashi's explanation, thereby excluding Rav Chisda's view.

items.text: Rav Chisda's defense
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's defense
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda responds: according to your reasoning, why does the Mishnah need to say 'in my presence it was written but not in my presence signed'? Rather, it teaches 'not only this but also that', and here too it teaches 'not only this but also that'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda defends his position by arguing that the Mishnah's phrase 'in my presence it was written but not in my presence signed' is extraneous unless it teaches 'not only this but also that', and the same applies to the case of one witness on the signature.

items.text: Rav Chisda and Marimar on grooving and partition
items.text_en: Rav Chisda and Marimar on grooving and partition
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says: a groove of five handbreadths and a partition of five handbreadths do not combine unless all is in a partition or all in a groove. Marimar taught that they do combine, and the halakha is that they combine.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a groove of five handbreadths and a partition of five handbreadths do not combine to form a valid partition unless the entire measure is in one type.
Marimar teaches that they do combine, and the halakha (הלכה) is ruled in accordance with his position.

items.text: Ilefa's question about hands being pure in halves
items.text_en: Ilefa's question about hands being pure in halves
items.desc_en: Ilefa asks whether hands can be purified in halves. The Gemara considers cases: two people washing from a quarter-log (rejected), washing one hand (rejected), washing half a hand (rejected by Rabbi Yannai's school). It concludes the case involves residual liquid, and questions its significance.

sub.desc_en: Ilefa asks whether hands can be purified in halves.
The Gemara considers the case of two people washing from a quarter-log and rejects it because a quarter-log suffices for one or two.
The Gemara considers washing one hand and rejects it because washing one hand is valid.
The Gemara considers washing half a hand and rejects it because the school of Rabbi Yannai rules that hands cannot be purified in halves.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves residual liquid (משקה טופח) on the hand.
The Gemara questions the significance of residual liquid and cites a supporting baraita.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Liquids not connected for impurity or purity
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Liquids not connected for impurity or purity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a poured stream, a siphon, and a liquid film are not considered a connection for impurity or purity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a poured stream, a siphon, and a liquid film are not considered a connection for impurity or purity.

items.text: Gemara's clarification: The case of a film thick enough to moisten
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification: The case of a film thick enough to moisten
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling is necessary only when there is a film thick enough to moisten, but a film that can moisten is a connection. It suggests this might refer to a mikveh and follow Rabbi Yehuda's opinion about touching water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's ruling is necessary only when there is a film thick enough to moisten, but then objects that such a film is explicitly taught to be a connection.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's ruling might refer to the laws of a mikveh (ritual bath) and follows the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a mikveh with exactly forty se'ah, where two people immerse one after the other — the first is pure, the second impure.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that if the first person's feet were touching the water, even the second person is pure, illustrating the principle of a connecting film.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's unresolved question: Half by immersion, half by pouring
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's unresolved question: Half by immersion, half by pouring
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya raises a question about a case where half of a person's head and majority come by immersion and half by pouring of drawn water, and leaves it unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya cites the established rule that one who brings his head and most of his body into drawn water, or upon whom three לוגים (logs) of drawn water fall, becomes טמא (ritually impure).
Rabbi Yirmeya asks: what is the law if half the immersion comes by entry (ביאה) and half by pouring (נפילה)? The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Pappa's unresolved question: Half by immersion, half by pouring for a zav
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's unresolved question: Half by immersion, half by pouring for a zav
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa raises a similar question about a sick man with a seminal emission who is purified by nine kav of water, asking what if half is by immersion and half by pouring, and leaves it unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa raises an unresolved question (תיקו) about a sick man with a seminal emission who is purified by nine kav of water, asking what the law is if half the water is applied by immersion and half by pouring.

items.text: Dispute about a get: One says written in his presence, the other says signed in his presence
items.text_en: Dispute about a get: One says written in his presence, the other says signed in his presence
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's case of conflicting witness statements is addressed: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the dispute applies only when the get does not emerge from both their hands, but if it does, the get is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one witness says the get was written in his presence and the other says it was signed in his presence.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Shmuel bar Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Shmuel bar Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the dispute applies only when the get does not emerge from both witnesses' hands, but if it does, the get is valid.

items.text: Inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's ruling that if two witnesses bring a get and one says 'in my presence it was signed', the get is valid according to Rabbi Yehuda, implying that two witnesses who bring a get from overseas do not need to say 'in our presence it was written and signed'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that according to Rabbi Yehuda, two witnesses who bring a get from overseas do not need to say 'in our presence it was written and signed'.

items.text: Abaye's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the inference from the Mishnah's latter clause, where the Rabbis deem a get invalid even if it comes from both witnesses, unless both say 'in our presence it was written and signed'. The Gemara explains the dispute: one opinion fears confusion with the validation of other documents by a single witness, while the other does not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges the Gemara's inference from the Mishnah's latter clause: if the Rabbis invalidate a get even when both witnesses are present unless both say 'in our presence it was written and signed', then why would they validate it when the get comes from both witnesses without that statement?
The Gemara confirms Abaye's inference: yes, the Rabbis would validate a get when both witnesses are present without the declaration.

The Gemara explains the dispute between the two opinions: one opinion fears confusion with the validation of other documents by a single witness (עד אחד), so they require the declaration even when both witnesses are present; the other opinion does not fear this confusion.

items.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that even if the get comes from both witnesses, it is invalid, implying that two witnesses must say 'in our presence it was written and signed'. Abaye challenges this from the Mishnah's latter clause, and the Gemara explains the dispute: one opinion holds that witnesses are not proficient in writing for her sake, the other that witnesses are not available to validate it.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that even if the get comes from both witnesses, it is invalid, implying that two witnesses who bring a get from overseas must say 'in our presence it was written and signed'.

Abaye challenges: according to this version, in the Mishnah's latter clause where two say 'in our presence it was written' and one says 'in my presence it was signed', the Rabbis rule it invalid; but if the get comes from both witnesses, would the Rabbis really invalidate it?
The Gemara answers: yes, the Rabbis would invalidate it even when the get comes from both witnesses.

The Gemara explains the dispute between the two opinions: one holds that the witnesses are not proficient in writing for her sake (לשמה), and the other holds that witnesses are not available to validate the get.

items.text: Reconciling the dispute with Rabba and Rava
items.text_en: Reconciling the dispute with Rabba and Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute between Rabba and Rava corresponds to the Tannaic dispute. It answers that Rava resolves it according to the first version, while Rabba explains that everyone agrees that writing for her sake is required, but the dispute is about a decree lest the matter revert to its flawed state.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute between Rabba and Rava corresponds to a Tannaic dispute.
The Gemara answers that Rava resolves the dispute according to the first version, while Rabba explains that everyone agrees writing for her sake is required.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute is about a decree lest the matter revert to its flawed state, with one opinion decreeing and the other not.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's dispute in the first clause
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's dispute in the first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda does not also dispute the first clause of the Mishnah. Ulla says that Rabbi Yehuda disputed even the first clause. Rav Oshaya challenges Ulla from a baraita, and the Gemara resolves that the baraita excludes a case where one says 'in my presence it was signed but not written', teaching that Rabbi Yehuda does not decree in that case either.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda does not also dispute the first clause of the Mishnah.
Ulla answers that Rabbi Yehuda did dispute even the first clause.
Rav Oshaya challenges Ulla from a baraita that says Rabbi Yehuda only validates this specific case, not another.
The Gemara infers that the baraita excludes the case where one says 'in my presence it was written' and another says 'in my presence it was signed'.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita excludes the case where one says 'in my presence it was signed but not written', teaching that Rabbi Yehuda does not decree even in that case.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling and the story of Rabba bar bar Chana
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling and the story of Rabba bar bar Chana
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that the case of two witnesses bringing a get from overseas is subject to the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis. The Gemara recounts that when Rabba bar bar Chana was ill, Rav Yehuda and Rabba visited him and asked whether two witnesses need to say 'in our presence it was written and signed'. He answered that they do not, comparing it to their testimony that he divorced her.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that the case of two witnesses bringing a get from overseas is subject to the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

sub.text: Story of Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.text_en: Story of Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that when Rabba bar bar Chana was ill, Rav Yehuda and Rabba visited him and asked whether two witnesses need to say 'in our presence it was written and signed'; he answered that they do not, comparing it to their testimony that he divorced her.

items.text: Story of the lamp and the exile to Babylonia
items.text_en: Story of the lamp and the exile to Babylonia
items.desc_en: A story is told about a friend who took a lamp from before them and prayed for either God's protection or that of Esau's descendant. The Gemara questions whether Romans are superior to Persians, citing a baraita that God exiled Israel to Babylonia because they could not bear Roman decrees. The contradiction is resolved by distinguishing between before and after the friends came to Babylonia.

sub.desc_en: A friend takes a lamp from before them and prays for either God's protection or that of Esau's descendant.
The Gemara questions whether the story implies Romans are superior to Persians.
Rabbi Chiyya's baraita explains that God exiled Israel to Babylonia because they could not bear Roman decrees.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before and after the friends came to Babylonia.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's ruling on a get from witnesses of writing vs. signing
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's ruling on a get from witnesses of writing vs. signing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'in my presence it was written' and two say 'in our presence it was signed,' the get is valid. Rabbi Ami quoting Rabbi Yochanan limits this to when the get comes from the hand of the witness of writing, but if from the hand of witnesses of signing, it is invalid. This implies that two who bring a get from overseas must say 'in our presence it was written and in our presence it was signed.' Rabbi Asi objects, citing the first clause where two say 'in our presence it was written' and one says 'in my presence it was signed' is invalid, and even if the get comes from both their hands, the Rabbis invalidate it. Rabbi Ami confirms.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one witness says 'in my presence it was written' and two say 'in our presence it was signed,' the get is valid.
Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan limits the Mishnah's validity to when the get comes from the hand of the witness of writing, but if from the hand of witnesses of signing, it is invalid.
The Gemara infers that Rabbi Ami holds that two who bring a get from overseas must say 'in our presence it was written and in our presence it was signed.'

Rabbi Asi objects: according to the first clause where two say 'in our presence it was written' and one says 'in my presence it was signed' is invalid, would the Rabbis invalidate even if the get comes from both their hands?
Rabbi Ami confirms that indeed the Rabbis invalidate it even in that case.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's contradictory ruling and Rabbi Asi's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's contradictory ruling and Rabbi Asi's objection
items.desc_en: Sometimes Rabbi Ami was found sitting and saying that even if the get comes from the hand of witnesses of signing, it is valid, implying that two who bring a get from overseas do not need to say 'in our presence it was written and in our presence it was signed.' Rabbi Asi objects, citing the first clause: if two say 'in our presence it was written' and one says 'in my presence it was signed,' it is invalid, and Rabbi Yehuda validates; the reason is that the get does not come from both their hands, but if it did, the Rabbis would validate it. Rabbi Ami confirms, and when asked why he didn't say so earlier, he responds that it is a peg that will not be moved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that sometimes Rabbi Ami was found sitting and ruling that even if the get comes from the hand of witnesses of signing, it is valid, implying that two who bring a get from overseas do not need to say 'in our presence it was written and in our presence it was signed.'

Rabbi Asi objects, citing the first clause of the Mishnah: if two say 'in our presence it was written' and one says 'in my presence it was signed,' it is invalid, and Rabbi Yehuda validates; the reason is that the get does not come from both their hands, but if it did, the Rabbis would validate it.
Rabbi Ami confirms Rabbi Asi's inference, and when asked why he didn't say so earlier, he responds that it is a peg that will not be moved.

items.text: Mishnah: Timing of writing and signing a get
items.text_en: Mishnah: Timing of writing and signing a get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a get is written and signed on the same day, or at night and signed at night, or at night and signed the next day, it is valid. If written by day and signed at night, it is invalid, but Rabbi Shimon validates. Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is that all gittin written by day and signed at night are invalid except for gittin of women.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the valid and invalid timing combinations for writing and signing a get, concluding that Rabbi Shimon validates a get written by day and signed at night.
Rabbi Shimon explains his position: all gittin written by day and signed at night are invalid except for gittin of women.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for dating a get
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for dating a get
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a date was instituted in gittin. Rabbi Yochanan says because of his sister's daughter (to prevent her from being disadvantaged if the get is backdated). Reish Lakish says because of produce (to prevent the husband from collecting produce from her property after the get). The Gemara then asks why Reish Lakish does not hold like Rabbi Yochanan, and answers that he would say... (the text cuts off).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a date was instituted in gittin (bills of divorce).
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the date was instituted because of his sister's daughter (to prevent her from being disadvantaged if the get is backdated).
Reish Lakish answers that the date was instituted because of produce (to prevent the husband from collecting produce from her property after the get).
The Gemara asks why Reish Lakish does not hold like Rabbi Yochanan's reason.
The Gemara begins to present Reish Lakish's response, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's reason for not adopting Reish Lakish's view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's reason for not adopting Reish Lakish's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that he does not hold like Reish Lakish because he maintains that the husband has rights to the produce until the moment of delivery (נתינה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan does not adopt Reish Lakish's view because he holds that the husband has rights to the produce (פֵּירוֹת) until the moment of delivery (נְתִינָה).

items.text: Question on Rabbi Shimon's position according to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Question on Rabbi Shimon's position according to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Reish Lakish, Rabbi Shimon's lenient ruling makes sense, but according to Rabbi Yochanan, why does Rabbi Shimon validate the get? Rabbi Yochanan responds that he is only speaking according to the Rabbis, not Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Reish Lakish, Rabbi Shimon's lenient ruling makes sense, but according to Rabbi Yochanan, why does Rabbi Shimon validate the get?
Rabbi Yochanan responds that he is only speaking according to the Rabbis, not Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: The practical difference between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.text_en: The practical difference between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yochanan, there is a clear difference between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis; but according to Reish Lakish, what is the difference? The answer: produce from the time of writing until the time of signing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yochanan, there is a clear difference between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis; but according to Reish Lakish, what is the difference?
The Gemara answers: the difference is produce from the time of writing until the time of signing.

items.text: Contradiction and reversal of opinions
items.text_en: Contradiction and reversal of opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that we heard the opposite from these sages regarding when produce is released, and therefore reverses their positions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that we heard the opposite positions from Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding when produce is released, citing the earlier dispute.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reversing the opinions: Rabbi Yochanan now holds the position attributed to Reish Lakish and vice versa.

items.text: Abaye's question about the benefit of the Sages' enactment
items.text_en: Abaye's question about the benefit of the Sages' enactment
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef: if three invalid gittin produce a valid child, what benefit did the Sages achieve? Rav Yosef answers that initially she may not marry. Abaye then asks about cutting the date and giving it to her, and Rav Yosef says we do not suspect a deceiver.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef: if three invalid gittin produce a valid child, what benefit did the Sages achieve through their enactment?
Rav Yosef answers that the benefit is that initially (לכתחילה) she may not marry.
Abaye asks: if he cuts the date and gives it to her, what then?
Rav Yosef answers that we do not suspect a deceiver (רמאי).

items.text: The case of a get with a week date
items.text_en: The case of a get with a week date
items.desc_en: Abaye asks about a get written with a week, year, month, or Sabbath date. Rav Yosef says it is valid, and explains that the enactment benefits by limiting the date to the surrounding weeks, just as a day date is limited to the surrounding days.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef about the validity of a get (גט) written with a week, year, month, or Sabbath date instead of a specific day.
Rav Yosef rules that such a get (גט) is valid (כשר).
Abaye asks what benefit the Sages' enactment provides if the date is so broad.
Rav Yosef explains that the enactment benefits by limiting the date to the surrounding weeks, just as a day date is limited to the surrounding days.
Rav Yosef supports his answer with an analogy: even a specific day date does not indicate morning or evening, yet it is valid by limiting to the surrounding days.
Rav Yosef concludes that the same logic applies here: the week date limits the get (גט) to the surrounding weeks.

items.text: Ravina's question about writing the date
items.text_en: Ravina's question about writing the date
items.desc_en: Ravina begins a question to Rava about a get where the date was written, but the segment is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava about a get where the date was written, but the question is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's question about a get placed in a pouch
items.text_en: Gemara's question about a get placed in a pouch
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a case where a husband places a get in a pouch, intending to reconcile with his wife if she appeases him. Rav Ashi responds that a person does not bring calamity upon themselves prematurely.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a case where a husband places a get in a pouch, intending to reconcile if his wife appeases him, questioning the validity of the get.
Rav Ashi responds that a person does not bring calamity upon themselves prematurely, so the get is valid despite the husband's conditional intent.

items.text: Question about gittin from overseas
items.text_en: Question about gittin from overseas
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi about gittin written in Nisan but not delivered until Tishrei, questioning the benefit of the Sages' enactment. Rav Ashi answers that such gittin have a known reputation (קלא).

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if a get (גט) from overseas is written in Nisan but not delivered until Tishrei, what benefit did the Sages achieve by their enactment?
Rav Ashi answers that such gittin (גיטין) have a known reputation (קלא), so the enactment's purpose is served.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on when to count for a get
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on when to count for a get
items.desc_en: Rav says the count begins from the time of delivery, while Shmuel says from the time of writing. Rav Nathan bar Hoshaya objects to Shmuel's view, and Abaye responds that the time of the get itself testifies to its validity.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with a dispute: Rav says the count for a get begins from the time of delivery (משעת נתינה), while Shmuel says from the time of writing (משעת כתיבה).

sub.text: Rav Nathan bar Hoshaya's objection to Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nathan bar Hoshaya's objection to Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nathan bar Hoshaya objects to Shmuel's view: if two women in the same courtyard receive gittin written at different times, one would be forbidden and the other permitted, creating an absurd inconsistency.
Abaye responds that the time written in each get itself testifies to its validity, so no confusion arises.

items.text: Baraitot supporting Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Baraitot supporting Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav: a get delayed three months requires a three-month wait, but no concern for an old get. Another baraita supports Shmuel: a deposited get given after three months allows immediate marriage, with no concern for an old get.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav: a get delayed three months requires a three-month wait, but no concern for an old get.
Another baraita supports Shmuel: a deposited get given after three months allows immediate marriage, with no concern for an old get.

items.text: Practice of Amoraim and halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: Practice of Amoraim and halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana, Rav Papi, and Rav Ashi follow Shmuel's view (from writing), while Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua follow Rav's view (from delivery). The halakha is decided in favor of Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana, Rav Papi, and Rav Ashi practice counting from the time of writing.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua practice counting from the time of giving.
The halakha is decided in favor of counting from the time of writing.

items.text: Dispute on when a ketubah is subject to remission
items.text_en: Dispute on when a ketubah is subject to remission
items.desc_en: Rav says a ketubah is remitted only when the wife both impairs it and converts it to a loan. Shmuel says either action suffices. Baraitot support both views: one requires both, another lists cases where conversion to a loan triggers remission from the time of court standing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: from when does a ketubah become subject to remission (שמיטה)?
Rav rules that the ketubah is remitted only when the wife both impairs it (פוגמת) and converts it to a loan (זוקפת).
Shmuel rules that either impairing the ketubah or converting it to a loan alone suffices for remission.
A baraita supports Rav: the ketubah is remitted only when both impairing and converting to a loan occur.
A baraita supports Shmuel: various obligations, including a ketubah, are remitted once converted to a loan, and the time of remission is from court standing.

items.text: Shmuel's comparison of ketubah to a court document
items.text_en: Shmuel's comparison of ketubah to a court document
items.desc_en: Shmuel compares a ketubah to a court document: both can be written by day and signed at night. The case of Rabbi Chiya bar Rav's ketubah is cited, where Rav was present and said nothing, implying agreement. The Gemara explains they were engaged in that matter, citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel compares a ketubah to a court document: both can be written by day and signed at night.

sub.text: Narrative of Rabbi Chiya bar Rav's ketubah
sub.text_en: Narrative of Rabbi Chiya bar Rav's ketubah
sub.desc_en: The case of Rabbi Chiya bar Rav's ketubah is cited: it was written by day and signed at night, and Rav was present and said nothing, implying tacit agreement.
The Gemara questions whether Rav's silence indicates he agrees with Shmuel's ruling.
The Gemara answers that they were engaged in that matter, so Rav's silence does not necessarily indicate agreement.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok
sub.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok is cited: the rule that a document written by day and signed at night is invalid only when not engaged in that matter, but if engaged in that matter it is valid.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's leniency and Resh Lakish's limitation
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's leniency and Resh Lakish's limitation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon validates a get written close to the divorce, as the husband has no further rights to the produce. Resh Lakish limits this leniency to immediately (אלתר), not within ten days.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens by citing Rabbi Shimon's leniency that a get written close to the divorce is valid, and Rava explains the reasoning: once the husband has set his eyes on divorcing her, he has no further rights to the produce.
Resh Lakish limits Rabbi Shimon's leniency to only when the get is given immediately (אלתר), not when given within ten days.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's position on the concern of appeasement
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's position on the concern of appeasement
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts Rav's concern that the husband might appease his wife within ten days with Rabbi Yochanan's view that if he appeased, there would be a public outcry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states Rav's concern that the husband might appease his wife within ten days.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that even if the husband appeased within ten days, the matter would have a public outcry, so there is no concern.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the core disagreement: when a man tells ten people to write a get, Rabbi Yochanan says two act as witnesses and the rest as a condition, while Reish Lakish says all act as witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says that when a man tells ten people to write a get, two act as witnesses and the rest as a condition.
Reish Lakish states the opposing view: all ten act as witnesses.

items.text: Clarifying the case: he said 'all of you'
items.text_en: Clarifying the case: he said 'all of you'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute applies only when the husband said 'all of you' write the get, as otherwise the Mishnah already rules that one writes and two sign.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks under what circumstances the dispute applies, noting that if the husband did not say 'all of you', the Mishnah already rules that one writes and two sign.
The Gemara answers that the dispute applies only when the husband explicitly said 'all of you' to the ten people.

items.text: Practical difference: delayed signatures
items.text_en: Practical difference: delayed signatures
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies a practical difference: if two signed on the day and the rest within ten days, according to the condition view it is valid, but according to the witnesses view it is invalid. Similarly, if one signatory is found to be a relative or invalid, the condition view validates the get while the witnesses view invalidates it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two positions (condition vs. witnesses).
The Gemara answers: if two signed on the day and the rest within ten days, the condition view validates the גט (get) while the witnesses view invalidates it.
Alternatively, if one signatory is found to be a relative or invalid, the condition view validates the גט (get) while the witnesses view invalidates it.

items.text: Further nuance: a relative or invalid signed first
items.text_en: Further nuance: a relative or invalid signed first
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where a relative or invalid signed first, leading to a dispute: some say it is valid (since it is a condition), while others say it is invalid due to concern of confusion with regular documents.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a case where a relative or invalid person signed first among the ten.
Some say the get is valid because the signing is merely a condition (תנאי), not testimony.
Others say the get is invalid due to concern that it will be confused with regular documents (שטרות דעלמא).

items.text: A case brought before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: A case brought before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a specific incident where a man told ten people to write a get, two signed on the day and the rest within ten days, and the case was brought to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi for judgment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a man told ten people to write a get, two signed on the day and the rest within ten days, and the case was brought to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi for judgment.

items.text: Resolving the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages
items.text_en: Resolving the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon's opinion can be relied upon in pressing circumstances. It then addresses a contradiction between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan regarding Rabbi Shimon's ruling, explaining that the anonymous ruling follows Rabbi Yochanan in one case and Resh Lakish in another.

items.text: Mishnah: Permitted and prohibited writing materials and surfaces
items.text_en: Mishnah: Permitted and prohibited writing materials and surfaces
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists materials that may be used to write a get (ink, gum, red dye, etc.) and those that may not (liquids, fruit juices). It also lists surfaces that may be used (olive leaf, cow's horn, slave's hand) and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's prohibition against writing on living beings or food.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the materials and adding more
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the materials and adding more
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the names of the materials listed in the Mishnah. It then asks what additional materials are included by the phrase 'anything that is permanent,' and cites baraitot from Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Chiya that add other permanent substances.

items.text: Liability for writing over ink on Shabbat
items.text_en: Liability for writing over ink on Shabbat
items.desc_en: An amoraic dispute is presented: if one passes ink over red dye on Shabbat, Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish both rule he is liable for two sins (writing and erasing). For ink over ink or dye over dye, he is exempt. For dye over ink, there is a dispute: one view says he is liable because he is erasing, the other says he is exempt because he is merely spoiling.

items.text: Resh Lakish's question: Is upper writing considered writing?
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's question: Is upper writing considered writing?
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan whether witnesses who cannot sign may have red dye written for them and then sign over it with ink, and whether the upper writing is considered valid. Rabbi Yochanan says it is not considered writing. Resh Lakish objects that Rabbi Yochanan himself taught that upper writing is considered writing for Shabbat purposes, but Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between theoretical and practical halakha.

items.text: Practical solutions for witnesses who cannot sign
items.text_en: Practical solutions for witnesses who cannot sign
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel offer solutions: Rav says to tear blank paper and fill the tears with ink; Shmuel says to use אבר (a type of ink). The Gemara questions Shmuel's solution because Rabbi Chiya taught that writing with אבר is valid, implying it is permanent. The Gemara resolves that there are two types: אברא (the substance) and מי דאברא (its liquid). Rabbi Avahu suggests מי מילין, and the Gemara distinguishes between processed and unprocessed forms.

items.text: Rav Pappa's solution: use רוק (spit)
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's solution: use רוק (spit)
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa suggests using spit (רוק) for witnesses to sign, and he instructed Pappa Torah'ah accordingly. This applies only to gittin, not to other documents, as Rav Kahana once flogged someone who did so for other documents.

items.text: Baraita on witnesses who cannot sign
items.text_en: Baraita on witnesses who cannot sign
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav's view: witnesses who cannot sign have paper cut and filled with ink. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel limits this to gittin; for other documents, witnesses must know how to read and sign. The Gemara suggests the baraita is missing a clause about reading.

items.text: Rava's ruling and dispute
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning: to prevent agunot. Rava rules the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but Rav Gamda reports in Rava's name that the halakha does not follow him, implying it follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Rav Kahana's action explained
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's action explained
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Kahana flogged someone who acted with other documents, but explains that this was regarding reading, not signing.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's distress and precedent
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's distress and precedent
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda was distressed because he could not read or sign. Ulla reassures him that Rabbi Elazar and Rav Nachman had others read and sign before them, but only with court scribes who are in awe.

items.text: Persian documents and their validity
items.text_en: Persian documents and their validity
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa would collect debts based on Persian documents by having two gentiles testify separately. Rav Ashi reports that Amemar allows collection from liened property if Jewish witnesses signed, but the Gemara raises concerns about reading ability, forgery, and the need to repeat the document's content in the last line, all of which are addressed.

items.text: Teaching that any language is valid
items.text_en: Teaching that any language is valid
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Amemar teaches, since a mishnah already states that a get written in Hebrew with Greek witnesses is valid. It answers that the mishnah applies only to gittin, but Amemar teaches that it applies to other documents as well.

items.text: Shmuel's concern about invisible ink
items.text_en: Shmuel's concern about invisible ink
items.desc_en: Shmuel says that if a husband gave his wife a blank paper and said 'This is your get,' she is divorced, because we suspect he wrote it with mei milin (invisible ink). The Gemara raises an objection from a mishnah that implies writing is required, and answers that Shmuel refers to testing with water; if ink appears, it is valid. The Gemara questions the test, but Shmuel only said 'we suspect.'

items.text: Witnesses must read the get
items.text_en: Witnesses must read the get
items.desc_en: Ravina reports that Marimar said in Rav Dimi's name that two witnesses must read the get. An objection is raised from a mishnah where the husband later claims it was a fake, but the Gemara answers that the mishnah refers to a case where the get was read and then hidden, so we do not suspect substitution.

items.text: Get found among barrels
items.text_en: Get found among barrels
items.desc_en: A man threw a get to his wife among barrels, and a mezuzah was found. Rav Nachman says a mezuzah is not commonly found among barrels, so the get is valid. But if two or three mezuzot are found, we assume the get was also there, and we suspect mice took it.

items.text: Get given with a Torah scroll
items.text_en: Get given with a Torah scroll
items.desc_en: A man entered a synagogue, took a Torah scroll, gave it to his wife, and said 'This is your get.' Rav Yosef says there is no concern about invisible ink because there is no invisible ink on top of invisible ink.

items.text: Gemara's objection: concern about writing for her sake
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: concern about writing for her sake
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if the concern is that the get was written without intent for the woman (כריתות), we require 'and he wrote for her' (לשמה), which is lacking. It then considers the possibility that the husband gave the scribe a coin in advance, but notes that the names of the couple and their city were not changed, so the get is still invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if the concern is that the get was written without intent for the woman (כריתות), we require 'and he wrote for her' (לשמה), which is lacking.
The Gemara considers the possibility that the husband gave the scribe a coin in advance, but notes that the names of the couple and their city were not changed, so the get is still invalid.

items.text: Rav Yosef's teaching: water on water
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's teaching: water on water
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Yosef's statement teaches that water (ink) cannot be written on top of water (ink), meaning that writing must be distinct and not overlapping.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel teaching Rav Yosef intended with his statement about a Torah scroll not being usable as a גט (bill of divorce).
The Gemara answers that Rav Yosef teaches that gall water (ink) cannot be written on top of gall water, meaning that writing must be distinct and not overlapping.

items.text: Rav Chisda: correcting a get written not for her sake
items.text_en: Rav Chisda: correcting a get written not for her sake
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that if a get was written not for the woman's sake and then the scribe traced over it for her sake, this is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis. The baraita discusses a case where one intended to write 'Yehuda' but omitted the dalet, and Rabbi Yehuda permits tracing over it to sanctify the name, while the Rabbis disqualify it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that a גט (bill of divorce) written not for her sake and then traced over for her sake falls into the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.
The baraita cites a case where one intended to write 'Yehuda' but omitted the dalet, and Rabbi Yehuda permits tracing over it to sanctify the name, while the Rabbis disqualify it.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's distinction
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov challenges Rav Chisda's comparison, arguing that the Rabbis' ruling there (about the name) is based on the requirement of 'this is my God and I will glorify Him' (זה אלי ואנוהו), which is not applicable to a get, so the cases are different.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov challenges Rav Chisda's comparison, arguing that the Rabbis' ruling there (about the name) is based on the requirement of 'זה אלי ואנוהו' (this is my God and I will glorify Him), which is not applicable to a גט (bill of divorce), so the cases are different.

items.text: Rav Chisda's attempt to invalidate all gittin and Rava's response
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's attempt to invalidate all gittin and Rava's response
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda claims he could invalidate all gittin, but Rava questions this: if because 'and he wrote' implies the husband writes, but the woman writes it, perhaps the Rabbis transferred ownership? And if because 'and he gives' is lacking, perhaps giving the get itself suffices, as they sent from there that writing on forbidden items is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda claims he could invalidate all bills of divorce in the world.
Rava asks Rav Chisda for the reason behind his claim.
Rava objects: if the concern is that the woman writes the גט (bill of divorce) rather than the husband, perhaps the Rabbis transferred ownership to him.
Rava objects further: if the concern is that the husband gives nothing of value, perhaps the giving of the גט (bill of divorce) itself suffices.
The Gemara supports Rava's second objection by citing that the Sages sent from Eretz Yisrael that a גט (bill of divorce) written on forbidden items is valid, showing monetary value is not required.

items.text: Support from the Mishnah and Rabbi's ruling
items.text_en: Support from the Mishnah and Rabbi's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi supports the ruling that writing on forbidden items is valid, citing the Mishnah about writing on an olive leaf. A baraita records that Rabbi ruled it valid, and when Levi taught it in Rabbi's name it was not praised, but in the name of the many it was, indicating the halakha follows Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi supports the ruling by citing the Mishnah that a גט (bill of divorce) can be written on an olive leaf, but the Gemara objects that an olive leaf is different because it can combine with others to have value.

A baraita records that Rabbi ruled a גט (bill of divorce) written on forbidden items is valid; when Levi taught it in Rabbi's name it was not praised, but in the name of the many it was, indicating the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi.

items.text: Engraving vs. writing: the dispute about חק תוכות and חק יריכות
items.text_en: Engraving vs. writing: the dispute about חק תוכות and חק יריכות
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether engraving (חקיקה) is considered writing. A baraita states 'and he wrote' excludes engraving, but a contradiction is raised from a slave freed by writing on a tablet. Ulla resolves it: engraving the inside (תוכות) is not writing, but engraving the sides (יריכות) is. A further contradiction about dinarim of gold is resolved by distinguishing between protruding (בולט) and sunken (שוקע) writing.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the verse 'and he writes' excludes engraving, but a contradiction is raised from a slave freed by writing on a tablet or slate.
Ulla in the name of רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) resolves the contradiction: engraving the inside (חק תוכות) is not writing, but engraving the sides (חק יריכות) is writing.

The Gemara objects: is engraving the inside not considered writing? A contradiction is raised from the High Priest's frontplate, where the writing protrudes like gold dinars, and gold dinars are made by engraving the inside.

The Gemara resolves: the frontplate was like gold dinars in that the writing protrudes, but unlike them in that there the letters were formed by engraving the inside, while here they were formed by engraving the sides (from the back).

items.text: Ravina's question about the nature of a mark (רושמא)
items.text_en: Ravina's question about the nature of a mark (רושמא)
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether a mark (רושמא) is made by cutting a groove or by gathering material. Rav Ashi answers it is by cutting a groove. An objection is raised from the case of dinarim of gold, which suggests it is not a groove, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether a mark (רושמא) is made by cutting a groove or by gathering material.
Rav Ashi answers that it is by cutting a groove.
An objection is raised from the case of dinarim of gold, which suggests it is not a groove.
The Gemara begins to explain the objection but the text is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to the Mishnah's ruling on a slave writing a get
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to the Mishnah's ruling on a slave writing a get
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a slave cannot write a get, given that a woman can write her own get. Rava initially suggests a proof from the case of a guarantor who signs after the witnesses, but Rav Ashi rejects this, arguing that a man (the guarantor) is different because he knows how to transfer ownership. Rav Ashi then brings a proof from the Mishnah itself: a woman writes her own get and a man writes his receipt, because the validity of the get depends on its signatures.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a slave cannot write a get, given that a woman can write her own get, and Rava initially suggests a proof from the case of a guarantor who signs after the witnesses.
Rav Ashi rejects Rava's proof, arguing that a man (the guarantor) is different because he knows how to transfer ownership.
Rav Ashi brings a proof from the Mishnah itself: a woman writes her own get and a man writes his receipt, because the validity of the get depends on its signatures.

items.text: Rava's case of a get placed in a slave's hand with a gift document
items.text_en: Rava's case of a get placed in a slave's hand with a gift document
items.desc_en: Rava presents a case where a husband writes a get for his wife and places it in his slave's hand, also writing a gift document transferring the slave to her. The woman acquires the slave and is divorced through him. The Gemara objects: the slave is a moving courtyard, which does not acquire. Even if the slave is standing still, Rava's principle states that if a moving object does not acquire, a stationary one also does not acquire. The Gemara concludes that the case involves a bound slave.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents a case where a husband writes a get and places it in his slave's hand, also writing a gift document transferring the slave to the wife, so she acquires the slave and is divorced through him.

The Gemara objects that the slave is a moving courtyard, which does not acquire, and even if standing still, Rava's principle holds that if a moving object does not acquire, a stationary one also does not acquire.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves a bound slave, so the objection is deflected.

items.text: Rava's second case: get placed in the courtyard with a gift document
items.text_en: Rava's second case: get placed in the courtyard with a gift document
items.desc_en: Rava presents another case: the husband writes a get and places it in his courtyard, also writing a gift document transferring the courtyard to her. She acquires the courtyard and is divorced through it. The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: if only the slave case were taught, one might think only a slave works, but a courtyard might be subject to a decree due to her courtyard that comes later; if only the courtyard case were taught, one might think only a courtyard works, but a slave might be subject to a decree due to an unbound slave. The combined teaching shows both are valid.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents a second case: the husband writes a get and places it in his courtyard, also writing a gift document transferring the courtyard to her, so she acquires the courtyard and is divorced through it.
The Gemara explains that both cases (slave and courtyard) are necessary to teach: each alone might have been subject to a decree, so the combined teaching shows both are valid.

items.text: Abaye's challenge and resolution regarding the courtyard's acquisition
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge and resolution regarding the courtyard's acquisition
items.desc_en: Abaye questions how a courtyard can acquire a get for a woman against her will, since the courtyard is derived from her hand, which acquires both willingly and unwillingly, but a gift (the courtyard itself) requires her consent. Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects, noting that agency for receiving a get also works only with consent, yet it is valid. Abaye responds that agency is derived from a different verse. Alternatively, agency for receiving can be found against her will, as a father receives a get for his minor daughter against her will.

sub.desc_en: Abaye questions how a courtyard can acquire a get against the woman's will, since the courtyard is derived from her hand (which works both willingly and unwillingly), but a gift requires her consent.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects that agency for receiving a get also requires consent, yet it is valid against her will.
Abaye responds that agency is derived from a different verse (וְשִׁלַּח וְשִׁלְּחָהּ), not from the hand, so the objection does not apply.
Alternatively, agency for receiving a get can be found against her will, as a father receives a get for his minor daughter against her will.

items.text: Beginning of discussion on the Mishnah's case of writing on an olive leaf
items.text_en: Beginning of discussion on the Mishnah's case of writing on an olive leaf
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins analyzing the Mishnah's case of writing a get on an olive leaf, questioning the status of a slave's hand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins analyzing the Mishnah's case of writing a get on an olive leaf, questioning the status of a slave's hand.

items.text: Gemara's objection to writing on a cow's horn
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to writing on a cow's horn
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one writes a get on a cow's horn, it cannot be given without cutting it off, which violates the requirement that the writing and giving be the only missing steps. The verse 'and he shall write and give to her' excludes a case where cutting is also needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one writes a get on a cow's horn, it cannot be given without cutting it off, which violates the requirement that the writing and giving be the only missing steps.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'and he shall write and give to her' excludes a case where cutting is also needed.

items.text: Rabbi Yose HaGlili's derivation from 'sefer'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose HaGlili's derivation from 'sefer'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yose HaGlili's reasoning: the word 'sefer' teaches that only items without a life force and not edible are valid, based on a baraisa that expands 'sefer' to include all such items.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
A baraita is cited explaining Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's position: the word 'ספר' (document) excludes anything with a life force or food, but the word 'וכתב' (and he shall write) includes all materials.

items.text: Rabbis' interpretation of 'sefer'
items.text_en: Rabbis' interpretation of 'sefer'
items.desc_en: The Rabbis explain that 'sefer' is not for exclusion but for the requirement of 'counting of matters' (a formal document), as opposed to 'besefer' which would have excluded other materials.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis respond that if the verse said 'בספר' (in a document), it would exclude other materials, but since it says 'ספר' (a document), it comes to teach the counting of matters (ספירת דברים).

items.text: Rabbis' use of 'vechatav' for divorce by document only
items.text_en: Rabbis' use of 'vechatav' for divorce by document only
items.desc_en: The Rabbis use 'vechatav' to teach that divorce is only by writing, not by money, countering a possible analogy from betrothal which can be by money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the word 'וכתב' (and he shall write).
The Gemara answers that the Rabbis derive from 'וכתב' that a woman is divorced only through a written document, not through money, countering a possible analogy from betrothal.

items.text: Alternative derivation from 'sefer keritut'
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from 'sefer keritut'
items.desc_en: Another view derives from 'sefer keritut' that only a document cuts off the marriage, not any other thing.

sub.desc_en: Another opinion derives from 'ספר כריתות' (a book of severance) that only a document severs the marriage, not any other object.

items.text: Derivation for conditional divorce from 'koret'
items.text_en: Derivation for conditional divorce from 'koret'
items.desc_en: Another view uses 'koret' to require that the divorce be absolute, not conditional on a permanent prohibition, as taught in a baraisa about conditional clauses.

sub.desc_en: Another opinion derives from 'ספר כריתות' the requirement of a complete severance between husband and wife, as illustrated by a baraita about conditional gittin.

items.text: Dispute over 'karet-keritut' derivation
items.text_en: Dispute over 'karet-keritut' derivation
items.desc_en: One view derives from the double language 'karet-keritut', while another does not derive from it.

sub.desc_en: One view derives the law from the double language 'כרת-כריתות' (cutting off-utter cutting off).
The other view does not derive anything from the double language 'כרת-כריתות'.

items.text: Mishnah: Writing on attached material and other invalid surfaces
items.text_en: Mishnah: Writing on attached material and other invalid surfaces
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a get cannot be written on something attached to the ground; if written attached, then detached, signed, and given, it is valid. Rabbi Yehuda disqualifies unless both writing and signing are on detached material. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira prohibits writing on erased paper or parchment due to forgery, while the Sages permit it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a get cannot be written on something attached to the ground, but if written attached, then detached, signed, and given, it is valid.
Rabbi Yehuda disqualifies the get unless both writing and signing are performed on detached material.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of writing on attached material
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of writing on attached material
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's contradiction, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that the Mishnah refers to writing the 'tofes' (form) while leaving space for the 'toref' (essential part). Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan agree, linking it to Rabbi Elazar's view that witnesses of delivery are essential. Reish Lakish explains that the Mishnah refers to signing, following Rabbi Meir's view that witnesses of signature are essential.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the contradiction in the Mishnah: it first says one may not write on attached material, then says if one wrote on attached material and detached it, it is valid.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that the Mishnah refers to writing the 'tofes' (form) while leaving space for the 'toref' (essential part).

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya agrees with the same explanation.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan also agrees with the same explanation.
The Gemara notes that this explanation aligns with Rabbi Elazar's view that witnesses of delivery (עדי מסירה) are the essential witnesses for the get.
The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's intent: one may not write the 'tofes' (form) lest one write the 'toref' (essential part); but if one wrote the 'toref' and gave it to her, it is valid.
Reish Lakish offers an alternative explanation: the Mishnah refers to signing (חתמו), not writing, and follows Rabbi Meir's view that witnesses of signature (עדי חתימה) are essential.
The Gemara notes that Reish Lakish's explanation aligns with Rabbi Meir's view that witnesses of signature (עדי חתימה) are the essential witnesses for the get.
The Gemara clarifies Reish Lakish's intent: one may not write the 'toref' (essential part) lest one sign it; but if one wrote the 'toref', detached it, signed it, and gave it to her, it is valid.

items.text: Dispute about writing on a perforated flowerpot or leaf
items.text_en: Dispute about writing on a perforated flowerpot or leaf
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses writing on a sherd of a perforated flowerpot, which is valid because it can be taken and given. For a leaf of a perforated flowerpot, Abaye says it is valid, while Rava says it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one wrote a get on a potsherd of a perforated flowerpot, it is valid because he can take it and give it to her.
The Gemara raises the case of writing on a leaf of a perforated flowerpot.
Abaye rules that it is valid.
Rava rules that it is invalid.

items.text: Rava's decree regarding cutting
items.text_en: Rava's decree regarding cutting
items.desc_en: Rava declares that a get written on a detached plant is invalid due to a decree lest one cut the plant.

sub.desc_en: Rava declares that a get written on a detached plant is invalid due to a decree lest one cut the plant.

items.text: Laws of acquisition with a pot and seeds
items.text_en: Laws of acquisition with a pot and seeds
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses cases of selling a pot and seeds, explaining when acquisition is effected by pulling or by taking possession of the seeds, and connects this to the Mishnah's rule about acquiring movable property with immovable property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the case of a pot belonging to one person and seeds to another, explaining that if the pot owner sells to the seed owner, pulling acquires the pot, but if the seed owner sells to the pot owner, the pot owner does not acquire the seeds until taking possession of them.

The Gemara continues with the case where pot and seeds belong to one person and are sold to another, stating that taking possession of the seeds acquires the pot, citing the Mishnah's principle that movable property is acquired with immovable property through money, document, or possession.
The Gemara concludes that if the buyer took possession of only the pot, he does not acquire even the pot until he takes possession of the seeds.

items.text: Dispute about a perforated pot in Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Dispute about a perforated pot in Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava argue whether a perforated pot with its hole in Eretz Yisrael and its foliage outside follows the hole or the foliage for halachic status. They agree when the pot is not perforated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a perforated pot with its hole in Eretz Yisrael and its foliage outside, and presents the dispute between Abaye and Rava.
The Gemara resolves that when the plant took root, all agree; the dispute is only when it did not take root.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah of two gardens
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah of two gardens
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the agreement on a non-perforated pot with a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda dispute about vegetables growing between two gardens, one above the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the claim that there is no dispute when the plant took root, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda argue about vegetables growing between two gardens, one above the other.
The Gemara distinguishes the Mishnah case, explaining that Rabbi Meir's reasoning is based on the upper owner's ability to remove his earth, not on the location of the roots.
The Gemara continues the distinction, citing Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning that the lower owner can fill the airspace with earth, showing the dispute is about control, not root location.

items.text: Further challenge from a tree partly in Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Further challenge from a tree partly in Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another challenge from a baraita about a tree partly in Eretz Yisrael and partly outside, where Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dispute. The Gemara resolves that the dispute is about roots, not foliage, and explains their reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier claim that there is no dispute when the plant took root, citing a baraita about a tree partly in Eretz Yisrael and partly outside, where Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagree.
The Gemara suggests that the baraita deals with a case where some branches are in Eretz Yisrael and some outside, implying the roots are in one place.

The Gemara rejects the interpretation, explaining that the baraita discusses a case where some roots are in Eretz Yisrael and some outside, and a rock divides them, allowing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel to distinguish.
The Gemara asks for Rabbi's reasoning, and answers that he holds the roots become mixed in the tree's body.
The Gemara resolves the dispute: one Sage holds that the air mixes the nutrients, the other holds that each part stands alone.

items.text: Types of parchment for a get
items.text_en: Types of parchment for a get
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's statement about three types of parchment is explained: matza, hipa, and diftera. Their definitions, halachic uses, and sizes are detailed, and the Gemara asks who are the 'Sages' who validate a get on diftera.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira states that a get written on diftera is invalid, and Rabbi Chiya bar Asi in the name of Ulla introduces three types of parchment: matza, hipa, and diftera.

Matza is defined as untanned, unsalted, and unprocessed parchment; its halachic use is for carrying on Shabbat (הוצאה), and its minimum size is given by Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda and quantified by Abaye as a quarter of a quarter of a Pumbedita measure.
Hipa is defined as salted but not tanned or processed parchment; its halachic use is for carrying on Shabbat, and its minimum size is the amount needed to make an amulet.
Diftera is defined as salted and tanned but not processed parchment; its halachic use is for carrying on Shabbat, and its minimum size is the amount needed to write a get on it.
The Gemara asks: who are the 'Sages' who validate a get written on diftera, as mentioned in the Mishnah?
Rabbi Elazar begins to answer the question about the identity of the Sages who validate a get on diftera.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the Mishnah's ruling aligns with Rabbi Elazar, who holds that the validity of a get depends on the witnesses of its delivery, not its writing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the Mishnah's ruling aligns with Rabbi Elazar, who holds that the validity of a get depends on the witnesses of its delivery, not its writing.

items.text: Dispute about the time gap between writing and delivery
items.text_en: Dispute about the time gap between writing and delivery
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar limits the Mishnah's leniency to a get written immediately before delivery, fearing a condition might have been stipulated and later falsified. Rabbi Yochanan permits even a gap of up to ten days, as the witnesses would remember any condition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar limits the Mishnah's leniency to a get written immediately before delivery, fearing a condition might have been stipulated and later falsified.
Rabbi Yochanan permits even a gap of up to ten days, as the witnesses would remember any condition.

items.text: Dispute about applying the leniency to other documents
items.text_en: Dispute about applying the leniency to other documents
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar restricts the leniency to gittin, citing the verse about storing documents in earthenware jars for longevity. Rabbi Yochanan extends it to all documents, explaining the verse as mere good advice.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar restricts the leniency of writing a get (גט) on a surface that can be erased to only gittin (גיטין), not other documents, citing the verse about storing documents in earthenware jars for longevity.
Rabbi Yochanan extends the leniency to all documents, explaining that the verse about storing in earthenware jars is merely good advice (עצה טובה) for longevity, not a halachic (הלכתי) requirement.

items.text: Mishnah: Who is fit to write a get
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who is fit to write a get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone is fit to write a get, including a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor. A woman may write her own get, and a man may write his receipt, since the get's validity depends on its signatories.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone is fit to write a get, including a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, and that a woman may write her own get and a man his receipt, because the get's validity depends on its signatories.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Huna's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Huna's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor can write a get since they lack mental competence. Rav Huna begins to answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor can write a get, since they lack mental competence (דֵּיעָה).
Rav Huna begins to answer the Gemara's question about the fitness of these individuals to write a get.

items.text: Opening condition for a minor writing a get
items.text_en: Opening condition for a minor writing a get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's condition that a minor may write a get only if an adult stands over him is cited, setting the stage for the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the condition that a minor may write a get only if an adult stands over him.

items.text: Rav Nachman's challenge and retraction regarding a gentile
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's challenge and retraction regarding a gentile
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman initially argues that if a gentile writes a get with an Israelite standing over him, it should be valid, but is refuted by a baraitha disqualifying a gentile. He retracts, concluding that a gentile is disqualified only for delivery (hav'ah) but not for writing, and attributes the baraitha to Rabbi Elazar who requires lishmah for writing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman challenges: if a gentile writes a get with an Israelite supervising, would it be valid? He cites a baraitha disqualifying a gentile.
The Gemara explains that a gentile acts for his own intent, not for the sake of the get.
Rav Nachman retracts, arguing that since a gentile is disqualified only for delivery (הֲבָאָה), it implies he is valid for writing.
The Gemara objects by citing the baraitha that disqualifies a gentile from writing a get.
Rav Nachman resolves that the baraitha follows Rabbi Elazar, who requires writing לִשְׁמָהּ (for her sake), and a gentile acts for his own intent.

items.text: Rav Nachman cites Rabbi Meir; Rava's objections and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman cites Rabbi Meir; Rava's objections and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports that Rabbi Meir validates a get even if found in a garbage dump, implying no need for lishmah in writing. Rava objects with three sources requiring lishmah, but Rav Nachman deflects each by interpreting them as referring to signature (chatimah) rather than writing. The section concludes with an alternative answer attributing all those sources to Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports that Rabbi Meir validates a get even if found in a garbage dump, implying no need for לכתחילה (the ideal standard) of writing לִשְׁמָהּ (for her sake).
Rava objects by citing the verse 'וְכָתַב לָהּ' (and he writes for her), which implies the writing must be לִשְׁמָהּ (for her sake), challenging Rabbi Meir's leniency.
Rav Nachman deflects by interpreting the verse as referring to the signature (חֲתִימַת עֵדִים) of witnesses, not the writing of the get itself.
Rava objects with a baraita stating that any get written not for the sake of a specific woman is invalid, implying the writing itself requires לִשְׁמָהּ (for her sake).
Rav Nachman deflects again by reinterpreting the baraita as referring to the signing (חֲתִימָה) of the witnesses, not the writing.
Rava objects with a baraita that compares writing a get to writing a formulaic copy (טוֹפֶס), implying the writing itself must be לִשְׁמָהּ (for her sake).
Rav Nachman deflects a third time by reinterpreting the baraita as referring to the signing (חֲתִימָה) of the witnesses, not the writing.
