The gemara offers an alternative resolution: all those baraitot that require לִשְׁמָהּ (for her sake) are attributed to Rabbi Elazar, who holds that the witnesses of delivery (עֵדֵי מְסִירָה) are the essential witnesses, thus requiring the writing to be לִשְׁמָהּ (for her sake).

items.text: Amoraic dispute on the requirement to leave space for the toref
items.text_en: Amoraic dispute on the requirement to leave space for the toref
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel and Rabbi Chaggai citing Ulla require leaving space for the toref (top part) in a get, attributing this to Rabbi Elazar. Rabbi Zerika citing Rabbi Yochanan says 'einah Torah' (it is not a law), meaning lishmah has no power, and attributes this to Rabbi Meir. The contradiction between Rabbi Yochanan's two statements is resolved by noting different amoraim reporting his view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel states that the get is valid only if space was left for the toref (top part), and attributes this requirement to Rabbi Elazar.
Rabbi Zerika citing Rabbi Yochanan says 'אֵינָהּ תּוֹרָה' (it is not a law), challenging the previous statement.

Rabbi Abba explains that Rabbi Yochanan's statement means that lishmah (writing for the sake of the woman) has no power, and attributes this view to Rabbi Meir, who holds that the witnesses' signatures effect the divorce.
The Gemara objects that Rabbah bar bar Chanah cited Rabbi Yochanan as attributing the requirement to Rabbi Elazar, contradicting Rabbi Abba's attribution to Rabbi Meir.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by noting that the two statements are from different amoraim (Rabbah bar bar Chanah and Rabbi Zerika) reporting Rabbi Yochanan's view, so no contradiction exists.

items.text: Mishnah: Who is fit to deliver a get
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who is fit to deliver a get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those disqualified from bringing a get: a deaf-mute, an imbecile, a minor, a blind person, and a gentile. It then discusses cases where a disqualified person becomes qualified after the fact, and the general rule: if both the beginning and end are with awareness, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing those who are fit to deliver a get, excluding a deaf-mute, an imbecile, a minor, a blind person, and a gentile.
The Mishnah rules that if a disqualified person (minor, deaf-mute, blind, imbecile, gentile) becomes qualified after receiving the get, it is still invalid.
The Mishnah states that if a qualified person becomes disqualified and then requalifies, the get is valid, and gives the general rule: if both the beginning and end are with awareness, it is valid.

items.text: Gemara: Why is a blind person disqualified?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why is a blind person disqualified?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a blind person (someh) is disqualified, given that he can rely on voice recognition (tvi'ut eina d'kala). Rav Yosef answers that the case is outside of Israel where the messenger must say 'befanai nichtav uvefanai nechtam', which a blind person cannot say. Abaye objects with the case of a sighted person who became blind, and Rav Ashi supports the distinction by noting the Mishnah's general rule uses 'da'at' (awareness) not 'kashrut' (fitness).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a blind person (someh) is disqualified from bringing a get, given that he is a person of awareness, unlike the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor.
Rav Sheshet answers that a blind person is disqualified because he cannot see from whom he receives the get and to whom he gives it.
Rav Yosef objects that a blind person is permitted to his wife through voice recognition (tvi'ut eina d'kala), so why can't he rely on the same for the get?
Rav Yosef answers that the case is outside of Israel, where the messenger must say 'בפני נכתב ובפני נחתם' (it was written and signed in my presence), which a blind person cannot say.
Abaye objects that a sighted person who became blind, who could have said the formula before becoming blind, is still disqualified unless he regains sight, as the Mishnah teaches.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's ruling is a structural parallel: just as the sane person who became insane is invalid unless he returns to sanity, so too the sighted person who became blind is invalid unless he regains sight, but the underlying law is the same.

Rav Ashi supports the distinction by noting that the Mishnah's general rule uses 'da'at' (awareness) not 'kashrut' (fitness), implying that the disqualification of a blind person is not due to lack of fitness but due to the inability to say the formula.

items.text: Question about a slave as a messenger to receive a get
items.text_en: Question about a slave as a messenger to receive a get
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new inquiry: whether a slave can serve as a messenger to receive a get from the husband, citing the disqualification of a gentile as a possible analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rabbi Ammi whether a slave can serve as a messenger to receive a get from the husband, citing the disqualification of a gentile as a possible analogy.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a slave as agent
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a slave as agent
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a slave cannot serve as an agent to receive a get for a woman from her husband, because the slave is not subject to the laws of gittin and kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a slave cannot serve as an agent to receive a get for a woman from her husband, because the slave is not subject to the laws of gittin and kiddushin.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's challenge and the response from the school of Rabbi Yannai
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's challenge and the response from the school of Rabbi Yannai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar challenges: if the reason is that the slave lacks legal capacity, then for matters where he does have capacity, he should be fit. He cites the case of a gentile and a Cuthean who can give terumah from their own produce but not from an Israelite's. The school of Rabbi Yannai explains that the verse 'גם אתם' teaches that the agent must be a member of the covenant, like the principal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar challenges: if the reason a slave cannot be an agent is that he lacks legal capacity in that matter, then for matters where he does have capacity, he should be fit.
Rabbi Elazar cites the case of a gentile and a Cuthean, who can give תרומה (priestly portion) from their own produce but not from an Israelite's, to support his challenge.
The Gemara asks: is the reason not the verse 'גם אתם' (you also), teaching that the agent must be an Israelite like the principal?
The school of Rabbi Yannai answers: no, the verse teaches that the agent must be a member of the covenant (בני ברית), like the principal.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's restated ruling with a seeming contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's restated ruling with a seeming contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan repeats his ruling, noting that it seems to contradict a mishnah where a pregnant slave woman acquires freedom for her child. The Gemara sets up the contradiction.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan restates his ruling that a slave cannot be an agent to receive a get for a woman because he is not subject to the laws of gittin and kiddushin.
The Gemara objects that this ruling seems to contradict a mishnah where a pregnant slave woman acquires freedom for her child, implying the child can act as an agent.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction by Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction by Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that a slave can receive a get for a fellow slave from the fellow's master, but not from his own master. The apparent contradiction is resolved by two great sages: one says the mishnah follows Rabbi's view that freeing half a slave acquires him, and the other says Rabbi holds that a fetus is a limb of its mother, so the slave's statement effectively grants her one of her own limbs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the mishnah's statement 'if she was pregnant, she acquires for him' means, given the earlier ruling that a slave cannot receive a get for a woman.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports that Rabbi Yochanan said two things: a slave can receive a גט (bill of divorce) for a fellow slave from the fellow's master, but not from his own master.

The Gemara raises a hypothetical objection: the mishnah explicitly states that if the slave's wife was pregnant, she acquires freedom for the child, contradicting the rule that a slave cannot act as an agent.
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing two great sages, Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak, who explained the mishnah.
One of the sages (Rabbi Zeira) explains that the mishnah follows Rabbi's view that freeing half a slave acquires him, so the slave's statement 'you and your child are free' is effective.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's explanation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's explanation
sub.desc_en: The other sage (Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak) explains that Rabbi holds a fetus is a limb of its mother (עובר ירך אמו), so the slave's statement effectively grants her one of her own limbs, making the child free.

items.text: Mishnah: Women who are not trusted to say 'her husband died' are trusted to bring her get
items.text_en: Mishnah: Women who are not trusted to say 'her husband died' are trusted to bring her get
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists women (mother-in-law, daughter-in-law, co-wife, etc.) who are not believed to testify that a husband died, but are believed to bring a get. The difference is that the writing of the get proves its validity. A woman herself may bring her own get, provided she says 'it was written and signed in my presence.'

sub.desc_en: The mishnah lists women who are not trusted to say 'her husband died' but are trusted to bring a get, because the writing proves its validity, and a woman may bring her own get if she says it was written and signed in her presence.

items.text: Gemara: Distinction between the Land of Israel and abroad regarding trustworthiness
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinction between the Land of Israel and abroad regarding trustworthiness
items.desc_en: A baraisa contradicts the mishnah, saying these women are not trusted to bring a get. Rav Yosef resolves: in the Land of Israel, where we do not rely on her word, she is trusted; abroad, where we rely on her word, she is not. Abaye objects, arguing the opposite: in the Land of Israel, where the husband can contest and we investigate, she is not trusted; abroad, where we do not investigate, she is trusted. A baraisa supports Abaye, with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rabbi Akiva's a fortiori argument that a woman is trusted to bring her own get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraisa that states these women are not trusted to bring a get, unlike the mishnah.
Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the Land of Israel, where we do not rely on her word and she is trusted, and abroad, where we rely on her word and she is not trusted.
Abaye objects, arguing the opposite: in the Land of Israel, where the husband can contest and we investigate, she is not trusted; abroad, where we do not investigate, she is trusted.
A baraisa supports Abaye, with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rabbi Akiva's a fortiori argument that a woman is trusted to bring her own get.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah that a woman must say 'in my presence'
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah that a woman must say 'in my presence'
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a woman who brings her own get must declare 'in my presence it was written and signed', as Rav Ashi proves from the wording of the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's analogy that a woman bringing her own get must declare 'in my presence it was written and signed'.
Rav Ashi proves from the Mishnah's precise wording that the woman must make the declaration.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution: Mishnah mixed between Land and outside
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution: Mishnah mixed between Land and outside
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves a contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah's first and last clauses refer to outside the Land, while the middle clause refers to the Land, as evidenced by the omission of 'and the mouth' in the distinction between get and death.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef proposes that the Mishnah's first and last clauses refer to outside the Land, while the middle clause refers to the Land.

Rav Yosef supports his resolution by noting that the Mishnah only says 'the writing proves' without mentioning 'the mouth', indicating the middle clause is about the Land where the messenger's oral testimony is not needed.

items.text: Problem: woman is divorced upon receiving the get
items.text_en: Problem: woman is divorced upon receiving the get
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a woman can bring her own get, since she is divorced upon receiving it. Rav Huna answers that the husband said 'you shall not be divorced by it except before a certain court', but the Gemara objects that she is divorced when she arrives there. Rav Huna bar Manoach offers a different answer: the husband said to place it on the ground and take it there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a woman can bring her own get, since she is divorced upon receiving it.
Rav Huna answers that the husband said 'you shall not be divorced by it except before a certain court'.
The Gemara objects that even so, she is divorced when she arrives there.
Rav Huna bar Manoach offers a different answer: the husband said to place it on the ground and take it there.

items.text: Objection: 'take your get from the ground' is invalid
items.text_en: Objection: 'take your get from the ground' is invalid
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the husband said 'take your get from the ground', Rava ruled that such a statement is ineffective.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the husband said 'take your get from the ground', Rava ruled that such a statement is ineffective.

items.text: Solution: dual agency for delivery and receipt
items.text_en: Solution: dual agency for delivery and receipt
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the husband appoints her as an agent for delivery until she reaches the court, and then as an agent for receipt, so she receives the get there. The Gemara notes that this avoids the problem of agency returning to the husband, as he appoints her as an agent for receipt at the court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the husband appoints her as an agent for delivery (שליח להולכה) until she reaches the court, and then as an agent for receipt (שליח לקבלה) at the court, so she receives the get there.

The Gemara notes that this avoids the problem of agency returning to the husband (חזרת שליחות אצל הבעל), as he appoints her as an agent for receipt at the court, not as an agent for delivery returning to him.

items.text: Objection from those who deny woman as agent for receipt
items.text_en: Objection from those who deny woman as agent for receipt
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that this works only for those who allow a woman to appoint an agent to receive her get from the husband's agent. For those who forbid it due to the husband's dignity, the Gemara answers that here the husband does not mind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the proposed solution works only for the opinion that a woman can appoint an agent to receive her get from the husband's agent, but asks what can be said for the opinion that she cannot.
The Gemara answers that the reason for the prohibition is the husband's dignity (ביזיון דבעל), and here the husband does not mind because he himself appointed her as an agent.

items.text: Objection from those who say it's due to her future courtyard
items.text_en: Objection from those who say it's due to her future courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara further objects for those who say the prohibition is due to her future courtyard. The answer is that the husband appoints her as an agent for delivery until the court, and then as an agent for delivery again, and she receives the get from him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: this works for the opinion that the prohibition is due to the husband's degradation, but for the opinion that it is due to her future courtyard, what can be said?
The Gemara answers: the husband says to her, 'Be an agent for delivery until you reach there, and when you reach there, I appoint you an agent for delivery again, and you receive your get from him.'

items.text: Alternative: court as agent
items.text_en: Alternative: court as agent
items.desc_en: An alternative answer is that the husband appoints her as an agent for delivery until the court, where she declares 'in my presence it was written and signed', and the court appoints an agent to give it to her.

sub.desc_en: An alternative answer proposes that the husband appoints her as an agent for delivery until the court, where she declares 'in my presence it was written and signed', and the court appoints an agent to give it to her.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of invalid gittin
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of invalid gittin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two additional cases beyond the first: if a man has two wives with the same name and writes a get to divorce the older one, he cannot use it for the younger; if he tells a scribe to write for whichever he chooses, the get is invalid for any divorce.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two additional cases of invalid gittin: a man with two wives of the same name cannot use a get written for the older to divorce the younger, and if he tells a scribe to write for whichever he chooses, the get is invalid for any divorce.

items.text: Gemara's question on the first case and answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the first case and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the first case of the Mishnah is referring to, since it seems to be about a get written for one woman but used for another. Rav Pappa answers that we are dealing with scribes who are learning, and Rav Ashi supports this from the language 'scribes dictate' rather than 'scribes read'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the first case of the Mishnah refers to, since it seems to describe a get written for one woman but used for another.
Rav Pappa answers that the case involves scribes who are learning to write gittin.
Rav Ashi supports this interpretation by noting that the Mishnah uses the language 'scribes dictate' rather than 'scribes read,' implying they are learning.

items.text: Derivation of the laws from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of the laws from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the meaning of 'more than this' and derives the three cases from the verse: the first case is excluded by 'and he gives', the second by 'and he writes', and the third by 'for her' (for her sake). The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael explains that each case is invalid because it lacks a specific requirement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'more than this'.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael explains that the Mishnah's cases are not merely invalid because they were written without any intent of divorce, but even when written with intent for divorce, they are still invalid.

The Gemara explains the derivation: the first case (writing for another woman) would be excluded by the verse 'and he gives', but since he wrote for divorce, it might be valid, so the Torah added 'and he writes' to exclude it.

The Gemara continues: the second case (writing for two wives with same name) would be excluded by 'and he writes', but since he himself wrote it, it might be valid, so the Torah added 'for her' (for her sake) to exclude it.

items.text: Purpose of the last clause: no retroactive selection
items.text_en: Purpose of the last clause: no retroactive selection
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the last clause of the Mishnah (the case of two wives with the same name) teaches that there is no retroactive selection (ברירה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the last clause of the Mishnah is needed and answers that it teaches there is no retroactive selection (ברירה).

items.text: Rava's inference and Abaye's objection, resolved with Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Rava's inference and Abaye's objection, resolved with Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: Rava infers from the Mishnah that two people named Yosef ben Shimon living in the same city can issue a debt document against others. Abaye objects from the first case of the Mishnah, but the Gemara resolves that both cases follow Rabbi Elazar's view of delivery witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's ruling that if one wrote a get for the older wife, he may not divorce the younger with it, implying that he may divorce the older with it.
Rava infers from this that two men named Yosef ben Shimon living in the same city can issue a debt document against others.

Abaye objects from the first case of the Mishnah: if the rule applied there, the first husband could divorce with the get, but the Gemara elsewhere says that no other person can issue a debt document against them.
The Gemara resolves that the first case follows the view of Rabbi Elazar, who holds that delivery witnesses validate the get, not the writing witnesses.
The Gemara applies the same resolution to Rava's case: the Mishnah's ruling about two wives with the same name also follows Rabbi Elazar's view of delivery witnesses.

items.text: Debate on whether invalid get disqualifies from priesthood
items.text_en: Debate on whether invalid get disqualifies from priesthood
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether an invalid get disqualifies the woman from marrying a priest. Shmuel holds that any get called 'invalid' disqualifies, consistent with his general principle. In the West, they say in the name of Rabbi Elazar that left-handed and nighttime gittin are invalid and disqualify.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that all invalid gittin disqualify a woman from marrying a priest, except for the first case (a get written for a different woman).
Shmuel argues that even the first case disqualifies the woman from priesthood.
The gemara notes that Shmuel follows his general principle: wherever the sages say 'a get is invalid', it is invalid and disqualifies; similarly for 'invalid חליצה (halitza)'.

sub.text: Western tradition in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Western tradition in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: In the West, they say in the name of Rabbi Elazar that gittin written with the left hand or at night are invalid and disqualify from priesthood.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a small get and an 'anpilya' (a folded get) are invalid and do not invalidate other women.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a small get and an 'anpilya' (a folded get) are invalid and do not invalidate other women.

items.text: Amoraic dispute about the last get
items.text_en: Amoraic dispute about the last get
items.desc_en: Ze'iri and Rav Asi rule that only the last get is invalid, while Rabbi Yochanan holds that even the last get is valid. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan's position follows his view on ברירה (retroactive designation) in the context of brothers dividing an inheritance, and it justifies why both cases are necessary.

sub.desc_en: Ze'iri states that all invalid gittin do not disqualify other women, except the last one.
Rav Asi agrees with Ze'iri that all invalid gittin do not disqualify, except the last one.
Rabbi Yochanan disagrees, ruling that even the last get does not disqualify other women.

The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling aligns with his general view that there is no retroactive selection (ברירה), as seen in his statement about brothers dividing an inheritance who are considered purchasers and must return property in the Jubilee year.

The Gemara explains why both cases (the get and the inheritance) are necessary to demonstrate Rabbi Yochanan's consistent rejection of retroactive selection (ברירה), as each case has a unique factor that might otherwise distinguish it.

items.text: Rav Hoshaya's inquiry about a conditional get
items.text_en: Rav Hoshaya's inquiry about a conditional get
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks Rav Yehuda about a case where the husband tells the scribe to write a get for whichever wife leaves the door first. Rav Yehuda responds that a similar case was taught in a baraita where the get is invalid, proving that there is no ברירה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks Rav Yehuda about the validity of a get written for whichever wife leaves the door first.
Rav Yehuda answers by citing a baraita that if one tells a scribe to write a get for whichever wife he chooses, it is invalid, proving that retroactive selection (ברירה) does not apply.

items.text: Objection from the Passover offering
items.text_en: Objection from the Passover offering
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya objects from a Mishnah about the Passover offering, where the first son to enter Jerusalem acquires a portion for himself and his brothers, implying that ברירה works. Rav Yehuda dismisses this, citing Rabbi Yochanan's explanation that it is only to encourage alacrity. The Gemara supports this with a baraita about daughters preceding sons.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya objects from a Mishnah about the Passover offering, where the first son to enter Jerusalem acquires a portion for himself and his brothers, implying that ברירה (retroactive selection) works.
Rav Yehuda dismisses the objection, citing Rabbi Yochanan's explanation that the Mishnah's rule is only to encourage alacrity (לזרזן במצות), not a case of genuine ברירה.
The Gemara supports Rav Yehuda's dismissal by noting that the Mishnah's language implies the sons were already registered from the outset, as one cannot register after slaughter.
A baraita is cited, recounting a case where daughters preceded sons, confirming that the rule is about encouraging alacrity, not retroactive selection.

items.text: Abaye's analysis of the inquiry
items.text_en: Abaye's analysis of the inquiry
items.desc_en: Abaye notes that Rav Hoshaya asked about a case dependent on others' will (תולה בדעת אחרים), but Rav Yehuda answered with a case dependent on his own will (תולה בדעת עצמו), and then Rav Hoshaya objected with another case dependent on others' will.

sub.desc_en: Abaye notes the inconsistency: Rav Hoshaya asked about a case dependent on others' will (תולה בדעת אחרים) but was answered with a case dependent on his own will (תולה בדעת עצמו), and then he raised an objection from another case dependent on others' will.

items.text: Rava's response: no distinction
items.text_en: Rava's response: no distinction
items.desc_en: Rava argues that there is no distinction between the two types of cases; one who holds ברירה applies it to both, and one who rejects it rejects it in both.

sub.desc_en: Rava rejects Abaye's observation, arguing that one who accepts retroactive selection (ברירה) applies it uniformly to both cases dependent on one's own will and others' will, and one who rejects it rejects it uniformly.

items.text: Rav Mesharshiya's objection from Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya's objection from Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects to Rava from Rabbi Yehuda, who rejects ברירה when dependent on his own will but accepts it when dependent on others' will, as shown in a baraita about separating terumah from wine bought from Cutheans.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects to Rava by citing Rabbi Yehuda, who rejects ברירה (retroactive designation) when dependent on one's own will but accepts it when dependent on others' will.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: The gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that one who buys wine from Cutheans cannot retroactively designate תרומה (priestly portion) and מעשרות (tithes) based on his own future choice, proving he rejects ברירה when dependent on his own will.

items.text: Opening Mishnah dispute on ברירה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah dispute on ברירה
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir permits drinking from a wine libation immediately (relying on retroactive clarification), while Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosi, and Rabbi Shimon forbid it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a dispute: Rabbi Meir permits drinking from a wine libation immediately (relying on retroactive clarification), while Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosi, and Rabbi Shimon forbid it.

items.text: Evidence that Rabbi Yehuda accepts ברירה when relying on others
items.text_en: Evidence that Rabbi Yehuda accepts ברירה when relying on others
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a conditional get becomes valid only upon the husband's death, showing that he accepts retroactive clarification when the condition depends on another person's will.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that Rabbi Yehuda accepts ברירה (retroactive clarification) when the condition depends on the will of others.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a conditional get (גט) is valid only upon the husband's death, demonstrating his acceptance of ברירה (retroactive clarification) when the condition depends on another person's will.

items.text: Rav Mesharshiya's challenge: Rabbi Shimon's inconsistency
items.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya's challenge: Rabbi Shimon's inconsistency
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya asks Rava: Rabbi Shimon rejects ברירה when relying on his own will, but accepts it when relying on others? This highlights an apparent contradiction in Rabbi Shimon's position.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya challenges Rava by pointing out an apparent inconsistency in Rabbi Shimon's position: he rejects ברירה (retroactive selection) when relying on his own will, but accepts it when relying on the will of others.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Shimon's distinction and supporting baraita
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Shimon's distinction and supporting baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: Rabbi Shimon rejects ברירה when relying on his own will (as previously stated), but accepts it when relying on others, as shown in a baraita where a conditional betrothal depends on the father's consent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the first half of the resolution: Rabbi Shimon rejects ברירה (retroactive selection) when the condition depends on his own will, as previously established.

The Gemara states the second half of the resolution: Rabbi Shimon accepts ברירה when the condition depends on others, citing a baraita where a conditional betrothal is valid only if the father consents.

items.text: Opening discussion on ברירה and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Opening discussion on ברירה and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon agree that ברירה applies whether the condition depends on one's own will or another's. It then cites the dispute about the wine barrel, where the Sages argue that if the barrel bursts, the drinker would have consumed טבלים retroactively, and Rabbi Meir responds 'when it bursts'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's case where if the father does not consent, the betrothal is not valid.
The Gemara clarifies that both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon hold that ברירה (retroactive selection) applies whether the condition depends on one's own will or another's.

The Gemara cites the dispute about the wine barrel: the Sages argue that if the barrel bursts, the drinker would have consumed טבלים (untithed produce) retroactively, and Rabbi Meir responds 'when it bursts' (לִכְשֶׁיִּבָּקַע), implying that the retroactive concern is irrelevant until the event actually occurs.

items.text: Mishnah: Requirements for writing form documents
items.text_en: Mishnah: Requirements for writing form documents
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who writes form documents (טופסי גיטין) must leave blank spaces for the man's name, woman's name, and date. For loan documents, spaces for lender, borrower, amount, and date. For sales documents, spaces for buyer, seller, amount, field, and date, due to the enactment. Rabbi Yehuda invalidates all, while Rabbi Elazar validates all except for divorce documents, based on the verse 'and he shall write for her' – for her sake.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the requirement for writing form documents (טופסי גיטין): one must leave blank spaces for the man's name, woman's name, and date.
The Mishnah continues with the requirements for loan documents: spaces for lender, borrower, amount, and date.
The Mishnah states the requirements for sales documents: spaces for buyer, seller, amount, field, and date, due to the enactment (מפני התקנה).

The Mishnah records the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda invalidates all form documents, while Rabbi Elazar validates all except divorce documents, based on the verse 'וְכָתַב לָהּ' (and he shall write for her) – for her sake.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel adds a requirement, and the necessity of both statements
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel adds a requirement, and the necessity of both statements
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that one must also leave space for the phrase 'you are permitted to any man'. This follows Rabbi Elazar, who holds that delivery witnesses effect the divorce and requires writing for her sake. The Gemara explains why both this statement and the earlier one about not writing a get for a man's wife are necessary, as each could otherwise be attributed to a different Tanna.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that one must also leave space for the phrase 'you are permitted to any man', and this follows Rabbi Elazar who holds that delivery witnesses effect the divorce and requires writing for her sake.
The Gemara states that both this statement and the earlier one are necessary.
The Gemara explains that if only the earlier statement were taught, one might attribute it to Rabbi Elazar, but the later clause about signatures could be attributed to Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara concludes that if only the later statement were taught, one might think the earlier one is not Rabbi Elazar's, so both are necessary.

items.text: Explanation of 'due to the enactment'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'due to the enactment'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan explains that the enactment is for the benefit of scribes (תקנת סופר). This follows Rabbi Elazar, who holds that delivery witnesses effect the divorce; in principle, even a form should not be written, but the Sages permitted it due to the scribes' livelihood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what enactment is referred to by the phrase 'due to the enactment' in the Mishnah.

Rabbi Yonatan explains that the enactment is for the benefit of scribes (תקנת סופרים), and this follows Rabbi Elazar's view that delivery witnesses effect the divorce; in principle even a form should not be written, but the Sages permitted it due to the scribes' livelihood.

items.text: Reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar on forms
items.text_en: Reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar on forms
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda invalidates all forms because he decrees that a form (טופס) is like the essential part (תורף), and other documents are like divorce documents. Rabbi Elazar validates all except divorce documents: he decrees that a form is like the essential part, but does not decree that other documents are like divorce documents.

sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda invalidates all forms because he decrees that a form (טופס) is like the essential part (תורף), and also decrees that other documents are like divorce documents.

The gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar validates all forms except divorce documents: he decrees that a form is like the essential part, but does not decree that other documents are like divorce documents.

items.text: Clarification of the verse for Rabbi Elazar's position
items.text_en: Clarification of the verse for Rabbi Elazar's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions that the verse 'and he shall write for her' is written about the essential part (תורף), not the form. It then corrects: rather, say that it is because of the verse 'and he shall write for her' – for her sake, meaning the entire document must be written for her sake.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'and he shall write for her' is written about the essential part (תורף) of the get, not the form (טופס).
The Gemara corrects itself: rather, say that the verse teaches that the entire document must be written for her sake (לשמה).

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Elazar's statements
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Elazar's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Elazar and resolves it by attributing them to two different Tannaim who follow Rabbi Elazar's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Elazar.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the two statements to two different Tannaim who both follow Rabbi Elazar's view.

items.text: First explanation: Rabbi Shabtai citing Hezekiah
items.text_en: First explanation: Rabbi Shabtai citing Hezekiah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shabtai citing Hezekiah explains that the concern is due to quarreling (קטטה), and this follows Rabbi Meir's view that witnesses of signature effect the divorce. The husband might write the get in advance, and the wife might hear the scribe and think the husband is instructing him, leading to quarreling.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shabtai citing Hezekiah explains that the concern is due to quarreling (קטטה), and this follows Rabbi Meir's view that witnesses of signature effect the divorce.
The Gemara elaborates that the husband could even write the get in advance, but the wife might hear the scribe and think the husband is instructing him, leading to quarreling.

items.text: Second explanation: Rav Chisda citing Avimi
items.text_en: Second explanation: Rav Chisda citing Avimi
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda citing Avimi explains that the concern is due to the enactment for agunot (תקנת עגונות). This explanation is attributed to either Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Elazar. For Rabbi Meir, the husband might quarrel with his wife and throw the get at her, causing her to be an agunah. For Rabbi Elazar, who holds that witnesses of delivery effect the divorce, the husband might need to travel overseas and not find a scribe, leaving her as an agunah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda citing Avimi introduces a second explanation for the mishna's ordinance: it is due to the enactment for deserted wives (תקנת עגונות), and notes that this explanation is attributed to either Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Elazar.

sub.text: Some say in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Some say in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Some explain the mishna according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that signatory witnesses effect the divorce; the concern is that a husband in a quarrel might throw a pre-written get at his wife, leaving her as an agunah.

sub.text: Some say in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Some say in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Some explain the mishna according to Rabbi Elazar, who holds that witnesses of transmission effect the divorce; the concern is that a husband traveling overseas might not find a scribe and would abandon his wife, leaving her as an agunah.

items.text: Discussion of the location of the date
items.text_en: Discussion of the location of the date
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's ruling that the date in a get must be written from the time of the marriage, not from the time of the betrothal. It questions why the date is not written from the betrothal, and explains that according to the reason of preventing the daughter of his sister (בת אחותו) or the reason of preventing the husband from enjoying the produce (פירות), there is a concern for both marriage and betrothal. However, for the reason of produce, a betrothed woman has no produce, so the date from betrothal would be unnecessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's rule about leaving a place for the date applies equally to divorce from marriage and from betrothal.
The Gemara explains that for divorce from marriage, the date is needed according to both reasons (בת אחותו and פירות).
The Gemara questions why the date is needed for betrothal according to the reason of פירות (produce), since a betrothed woman has no produce.

items.text: Rav Amram's tradition from Ulla
items.text_en: Rav Amram's tradition from Ulla
items.desc_en: Rav Amram reports a tradition from Ulla that the reason is due to the enactment for the child (תקנת ולד), but he did not know what it meant. After hearing a baraita about a man who says 'write a get for my betrothed, when I marry her I will divorce her,' and Ulla's explanation that it is a decree lest people say the get precedes the child, Rav Amram applies this reasoning here as well.

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram reports a tradition from Ulla that the reason is due to the enactment for the child (תקנת ולד), but he did not know what it meant.
Rav Amram recalls a baraita about a man who says 'write a get for my betrothed, when I marry her I will divorce her,' which is not a valid get.
Ulla explains that the reason is a decree lest people say the get precedes the child.
Rav Amram applies the same reasoning here: it is a decree lest people say the get precedes the child.

items.text: Halakhah like Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Halakhah like Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports a chain of tradition from Rav that the halakhah follows Rabbi Elazar, and Rav praised Rabbi Elazar as 'the best of the sages' (טוביאנא דחכימי).

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira citing a chain of tradition from Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira citing a chain of tradition from Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira transmits a chain of tradition that the halakhah follows Rabbi Elazar, and Rav praised Rabbi Elazar as 'the best of the sages' (טוביאנא דחכימי).

items.text: Application to other documents
items.text_en: Application to other documents
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the leniency of writing a get in advance applies to other documents, citing Rav Pappi in the name of Rava that a court document signed before witnesses is invalid because it appears false. However, the Gemara rejects this based on Rav Nachman's statement that Rabbi Meir allows even a get found in the garbage if signed and given, and the Sages only disagree regarding gittin because they require writing for her sake, but for other documents they agree. Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan adds that a loan document cannot be reused after repayment because the lien is void, not because of falseness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the leniency of writing a get in advance applies also to other documents.

sub.text: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappi citing Rava objects that a court document (אשרתא דדייני) written before witnesses sign is invalid because it appears false (שיקרא), implying the same concern applies here.

The Gemara rejects the objection by citing Rav Nachman that Rabbi Meir permits even a get found in the garbage if signed and given, and the Sages only disagree regarding gittin because they require writing for her sake (לשמה), but for other documents they agree.

Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan adds that a loan document cannot be reused after repayment because the lien is void (נמחל שעבודו), not because of falseness (שיקרא), supporting that the concern for falseness does not apply to other documents.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if a messenger loses a get and finds it immediately, it is valid; otherwise it is invalid. If found in a container and he recognizes it, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the rules for a messenger who loses a get: if found immediately it is valid, otherwise invalid; if found in a container and recognized, it is valid.

items.text: Gemara's Contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's Contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita: found divorce documents should not be returned, even if the messenger says 'give it', they may be returned even after a long time, contradicting the mishnah's time limit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita: found divorce documents should not be returned, yet if the messenger says 'give it', they may be returned even after a long time, contradicting the mishnah's time limit.

items.text: Rabba's Resolution
items.text_en: Rabba's Resolution
items.desc_en: Rabba resolves the contradiction: the mishnah deals with a place where caravans are common (so the get might have been dropped by someone else), while the baraita deals with a place where caravans are not common.

sub.desc_en: Rabba resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a place where caravans are common (mishnah case) and where they are not (baraita case).

items.text: Refining Rabba's Rule
items.text_en: Refining Rabba's Rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara adds that even where caravans are common, the get is only invalid if there are two people named Yosef ben Shimon in the city. This is proven from a story in Rav Huna's court, where a get from Shviri was found and Rav Huna suspected two Shviris, but Rav Chisda told Rabba to investigate, and Rabba found a baraita that court documents are always returned, implying the concern only applies when duplicate names are established.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that even where caravans are common, the get is only invalid if there are two people named Yosef ben Shimon in the city.

sub.text: Gemara's proof from Rav Huna's court
sub.text_en: Gemara's proof from Rav Huna's court
sub.desc_en: The Gemara proves the rule from a story where a get from Shviri was found in Rav Huna's court, Rav Huna suspected two Shviris, Rav Chisda told Rabba to investigate, and Rabba found a baraita that court documents are always returned.
The Gemara concludes that Rav Huna's court, which is like a place where caravans are common, still returns the get, proving the concern only applies when duplicate names are established.

items.text: Rabba's Practical Ruling
items.text_en: Rabba's Practical Ruling
items.desc_en: Rabba applied his ruling in practice regarding a get found in a flax shop in Pumpedita. There are two versions: one where it was in a place where flax is threshed (no caravans), even with duplicate names; another where it was in a place where flax is sold (caravans present), and without duplicate names.

sub.text: Stam's summary of Rabba's practical ruling
sub.text_en: Stam's summary of Rabba's practical ruling
sub.desc_en: Rabba applied his ruling in practice regarding a get found in a flax shop in Pumpedita.
One version says the flax shop was where flax is threshed, so no caravans are present, and the get is valid even with duplicate names.
Another version says the flax shop was where flax is sold, so caravans are present, and the get is valid only without duplicate names.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's Alternative Resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's Alternative Resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises a different contradiction between the mishnah and a baraita about finding a get in the market, and begins to resolve it, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises a contradiction between the mishnah (which says a get found immediately is valid, otherwise invalid) and a baraita (which distinguishes based on the husband's admission).
Rabbi Zeira begins to resolve the contradiction, but the text is cut off before the resolution is completed.

items.text: Dispute about returning a get when the husband admits
items.text_en: Dispute about returning a get when the husband admits
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two versions of a dispute: one where the husband's admission allows return even after a long time, distinguishing between places where caravans are common or not; another version argues that even without established suspicion, the get should not be returned, contradicting Rabbah's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can allow returning a get even after a long time when the husband admits.
The Gemara answers that the distinction depends on whether caravans are common in that place, affecting the likelihood of the get being lost and found.
One version states that the get is not returned only when suspicion has been established, which aligns with Rabbah's view.
Another version argues that even without established suspicion the get should not be returned, contradicting Rabbah's view.

items.text: Why Rabbi Zeira disagrees with Rabbah
items.text_en: Why Rabbi Zeira disagrees with Rabbah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbah does not follow Rabbi Zeira because the Mishnah is strong evidence for his objection. Rabbi Zeira, however, does not follow Rabbah because the Mishnah's phrase 'if he said 'give'' might only mean immediately, not after a long time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbah does not follow Rabbi Zeira because the Mishnah is strong evidence for his objection.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Zeira does not follow Rabbah's position.
Rabbi Zeira argues that the Mishnah's phrase 'if he said give' might only mean immediately, not after a long time.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's criterion: witnesses' testimony
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's criterion: witnesses' testimony
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya suggests that the case is where witnesses say they only ever signed one get for Yosef ben Shimon. The Gemara questions why this is necessary, and explains it teaches that we do not suspect a coincidental match of names and witnesses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya proposes that the case is where witnesses testify that they only ever signed one get for Yosef ben Shimon.
The Gemara questions why this testimony is necessary, since it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling teaches that we do not suspect a coincidental match of names and witnesses.

items.text: Rav Ashi's criterion: a prominent siman
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's criterion: a prominent siman
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says the case is where one says 'there is a hole next to such-and-such letter,' which is a מובהק siman. The Gemara notes that this raises a doubt whether simanim are d'oraita or d'rabbanan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi defines the case as one where the finder says 'there is a hole next to such-and-such letter,' which is a מובהק (prominent) siman.
The Gemara notes that this raises a doubt whether simanim are דאורייתא (biblical) or דרבנן (rabbinic).

items.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's lost get and its return
items.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's lost get and its return
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah lost a get in the study hall and it was returned to him based on either a siman or visual recognition. He was unsure whether it was returned due to simanim (implying they are d'oraita) or due to visual recognition (which is reliable only for a Torah scholar).

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah lost a get in the study hall and noted that he had both a siman (identifying mark) and visual recognition of it.
The finders returned the get to him.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah expressed uncertainty whether the return was due to the siman (implying simanim are d'oraita) or due to visual recognition.
The Gemara concludes that visual recognition is reliable only for a Torah scholar (צורבא מרבנן), not for an ordinary person.

items.text: Definitions of 'not immediately' and simanim for a get
items.text_en: Definitions of 'not immediately' and simanim for a get
items.desc_en: A baraisa lists various opinions on how long constitutes 'not immediately' (e.g., time for a caravan to pass, to write the get). It also states that even if delayed, if there are simanim like a hole next to a letter, one can testify, but not for general physical marks like 'long and short'.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa opens by asking the definition of 'not immediately' and presents Rabbi Natan's opinion that it is the time for a caravan to pass and encamp.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar defines 'not immediately' as the time a person stands and sees that no one passed there.
Yesh Omrim defines 'not immediately' as the time a person did not stay there.
Rabbi defines 'not immediately' as the time to write the get.
Rabbi Yitzchak defines 'not immediately' as the time to read the get.
Acherim defines 'not immediately' as the time to write and read the get.
The baraisa rules that even if delayed, if the get has simanim (e.g., a hole next to a specific letter), one may testify about it.
The baraisa concludes that one does not testify based on physical marks like 'long and short'.

items.text: Finding a get tied to a pouch or ring
items.text_en: Finding a get tied to a pouch or ring
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a get is found tied to a pouch, money bag, or ring, it is considered a siman and may be returned.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a get is found tied to a pouch, money bag, or ring, it is considered a siman and may be returned.

items.text: Opening Mishnah clause
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah clause
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a get is found among one's vessels, even after a long time, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a get found among one's vessels is valid even after a long time.

items.text: Gemara's dispute on the condition for validity
items.text_en: Gemara's dispute on the condition for validity
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel and Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel argue whether the get is valid only if no person stayed there or if no person passed there. The Gemara explains that they actually reverse each other's opinions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the halacha requires that no person stayed there.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel that the halacha requires that no person passed there.
The Gemara asks why each authority states his own version of the halacha without acknowledging the other.
The Gemara answers that they actually reverse each other's opinions, so each states his own version as the halacha.
The Gemara digresses to explain the terms 'חפיסה' (a small leather bag) and 'דלוסקמא' (an old man's cloak) from the Mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: Presumption of life for agent and wife
items.text_en: Mishnah: Presumption of life for agent and wife
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if an elderly or sick agent brings a get, the husband is presumed alive. Similarly, a bat Yisrael married to a kohen may eat terumah if her husband went overseas, and a sin-offering sent from overseas is offered, all based on the presumption that the person is alive.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an agent bringing a גט (bill of divorce) who left the husband elderly or sick gives it based on the presumption that the husband is alive.

The Mishnah rules that a בת ישראל (Israelite woman) married to a כהן (priest) whose husband went overseas may eat תרומה (priestly portion) based on the presumption he is alive, and a חטאת (sin-offering) sent from overseas is offered based on the presumption the sender is alive.

items.text: Rava's limitation and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rava's limitation and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rava limits the Mishnah: only an old man who has not reached 'gevurot' (80 years) and a sick person who is not moribund are presumed alive. Abaye objects from a baraita that even a 100-year-old agent is presumed alive. The Gemara concludes with a forced resolution.

sub.desc_en: Rava limits the Mishnah's presumption: it applies only to an old man who has not reached the age of 'גבורות' (strength, i.e., eighty) and to a sick person who is not moribund, but not to one who has reached eighty or is moribund, since most such people die.
Abaye objects by citing a baraita that even a one-hundred-year-old agent is presumed alive, refuting Rava's limitation.
The Gemara offers a forced resolution: since the baraita deals with an exceptionally old man who has already lived past the norm, it is a special case, so Rava's general rule stands.

items.text: Abaye's contradiction between get and terumah
items.text_en: Abaye's contradiction between get and terumah
items.desc_en: Abaye raises a contradiction: the Mishnah presumes the husband alive for a get, but a Mishnah says that if a man says 'This is your get one hour before my death,' she is immediately forbidden to eat terumah. Rabba answers that terumah is lenient (possible to avoid transgression) while get is stringent (cannot be undone).

sub.desc_en: Abaye raises a contradiction: the Mishnah presumes the husband alive for a get, but a Mishnah says that if a man says 'This is your get one hour before my death,' she is immediately forbidden to eat terumah.
Rabba answers that terumah is lenient (possible to avoid transgression) while get is stringent (cannot be undone).

items.text: Contradiction within terumah and resolution attempts
items.text_en: Contradiction within terumah and resolution attempts
items.desc_en: Abaye then raises a contradiction within terumah itself: the Mishnah presumes the husband alive, but another Mishnah forbids terumah immediately if the get is conditional on death. Rav Adda bar Yitzchak distinguishes because the husband forbade her one hour before his death. Rav Pappa objects that we don't know who dies first. The Gemara leaves this unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Abaye raises a contradiction within the laws of תרומה (priestly portion): one Mishnah permits a woman to eat תרומה while her husband is away, but another Mishnah forbids her immediately if the husband gave a conditional גט (bill of divorce) effective one hour before his death.
Rav Adda bar Yitzchak distinguishes the case because the husband explicitly forbade her from eating תרומה one hour before his death, creating a specific prohibition.
Rav Pappa objects that we do not know who dies first — the husband or the wife — so the conditional prohibition cannot be applied with certainty.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing the lenient view to Rabbi Meir, who does not worry about death, and the stringent view to Rabbi Yehuda, who does. Rava begins to speak but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing the lenient view to Rabbi Meir, who does not worry about death, and the stringent view to Rabbi Yehuda, who does.
A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi Meir permits immediate action without concern for death, while Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon forbid it, supporting Abaye's attribution.
Rava begins to speak but the text cuts off, indicating a shift to a new argument.

items.text: Distinguishing between 'perhaps died' and 'perhaps will die'
items.text_en: Distinguishing between 'perhaps died' and 'perhaps will die'
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially asserts that we do not worry about a messenger having died, but we do worry about him dying in the future. Rav Adda bar Masna challenges this from the case of a wine vat (נוד), where the concern is about future death and yet the Sages disagree. Rav Yehuda of Diskarta answers that a vat is different because it can be entrusted to a guard. Rav Mesharshiya objects that a guarantor is still needed, so Rava concludes that the distinction between 'perhaps died' and 'perhaps will die' is a dispute among Tanna'im.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that we do not worry about a messenger having died, but we do worry about him dying in the future.
Rav Adda bar Masna challenges Rava from the case of a wine vat (נוד), where the concern is about future death and yet the Sages disagree.
Rav Yehuda of Diskarta answers that a wine vat is different because it can be entrusted to a guard.
Rav Mesharshiya objects that even with a guard, a guarantor is still needed.
Rava concludes that the distinction between 'perhaps died' and 'perhaps will die' is a dispute among Tanna'im.

items.text: The case of sending a sin-offering from overseas
items.text_en: The case of sending a sin-offering from overseas
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses sending a sin-offering from overseas, and the Gemara asks how this is possible since the owner must perform semikhah (laying of hands). Rav Yosef answers that it refers to a women's offering, and Rav Pappa says it refers to a bird sin-offering. The Gemara then explains why both cases (get and terumah) needed to be stated, and why the case of a bird sin-offering is also necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a sin-offering can be sent from overseas, since the owner must perform סמיכה (laying of hands).
Rav Yosef answers that the mishna refers to a women's offering, which does not require סמיכה.
Rav Pappa answers that the mishna refers to a bird sin-offering, which does not require סמיכה.
The Gemara explains why both answers are necessary: each case has a unique reason why the leniency might not apply.
The Gemara further explains why the case of a bird sin-offering is also necessary, since one might think it is forbidden to bring unconsecrated animals into the Temple courtyard.

items.text: Mishnah: Three things Rabbi Elazar ben Parta said
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three things Rabbi Elazar ben Parta said
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Elazar ben Parta said three things before the Sages, and they upheld his words: a city besieged by a siege-engine, a ship tossed at sea, and one going out to be judged are presumed alive. But if the city was captured, the ship lost, or the person executed, we apply the stringencies of both the living and the dead.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah lists three cases where Rabbi Elazar ben Parta's ruling was accepted: a besieged city, a storm-tossed ship, and one going to trial — all presumed alive.
The mishnah contrasts cases where the danger has already materialized, imposing stringencies of both life and death.

items.text: Rav Yosef's distinction between Jewish and non-Jewish courts
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's distinction between Jewish and non-Jewish courts
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says that the Mishnah's ruling (that one going out to be judged is presumed alive) applies only to a Jewish court, but in a non-Jewish court, once the verdict is issued, they will certainly kill him. Abaye objects that non-Jewish courts accept bribes, so the verdict is not final. Rav Yosef responds that they accept bribes only before the verdict is sealed, but after the seal, they do not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef distinguishes between a Jewish court, where the ruling is not final, and a gentile court, where once sentenced the prisoner is executed.
Abaye objects that gentile courts also accept bribes, so the verdict may not be final; Rav Yosef responds that bribes are only taken before the verdict is sealed.
Rav Yosef responds that non-Jewish courts accept bribes only before the verdict is sealed (פורסי שנמג), but after the seal, they do not accept bribes, so the verdict is final.

items.text: Challenges and resolution regarding non-Jewish court testimony
items.text_en: Challenges and resolution regarding non-Jewish court testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that if two witnesses say a person's trial was completed in a certain court, he is executed, implying that even a non-Jewish court's verdict is reliable. The Gemara deflects that this refers to a fugitive. Another baraita states that if a Jewish court says 'so-and-so died' or 'was killed,' his wife may remarry, but if non-Jewish court officials say so, she may not. The Gemara questions why non-Jewish testimony is not trusted, given the principle that one who speaks casually is believed. The answer is that this applies only to matters in which they have no interest, but here they have an interest in establishing their falsehood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita that if two witnesses say a person's trial was completed in a certain court, he is executed, implying non-Jewish court verdicts are reliable.
The Gemara deflects that the baraita refers to a fugitive, not a standard case.

sub.text: Gemara's further challenge from another baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's further challenge from another baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita: if a Jewish court says 'so-and-so died' or 'was killed,' his wife may remarry, but if non-Jewish court officials say so, she may not.
The Gemara questions why non-Jewish testimony is not trusted, given the principle that one who speaks casually (מסיח לפי תומו) is believed.
The Gemara suggests that 'died' and 'was killed' in the baraita refer to 'sentenced to death' and 'sentenced to execution,' yet the Jewish court still permits remarriage.

The Gemara resolves that the principle of believing one who speaks casually applies only to matters in which they have no interest, but here non-Jewish officials have an interest in establishing their falsehood.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's statement
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Yosef said the Mishnah's ruling applies only to a non-Jewish court, implying a different distinction.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Yosef's distinction applies specifically to a gentile court.

items.text: Opening statement about Jewish court
items.text_en: Opening statement about Jewish court
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that in a Jewish court, once the verdict of death is issued, they execute him immediately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that in a Jewish court, once the verdict of death is issued, they execute him immediately.

items.text: Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that even in a Jewish court, they might find merit for the accused after the verdict, but the Gemara clarifies that after the verdict is finalized, they no longer seek merit.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects: even in a Jewish court, they might find merit for the condemned, but only before the verdict is finalized, not after.

items.text: Attempted support and rejection
items.text_en: Attempted support and rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support the earlier statement with a baraita about witnesses testifying that a verdict was finalized, but rejects it because the case of a fugitive is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that seems to support Abaye: witnesses can testify that a person's verdict was finalized, and he is executed, but this is distinguished because a fugitive is different.
The Gemara rejects the support, arguing that the case of a fugitive (בורח) is different from the general rule.

items.text: Baraita about testimony from Jewish and gentile courts
items.text_en: Baraita about testimony from Jewish and gentile courts
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: testimony from a Jewish court that a man died or was killed allows his wife to remarry, but from gentile courts it does not. The Gemara questions the meaning of 'died' and 'killed', suggesting they refer to being sentenced to death, and concludes that from a Jewish court the wife may remarry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: testimony from a Jewish court that a man died or was killed allows his wife to remarry, but from gentile courts it does not.
The Gemara questions the meaning of 'died' and 'killed', suggesting they refer to actual death, and asks why gentile testimony would not be credible.
The Gemara concludes that 'died' and 'killed' refer to being sentenced to death, and from a Jewish court the wife may remarry.

items.text: Alternative explanation for gentile courts
items.text_en: Alternative explanation for gentile courts
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: 'died' and 'killed' mean literally dead, but gentiles are not believed because they are involved in the matter and would lie to strengthen their falsehood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that 'died' and 'killed' are literal, but gentiles are not believed because they are involved in the matter and would lie to reinforce their falsehood.

items.text: Mishnah: Messenger who falls ill
items.text_en: Mishnah: Messenger who falls ill
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: One who brings a get in Eretz Yisrael and falls ill may send it with another. But if he said 'Take for me from her such-and-such an object', he may not send it with another, because he does not want his deposit in another's hand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one who brings a get in the Land of Israel and falls ill may send it with another agent; but if he said 'take me a certain object from her,' he may not send it with another, because he does not want his deposit in another's hand.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's condition of illness
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's condition of illness
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana emphasizes that the Mishnah specifically says 'fell ill'. The Gemara explores possible interpretations: whether it is always permitted, or only when he said 'go' vs. 'you go', or according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Three resolutions are offered.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana emphasizes that the Mishnah specifically reads 'fell ill', teaching that the permission to appoint a substitute agent applies only when the original agent actually fell ill, not as a generic description.

The Gemara questions how Rav Kahana’s ruling aligns with the known halachot: if the sender said 'go' (a general agency), the agent may delegate even without illness; if said 'you go' (personal agency), even illness should not permit delegation; and according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, delegation is never permitted, so illness is irrelevant.

The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between 'go' (delegation permitted), 'you go' (delegation forbidden), and the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that delegation is never permitted at all.

Three alternative resolutions: the Mishnah refers to a case where the agent was told 'go' and fell ill; or 'you go' and illness is exceptional; or the Mishnah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and illness is an exceptional case permitting delegation.

items.text: Contradiction and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita where a husband tells two or three to give a get, implying only they may do so, not a messenger. Abaye resolves: there the husband is concerned about his dignity, but here he is not particular.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita where a husband tells two or three to give a get, implying only they may do so, not a messenger.
Abaye resolves the contradiction: there the husband is concerned about his dignity, but here he is not particular.

items.text: Rava's alternative and the difference between them
items.text_en: Rava's alternative and the difference between them
items.desc_en: Rava says the reason is that words cannot be transferred to a messenger. The difference between them is a case of a messenger for a gift, which is disputed by Rav and Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Rava gives an alternative reason: the matter is one of words (מלי), and words cannot be transferred to a messenger.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Abaye's and Rava's explanations.
The Gemara resolves that the difference lies in the case of a messenger for a gift, which is disputed by Rav and Shmuel: Rav says a gift is not like a גט (bill of divorce), while Shmuel says it is.

items.text: Discussion of the second clause: 'Take for me an object'
items.text_en: Discussion of the second clause: 'Take for me an object'
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish says the Mishnah teaches that a borrower cannot lend, etc. Rabbi Yochanan objects that even schoolchildren know this, and explains that sometimes the get itself is invalid, like if he said 'do not divorce her except in the house' and he divorced her in the attic. The Gemara then clarifies a case where all agree the get is valid.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that the Mishnah's second clause teaches that a borrower cannot lend, and a renter cannot sublet.

Rabbi Yochanan objects that even schoolchildren know this rule, and explains that the Mishnah's real novelty is that sometimes the get itself is invalid, analogous to cases where the husband's instructions about location or hand are violated.

The Gemara clarifies that all agree the get is valid when the wife comes out to meet the agent and exchanges the object for the get; the dispute is only when the agent goes inside to retrieve the object.

items.text: Opening dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Opening dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a husband takes a gift from his wife and then gives her a get, or vice versa. Rabbi Yochanan invalidates the get in such a case, while Reish Lakish validates it when done through an agent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a husband takes a gift from his wife and then gives her a get, or vice versa, and states that Rabbi Yochanan invalidates the get in such a case, while Reish Lakish validates it when done through an agent.

items.text: Mishnah: Agent from overseas appoints a second agent in court
items.text_en: Mishnah: Agent from overseas appoints a second agent in court
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an agent bringing a get from overseas who falls ill may appoint another agent in court, and the second agent need not say 'in my presence it was written and signed' but only 'I am an agent of the court'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that an agent bringing a get from overseas who falls ill may appoint a second agent in court, and the second agent only needs to say 'I am an agent of the court'.

items.text: Gemara's question: Can a second agent appoint a third?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Can a second agent appoint a third?
items.desc_en: The rabbis ask Rabbi Avahu whether a second agent can appoint another agent. He answers from the Mishnah that it is implied, but they then ask whether this must be done in court or can be done outside court. He answers from the Mishnah that the second agent says 'I am an agent of the court', implying it must be in court.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis ask Rabbi Avahu whether a second agent (שליח דשליח) can appoint another agent.
Rabbi Avahu answers that the question is unnecessary, because the Mishnah's phrase 'אין השליח האחרון' implies that a second agent can indeed appoint a third.
The rabbis then ask whether the second agent's appointment must be in court (בית דין) or can be done outside court.
Rabbi Avahu answers that this too is unnecessary, because the Mishnah says the second agent says 'שליח בית דין אני' (I am an agent of the court), implying it must be in court.

items.text: Alternate version of the inquiry by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.text_en: Alternate version of the inquiry by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak teaches a different version where the rabbis first ask whether a second agent can appoint an agent at all, and then whether it must be in court. Rabbi Avahu answers both from the Mishnah.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternate version
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternate version
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak presents an alternate version of the inquiry: the rabbis ask Rabbi Avahu whether a second agent may appoint an agent in court or outside court.
Rabbi Avahu challenges the rabbis: should you not first ask whether a second agent can appoint an agent at all?
The rabbis reply that this is not in question, as the Mishnah's phrase 'the last agent' implies that an agent can appoint an agent.
The rabbis clarify that their question is only whether the appointment must be in court or can be outside court.
Rabbi Avahu answers that this too is not in question, citing the Mishnah's statement that the agent says 'I am an agent of the court.'

items.text: Rabba and Rav Ashi on multiple agents in Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Rabba and Rav Ashi on multiple agents in Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: Rabba says an agent in Eretz Yisrael can appoint many agents. Rav Ashi adds that if the first agent dies, all are void. Mar bar Rav Ashi objects, arguing that all agents derive their power from the husband, so if the husband dies they are void, but if the first agent dies they remain valid.

sub.desc_en: Rabba states that an agent in Eretz Yisrael can appoint multiple agents.
Rav Ashi adds that if the first agent dies, all subsequent agents are void.
Mar bar Rav Ashi objects, arguing that all agents derive their power from the husband, so if the husband dies they are void, but if the first agent dies they remain valid.

items.text: Story of the agent who did not know the wife
items.text_en: Story of the agent who did not know the wife
items.desc_en: A man sends a get with an agent who does not know the wife, so he instructs him to give it to Abba bar Minyomi. The agent cannot find him, so the rabbis suggest appointing them as agents. Rav Safra objects that this agent was not appointed for divorce. Rava says Rav Safra refuted three ordained rabbis, but Rav Ashi questions this.

sub.desc_en: The story is introduced: a man sends a גט (bill of divorce) with an agent who does not know the wife; the husband instructs him to give it to אבא בר מיניומי (Abba bar Minyumi), but the agent cannot find him and instead encounters three rabbis who suggest appointing themselves as agents.
Rav Safra objects that the agent was not appointed for divorce (שליח שלא ניתן לגירושין), and the rabbis are embarrassed.
Rava says that Rav Safra refuted three ordained rabbis, but Rav Ashi questions this, arguing that the husband did not explicitly say 'Abba bar Minyumi and not you'.

An alternative version: Rava says Rav Safra struck the three ordained rabbis mistakenly, but Rav Ashi clarifies that the husband's instruction was indeed 'Abba bar Minyumi and not you', so Rav Safra was correct.

items.text: Case of an agent instructed to delay delivery due to illness
items.text_en: Case of an agent instructed to delay delivery due to illness
