items.desc_en: A man tells an agent not to give the get for thirty days, but the agent falls ill within that time. Rava rules that since he is forced, he can appoint another agent after thirty days. The rabbis object that this agent was not appointed for divorce, but Rava says since the husband can divorce after thirty days, it is as if he was appointed. The Gemara raises a concern about possible reconciliation, citing a similar case.

sub.desc_en: A man sends a גט (bill of divorce) with an agent, instructing him not to give it for thirty days; the agent becomes ill within that period.
Rava rules that since the agent is forced (אונס), he can appoint another agent after thirty days, and the agent is considered one granted for divorce.
The Gemara objects: we should worry that the husband was mollified and canceled the גט, citing a mishna about a conditional divorce.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna resolves that the mishna refers to a case where the husband says his wife is believed to say he did not come, so no concern about mollification.

items.text: Conclusion: The case involved an arusah, not a nesuah
items.text_en: Conclusion: The case involved an arusah, not a nesuah
items.desc_en: Rava was embarrassed, but it was later revealed that the woman was an arusah (betrothed), not a nesuah (married). Rava questions whether the same ruling would apply to a nesuah, and states that this is a matter that requires further inquiry.

sub.desc_en: The narrator reports that Rava was embarrassed, but later the matter was revealed that the woman was an arusah (betrothed), not a nesuah (married).
Rava questions whether the same ruling that applied to an arusah would apply to a nesuah, implying a distinction.
Rava states that this matter certainly requires further inquiry, leaving the question unresolved.

items.text: Question about court appointing an agent
items.text_en: Question about court appointing an agent
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a court appoints an agent in the presence of the husband or even in his absence, and resolves that it is valid either way, as confirmed by a message from the academy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a court appoints an agent in the presence of the husband or even in his absence.
The Gemara resolves that the court may appoint an agent either in the husband's presence or in his absence.
A message from the academy confirms that the court may appoint an agent either in the husband's presence or in his absence.

items.text: Cases of conditional gittin with unforeseen circumstances
items.text_en: Cases of conditional gittin with unforeseen circumstances
items.desc_en: Two cases are presented: one where a man set a condition for a get but was prevented by a river crossing, and another where he tried to appease his wife but failed. Rav Yosef comments on the second case, and the Gemara distinguishes between opinions on whether force majeure applies to gittin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the first case: a man set a condition for a get that if he does not return within thirty days it should be a get, but a river crossing prevented him; Shmuel ruled that he is not considered to have arrived.
The Gemara presents the second case: a man set a condition for a get that if he does not appease his wife within thirty days it should be a get, but he failed to appease her.
Rav Yosef questions: Did he give her a tarqav of dinars and she was not appeased? (implying that the condition was impossible to fulfill, so the get is valid).

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports Rav Yosef saying: Does he need to give her a tarqav of dinars? He did appease her and she was not appeased (implying the condition was fulfilled, so the get is not valid).
The Gemara resolves: the first case follows the opinion that there is an אונס (force majeure) in gittin, and the second case follows the opinion that there is no אונס in gittin.

items.text: Mishnah: lending to priests, Levites, and the poor
items.text_en: Mishnah: lending to priests, Levites, and the poor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one who lends money to a priest, Levite, or poor person may separate their tithes on their behalf assuming they are still alive, and if they die, he needs permission from the heirs unless the loan was made in court.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who lends money to a priest, Levite, or poor person may separate tithes on their behalf assuming they are alive, and if they die, he needs permission from heirs unless the loan was made in court.

items.text: Gemara's question and three answers
items.text_en: Gemara's question and three answers
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can separate tithes for someone who has not yet received them. Rav, Shmuel, and Ulla each offer different explanations, and the Gemara explains why each Amora rejects the others' views.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah allows separating tithes for recipients who have not yet received the produce.
Rav answers that the Mishnah deals with priestly and Levitical gifts that are already designated for them.
Shmuel answers that the lender acquires the tithes for the recipients through a third-party acquisition (זיכוי).
Ulla answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosi, who ruled that one who does not yet own the produce is treated as if he does.

The Gemara explains why each Amora rejects the others' views: Rav's view is rejected because the Mishnah does not mention designated gifts, Shmuel's because it does not mention acquisition through others, and Ulla's because the Mishnah is not established as a minority opinion.

items.text: Baraita and its analysis
items.text_en: Baraita and its analysis
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates on the Mishnah, including setting a price at the cheap rate, exemption from usury and shemittah, and the inability to retract. The Gemara explains each clause, with Rav Pappa distinguishing between the homeowner and the priest regarding retraction.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the rule that one who lends to a priest, Levite, or poor person may separate their gifts with the presumption they are alive.
The baraita adds that he may contract at the low market rate, it is exempt from interest, and the Sabbatical Year does not cancel it.
The baraita states that the lender cannot renege, and if the owners despaired, he may not separate on their behalf.
The Gemara questions why the baraita needs to state that he may contract at the low market rate, as it seems obvious.
The Gemara answers that the baraita teaches that even if he did not explicitly contract at the low rate, he is considered as if he did.
The Gemara asks for the reason why this arrangement is exempt from the prohibition of interest.
The Gemara answers that since when the borrower has no produce he gives nothing, it is not a true loan, so there is no interest.
The Gemara explains that the Sabbatical Year does not cancel this loan because the verse 'לֹא יִגּוֹשׂ' (He shall not exact) does not apply to it.
Rav Pappa distinguishes: a homeowner cannot renege on the priest, but a priest can renege on the homeowner, citing the mishna that one who gave money without pulling produce may renege.
The Gemara questions why the baraita needs to state that if the owners despaired, one may not separate, as it seems obvious.
The Gemara answers that it is necessary in a case where the seeds produced dried stalks, lest one think that growth is significant and he does not despair; the baraita teaches that he does despair.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and Rabbi Achai
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and Rabbi Achai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that if the borrower died, one may separate tithes assuming the recipient belongs to the same tribe or is a poor person of Israel, while Rabbi Achai says assuming poor people of the world. The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between them.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling: one who lent to a priest or Levite in court and they died may separate tithes assuming the recipient is from that tribe; for a poor person who died, assuming poor people of Israel.
Rabbi Aḥai offers a different opinion: one may separate tithes assuming the poor of the world, not just Israel.
The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two opinions.

items.text: Distinction between Kutite poor and Israelite poor
items.text_en: Distinction between Kutite poor and Israelite poor
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a practical difference: Kutite poor and Israelite poor are considered distinct categories, so if a Kutite poor person becomes wealthy, one does not separate tithes on his behalf, and the Kutite keeps what he has.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a practical difference between Kutite poor and Israelite poor: if a Kutite poor person becomes wealthy, one does not separate tithes on his behalf, and the Kutite keeps what he has.

items.text: Why enactment for death but not wealth?
items.text_en: Why enactment for death but not wealth?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the rabbis enacted a rule regarding death but not regarding wealth, and answers that death is common whereas wealth is uncommon, citing a popular saying from Rav Pappa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the rabbis enacted a rule for death but not for wealth.
The Gemara answers that death is common whereas wealth is uncommon.
Rav Pappa cites a popular saying: if your friend dies, support him; if he becomes wealthy, do not support him.

items.text: Ruling on 'dead – needs permission' explained
items.text_en: Ruling on 'dead – needs permission' explained
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Rabbi says heirs inherit, but this seems obvious. Rabbi Yochanan clarifies: heirs inherit only land, not cash.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Rabbi says 'heirs who inherited' regarding the case of a dead person needing permission.
The Gemara asks: are there heirs who do not inherit? — the phrase seems redundant.
Rabbi Yochanan explains: the phrase means heirs who inherited land, not those who inherited cash.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yochanan on collateral
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yochanan on collateral
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan rules that if a debtor left only a needle's worth of land, the creditor collects only a needle's worth. Rabbi Yochanan says even if left a needle, the creditor collects a full axe's worth, citing the precedent of Abaye's Katinah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan rules that the creditor collects only the value of the land left by the debtor, whether a needle's worth or an axe's worth.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that even if the debtor left only a needle's worth of land, the creditor collects a full axe's worth, citing the precedent of Abaye's Katinah.

items.text: Maaser declaration: first version by Abaye
items.text_en: Maaser declaration: first version by Abaye
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa about an Israelite telling a Levi he has maaser of his, and explains: if unspecified, no concern for terumat maaser; if a specific kor, concern arises. Abaye explains the Israelite says 'take its value' and the concern is about the Levi possibly having separated terumat maaser elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that if an Israelite tells a Levi 'I have maaser of yours', there is no concern for terumat maaser; but if he specifies a kor, there is concern.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means, since the Levi's claim is unclear.
Abaye explains that the Israelite says 'take its value', and the concern is that the Levi may have already separated terumat maaser from this maaser onto another batch.

items.text: Objection to Abaye: Are we dealing with wicked people?
items.text_en: Objection to Abaye: Are we dealing with wicked people?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why would we suspect the Levi of being wicked enough to take money and then designate the produce as terumat maaser?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Abaye's explanation: are we dealing with wicked people who would take money and then designate the produce as תרומת מעשר (terumat maaser)?

items.text: Second version by Rav Mesharshiya bar Rav Idi
items.text_en: Second version by Rav Mesharshiya bar Rav Idi
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya bar Rav Idi revises: the case is about a son claiming maaser from his father's estate; if unspecified, no concern; if a specific kor, concern that his father may have separated terumat maaser elsewhere.

sub.text: Rav Mesharshiya bar Rav Idi's revision
sub.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya bar Rav Idi's revision
sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya bar Rav Idi revises the baraita: the case involves a son claiming maaser from his father's estate; if unspecified, no concern about terumat maaser; if a specific kor, concern that the father may have separated terumat maaser elsewhere.

items.text: Objection: Would associates be suspected of separating without adjacent produce?
items.text_en: Objection: Would associates be suspected of separating without adjacent produce?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: are we to suspect fellows (chaverim) of separating terumah not from the contiguous produce?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: are we to suspect fellows (chaverim) of separating תרומה (priestly portion) not from the contiguous produce?

items.text: Third version by Rav Ashi: concern if not fixed
items.text_en: Third version by Rav Ashi: concern if not fixed
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi revises: the case is where a son says his father told him 'maaser is yours' or 'maaser for your father is with me' – then concern because it was not fixed, so the owner did not prepare it. If a specific kor was mentioned, no concern because it was fixed and the owner prepared it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi introduces a third version of the baraita's interpretation.
Rav Ashi explains that when the son says 'maaser is yours' or 'maaser for your father is with me' without specifying a fixed amount, there is concern because the owner did not prepare it.
Rav Ashi concludes that when a specific kor is mentioned, there is no concern because the owner fixed and prepared it.

items.text: Abba Elazar ben Gamla: owner may designate terumat maaser
items.text_en: Abba Elazar ben Gamla: owner may designate terumat maaser
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: does the owner have authority to separate terumat maaser? It answers: yes, according to Abba Elazar ben Gamla, who expounds the verse 'and your terumah shall be counted to you' to permit this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the owner has authority to separate תרומת מעשר (the priestly portion from the tithe).

The Gemara answers that this follows Abba Elazar ben Gamla, who expounds the verse 'וְנֶחְשַׁב לָכֶם תְּרוּמַתְכֶם' (and your terumah shall be counted to you) to permit the owner to separate תרומת מעשר.

items.text: Opening baraita on terumot
items.text_en: Opening baraita on terumot
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that the Torah speaks of two terumot: terumah gedolah and terumat ma'aser, drawing analogies between them regarding estimation and the owner's authority.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the Torah speaks of two terumot (terumah gedolah and terumat ma'aser) and draws analogies between them regarding estimation and the owner's authority.

items.text: Mishnah: separating terumot and ma'asrot from designated produce
items.text_en: Mishnah: separating terumot and ma'asrot from designated produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who leaves produce or money for separating terumot and ma'asrot may do so assuming they still exist; if lost, he must be concerned from time to time, according to Rabbi Elazar. Rabbi Yehuda adds that wine is inspected at three specific periods.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who leaves produce or money for separating terumot and ma'asrot may do so assuming they still exist, but if lost, he must be concerned from time to time, according to Rabbi Elazar.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that wine is inspected at three specific periods: after Sukkot, when the grape blossoms appear, and when water enters the unripe grapes.

items.text: Gemara: clarifying 'from time to time'
items.text_en: Gemara: clarifying 'from time to time'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'from time to time' means. Rabbi Yochanan explains it refers to the time of inspection, and Rabbi Elazar ben Antignos cites Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yannai with an alternative view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'from time to time' in the Mishnah means.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'from time to time' refers to the time of inspection.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Antignos citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Antignos citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Antignos cites Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yannai with an alternative view on the meaning of 'from time to time'.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrasing
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrasing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's use of 'mei'ein l'ein' (from time to time) according to the opinion that it refers to the time of placement, arguing it should say 'ad mei'ein l'ein' (until from time to time).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrasing 'מעת לעת' (from time to time) according to the opinion that it refers to the time of placement, arguing it should say 'עד מעת לעת' (until from time to time).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's statement and clarification
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's statement and clarification
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says that his colleagues disagree with him, citing a Mishnah about a mikveh found deficient. The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's 'l'mafrei'a' means 'mei'ein l'ein', teaching that the dispute is about the retroactive effect.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that his colleagues disagree with him, citing a Mishnah about a mikveh found deficient, where all purities performed on its basis retroactively become impure.
The Gemara asks: It is obvious that they disagree — why does Rabbi Elazar need to state this?

The Gemara answers: Lest you think that 'l'mafrei'a' means 'from that time onward' (i.e., only from the moment of measurement), the Mishnah teaches that it means 'mei'ein l'ein' (retroactively from the last valid measurement).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's three periods for selling produce
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's three periods for selling produce
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches Rabbi Yehuda's three periods for selling grain, wine, and oil, and Rava explains that this applies to partners. After these periods, any day is its own time.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's three periods for selling grain, wine, and oil.
The gemara asks what practical halachic purpose these periods serve.
Rava (or alternatively Rav Pappa) answers that the periods apply to partners who share produce.
The gemara asks what the rule is after these periods have passed.
Rava resolves that after the designated periods, any day is considered its own time for selling.

items.text: Interpretation of the east wind
items.text_en: Interpretation of the east wind
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rabbah debate the meaning of 'charishit' in the verse about the east wind. Rav Yehuda says it makes furrows in the sea; Rabbah objects and says it silences all other winds, citing a verse about garments being warm.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the verse about the east wind and asks the meaning of the word 'charishit'.
Rav Yehuda explains that the east wind makes furrows in the sea.
Rabbah objects that if the wind makes furrows, it would contradict the verse about the sun beating down on Jonah's head.
Rabbah explains that the east wind silences all other winds.
Rabbah cites a verse about garments being warm when the earth is still from the south wind to support his interpretation.

sub.text: Rabbi Tachlifa bar Rav Chisda's supporting statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tachlifa bar Rav Chisda's supporting statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tachlifa bar Rav Chisda in the name of Rav Chisda explains that the verse about garments being warm refers to when the south wind is stilled, because the east wind silences all other winds.

items.text: Discussion about winds and the world's sustenance
items.text_en: Discussion about winds and the world's sustenance
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda discuss whether to stand for Geniva, who is a Torah scholar. Geniva then teaches in the name of Rav Chanan bar Rava that four winds blow daily, the north wind accompanies all, and the south wind is harsh but held back by the 'netz' (hawk).

sub.text: Narrative setting (Rav Huna and Rav Chisda sitting)
sub.text_en: Narrative setting (Rav Huna and Rav Chisda sitting)
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda are sitting; Geniva passes by, and one suggests standing for him because he is a Torah scholar.
The other (Rav Chisda) objects: should we stand before a disputant (one who argues with the rabbis)?
Meanwhile, Geniva comes to them and asks what they were discussing.

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda answer
sub.desc_en: They answer that they were discussing winds.

sub.text: Geniva's teaching in the name of Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Geniva's teaching in the name of Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Geniva teaches in the name of Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav that four winds blow daily, the north wind accompanies all, and the south wind is harsh but held back by the 'netz' (hawk), as per the verse.

items.text: The east wind's destructive power and three interpretations
items.text_en: The east wind's destructive power and three interpretations
items.desc_en: Rava and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak encounter Rav Nachman bar Yaakov, who reveals his arm and says the east wind blows. Rava, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan each interpret a verse to describe the east wind's effect: causing miscarriage, rotting pearls, and spoiling semen. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes all three derive from the same verse.

sub.desc_en: The gemara sets the scene: Rava and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak are sitting; Rav Nachman bar Yaakov passes by in a golden chair, and Rava goes to greet him while Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak initially hesitates, thinking he might be from the Exilarch's household.
When Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak realizes it is Rav Nachman bar Yaakov, he goes to him; Rav Nachman bar Yaakov reveals his arm and declares that the east wind (קדים) is blowing.
Rava cites Rav: the east wind causes a woman to miscarry.
Shmuel says the east wind rots even a pearl in the sea.
Rabbi Yochanan says the east wind spoils the semen in a woman's womb.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes that all three derive their interpretations from the same verse (Hosea 13:15), applying each phrase to a different destructive effect of the east wind.

items.text: Rava's praise and further interpretation
items.text_en: Rava's praise and further interpretation
items.desc_en: Rava praises Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak as a sharp scholar from Sura who delves into verses, and begins to interpret the phrase 'ki hu bein achim yafri'.

sub.desc_en: Rava praises Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak as a sharp scholar from Sura who delves into verses.
Rava asks about the meaning of the verse 'כי הוא בין אחים יפריא'.
Rava begins to interpret the verse, starting with 'אפילו' (even).

items.text: Opening mnemonic or introductory phrase
items.text_en: Opening mnemonic or introductory phrase
items.desc_en: A brief mnemonic about a loose joint in a basket, followed by three Amoraim's expansions on the concept of looseness.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with a mnemonic about a loose joint in a basket, indicating looseness.
Rav Yosef expands the concept of looseness to include a peg in a wall.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov further expands the concept to a reed in a basket.

items.text: Mishnah: Revoking a get before delivery
items.text_en: Mishnah: Revoking a get before delivery
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a husband can revoke a get by telling the messenger or his wife that the get is void, but once it reaches her hand, he cannot revoke it. Rabban Gamliel the Elder instituted a decree to prevent revocation before a distant court for the sake of social order.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: a husband can revoke a get (גט) by telling the messenger or his wife that it is void, but once it reaches her hand, he cannot revoke it.
The Mishnah adds that Rabban Gamliel the Elder instituted a decree preventing revocation before a distant court, for the sake of social order (תיקון העולם).

items.text: Gemara: 'He arrived' vs. 'It arrived'
items.text_en: Gemara: 'He arrived' vs. 'It arrived'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'it arrived' (הִגִּיעַ) rather than 'he arrived' (הִגִּיעוֹ), implying that even if the get arrives on its own, it is effective, and we do not say the husband only intended to distress her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah uses 'הִגִּיעַ' (it arrived) rather than 'הִגִּיעוֹ' (he arrived), implying that even if the get arrives on its own, it is effective, and we do not say the husband only intended to distress her.

items.text: Gemara: Why mention each case of revocation?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why mention each case of revocation?
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah separately mentions revoking via a second messenger, by going to the wife himself, or by sending a messenger to her. Each case might have been thought ineffective due to the messenger's authority or the husband's intent, so the Mishnah teaches that all are valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah separately mentions the case of sending a second agent after the first, and answers that it might have been thought the second agent cannot nullify the first's agency, so the Mishnah teaches that he can.

The Gemara asks why the Mishnah separately mentions the husband going to his wife himself, and answers that it might have been thought he only intends to vex her, so the Mishnah teaches that the bill of divorce is void.

The Gemara asks why the Mishnah separately mentions sending an agent to the wife, and answers that it might have been thought the agent would only intend to vex her, so the Mishnah teaches that the bill of divorce is void.

items.text: Gemara: Once the get reaches her hand
items.text_en: Gemara: Once the get reaches her hand
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah states the obvious that after the get reaches her hand he cannot revoke it, and answers that it is necessary to teach that even if he later retracts his revocation, it is not retroactively void.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah states the obvious that once the גט (bill of divorce) reaches her hand, he cannot revoke it.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is necessary to teach that even if he later retracts his revocation, it is not retroactively void.

items.text: Gemara: Language of nullification
items.text_en: Gemara: Language of nullification
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that saying 'it is void' or 'I do not want it' is effective, but 'it is invalid' or 'it is not a get' is not. The Gemara questions whether 'void' implies retroactive nullification, citing a parallel case of gifts, and Abaye resolves the apparent contradiction.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that saying 'it is void' or 'I do not want it' is effective, but 'it is invalid' or 'it is not a get' is not.
The Gemara questions whether 'void' implies retroactive nullification, citing a parallel case of gifts where Rabbah bar Avuha and Rav Sheshet rule that 'void' means from the outset.
Abaye resolves the apparent contradiction by explaining that 'void' in the context of a get means retroactive nullification, consistent with the gift case.

items.text: Opening ambiguity of 'בטל' language
items.text_en: Opening ambiguity of 'בטל' language
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the phrase 'בטל' can be interpreted either as past tense (already void) or future tense (should be void). In the context of a get, the language that takes effect is used; similarly for a gift.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the phrase 'בטל' can be interpreted either as past tense (already void) or future tense (should be void), and in the context of a get or a gift, the effective language is used.

items.text: Abaye's principle: gift agent like get agent
items.text_en: Abaye's principle: gift agent like get agent
items.desc_en: Abaye states a principle: a gift agent is like a get agent; the practical difference is that 'הולך' is not equivalent to 'זכי'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states a principle: a gift agent is like a get agent; the practical difference is that 'הולך' is not equivalent to 'זכי'.

items.text: Ravina's question about 'בטל' left unresolved
items.text_en: Ravina's question about 'בטל' left unresolved
items.desc_en: Ravina found Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak pondering the meaning of 'בטל' in a certain context, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Ravina finds Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak pondering the meaning of 'בטל' in a certain context, and the question remains unresolved.
The gemara declares the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Baraita on effective and ineffective annulment formulas
items.text_en: Baraita on effective and ineffective annulment formulas
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita listing formulas that are effective (e.g., 'לא יועיל', 'לא יתיר') and those that are ineffective (e.g., 'אינו מועיל', 'אינו מתיר').

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita listing effective annulment formulas (e.g., 'לֹא יוֹעִיל', 'יְהֵא חֶרֶס') that render the get validly annulled.
The baraita then lists ineffective formulas (e.g., 'אֵינוֹ מוֹעִיל', 'חֶרֶס הוּא') that have no legal effect.

items.text: Question about 'הרי הוא חרס'
items.text_en: Question about 'הרי הוא חרס'
items.desc_en: A question is raised about the formula 'הרי הוא חרס' – is it effective? Ravina asks Rav Acha bar Rava, comparing it to 'הרי הוא הקדש' and 'הרי הוא הפקר'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the formula 'הרי הוא חרס' (it is a potsherd) – is it effective to annul the get? Ravina asks Rav Acha bar Rava, comparing it to 'הרי הוא הקדש' (it is consecrated) and 'הרי הוא הפקר' (it is ownerless).

items.text: Dispute on reusing a canceled get
items.text_en: Dispute on reusing a canceled get
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet dispute whether a husband can reuse a get after canceling the agency. The halakha follows Rav Nachman that he can. The Gemara questions this based on Rabbi Yochanan's ruling, but distinguishes between canceling speech (agency) and the get itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a husband who canceled the agency of a get can later reuse that same get to divorce his wife.
Rav Nachman rules that the husband may indeed reuse the get.
Rav Sheshet rules that the husband may not reuse the get.
The Gemara states that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rav Nachman's lenient position.
The Gemara objects: the established הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yochanan, who rules that a canceled agency cannot be reinstated, contradicting Rav Nachman's ruling.
The Gemara distinguishes: Rabbi Yochanan's case involves speech canceling speech (the agency), but here the get document itself was never nullified, so it remains valid for reuse.

items.text: Dispute on number of witnesses for cancellation
items.text_en: Dispute on number of witnesses for cancellation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet dispute whether a get must be canceled before two or three people. Rav Sheshet requires three because the Mishnah says 'בית דין'; Rav Nachman argues that two can also be called 'בית דין'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks before how many people one must cancel a get.
Rav Nachman rules that cancellation requires two people.
Rav Sheshet rules that cancellation requires three people.
Rav Sheshet supports his position by noting that the Mishnah uses the term 'בית דין' (court), which implies three judges.
Rav Nachman counters that even two people can be called a 'בית דין' (court).

sub.text: Rav Nachman's proof from a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's proof from a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a baraita where the phrase 'before you' (plural) is used for two people, proving that two can constitute a court.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's formula for a get, which includes the names of the judges and the location.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's formula for a get, which includes the names of the judges and the location.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Nachman's proof
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Nachman's proof
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishes questions the Mishnah's listing of judges, and Rav Nachman brings a proof from a Mishnah that judges sign like witnesses, implying two judges. Rav Sheishes distinguishes between the two cases.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishes questions why the Mishnah lists judges in a detailed manner, as if the Tanna were a peddler counting items.
Rav Nachman brings a proof from a Mishnah that judges sign below, like witnesses, implying that judges are two, just as witnesses are two.
Rav Sheishes rejects the proof, arguing that the two cases are distinct and each stands on its own.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that it makes no difference whether the document is written in the language of judges and signed by witnesses, or written in the language of witnesses and signed by judges.

items.text: Dispute over the reason for the enactment
items.text_en: Dispute over the reason for the enactment
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'for the betterment of the world' means. Rabbi Yochanan says it is to prevent mamzerim, and Reish Lakish says it is to prevent agunot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'for the betterment of the world' means, and Rabbi Yochanan answers it is to prevent mamzerim.
Reish Lakish answers that it is to prevent agunot (anchored women).
Reish Lakish answers that the enactment is to prevent agunot (women chained to their marriages).

items.text: Explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds like Rav Nachman that the get is given before two, so the woman might not hear and remarry, causing mamzerim. Reish Lakish holds like Rav Sheishes that it is before three, so she hears and does not remarry, only preventing agunot.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds like Rav Nachman that the get is given before two, so the woman might not hear and remarry, causing mamzerim.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Reish Lakish's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Reish Lakish's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish holds like Rav Sheishes that the get is given before three, so she hears and does not remarry, only preventing agunot.

items.text: Baraita on annulling a get and the power of the court
items.text_en: Baraita on annulling a get and the power of the court
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if the husband annuls the get, it is annulled according to Rabbi, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says he cannot annul or add conditions because of the power of the court. The Gemara questions how the court can permit a married woman, and answers that betrothal is contingent on rabbinic consent, which the court can revoke.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi holds that if the husband annuls the get, it is annulled, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel argues he cannot annul or add conditions because of the power of the court (מה כח בית דין יפה).
The Gemara questions how the court can permit a married woman (אשת איש) if the get is annulled by Torah law (מדאורייתא), merely because of the principle of 'מה כח בית דין יפה'.
The Gemara answers that betrothal (קידושין) is contingent on rabbinic consent (אדעתא דרבנן), so the court can retroactively annul the betrothal, permitting the woman.

items.text: Ravina's question about betrothal through intercourse
items.text_en: Ravina's question about betrothal through intercourse
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi about a case where betrothal was through intercourse, and the Gemara answers that the rabbis treat such intercourse as licentious.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if the betrothal was through intercourse, what can be said?
Rav Ashi answers that the rabbis render his intercourse an act of licentiousness.

items.text: Baraita on annulling a get before ten people
items.text_en: Baraita on annulling a get before ten people
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a case where a husband tells ten people to write a get; Rabbi says he can annul each one separately, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says he must annul in front of all. The Gemara explains they dispute the principle of partial nullification of testimony.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi holds a husband who told ten people to write a get can annul each one separately, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds he must annul in front of all.
The Gemara explains that the dispute revolves around the principle of whether partial nullification of testimony nullifies the entire testimony (עדות שבטלה מקצתה בטלה כולה).

items.text: The dispute between the first Tanna and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: The dispute between the first Tanna and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the disagreement: the first Tanna holds that partial nullification of testimony does not nullify the whole, so the other witnesses can still write and deliver the get. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that partial nullification nullifies the whole, and since the other witnesses are unaware, they might write and deliver, causing a married woman to be permitted to remarry.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the first Tanna's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the first Tanna's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the first Tanna holds that partial nullification of testimony does not nullify the whole, so the other witnesses may write and deliver the get.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that partial nullification nullifies the whole, and since the other witnesses are unaware, they might write and deliver, causing a married woman to be permitted to remarry.

items.text: Alternative explanation for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning
items.text_en: Alternative explanation for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: everyone agrees that partial nullification does not nullify the whole, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that a matter performed in the presence of ten requires ten to undo it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: all agree that partial nullification does not nullify the whole, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that a matter performed in the presence of ten requires ten to undo it.

items.text: Inquiry regarding the term 'Kulchem'
items.text_en: Inquiry regarding the term 'Kulchem'
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the husband said 'Kulchem' (all of you), does that affect the dispute? One possibility is that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning is based on partial nullification, and with 'Kulchem' the witnesses cannot write and deliver. Alternatively, his reasoning is based on the need for ten to undo the act, so even 'Kulchem' would not help.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the husband said 'Kulchem' (all of you), what is the law? One possibility is that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning is based on partial nullification, and with 'Kulchem' the witnesses cannot write and deliver.
The Gemara presents the alternative possibility: perhaps Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning is that a matter done before ten requires ten to undo it, so even 'Kulchem' would not help.

items.text: Proof from a Mishnah about two agents
items.text_en: Proof from a Mishnah about two agents
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing a Mishnah where a husband tells two people to give a get, and Rabbi allows nullification before each other, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires both together. This parallels the 'Kulchem' case, but Rav Ashi distinguishes between witnesses of writing and witnesses of delivery, concluding the Mishnah deals with delivery witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where a husband tells two agents to give a get, and Rabbi allows nullification before each other while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires both together, arguing that two agents are parallel to 'Kulchem' and they still dispute.
Rav Ashi distinguishes the Mishnah as dealing with witnesses of delivery (עדי הולכה), not witnesses of writing, so it does not prove the 'Kulchem' case.

The Gemara supports Rav Ashi by noting that the Mishnah's continuation, where each agent is addressed separately, only makes sense with delivery witnesses, not writing witnesses who must see the act together.

items.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's tradition and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's tradition and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda heard two rulings from Rabbi Abba, one like Rabbi and one like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but did not know which was which. Rav Yosef resolves this by citing a story where Rabbi initially acted like the Sages but then reversed to follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, indicating that the other ruling was like Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports that he heard two rulings from Rabbi Abba, one like Rabbi and one like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but he does not know which is which.
Rav Yosef resolves the ambiguity by citing a story from Rav Dimi: Rabbi initially acted like the Sages, but then reversed and followed Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
The gemara concludes: since the story shows that Rabbi's final position was like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the other ruling from Rabbi Abba must be the one like Rabbi.

items.text: Support from Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha
items.text_en: Support from Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha also held one ruling like Rabbi and one like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, as shown by a story where he instructed witnesses to hide and write a get. The Gemara deduces that this follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (requiring concealment), and the other ruling must be like Rabbi (allowing dispersal).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha also held one ruling like Rabbi and one like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah recounts that Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha extracted a get against the husband's will and instructed the elders to hide and write it for the wife.
The Gemara argues that if Rabbi Yoshiya followed Rabbi's view, hiding would be pointless, so he must follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view that nullification requires the agent's presence.

The Gemara argues that if Rabbi Yoshiya also followed Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the other dispute, scattering would suffice; thus he must hold one like Rabbi and one like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

items.text: Rava's ruling in the name of Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Rava's ruling in the name of Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rava states that Rav Nachman ruled the halakha follows Rabbi in both cases, and the Gemara questions how Rav Nachman could ignore the principle of 'the power of the court is beneficial', citing a statement from Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports that Rav Nachman ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi in both disputes.
The Gemara questions how Rav Nachman could ignore the principle of 'the power of the court is beneficial'.

sub.text: Gemara citing Rav Nachman citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Gemara citing Rav Nachman citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites that Rav Nachman himself reported a statement from Shmuel that presumably affirms the principle, creating a contradiction.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rav Nachman's gloss
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rav Nachman's gloss
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when orphans come to divide their father's estate, the court appoints an appraiser and selects a good portion for them; when they grow up, they can protest the division. Rav Nachman adds that they cannot protest, otherwise what power does the court have?

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that when orphans divide their father's estate, the court appoints an appraiser and selects a good portion for them, and when they grow up they can protest.
Rav Nachman adds his own gloss that when they grow up they cannot protest, otherwise what power does the court have?

items.text: Distinction between monetary and prohibitory matters
items.text_en: Distinction between monetary and prohibitory matters
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes the Mishnah's case (monetary) from the case of a get (prohibitory), implying that the court's power applies only to monetary matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the Mishnah's case (monetary) from the case of a get (prohibitory), limiting the court's power to monetary matters.

items.text: Story of Gidul bar Re'ilai's get
items.text_en: Story of Gidul bar Re'ilai's get
items.desc_en: Gidul bar Re'ilai sent a get to his wife via a messenger. The messenger found her sitting and spinning, gave her the get, but she asked him to come back tomorrow. The messenger returned to Gidul and reported; Gidul then recited the blessing 'Baruch HaTov VeHaMeitiv'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara tells the story of Gidul bar Re'ilai who sent a get to his wife via a messenger; the messenger found her spinning and gave her the get, but she asked him to return tomorrow.
The messenger returned to Gidul and reported; Gidul then recited the blessing 'Baruch HaTov VeHaMeitiv' (Blessed is the Good and the Beneficent).

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on גילוי דעתא
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on גילוי דעתא
items.desc_en: Abaye says that reciting 'Baruch HaTov VeHaMeitiv' does not nullify the get, while Rava says it does. The Gemara explains they disagree about whether revealing intent (גילוי דעתא) in a get is significant: Abaye holds it is not, Rava holds it is.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that reciting 'ברוך הטוב והמטיב' (Blessed is the Good and the Beneficent) does not nullify the get.
Rava states that reciting 'ברוך הטוב והמטיב' does nullify the get.
The Gemara explains that Abaye and Rava disagree about whether גילוי דעתא (revealing intent) in a get is significant: Abaye holds it is not, Rava holds it is.

items.text: Rava's proof from Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: Rava's proof from Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: Rava cites a case where Rav Sheshet took a get from a man by force and told witnesses to nullify it, requiring another get. Abaye deflects: Rav Sheshet nullified his own get, not others', and his statement was to avoid embarrassment.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a case where Rav Sheshet took a get by force and told witnesses to nullify it, requiring another get, to prove that גילוי דעתא (revealed intent) in a get is significant.
Abaye deflects: Rav Sheshet nullified his own get, not others', and his statement to witnesses was only to avoid embarrassment (דפוניי), not because גילוי דעתא is significant.

items.text: Abaye's proof from Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a case where Rav Yehuda took a get from his son-in-law, nullified it, then later forced him to give another get, telling witnesses to write it. If גילוי דעתא were significant, why did Rav Yehuda run after the witnesses? Rava explains he ran to tell them to give the get quickly to end the man's suffering.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a case where Rav Yehuda nullified a get and then ran after witnesses to give another, arguing that if גילוי דעתא (revealed intent) were significant, Rav Yehuda would not have needed to run.
Rava explains that Rav Yehuda ran not to nullify the first get but to tell the witnesses to write the new get quickly to end the man's suffering.

items.text: Abaye's proof from a conditional get
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from a conditional get
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a case where a man said 'If I don't come within 30 days, let this be a get.' He came but the river blocked him; he said 'See I have come.' Shmuel ruled this is not considered coming. Rava distinguishes: there he wanted to fulfill the condition, not nullify the get.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a case where a man said 'If I don't come within 30 days, let this be a get'; he came but the river blocked him, and Shmuel ruled this is not considered coming, to prove that גילוי דעתא (revealed intent) is not significant in gittin.
Rava rejects Abaye's proof by distinguishing that there the husband wanted to fulfill the condition, not to nullify the get, so the condition was not fulfilled.

items.text: Two cases of conditional gets and the dispute
items.text_en: Two cases of conditional gets and the dispute
items.desc_en: Two cases are presented: one where a man said 'If I don't marry within 30 days, let this be a get' and then said 'I have troubled myself'; another where he said 'by Rosh Chodesh Adar' but later claimed he meant Nisan. The Gemara analyzes: if due to coercion, there is no coercion in gittin; if due to גילוי דעתא, it is the dispute of Abaye and Rava.

sub.desc_en: Presents the first case: a man stipulated that if he does not marry within thirty days the get takes effect, and when the time came he said he had troubled himself.
Asks what concern applies: if due to coercion, there is no coercion in gittin; if due to גילוי דעתא, it is the dispute of Abaye and Rava.
Presents the second case: a man stipulated by Rosh Chodesh Adar but later claimed he meant Nisan.
Asks the same analysis for the second case: if due to coercion, no coercion in gittin; if due to גילוי דעתא, it is the dispute of Abaye and Rava.

items.text: Halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: Halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: the halakha is like Nachman (Rav Nachman) in both instances (the Mishnah and the dispute).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that the halakha follows Rav Nachman in both the Mishnah and the dispute.

items.text: Halakhic ruling in Nehardea
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling in Nehardea
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Nachmani's view regarding the earlier dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that the halakha follows Nachmani's view.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rabban Gamliel's enactment for names
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rabban Gamliel's enactment for names
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that originally a man would change his name and his wife's name in a get, but Rabban Gamliel the Elder enacted that one writes 'Ish Ploni and any name he has' for tikkun ha'olam.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the earlier practice of changing names in a get and Rabban Gamliel's enactment to write 'so-and-so and any name he has' for the sake of tikkun ha'olam.

items.text: Gemara: The question from overseas and Rav Ashi's condition
items.text_en: Gemara: The question from overseas and Rav Ashi's condition
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel reports that the people of the sea province asked Rabban Gamliel about men with two names, leading to his enactment. Rav Ashi adds that this applies only when the person is established with two names, and Rabbi Abba confirms that Rabbi Mari and Rabbi Elazar agree.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that the people of the maritime province asked Rabban Gamliel how to write a get for a man known by two different names in different places.
Rabban Gamliel enacted that they should write 'so-and-so and any name he has' for the sake of tikkun ha'olam.
Rav Ashi qualifies that this enactment applies only when the man is established with two names.
Rabbi Abba tells Rav Ashi that Rabbi Mari and Rabbi Elazar agree with him.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a man has two wives in different regions and two names, he must include both names when divorcing each wife, but if he goes to another place and divorces with one name, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Ashi's qualification, detailing the case of a man with two wives and two names who must include both names when divorcing each wife, but if he goes elsewhere and divorces with one name it is valid.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the baraita's contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the baraita's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's last case, which seems to contradict the requirement to include both names. It resolves that the distinction is whether the person is established with two names or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita itself requires the Galilean name to be included, contradicting the leniency for a man who goes elsewhere.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita distinguishes between a case where the man is established with two names (requires both) and where he is not (only one name suffices).

items.text: Practical ruling from Nehardea
items.text_en: Practical ruling from Nehardea
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a case of a woman called Miriam and also Purtah Sarah, and the Nehardeans rule that one writes 'Miriam and any name she has', not 'Sarah and any name she has'.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans rule that a woman called Miriam and also Purta Sarah should have her get written with 'Miriam and any name she has' but not 'Sarah and any name she has'.

items.text: Mishnah: Widow's oath and other enactments
items.text_en: Mishnah: Widow's oath and other enactments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a widow collects her ketubah from orphans only with an oath, but Rabban Gamliel enacted that she takes a vow instead. It also mentions that witnesses sign the get and Hillel instituted the prozbul, all for tikkun ha'olam.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three enactments for tikkun ha'olam: a widow collects her ketubah only with an oath (or a vow by Rabban Gamliel's enactment), witnesses sign the get, and Hillel instituted the prozbul.

items.text: Gemara's question on the widow's oath
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the widow's oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies a widow, since anyone collecting from orphans requires an oath. It suggests that the widow's case was necessary because one might have thought otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifically mentions a widow, since anyone collecting from orphans requires an oath.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah needed to specify a widow because one might have thought she is exempt from the oath.

items.text: Conclusion of the Mishnah's reason
items.text_en: Conclusion of the Mishnah's reason
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Sages were lenient with the widow because of the concern for her reputation (חינא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Sages were lenient with the widow because of the concern for her reputation (חינא).

items.text: The story of the widow and the dinar
items.text_en: The story of the widow and the dinar
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages refrained from making widows swear, and recounts a story of a widow who swore falsely and was punished, leading the Sages to declare that one who swears truthfully is punished, so one who swears falsely is even more so.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages refrained from making widows swear.

sub.text: Rav Kahana / Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana / Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the reason is a story told by Rav Kahana (or Rav Yehuda citing Rav) about a widow who deposited a gold dinar in a jar of flour, baked it into bread, and gave it to a poor person.

The story continues: the owner demanded the dinar, the widow swore falsely, her son died, and the Sages concluded that if one who swears truthfully is punished, one who swears falsely is even more so.
The Gemara asks why the widow was punished despite swearing truthfully.
The Gemara answers that she was punished because she misappropriated the place where the dinar was kept (using the flour for bread).
The Gemara clarifies that the phrase 'one who swears truthfully' means 'like one who swears truthfully' (i.e., she was treated as if she had sworn falsely due to her indirect benefit).

items.text: Distinction between widow and divorcee
items.text_en: Distinction between widow and divorcee
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the story specifically involves a widow, and Rabbi Zeira cites Shmuel that the exemption applies only to a widow, not a divorcee, because a widow might come to permit herself due to the effort she exerts for the orphans.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the story specifically involves a widow, arguing that the same concern should apply to a divorcee.
Rabbi Zeira cites Shmuel that a widow is different because she might come to permit herself due to the effort she exerts for the orphans.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel: in court vs. outside court
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel: in court vs. outside court
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba that both Rav and Shmuel agree the exemption applies only in court, but outside court she is made to swear. However, this is contradicted by Rav's practice of not collecting a ketubah for a widow. The Gemara resolves that in Sura they taught one version, and in Nehardea another, where Shmuel limits the exemption to court, but Rav extends it even outside court. Rav's practice is consistent with his view, and the Gemara explains that Rav would not collect because he was lenient with vows.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba that both Rav and Shmuel agree the exemption from swearing applies only in court, but outside court she is made to swear.
The Gemara objects: But Rav himself did not collect a ketubah for a widow, contradicting the claim that he would swear her outside court.

The Gemara resolves that in Sura they taught one version where both agree, but in Nehardea they taught that Shmuel limits the exemption to court while Rav extends it even outside court, and Rav's practice is consistent with his view because he was lenient with vows.

items.text: Cases of widows who swore voluntarily
items.text_en: Cases of widows who swore voluntarily
items.desc_en: A widow came before Rav Huna, who cited Rav's practice. She swore voluntarily, and Rav Huna noted that Rav admits in the case of a 'jumping' widow (קופצת). Another widow came before Rabba bar Rav Huna, who also refused to collect, and when she asked for sustenance, he cited Shmuel that a claimant of her ketubah has no sustenance. She cursed him, and he fell ill and did not recover.

sub.desc_en: A widow came before Rav Huna, who told her that Rav does not collect a ketubah for a widow.
The widow swore voluntarily, invoking a curse on herself if she had benefited from her ketubah.
Rav Huna noted that Rav admits in the case of a 'jumping' widow (קופצת) who swears voluntarily.

sub.text: Narrative: another widow before Rabba bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Narrative: another widow before Rabba bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Another widow came before Rabba bar Rav Huna, who similarly refused to collect her ketubah, citing both Rav and his father's practice.
The widow asked Rabba bar Rav Huna for sustenance (מזונות).

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna's citation of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna's citation of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna cited Shmuel that a claimant of her ketubah has no sustenance.
The widow cursed Rabba bar Rav Huna, and despite attempts to overturn the curse, he fell ill and did not recover.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's advice to circumvent the exemption
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's advice to circumvent the exemption
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda advises Rav Yirmeya Bira'ah to have the widow vow in court and then swear outside court, so that the news reaches him and he can act upon it.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda to Rav Yirmeya Bira'ah
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda to Rav Yirmeya Bira'ah
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda advises Rav Yirmeya Bira'ah to have the widow vow in court and then swear outside court, so that the news reaches him and he can act upon it.

items.text: Reiteration of the rule for a divorcee and a counterexample
items.text_en: Reiteration of the rule for a divorcee and a counterexample
items.desc_en: The Gemara restates Rabbi Zeira's ruling that a divorcee is made to swear. It then questions this with a story of a divorcee who vowed and was believed, suggesting that even a divorcee might not be made to swear if she takes a vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara restates Rabbi Zeira's ruling in Shmuel's name: the leniency of not imposing an oath applies only to a widow, but a divorcee is made to swear.
The Gemara objects by citing a story of a divorcee who took a vow (נדר) and was believed without an oath, suggesting that even a divorcee might not be made to swear if she takes a vow.

items.text: Rav Ashi's identification of the case
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's identification of the case
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi clarifies that the earlier case of the Mishnah (about writing a get and stipulating payment) involved a yevamah (a woman subject to levirate marriage), not a regular divorce.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the earlier case by identifying it as a get for a yevamah (woman subject to levirate marriage), not a regular divorce.

items.text: Rav Huna's distinction: unmarried vs. remarried widow
items.text_en: Rav Huna's distinction: unmarried vs. remarried widow
items.desc_en: Rav Huna limits Rabban Gamliel's enactment to a widow who has not remarried; if she remarried, we do not make her vow because her husband can annul it. The Gemara questions this, noting that even if unmarried, she will eventually marry and her husband could annul, but answers that a husband cannot annul vows made before marriage. The Gemara then raises a concern that she might go to a sage to annul the vow, but Rav Huna holds that the sage requires the vow to be specified (which she will not do).

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna limits Rabban Gamliel's enactment to a widow who has not remarried; if she remarried, we do not make her vow.
The Gemara questions why remarriage matters, since even an unmarried widow will eventually marry and her husband could annul the vow.
The Gemara answers that a husband cannot annul vows made before marriage.
The Gemara raises a concern that the widow might go to a sage to annul the vow.
Rav Huna holds that the sage requires the vow to be specified, which the widow will not do.

items.text: Rav Nachman's opinion: even if remarried
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's opinion: even if remarried
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman argues that even a remarried widow can be made to vow, because we make her vow in public (before many people), which has no annulment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asserts that even a remarried widow can be made to vow, because we make her vow in public (before many people), which has no annulment.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the remarried widow
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the remarried widow
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that a remarried widow collects her ketubah if she vowed, implying she must vow now. The Gemara deflects: it means she vowed originally (before remarriage). Another baraita explicitly says she vows and collects, leading to the conclusion that this is a dispute between Tanna'im about whether a vow made in public can be annulled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that a remarried widow collects her ketubah if she vowed, implying she must vow now (after remarriage), contradicting Rav Huna's position.
The Gemara deflects: the baraita means she vowed originally (before remarriage), not now.
The Gemara cites another baraita that explicitly says she vows and collects, implying she vows now.
The Gemara resolves that this is a dispute between Tanna'im: one holds that a vow made in public (ברבים) can be annulled, the other holds it cannot.

items.text: Dispute: must the vow be specified to the sage?
items.text_en: Dispute: must the vow be specified to the sage?
items.desc_en: An inquiry is raised whether one must specify the details of the vow to the sage for annulment. Rav Nachman says no, because if required, the person might cut off his speech and the sage would annul only what he heard. Rav Pappa says yes, because it is a matter of prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry whether one must specify the details of the vow to the sage for annulment.
Rav Nachman rules that one does not need to specify the vow.
Rav Pappa rules that one must specify the vow.
Rav Nachman explains that if specification were required, the person might cut off his speech and the sage would annul only what he heard.
Rav Pappa explains that specification is required because it is a matter of prohibition.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Nachman from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Nachman from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita about one who marries women in transgression requires him to vow and then divorce. If, as Rav Nachman says, specifying the vow is unnecessary, one might go to a sage to annul it. This challenges Rav Nachman's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman by citing a baraita about one who marries women in transgression, requiring him to vow and then divorce, and argues that if specifying the vow is unnecessary, one might go to a sage to annul it.

items.text: Vow made in public vs. vow made with public consent
items.text_en: Vow made in public vs. vow made with public consent
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a court can force a recalcitrant husband to vow if a vow made in public can be annulled. It distinguishes between a vow made in public and one made with public consent, citing Amemar that the latter cannot be annulled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a court can force a recalcitrant husband to vow in public, given the dispute whether a vow made in public (נדר שהודר ברבים) can be annulled; for the opinion that it cannot, the court's action works, but for the opinion that it can, what is the court to do?

The Gemara answers that the court forces the husband to vow על דעת רבים (with public consent), and cites Amemar's ruling that even for those who hold a public vow can be annulled, a vow made על דעת רבים cannot be annulled.

items.text: Exception for a mitzvah matter
items.text_en: Exception for a mitzvah matter
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this rule applies only to discretionary matters, but for a mitzvah, such a vow can be annulled. It cites the case of Rav Acha who vowed against a teacher for neglecting children, and Ravina annulled it because no one else was as precise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the rule of no annulment applies only to discretionary matters, but for a mitzvah matter, annulment is possible.
The Gemara cites the case of Rav Acha who vowed against a children's teacher on the mind of the public, and Ravina annulled the vow because no one else was as precise.

items.text: Witnesses signing the get: Rabba's explanation
items.text_en: Witnesses signing the get: Rabba's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says witnesses sign a get 'for the betterment of the world,' since signing is a Torah requirement. Rabba explains that according to Rabbi Elazar, who holds that only witnesses of delivery are essential, the rabbis instituted signing witnesses for the betterment of the world, in case the delivery witnesses die or go abroad.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's phrase 'for the betterment of the world' seems misplaced, since the requirement for witnesses to sign a get is a Torah law, not a rabbinic enactment.

Rabba explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar, who holds that only witnesses of delivery (עדי מסירה) are essential by Torah law; the rabbis instituted signing witnesses (עדי חתימה) as a safeguard in case the delivery witnesses die or go abroad.

items.text: Rav Yosef's alternative: Witnesses must specify names
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's alternative: Witnesses must specify names
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says the enactment was for witnesses to write their names in the get, even according to Rabbi Meir. A baraita describes the earlier practice where a witness would write 'I, so-and-so, signed as a witness,' which was valid only if his handwriting was verified elsewhere. Rabban Gamliel praised this enactment as a great improvement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asserts that even according to Rabbi Meir, the enactment was for witnesses to specify their names in the get.
A baraita describes the earlier practice where a witness wrote 'I, so-and-so, signed as a witness,' valid only if his handwriting was verified elsewhere.
Rabban Gamliel praises the enactment of specifying names in gittin as a great improvement for the betterment of the world.

items.text: Objection: Why not use symbols?
items.text_en: Objection: Why not use symbols?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that rabbis used symbols (e.g., a fish, a palm branch) as signatures, so why require full names? It answers that rabbis are different because their symbols are well-known. Originally, they used disks (diskei) to identify witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that rabbis used symbols (e.g., a fish, a palm branch) as signatures, so why require full names?
The Gemara answers that rabbis are different because their symbols are well-known.
The Gemara notes that originally, witnesses were identified using disks (diskei) rather than signatures.

items.text: Hillel's enactment of prosbul
items.text_en: Hillel's enactment of prosbul
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Hillel instituted prosbul. The Gemara explains that Hillel saw people refraining from lending, violating the Torah's warning, so he enacted prosbul. The text of prosbul is given: the lender transfers his debts to the court for collection at any time.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Hillel instituted prosbul because he saw people refraining from lending, violating the Torah's warning.
The Gemara provides the text of prosbul: the lender transfers his debts to the court for collection at any time, and the judges or witnesses sign below.

items.text: How can Hillel override Torah law?
items.text_en: How can Hillel override Torah law?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Hillel could annul the Torah's shemittah cancellation of debts. Abaye answers that this applies only to the present-day rabbinic shemittah, and follows Rabbi's opinion that when the land is not released (i.e., not in the Jubilee cycle), monetary debts are not released either.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Hillel could annul the Torah's shemittah cancellation of debts.
Abaye answers that Hillel's prosbul applies only to the present-day rabbinic shemittah, and follows Rabbi's opinion.
A baraita cites Rabbi's opinion that the Torah links land release and debt release, so when the land is not released (as in the present era), monetary debts are not released either.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Hillel institutes the prosbul
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Hillel institutes the prosbul
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Hillel saw people refraining from lending due to the Sabbatical year's debt cancellation, so he instituted the prosbul to allow collection.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the rabbis instituted that the Sabbatical year should release debts as a remembrance, but Hillel saw people refraining from lending and instituted the prosbul.

items.text: Gemara's question and answers on the source of authority
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answers on the source of authority
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how rabbis can enact a debt cancellation that is not Torah-mandated. Abaye answers it is a passive directive, while Rava cites the principle that court-ordered confiscation is valid, supported by verses from Ezra and Joshua.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the rabbis can enact a debt cancellation (שמיטה) that is not Torah-mandated.
Abaye answers that the rabbinic enactment is merely a passive directive (שב ואל תעשה), not an active command.
Rava answers that the principle of court-ordered confiscation (הפקר בית דין הפקר) justifies the rabbinic enactment.
Rabbi Yitzchak cites a verse from Ezra (Ezra 10:8) to prove that court-ordered confiscation is valid.
Rabbi Eliezer cites a verse from Joshua (Joshua 14:1) to derive that leaders (ראשים) can allocate property as they wish, analogous to fathers.

items.text: Inquiry: Was the prosbul for Hillel's generation only?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Was the prosbul for Hillel's generation only?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Hillel enacted the prosbul only for his generation or for all generations, with the practical difference being whether a later court can annul it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Hillel enacted the prosbul only for his generation or for all generations.
The Gemara clarifies the practical difference: if for his generation only, a later court can annul it; if for all generations, a later court cannot annul it unless greater in wisdom and number.

items.text: First attempted proof from Shmuel's practice
items.text_en: First attempted proof from Shmuel's practice
items.desc_en: Shmuel says prosbul is only written in the courts of Sura or Nehardea, implying it was not for all generations. The Gemara deflects that Hillel's enactment applied only to courts as authoritative as his own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's statement that prosbul is only written in the courts of Sura or Nehardea, arguing that if Hillel's enactment applied to all generations, other courts would also write it.
The Gemara deflects that Hillel's enactment applied to all generations only for courts as authoritative as his own, like those of Rav Ami and Rav Asi, but not for ordinary courts.

items.text: Second attempted proof and Rav Nachman's statement
items.text_en: Second attempted proof and Rav Nachman's statement
items.desc_en: Shmuel calls the prosbul an 'affront to judges' and says he would annul it if he were more powerful. Rav Nachman says he would uphold it, meaning he would declare that an unwritten prosbul is considered as written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings Shmuel's statement that the prosbul is an affront to judges and that he would annul it if he were more powerful, and then raises the objection that a later court cannot annul the decree of an earlier court unless greater in wisdom and number.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel meant he would annul the prosbul only if he were greater than Hillel in wisdom and number.
Rav Nachman says he would uphold the prosbul, meaning he would declare that an unwritten prosbul is considered as written.

items.text: Meaning of 'עולבנא' and concluding aggadic passage
items.text_en: Meaning of 'עולבנא' and concluding aggadic passage
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether 'עולבנא' means insult or humility, citing Ulla's metaphor of a bride who sinned under the canopy. Rav Mari and Rava discuss the verse, and a baraita praises those who suffer insult without retaliating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the term 'עולבנא' (insult/humiliation) means a language of insolence or a language of humility.
Ulla provides a supporting metaphor: a bride who sinned under her wedding canopy is 'עלובה' (humiliated), suggesting the term means insult.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel's interpretation
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel's interpretation
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel cites the verse 'עַד שֶׁהַמֶּלֶךְ בִּמְסִבּוֹ נִרְדִּי נָתַן רֵיחוֹ' (Song of Songs 1:12) to support the interpretation of insult.
Rava objects that the verse still indicates affection, since it says 'נתן' (gave fragrance) and not 'הסריח' (stank), implying humility rather than insult.
A baraita praises those who suffer insult without retaliating, citing the verse 'וְאוֹהֲבָיו כְּצֵאת הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בִּגְבוּרָתוֹ' (Judges 5:31), concluding the aggadic passage.

items.text: Etymology of 'prosbul'
items.text_en: Etymology of 'prosbul'
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that 'prosbul' is a Greek compound meaning 'pros' (before) and 'bulei' (the council), i.e., a declaration before the court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'prosbul' means.
Rav Chisda explains that 'prosbul' is a Greek compound meaning 'pros' (before) and 'bulei' (the council), i.e., a declaration before the court.

items.text: Etymological explanation of 'bulot' and 'butot', and definition of 'prosbul'
items.text_en: Etymological explanation of 'bulot' and 'butot', and definition of 'prosbul'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the terms 'bulot' (rich people) and 'butot' (poor people) based on verses, and Rava asks La'ozah for the meaning of 'prosbul', which is explained as 'a disclosure of the matter'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'bulot' refers to rich people, citing a verse and Rav Yosef's teaching about the 'bulot' of Judah.
The Gemara explains that 'butot' refers to poor people, citing a verse about lending.
Rava asks La'ozah for the meaning of the term 'prosbul'.
La'ozah explains that 'prosbul' means 'a disclosure of the matter'.

items.text: Orphans do not need a prosbul
items.text_en: Orphans do not need a prosbul
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that orphans do not require a prosbul, and Rami bar Chama supports this with the reasoning that Rabban Gamliel and his court are considered the father of orphans.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that orphans do not need a prosbul.
Rami bar Chama supports this with a baraita, reasoning that Rabban Gamliel and his court are considered the father of orphans.

items.text: Requirements for writing a prosbul: land ownership
items.text_en: Requirements for writing a prosbul: land ownership
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a prosbul is only written on land; if the lender has no land, he can be granted a minimal amount. Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav says even a stalk of cabbage suffices, and Rav Yehuda adds that even lending a place for an oven or stove allows writing a prosbul.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a prosbul is only written on land, and if the lender has no land, one grants him a minimal amount within his field.
The Gemara asks how much is considered 'minimal amount'.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav answers that even a stalk of cabbage suffices.
Rav Yehuda adds that even lending a place for an oven or stove allows writing a prosbul.
