items.text: Challenge from a beraita about a perforated flowerpot
items.text_en: Challenge from a beraita about a perforated flowerpot
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Yehuda's leniency with a beraita from Hillel that a prosbul is only written on a perforated flowerpot, implying that an unperforated one is invalid. The Gemara resolves that the case involves placing the pot on sticks, so the place is not considered his.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Yehuda's leniency by citing a beraita from Hillel that a prosbul is only written on a perforated flowerpot, implying an unperforated one is invalid.
The Gemara objects: why is an unperforated pot invalid, since the pot itself has a place (the ground inside it)?
The Gemara resolves that the case involves placing the pot on sticks, so the place is not considered his.

items.text: Practical examples of acquiring land for prosbul
items.text_en: Practical examples of acquiring land for prosbul
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi acquires a palm branch to write a prosbul, the rabbis of Rav Ashi's house transfer their words to each other, and Rabbi Yonatan asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba if he needs anything else, who says no.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi acquires a palm branch (גִּידְמָא דְּדִיקְלָא) and writes a prosbul on it.
The rabbis of Rav Ashi's house transfer their words to each other (to acquire land for prosbul).
Rabbi Yonatan transfers words to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and asks if he needs anything else.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba responds that he does not need anything else.

items.text: Writing prosbul based on the debtor's land or Rabbi Natan's principle
items.text_en: Writing prosbul based on the debtor's land or Rabbi Natan's principle
items.desc_en: A beraita teaches that if the lender has no land but the guarantor does, a prosbul can be written. If neither has land but the debtor does, it can also be written based on Rabbi Natan's principle that a creditor can collect from the debtor's debtor.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if the lender has no land but the guarantor does, a prosbul can be written based on the guarantor's land.
The baraita adds that if neither lender nor guarantor has land but the debtor does, a prosbul can be written based on Rabbi Natan's principle that a creditor can collect from the debtor's debtor.

items.text: Dispute about shemittah and documents with lien property
items.text_en: Dispute about shemittah and documents with lien property
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel say that a document with lien property is considered a 'shtar' that is not remitted, while Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish argue that only a document without lien property is remitted; one with lien property is not remitted.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the Mishnah that shemittah (the Sabbatical year) remits all loans, whether documented in a שטר (contract) or not.

Rav and Shmuel explain that 'with a שטר' means a document with lien property (אחריות נכסים), which is remitted, and 'without a שטר' means one without lien property, and certainly an oral loan is remitted.

Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish argue that 'with a שטר' refers to a document without lien property, and 'without a שטר' means an oral loan, but a document with lien property is not remitted by shemittah.

items.text: Beraitot supporting Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Beraitot supporting Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: Two beraitot are cited: one states that a document with lien property is not remitted, and another adds that even if the debtor designated a field or wrote that all his property is surety, the loan is not remitted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited supporting Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish: a document with lien property (אחריות נכסים) is not remitted by the Sabbatical year.
Another baraita adds that even if the debtor designated a specific field or wrote that all his property is surety, the loan is not remitted.

items.text: Case of Rabbi Asi's relative and the dispute with Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Case of Rabbi Asi's relative and the dispute with Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A relative of Rabbi Asi had a document with lien property; Rabbi Asi ruled it is not remitted, but Rabbi Yochanan ruled it is remitted. When challenged, Rabbi Yochanan says they do not act based on reasoning, and suggests the beraita supporting Rabbi Asi might be Beit Shammai's view.

sub.desc_en: A relative of Rabbi Asi brings a document with lien property to Rabbi Asi, who rules it is not remitted by the Sabbatical year.
The relative leaves Rabbi Asi and goes to Rabbi Yochanan, who rules that the document is remitted.
Rabbi Asi comes before Rabbi Yochanan and asks whether the document is remitted, and Rabbi Yochanan again says it is remitted.
Rabbi Asi objects that Rabbi Yochanan himself previously ruled that such a document is not remitted.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that they do not act based on mere reasoning.
Rabbi Asi cites a baraita that supports Rabbi Yochanan's original ruling.
Rabbi Yochanan suggests that the baraita might reflect Beit Shammai's view that a document ready for collection is considered as already collected.

items.text: Loans on collateral and delivery of documents to court are not remitted
items.text_en: Loans on collateral and delivery of documents to court are not remitted
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a loan on collateral or delivering documents to court is not remitted. The Gemara explains that the court seizes the documents, and for collateral, Rava says it is because the lender seizes it. Abaye challenges with a case of living in the borrower's courtyard, and Rava distinguishes based on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that a creditor acquires the collateral.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who lends money on a collateral or delivers his documents to court is not subject to remission.
The Gemara asks: granted, for delivering documents to court, the court seizes them; but what is the reason for the exemption regarding a loan on collateral?
Rava answers: because the lender seizes the collateral.
Abaye objects: if so, if one lent money and lives in the borrower's courtyard, which he also seizes, would that also not be remitted?
Rava distinguishes: collateral is different because the creditor acquires it based on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that a creditor acquires the collateral.

items.text: Beginning of next Mishnah
items.text_en: Beginning of next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the next Mishnah with the phrase 'We learned there'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the next Mishnah with the phrase 'We learned there'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who returns a debt in the Sabbatical year must say 'I am remitting,' and if the debtor says 'even so,' he may accept it, based on the verse 'And this is the matter of the remission.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who returns a debt in the Sabbatical year must say 'I am remitting,' and if the debtor says 'even so,' he may accept it, citing the verse 'And this is the matter of the remission.'

items.text: Gemara's discussion on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Abaye debate the necessity of the debtor's statement. A story is told about Rabbah and Abba bar Marta, illustrating the practical application of the Mishnah's ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states that the debtor must explicitly say he is remitting the debt, and the creditor must wait until he says so.

Abaye objects by citing a baraita that when repaying a debt in the Sabbatical year, the debtor should say 'they are mine and I give them as a gift,' not 'in repayment of my debt,' implying a different formula.
Rabbah responds that the same principle applies: the creditor must wait until the debtor says that formula as well.

sub.text: Story about Rabbah and Abba bar Marta
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbah and Abba bar Marta
sub.desc_en: A story is told: Abba bar Marta owed Rabbah money; in the Sabbatical year he brought the money and said 'I remit,' and Rabbah took it and left, but later Abaye found Rabbah upset and Rabbah recounted the incident.

Abaye goes to Abba bar Marta, learns that Rabbah only said 'I remit' without the debtor saying 'even so,' instructs Abba bar Marta to bring the money again and say 'even so,' which he does; Rabbah then takes the money and remarks that he initially thought Abba bar Marta was not a Torah scholar.

items.text: The reliability of claiming a lost prosbul
items.text_en: The reliability of claiming a lost prosbul
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Nachman rules that a person is believed to say 'I had a prosbul and it was lost,' because the Sages instituted the prosbul and one would not abandon a permitted path for a forbidden one. Rav, however, considers such a claim as 'opening the mouth for the mute.'

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Nachman rules that a person is believed to claim he had a prosbul (פְּרוֹסְבּוּל) that was lost, because the Sages instituted the prosbul and one would not abandon a permitted path (הֶיתֵּירָא) for a forbidden one (אִיסּוּרָא).
Rav rejects such a claim, calling it 'opening the mouth for the mute' (פְּתַח פִּיךָ לָאִלֵּם), implying the claimant is not believed without evidence.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the need for a prosbul
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the need for a prosbul
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a Tannaitic dispute: one Tanna requires a prosbul when collecting a debt, while the Sages say it is not required.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a creditor who produces a debt document without a prosbul may not collect.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah reflects a Tannaitic dispute: one Tanna requires a prosbul, while the Sages say it is not required.

items.text: Mishnah on a captured slave
items.text_en: Mishnah on a captured slave
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a slave is captured and redeemed, if redeemed as a slave he is enslaved; if as a free man, he is not enslaved. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says in either case he is enslaved.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a slave was captured and redeemed, if redeemed as a slave he remains enslaved; if redeemed as a free man he is free; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says in either case he remains enslaved.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states his dissenting opinion: in either case the slave is enslaved.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the slave Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the slave Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the circumstances, with Abaye and Rava offering different interpretations. Abaye says it is before despair, Rava says after despair. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning is explained, including a statement by Hezekiah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what circumstances the Mishnah addresses, challenging both possibilities: before despair or after despair.
Abaye explains the Mishnah as referring to before despair, detailing the slave's status regarding the first and second masters.

sub.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position (Abaye's version)
sub.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position (Abaye's version)
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that in either case the slave is enslaved, because there is a מצוה (commandment) to redeem slaves just as to redeem free people.
Rava explains the Mishnah as referring to after despair, detailing the slave's status regarding the first and second masters.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling is explained by Hezekiah's reason: to prevent slaves from deliberately falling into captivity to escape their master.

items.text: Objection to Rava and resolution
items.text_en: Objection to Rava and resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised against Rava from the wording of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Rava explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was addressing both possibilities.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection against Rava from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement, noting that it fits Abaye's view (before יאוש) but not Rava's view (after יאוש).
The Gemara sharpens the objection: according to Rava's interpretation (after יאוש), the phrase 'just as' is inappropriate, since the reason is actually that of Hezekiah.

Rava resolves the objection by explaining that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was addressing both possibilities: if the Sages spoke before יאוש, his reason is 'just as'; if after יאוש, his reason is that of Hezekiah.

items.text: Question on acquisition from a gentile and answer
items.text_en: Question on acquisition from a gentile and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a second master can acquire the slave from the captor, and answers that the captor acquires the slave for his labor, citing Resh Lakish's derivation from a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how, according to Rava who holds the redemption occurs after יאוש (despair), the second master can acquire the slave from the captor, since the captor himself never acquired the slave.

The Gemara answers that the captor does acquire the slave for his labor, citing Resh Lakish's derivation from the verse 'מהם תקנו' (from them you shall buy) that a gentile can acquire another gentile for his labor.

items.text: Gentiles acquiring slaves from each other
items.text_en: Gentiles acquiring slaves from each other
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's statement 'they do not acquire from each other' refers to acquisition of the slave's body, not his earnings. It then argues that a gentile can acquire a slave from another gentile through money, using a kal vachomer from a gentile acquiring from a Jew.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that gentiles do not acquire slaves from each other, asking if this means they cannot acquire each other's slaves at all.
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah means they do not acquire the slave's body (גופו) from each other, but they may acquire his earnings.
The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah also means that gentiles do not acquire the slave's earnings from each other.
The Gemara answers with a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if a gentile can acquire a slave's earnings from a Jew, then certainly a gentile can acquire from another gentile.

items.text: Acquisition by chazakah and scriptural source
items.text_en: Acquisition by chazakah and scriptural source
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether acquisition by chazakah (presumptive possession) is valid for a gentile acquiring from another gentile. Rav Papa answers by citing the case of Ammon and Moab being purified through Sichon. The source for a gentile acquiring from a Jew is derived from the verse 'and he took a captive from them'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the rule of gentiles acquiring from each other applies only to acquisition by money (כַּסְפָּא) but not by chazakah (חזקה, presumptive possession).
Rav Papa answers by citing the case of Ammon and Moab being purified through acquisition by chazakah from Sichon, proving that a gentile can acquire from another gentile by chazakah.
The Gemara derives the source for a gentile acquiring from a Jew from the verse 'וַיִּשְׁבְּ מִמֶּנּוּ שֶׁבִי' (and he took a captive from them).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on a fugitive slave
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on a fugitive slave
items.desc_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan: a slave who escapes from prison goes free, and the court forces his master to write him a bill of manumission.

sub.text: Rav Shemen bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan: a slave who escapes from prison goes free, and the court forces his master to write him a bill of manumission.

items.text: Contradiction with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the slave remains enslaved, and Rabbi Yochanan rules like him in most cases. Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing before and after despair. Rava, who holds the case is after despair, faces a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Yochanan. Rava answers that a fugitive slave is different because he risks his life to escape, so he would not risk recapture.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that the slave remains enslaved, and notes that Rabbi Yochanan generally rules like him.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the case before יאוש (despair) and after יאוש (despair).
The Gemara objects that for Rava, who holds the case is after יאוש (despair), there is a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Yochanan.
Rava answers that a fugitive slave is different because he already risks his life to escape, so he would not risk recapture by the authorities.

items.text: Case of Shmuel's maidservant and the law of hefker
items.text_en: Case of Shmuel's maidservant and the law of hefker
items.desc_en: Shmuel's maidservant was captured. The captors redeemed her as a maidservant and sent her back. They followed Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but Shmuel ruled she did not need a bill of manumission because the redemption was after despair. Shmuel holds that one who declares his slave ownerless goes free without a bill, based on the verse 'every slave of a man' – only a slave with a master's authority is called a slave.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Shmuel's maidservant was captured, redeemed as a maidservant, and sent back to him.
The captors inform Shmuel that they follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view and redeemed her as a maidservant.
The Gemara explains that the captors thought the redemption was before despair, but it was after despair, so Shmuel ruled she needed neither re-enslavement nor a bill of manumission.

The Gemara cites Shmuel's own ruling that one who declares his slave ownerless goes free without a bill, based on the verse 'every slave of a man' — only a slave with a master's authority is called a slave.

items.text: Case of Rabbi Abba bar Zutra's maidservant and the gentile's motive
items.text_en: Case of Rabbi Abba bar Zutra's maidservant and the gentile's motive
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zutra's maidservant was captured, and a gentile redeemed her as a wife. The rabbis sent him a message to send a bill of manumission. The Gemara questions why a bill is needed: if they could redeem her, why the bill? Two answers are given: either the bill facilitates her redemption by the Jewish community, or it causes the gentile to release her. The Gemara notes that gentiles value their animals more than their wives, but in public they are ashamed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Abba bar Zutra's maidservant was captured, and a certain gentile from Tadmor redeemed her as a wife; the rabbis sent him a message to send a bill of manumission.
The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances? If they could redeem her, why is a bill needed? If they cannot redeem her, what good would a bill do?
First answer: they can redeem her, and the bill facilitates her redemption by uniting the Jewish community to act.
Second answer: they cannot redeem her, but the bill shames the gentile into releasing her.
The Gemara objects: but Mar said that gentiles value Jewish animals more than Jewish women; how would shaming work?
The Gemara resolves: that applies in private, but in public it is shameful for them.

items.text: Case of the maidservant in Pumpedita and the prohibition of freeing a slave
items.text_en: Case of the maidservant in Pumpedita and the prohibition of freeing a slave
items.desc_en: A maidservant in Pumpedita was being used for forbidden relations. Abaye wanted to force her master to free her, but refrained because of Shmuel's ruling that freeing a Canaanite slave violates a positive commandment. Ravina says that in such a case of sin, even Shmuel would agree. The Gemara questions Abaye's concern, citing a story of a half-slave half-free woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of a maidservant in Pumpedita who was being used for forbidden relations.
Abaye states that were it not for Shmuel's ruling that freeing a slave violates a positive commandment, he would force the master to free her.
Ravina objects that even Shmuel would agree in this case of sin, permitting the freeing of the slave.
The Gemara questions why Abaye did not consider the sin itself as sufficient reason to force the master, despite Shmuel's ruling.
The Gemara cites a story of a half-slave half-free woman, implying that in cases of sin, freeing a slave is permitted.

items.text: Clarification of the earlier incident
items.text_en: Clarification of the earlier incident
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the earlier case of a woman who was freed was treated as ownerless property, not a proper emancipation. The Gemara questions this, distinguishing between a woman unfit for slavery or freedom and a slave who could be designated for a specific task.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the earlier case of a woman freed by coercion was treated as ownerless property (הפקר), not a proper emancipation.
The Gemara objects: how can the case be compared? There, the woman was unfit for either slavery or freedom, but here a slave can be designated for a specific task.
The Gemara answers that here, the master could designate the slave for a specific task and guard her, so the comparison is valid.

items.text: The prohibition against freeing slaves and the exception for a mitzvah
items.text_en: The prohibition against freeing slaves and the exception for a mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel states that freeing a slave violates a positive commandment from Leviticus 25:46. A challenge is brought from a story where Rabbi Eliezer freed his slave to complete a minyan, and the Gemara answers that a mitzvah is different.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that freeing a slave violates a positive commandment (עשה) from the verse 'לעולם בהם תעבודו' (Leviticus 25:46).
The Gemara raises an objection from a story where Rabbi Eliezer freed his slave to complete a minyan (prayer quorum), implying that freeing a slave is permitted for a mitzvah.
The Gemara answers that a mitzvah (commandment) is different, i.e., the prohibition is waived for the sake of fulfilling a mitzvah.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on the verse
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on the verse
items.desc_en: A baraisa records a dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says the verse 'forever shall you work them' is optional, while Rabbi Akiva says it is obligatory. The Gemara considers whether Rabbi Eliezer might hold like Rabbi Yishmael, but rejects this because a baraisa explicitly states Rabbi Eliezer holds it is obligatory.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa records the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael interprets the verse 'forever shall you work them' as optional (רשות), while Rabbi Akiva interprets it as obligatory (חובה).
The Gemara raises a possibility: perhaps Rabbi Eliezer holds like the one who says the verse is optional (רשות), which would explain his action of freeing a slave for a minyan.
The Gemara rejects this possibility, citing an explicit baraisa where Rabbi Eliezer states that the verse is obligatory (חובה).

items.text: Three things that cause householders to lose their wealth
items.text_en: Three things that cause householders to lose their wealth
items.desc_en: Rabbah lists three actions that cause householders to lose their wealth: freeing slaves, inspecting property on Shabbat, and setting meals on Shabbat during study time. He supports this with a story from Rabbi Yochanan about two families in Jerusalem who set their meals at different times and were uprooted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah lists three actions that cause householders to lose their wealth: freeing slaves, inspecting property on Shabbat, and setting meals on Shabbat during study time.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan provides a supporting story about two families in Jerusalem who set their meals at different times and were uprooted.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef on consecrating vs. declaring ownerless
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef on consecrating vs. declaring ownerless
items.desc_en: Rabbah quoting Rav says that one who consecrates his slave goes free, because he only meant to consecrate his value. Rav Yosef quoting Rav says that one who declares his slave ownerless goes free. The Gemara explains the logical relationship between the two rulings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah in the name of Rav rules that one who consecrates his slave goes free, because the slave's body is not consecrated and the owner only meant to make him a holy people.

Rav Yosef in the name of Rav rules that one who declares his slave ownerless goes free, and the Gemara explains the logical relationship between the two rulings: the one who says consecration certainly agrees about ownerless, but the one who says ownerless may reject consecration because the owner might have meant the slave's monetary value.

items.text: Whether a bill of manumission is required
items.text_en: Whether a bill of manumission is required
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether a slave freed through consecration or ownerlessness requires a bill of manumission. Rav Chiyya bar Avin quoting Rav answers that in both cases the slave goes free but requires a bill of manumission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question whether a slave freed through consecration or ownerlessness requires a bill of manumission.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Rav answers that in both cases the slave goes free but requires a bill of manumission.

items.text: Challenges to Rav's ruling from a Mishnah and a Baraisa
items.text_en: Challenges to Rav's ruling from a Mishnah and a Baraisa
items.desc_en: Rabbah raises a Mishnah about consecrated property with slaves, which seems to contradict Rav. The Gemara defends Rav by saying he is a Tanna and can disagree. Further challenges are brought from a verse about herem and a baraisa about consecrating a slave, and the Gemara attempts to resolve them by distinguishing between consecrating the body and consecrating the value.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah raises a Mishnah about consecrating property with slaves, which seems to contradict Rav's ruling that a consecrated slave goes free.
The Gemara defends Rav by noting that Rav is a Tanna and can disagree with the Mishnah.

sub.text: Gemara's further challenge from a verse
sub.text_en: Gemara's further challenge from a verse
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a verse about herem that includes Canaanite slaves, and resolves it by saying the verse refers to consecrating the slave's value.
The Gemara objects that if the verse is about value, then the Mishnah about consecrating property should also be about value.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah is about value, why would treasurers be involved at all?
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah is about value, the details about selling and the slave paying for himself are incoherent.

sub.text: Gemara's final challenge from a baraisa
sub.text_en: Gemara's final challenge from a baraisa
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraisa that a consecrated slave may work and eat, because only his value was consecrated, supporting Rav's position.

items.text: Identifying the Mishnah's author as Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Identifying the Mishnah's author as Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the Mishnah must be Rabbi Meir's view, because he holds that a person does not utter words in vain. It supports this by noting that the latter clause about one who consecrates himself fits only Rabbi Meir, not the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by identifying the Mishnah as Rabbi Meir's view, because he holds that a person does not utter words in vain.
The Gemara argues that the conclusion is also logical, because the latter clause about one who consecrates himself fits only Rabbi Meir's view.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah were the Rabbis' view, the slave would be valued for his monetary worth, but the man himself would not be valued for his monetary worth.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about consecrating a slave
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about consecrating a slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's dispute might align with a tannaitic debate between the Sages and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding whether a consecrated slave has sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah's dispute aligns with a tannaitic debate between the Sages and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel about whether a consecrated slave has sanctity.

items.text: Rejection of the sanctity interpretation
items.text_en: Rejection of the sanctity interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous suggestion, pointing out that the terms 'me'ilah' and 'no me'ilah' are inappropriate for a dispute about sanctity; they should have said 'sanctified' and 'not sanctified'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the terms 'me'ilah' and 'no me'ilah' are inappropriate for a dispute about sanctity; they should have said 'sanctified' and 'not sanctified'.

items.text: Alternative interpretations of the tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Alternative interpretations of the tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative explanations: first, that all agree the slave is sanctified but dispute whether a slave is like land or movable property; second, that all agree a slave is like land but dispute whether hair destined to be cut is considered already cut.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that all agree the slave is sanctified (קָדוֹשׁ), and the dispute is whether a slave is classified as land (מְקַרְקְעֵי) or movable property (מִטַּלְטְלִי).
The Gemara objects: if the dispute were about the slave's status as land or movable property, they should have argued about the slave's body (גּוּפוֹ), not just his hair.
The Gemara revises: all agree a slave is like land, and the dispute is whether hair destined to be cut (עוֹמֵד לִיגָּזֵז) is considered already cut (כְּגָזוּז) or not.

items.text: Comparison with Rabbi Meir's view on attached produce
items.text_en: Comparison with Rabbi Meir's view on attached produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the dispute to a tannaitic debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about whether attached produce is considered like land, and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's explanation that grapes ready for harvest are at issue. It then distinguishes that case from the slave's hair, which improves while attached.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute about the slave's hair corresponds to a tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding attached produce.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's explanation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages concerns grapes ready for harvest, where Rabbi Meir considers them like already harvested, while the Sages do not.

The Gemara distinguishes the cases: Rabbi Meir's leniency regarding grapes applies because they deteriorate while attached, but the slave's hair improves while attached, so even Rabbi Meir would agree it is not considered detached.

items.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's report and Rabbi Yochanan's reaction
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's report and Rabbi Yochanan's reaction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef reports Rav's teaching before Rabbi Yochanan, who questions whether Rav actually said that, citing Ulla's statement in Rabbi Yochanan's name that one who declares his slave ownerless frees him and requires a writ of manumission. The Gemara clarifies that Rav agrees with Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef reports Rav's teaching before Rabbi Yochanan, who questions whether Rav actually said that, citing Ulla's statement in Rabbi Yochanan's name that one who declares his slave ownerless frees him and requires a writ of manumission.
The Gemara clarifies that Rav agrees with Rabbi Yochanan, and presents an alternative version where Rabbi Yochanan's reaction was based on the omission of the requirement for a writ of manumission.

items.text: Ulla's statement and Rabbi Abba's objection
items.text_en: Ulla's statement and Rabbi Abba's objection
items.desc_en: Ulla states in Rabbi Yochanan's name that one who declares his slave ownerless frees him and requires a writ of manumission. Rabbi Abba objects from a baraita about a convert's slaves, where they become free without a writ. Ulla explains that a convert's slaves are like his wife, who can be sent away without a get.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one who declares his slave ownerless frees him but requires a bill of manumission.
Rabbi Abba objects from a baraita about a convert's slaves who become free without a bill of manumission, challenging Rabbi Yochanan's requirement.
Ulla dismisses the objection and explains via Rav Nachman that a convert's slaves are like his wife, who is freed without a get, so they do not require a bill of manumission.

items.text: Further challenges and resolution
items.text_en: Further challenges and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla's reasoning: if a convert's slaves are like his wife, why not apply this to a Jewish master? The verse limits it. It then raises a difficulty from Ameimar's ruling about a master who declares his slave ownerless and dies, and concludes with Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the halakha follows Abba Shaul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla's reasoning: if a convert's slaves are like his wife, why not apply this to a Jewish master as well?
Rav Nachman answers that the verse limits the rule to a convert's slaves, as a Jewish master's slaves are inherited by his children.
The Gemara raises a difficulty from Ameimar's ruling that a master who declares his slave ownerless and dies leaves the slave without remedy, challenging the consistency of the reasoning.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the halakha follows Abba Shaul, resolving the difficulty.

items.text: First inquiry: Is Rabbi's ruling from explicit tradition or logical inference?
items.text_en: First inquiry: Is Rabbi's ruling from explicit tradition or logical inference?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's report of Rabbi's ruling (that a slave whose master says 'I despaired of him' requires a shtar) was heard explicitly or derived logically. Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi's reasoning via a gezerah shavah from a woman's divorce. The Gemara then infers that just as a woman's divorce involves issura (prohibition) not mammona (money), so too the slave's shtar. The interlocutor counters that one could instead infer that just as a woman can be any age, so too the slave. The first speaker clarifies he heard it explicitly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi heard Rabbi's ruling explicitly or inferred it, and cites the story where Rabbi ruled that a slave whose master said 'I despaired of him' requires a שטר (document).

Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi's reasoning: he derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'לה' (to her) used for a woman's divorce, teaching that just as a woman requires a שטר (document), so too a slave requires a שטר.
The interlocutor infers from the analogy that just as a woman's divorce involves איסורא (prohibition) and not ממונא (money), so too the slave's release involves איסורא and not ממונא.
The interlocutor counters that if the ruling is inferred, one could instead infer that just as a woman can be any age (adult or minor), so too a slave can be any age.
The first speaker clarifies that he heard the ruling explicitly, not inferred.

items.text: Second inquiry: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's ruling on Abba Shaul, with parallel debate
items.text_en: Second inquiry: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's ruling on Abba Shaul, with parallel debate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha does not follow Abba Shaul. Rabbi Zeira asks whether this was heard explicitly or derived logically, and the same logical debate recurs: one could infer either that the slave requires a shtar (like a woman's get) or that the slave can be any age. Again, the answer is that it was heard explicitly.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha does not follow Abba Shaul.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba whether he heard this ruling explicitly or inferred it logically.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's report and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's report and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains the logical inference: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's report about Rabbi's ruling, and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation that Rabbi derived a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from a woman's גט (bill of divorce) to require a שטר (document) for the slave.
The gemara infers from the analogy that just as a woman can be any age, so too the slave can be any age (not just a minor).
The interlocutor objects that one could infer the opposite: just as a woman involves איסור (prohibition) and not ממון (money), so too the slave involves איסור and not ממון.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba answers that he heard the ruling explicitly, not through logical inference.

items.text: Reconciling Rabbi's statement with a baraita and introducing Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Reconciling Rabbi's statement with a baraita and introducing Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi said a slave has no remedy except a shtar, but a baraita has Rabbi saying the slave can give his own money and go free. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi meant either money or a shtar, but in this case the money is ineffective. This is to exclude the view of Rabbi Shimon, who holds that money does not complete the maidservant's release, only a shtar does, based on a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's report that Rabbi said a slave has no remedy except a shtar (document of manumission).
The Gemara objects: a baraita has Rabbi saying the slave can give his own money and go free, contradicting the statement that only a shtar works.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi meant either money or a shtar, but in this case the money is ineffective because the master's declaration of despair nullifies the slave's ability to pay.

sub.text: Gemara's shift to exclude Rabbi Shimon's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's shift to exclude Rabbi Shimon's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi's statement was intended to exclude the view of a certain Tanna (Rabbi Shimon).

sub.text: Supporting baraita citing Rabbi Shimon in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita citing Rabbi Shimon in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says in the name of Rabbi Akiva that money does not complete the maidservant's release, only a shtar does, based on a verse.

items.text: Dispute over the halakha following Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Dispute over the halakha following Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama reports in the name of Rav Nachman that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, while Rav Yosef bar Chama reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Shimon.

sub.text: Rami bar Chama citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rami bar Chama citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama reports in the name of Rav Nachman that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Chama citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Practical case and clarification of the ruling
items.text_en: Practical case and clarification of the ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak encounters Rava bar Sheilta and asks about the halakha. Rava bar Sheilta says he holds it is not the halakha, but others from Machoza say Rabbi Zeira reported in the name of Rav Nachman that it is the halakha. A story is told of a maidservant whose master was dying; she cried to him, and he threw his cap at her, saying 'Acquire this and acquire yourself.' Rav Nachman ruled this was invalid. Some thought it was because the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon (money doesn't work), but the real reason is that the cap belonged to the master (not the slave), so it was not a valid acquisition.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak to Rava bar Sheilta
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak to Rava bar Sheilta
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak finds Rava bar Sheilta at the synagogue entrance and asks him whether the halakha (הלכה) follows Rabbi Shimon or not.
Rava bar Sheilta answers that in his view it is not the halakha (הלכה), but reports that the rabbis from Machoza say Rabbi Zeira cited Rav Nachman that it is the halakha.

When the narrator came to Sura, he found Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin and asked him about the actual case: a maidservant whose master was dying cried to him, and he threw his cap at her saying 'Acquire this and acquire yourself.'
The case came before Rav Nachman, who ruled that the master's action accomplished nothing (לא עשה ולא כלום).

Some thought the invalidation was because the halakha (הלכה) follows Rabbi Shimon (that money does not work), but the stam clarifies it was actually because the cap belonged to the master (כליו של מקנה), not the slave, so it was not a valid acquisition.

items.text: Final ruling: halakha does not follow Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Final ruling: halakha does not follow Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: A chain of tradition (Rav Shmuel bar Achitai, Rav Hamnuna Saba, Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ashyan, Rav Huna, Rav Hamnuna) reports that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, but the Gemara concludes that this is not correct—the halakha does not follow Rabbi Shimon.

sub.text: Chain of tradition (Rav Shmuel bar Achitai et al.)
sub.text_en: Chain of tradition (Rav Shmuel bar Achitai et al.)
sub.desc_en: A chain of tradition reports that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara rejects the tradition and concludes that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Introduction of a new topic: a slave who marries a free woman in the master's presence
items.text_en: Introduction of a new topic: a slave who marries a free woman in the master's presence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira, Rabbi Chanina, Rav Ashi, and Rabbi begin a new discussion about a slave who marries a free woman in the presence of his master, setting up the next sugya.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Chanina citing Rav Ashi citing Rabbi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Chanina citing Rav Ashi citing Rabbi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira introduces a new topic: a slave who marries a free woman in the presence of his master, setting up the next sugya.

items.text: Opening question about a slave who put on tefillin
items.text_en: Opening question about a slave who put on tefillin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges a statement that a slave who put on tefillin in front of his master goes free, citing a mishnah where Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute the status of a slave who received a betrothal document.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges the statement that a slave who put on tefillin goes free, citing a mishnah where Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute the status of a slave who received a betrothal document.

items.text: First answer: when the master put tefillin on him
items.text_en: First answer: when the master put tefillin on him
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Sheila explains that the case is when the master himself put tefillin on the slave, similar to when the master married him off.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Sheila resolves the contradiction by explaining that the slave put on tefillin only because his master placed them on him, and similarly the betrothal document was given when the master married him off.

items.text: Objection: can the slave cause a prohibition?
items.text_en: Objection: can the slave cause a prohibition?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: can it be that the master does not cause a prohibition for the slave, but the slave himself causes a prohibition?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: can it be that what is forbidden for the master to do to his slave is permitted for the slave to do to himself?

items.text: Second answer: the document's language
items.text_en: Second answer: the document's language
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the case involves a document that says 'Go out with this and be betrothed with it,' and the dispute is whether the language implies freedom.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the case involves the master saying 'Go out with this document and be betrothed with it,' and Rabbi Meir holds that this language implies emancipation while the Sages disagree.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a slave who put on tefillin in front of his master goes free. The Gemara challenges this with a baraita listing actions that do not free a slave, including putting on tefillin. Rabbah bar Rav Sheila answers that the baraita refers to when the master put tefillin on the slave.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a slave who put on tefillin in front of his master goes free.
The Gemara challenges with a baraita listing actions that do not free a slave, including putting on tefillin.
Rabbah bar Rav Sheila answers that the baraita refers to when the master put tefillin on the slave, not the slave acting independently.

items.text: Deathbed statement: 'let her not be enslaved'
items.text_en: Deathbed statement: 'let her not be enslaved'
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: if a master says at death 'Plonit my maidservant, let her not be enslaved after my death,' the heirs are forced to write her a bill of freedom. Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi object that her children would still be slaves.

sub.text: Rav Dimi's report of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi's report of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that if a master says at death 'Let my slavewoman Plonis not be enslaved after my death,' the heirs are compelled to write a bill of emancipation, but Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi object that her children remain slaves.
Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi object to Rabbi Yochanan that her children would still be slaves, implying the ruling is inconsistent.

items.text: Deathbed statement: 'let her have gratification'
items.text_en: Deathbed statement: 'let her have gratification'
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: if a master says at death 'Plonit my maidservant gave me gratification, let her have gratification,' the heirs are forced to give her gratification, because it is a mitzvah to fulfill the words of the deceased.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's report of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's report of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that if a master says at death 'My slavewoman Plonis gave me comfort, let comfort be done for her,' the heirs are compelled to give her comfort, because it is a מצוה (commandment) to fulfill the words of the deceased.

items.text: Amemar: an ownerless slave has no remedy
items.text_en: Amemar: an ownerless slave has no remedy
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that a master who declares his slave ownerless does not free him, because the master only has a prohibition over the slave, not ownership, and cannot transfer a prohibition. Rav Ashi objects citing Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan that such a slave goes free and needs a bill of freedom. Amemar responds that 'needs' means he has no remedy.

sub.desc_en: Amemar rules that a master who declares his slave ownerless leaves the slave without remedy, because the master only has a prohibition over the slave, not ownership, and cannot transfer a prohibition.
Rav Ashi objects, citing Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan (and Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Rav) that such a slave goes free and needs a bill of freedom.
Amemar responds that the word 'needs' in the cited statement means the slave has no remedy, not that he can actually obtain freedom.

items.text: Alternative version: ownerless slave after master's death
items.text_en: Alternative version: ownerless slave after master's death
items.desc_en: An alternative version has Amemar ruling that a slave declared ownerless after the master's death has no remedy, because the prohibition cannot be inherited. Rav Ashi objects citing Rav Dimi's report. The Gemara explains that Rav Dimi's report was a mistake, but only because it lacked explicit freedom language; if it had such language, it would be valid. Amemar follows Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's version.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version has Amemar ruling that a slave declared ownerless after the master's death has no remedy, because the prohibition cannot be inherited.
Rav Ashi objects to Amemar, citing Rav Dimi's report that Rabbi Yochanan ruled differently.
Amemar responds that Rav Dimi's report was a mistake, but only because it lacked explicit freedom language; if it had such language, it would be valid, and he follows Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's version.

items.text: Case of slaves sold to a gentile
items.text_en: Case of slaves sold to a gentile
items.desc_en: Slaves from a certain place were sold to a gentile. The later owners came before Ravina, who ruled that the earlier owners must write them a bill of freedom. The rabbis objected citing Amemar's ruling. Ravina responded that he follows Rav Dimi, and the mistake was only about lacking freedom language; here it is present. The halakha follows Ravina.

sub.desc_en: The narrator presents a case: slaves from a certain place were sold to a gentile, and the later owners came before Ravina, who ruled that the earlier owners must write them a bill of freedom.
The sages object to Ravina, citing Amemar's ruling that one who declares his slave ownerless has no remedy.
Ravina responds that he follows Rav Dimi's view, and the mistake in Rav Dimi's case was only about lacking freedom language.
The sages object further, asserting that Rav Dimi's ruling was a mistake.
Ravina resolves the objection: the mistake was only about lacking freedom language, but here it is present, so the halakha follows Ravina.

items.text: Case of a slave owned by two masters
items.text_en: Case of a slave owned by two masters
items.desc_en: A slave was owned by two masters; one freed his half. The other master, to avoid losing the slave, transferred his half to his minor son. Rav Yosef bar Rava sent a query to Rav Papa, who responded that since the minor is known to be money-oriented, they will appoint a guardian for him.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a slave owned by two masters, one freed his half, and the other transferred his half to his minor son to avoid loss.
Rav Yosef bar Rava sends a query to Rav Papa, citing the verse 'as he has done, so shall be done to him' to imply the master's intent to evade the law.
Rav Papa responds that since the minor is known to be money-oriented, the court will appoint a guardian for him to manage the slave's affairs.

items.text: Opening context: slave freed by jingling coins
items.text_en: Opening context: slave freed by jingling coins
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a scenario where a master jingles coins and writes a bill of manumission for his slave, setting the stage for the discussion of effective manumission formulas.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a scenario where a master jingles coins and writes a bill of manumission for his slave, setting the stage for the discussion of effective manumission formulas.

items.text: Baraita on manumission formulas
items.text_en: Baraita on manumission formulas
items.desc_en: A baraita lists effective and disputed formulations for freeing a slave: past tense (עשיתי, עשוי, הרי הוא) are effective, while future tense (אעשנו) is disputed between Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Sages. Rabbi Yochanan rules that all require a document.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three past-tense formulations for freeing a slave that are effective: עשיתי (I made), עשוי (made), הרי הוא (behold he is).
The baraita presents a dispute regarding the future-tense formulation אעשנו (I will make): Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds the slave is acquired, while the Sages hold he is not.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that all these formulations require a document (שטר) to effect manumission.

items.text: Parallel baraita on gift of a field
items.text_en: Parallel baraita on gift of a field
items.desc_en: A similar baraita discusses gift formulas for a field: past tense (נתתי, נתונה, הרי היא שלו) are effective, while future tense (אתננה) is disputed between Rabbi Meir and the Sages. Rabbi Yochanan again requires a document.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that past-tense or present-tense declarations of a gift of land ('I gave,' 'it is given,' 'it is his') are effective.
The baraita presents a dispute about a future-tense declaration ('I will give it'): Rabbi Meir rules the recipient acquires it, while the Sages rule he does not.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that all these cases are effective only when accompanied by a written document (שטר).

items.text: Dispute between master and slave/recipient
items.text_en: Dispute between master and slave/recipient
items.desc_en: When the master claims to have freed the slave or given a field, but the slave/recipient denies it, we suspect the master may have transferred rights through a third party. However, if the master claims to have written and given a document, the recipient's denial is accepted as conclusive (הודאת בעל דין כמאה עדים דמי).

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that if a master claims to have freed his slave but the slave denies it, we suspect the master may have transferred emancipation through a third party.
If the master claims to have written and given a bill of manumission, the slave's denial is accepted as conclusive, like the testimony of one hundred witnesses.
The same rule applies to a field: if the giver claims to have given it but the recipient denies, we suspect transfer through a third party.
If the giver claims to have written and given a document, the recipient's denial is accepted as conclusive, like the testimony of one hundred witnesses.

items.text: Dispute about who eats the produce
items.text_en: Dispute about who eats the produce
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah disagree about who eats the produce in the interim: Rav Chisda says the giver eats, Rabbah says the produce is divided. The Gemara resolves that they refer to different cases: the father (giver) vs. the son (recipient).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who consumes the produce of the field in the interim.
Rav Chisda rules that the giver (original owner) eats the produce.
Rabbah rules that the produce is deposited with a third party.
The Gemara resolves that they do not disagree: Rav Chisda's case is about the father (the giver), Rabbah's case is about the son (the recipient).

items.text: Mishnah: slave as אפותיקי and freed
items.text_en: Mishnah: slave as אפותיקי and freed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a master designates his slave as collateral (אפותיקי) and then frees him, the slave is not liable to the creditor. However, as a תיקון העולם, the court forces the master to free the slave and write a document for his value. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the master merely frees him without writing a document.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches: if a master designates his slave as collateral (אפותיקי) for others and then frees him, the strict law is that the slave owes nothing, but as a tikkun haolam (repair of the world) the court forces the master to free the slave and write a document for his value.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: the master does not write a document for the value, but rather simply frees the slave.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dissents, holding that the master merely frees the slave without writing a document for his value.

items.text: Gemara: who freed the slave?
items.text_en: Gemara: who freed the slave?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who freed the slave, and Rav answers: the first master. The slave is not liable to the second master (creditor) because of Rava's principle that sanctification, leaven, and manumission nullify liens. The concern of תיקון העולם is that the slave might be found in the market and sold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who freed the slave in the Mishnah's case where the master made him collateral and then freed him.
Rav answers that the first master freed the slave.
The Gemara explains that as a matter of strict law, the slave owes nothing to the second master (the creditor).
The Gemara cites Rava's principle that sanctification (הקדש), leaven (חמץ), and manumission (שחרור) nullify prior liens.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's concern for תיקון העולם (the betterment of the world) is that the slave might be found in the market and sold, causing confusion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah continuation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah continuation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a second master calls a slave 'my slave,' the court forces him to free the slave, and the slave writes a bond for his value. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says only the emancipator writes the bond.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: the first Tanna requires the slave to write a bond for his value, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says only the emancipator writes.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute is about whether one is liable for damaging another's lien. It cites a parallel tradition that the same dispute applies to one who damages another's security.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: over what principle do the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dispute?
The Gemara answers: they dispute about one who damages another's lien — one holds he is liable, the other holds he is exempt.
A parallel tradition is cited: the case of one who damages another's lien is explicitly brought to the dispute of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis.

items.text: Ulla's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Ulla's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Ulla reinterprets the Mishnah: the second master freed the slave. The dispute is about whether damage that is not physically noticeable is considered damage. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds it is not damage, while the Sages hold it is.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that the second master freed the slave, and explains the dispute: the first master is compelled to free the slave and write a document for his value due to the reputation of freedom.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the slave does not write a document for his value; rather, the one who freed him writes it.
The Gemara resolves the dispute: they disagree about whether damage that is not physically noticeable (היזק שאינו ניכר) is considered damage; one holds it is damage, the other holds it is not.

items.text: Debate between Rav and Ulla
items.text_en: Debate between Rav and Ulla
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Ulla does not hold like Rav, and vice versa. Ulla argues that the second master is called 'his master,' not 'emancipator'; Rav argues the opposite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Ulla does not hold like Rav.
Ulla argues that the second master is called 'his master' (רַבּוֹ), not 'emancipator'.
The Gemara asks why Rav does not hold like Ulla.
Rav argues that the second master is called 'emancipator' (מְשַׁחְרֵר), not 'his master'.

items.text: Case of a field designated as collateral
items.text_en: Case of a field designated as collateral
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where one designates a field as collateral (אפותיקי) and it is washed away. Rabbi Yochanan says the creditor cannot collect from other property; the father of Shmuel says he can. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reconciles the dispute by specifying that the debtor said 'you shall have payment only from this.' A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a dispute: one who designates his field as אפותיקי (collateral) and it is washed away — Rabbi Yochanan says the creditor does not collect from other property, while Shmuel's father says he does.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling must be interpreted as a case where the debtor said 'you shall have payment only from this field.'
A baraita supports the distinction: if the debtor merely designated the field, the creditor collects from other property; but if he said 'you shall have payment only from this,' he does not.

items.text: Another baraita on אפותיקי for a creditor and a wife's ketubah
items.text_en: Another baraita on אפותיקי for a creditor and a wife's ketubah
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one designates a field as collateral for a creditor and a wife's ketubah, both collect from other property. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes: the creditor collects from other property, but the wife does not, because it is not her way to go to court.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that if one designates his field as אפותיקי (designated repayment) for a creditor and for a wife's ketubah, both collect from other property.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes: the creditor collects from other property, but the wife does not collect from other property.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains the reason: it is not the way of a woman to go to court, so the designated field is presumed to be her sole recourse.

items.text: Mishnah: Half-slave half-free person
items.text_en: Mishnah: Half-slave half-free person
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a person who is half-slave and half-free. Beit Hillel says he works for his master one day and for himself one day. Beit Shammai objects that this solves the master's problem but not his own, as he cannot marry a slavewoman (since half-free) nor a freewoman (since half-slave).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a half-slave half-free person and states Beit Hillel's ruling that he works for his master one day and for himself one day.
Beit Shammai objects that Beit Hillel's solution only addresses the master's interest but leaves the half-slave unable to marry either a slavewoman or a freewoman.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a slave is half-free, the court forces the master to free him entirely and the slave writes a note for half his value; Beit Hillel retracted to agree with Beit Shammai.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a half-free slave cannot be fully freed by cancellation, so the court forces the master to free him and the slave writes a note for half his value; Beit Hillel retracted to agree with Beit Shammai.

items.text: Tannaic dispute and Rabbah's explanation
items.text_en: Tannaic dispute and Rabbah's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Baraita: Rabbi says the slave acquires himself, the Sages say he does not. Rabbah explains the dispute is over a document: Rabbi derives from a hekesh (analogy) between document and money, while the Sages derive from a gezeirah shavah (verbal analogy) from a woman.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states a dispute: Rabbi says the slave acquires himself, the Sages say he does not.

Rabbah explains the dispute is over a document: Rabbi derives from a hekesh (analogy) between document and money, while the Sages derive from a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) from a woman; but regarding money, all agree the slave is acquired.

items.text: Attempt to frame the dispute as hekesh vs. gezeirah shavah
items.text_en: Attempt to frame the dispute as hekesh vs. gezeirah shavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether hekesh or gezeirah shavah is superior, but rejects this: everyone agrees gezeirah shavah is superior, but here it is refutable because a woman cannot be freed with money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi and the Sages is about whether הֶקֵּשׁ (analogy) or גְּזֵרָה שָׁוָה (verbal analogy) is the superior interpretive method.
The Gemara rejects this: everyone agrees that גְּזֵרָה שָׁוָה is superior, but here the גְּזֵרָה שָׁוָה is refutable because a woman cannot be freed with money, unlike a slave.

items.text: Rav Yosef's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says the dispute is over money: Rabbi derives from the verse that she is redeemed and not redeemed, while the Sages say the Torah speaks in human language; but regarding a document, all agree he does not acquire.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that the dispute is about money: Rabbi derives partial redemption from a verse, while the Sages say the Torah speaks in human language; but regarding a document, all agree that half-manumission is invalid.

items.text: Refutation of Rav Yosef and defense
items.text_en: Refutation of Rav Yosef and defense
items.desc_en: A challenge is brought from the Baraita that explicitly states the dispute is over a document, refuting Rav Yosef. Rav Yosef defends by saying the dispute applies to both, but the Baraita chose to teach about a document to show Rabbi's lenient power.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that explicitly states the dispute over a document, refuting Rav Yosef's position that the dispute is over money.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita implies that the dispute is only about a document, making Rav Yosef's refutation doubly problematic.
Rav Yosef defends himself by saying the dispute applies to both document and money, but the baraita chose to teach about a document to show Rabbi's lenient power.

The Gemara objects that if the baraita wanted to show power, it could have taught the dispute over money to show the Sages' power, but Rav Yosef's answer is that the power of leniency (התירא) is preferred.

items.text: Brayta analysis supporting Rabbah
items.text_en: Brayta analysis supporting Rabbah
items.desc_en: A Baraita is cited deriving from verses that partial redemption applies to money and document, and that a document is analogous to money for both full and half freedom, supporting Rabbah's view.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited deriving from the verse 'והפדה' that partial redemption applies to money and its equivalent.
The baraita extends the derivation to include a document (שטר) through a verbal analogy from divorce.
The baraita concludes by deriving that a document, like money, can effect half-freedom, supporting Rabbah's view.

items.text: Reconciling the Baraita with the opinions
items.text_en: Reconciling the Baraita with the opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for Rav Yosef after his refutation, the Baraita is Rabbi's view; for Rabbah, the beginning is unanimous and the end is Rabbi's. Rav Ashi says the entire Baraita is Rabbi. The Mishnah is then analyzed: for Rabbah it fits with money and all agree; for Rav Yosef it must be Rabbi's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rav Yosef after his refutation, the baraita is Rabbi's view; but for Rabbah, is the beginning unanimous and the end Rabbi's?
Rabbah answers: yes, the beginning is unanimous and the end is Rabbi's view.
Rav Ashi says the entire baraita is Rabbi's view.
The Gemara asks: for Rabbah, the Mishnah fits with money and all agree; for Rav Yosef, must it be only Rabbi's view and not the Sages?
Ravina begins to answer the question (the continuation is on the next daf).

items.text: Opening statement of the dispute
items.text_en: Opening statement of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the case of a slave owned by two partners, with a dispute between Rabbi and the Sages. The exact parameters of the dispute are not yet clarified.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the case of a slave owned by two partners, with a dispute between Rabbi and the Sages.

items.text: Rabbah's clarification of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbah's clarification of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the dispute applies only when one partner frees his half and leaves the other half untouched. But if he frees half and sells or gives away the other half, since the slave entirely leaves him, all agree the slave is free.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah clarifies that the dispute is only when one partner freed his half and left the other half unfreed, but if he freed his half and sold or gave away the other half, all agree the slave is acquired.

items.text: Abaye's challenge and resolution via baraitot
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge and resolution via baraitot
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah, arguing that the dispute applies even when the entire slave is freed, citing two contradictory baraitot. The Gemara initially suggests one follows Rabbi and the other the Sages, but then resolves that both follow the Sages: one where the master said 'all' and the other where he said 'half-half'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah by citing two contradictory baraitot about a master giving all his property to two slaves, implying the dispute applies even when the entire slave is freed.
The Gemara initially suggests that one baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the other follows the Sages.
The Gemara resolves that both baraitot follow the Sages: one where the master said 'all' and the other where he said 'half-half'.

items.text: Rejection of the resolution and new interpretation
items.text_en: Rejection of the resolution and new interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the resolution because the second baraita explicitly states 'if he said half-half they do not acquire', implying the first case is 'all'. It then reinterprets: the second baraita explains the first, and the Tanna teaches the second case to reveal that even in the first case (all) they do not acquire.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the second baraita's explicit statement 'if he said half-half they do not acquire' implies the first case is 'all', contradicting the previous resolution.
The Gemara reinterprets that the second baraita is explaining the first: 'even themselves do not acquire' — how? For example, if he said half-half.
The Gemara supports this interpretation with a logical argument: if the first case were 'all', then 'all they do not acquire' would be obvious, and 'half-half' would be unnecessary to state.

The Gemara resolves that the second baraita is taught to reveal the first case: lest you think the first case is 'half-half' but 'all' they acquire, it teaches the second case 'half-half' to imply the first is 'all' — and even so they do not acquire.

items.text: Alternative resolution: one document vs. two documents
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: one document vs. two documents
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another resolution: the contradiction is between a case with one document (where even 'all' does not work) and two documents (where 'all' works, but 'half-half' does not). The baraita is explained as referring to one document, but with two documents they acquire.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative resolution: the contradiction is between a case with one document (where even 'all' does not work) and two documents (where 'all' works, but 'half-half' does not).

The Gemara explains the baraita: the statement 'even themselves did not acquire' refers to a single document, but with two documents they acquire; however, if he said 'half-half', even with two documents they do not acquire.

items.text: Another resolution: simultaneous vs. sequential
items.text_en: Another resolution: simultaneous vs. sequential
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the contradiction is between simultaneous and sequential gifts. However, it raises a difficulty: the first recipient should acquire himself and then his fellow, but this is rejected, and the Gemara concludes with the earlier resolution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the contradiction is between a simultaneous gift (בבת אחת) and a sequential gift (בזה אחר זה).
The Gemara objects: the later recipient does not acquire himself because the first already acquired him, but the first should acquire himself and then his fellow.
The Gemara concludes that the earlier resolution (the distinction between one document and two documents) is the correct one.

items.text: Rav Ashi's distinction: 'my slaves' implies past status
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's distinction: 'my slaves' implies past status
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the baraita where they do not acquire is because the master called them 'my slaves', implying they are still slaves. Rafram objects that it could mean 'who were already slaves', but the Gemara supports Rav Ashi from a Mishnah where calling a slave 'my slave' does not prevent freedom, showing 'my slaves' refers to past status.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi distinguishes the baraita where they do not acquire because the master called them 'my slaves', implying they are still slaves.
Rafram objects that 'my slaves' could mean 'who were already slaves', referring to past status.
The Gemara supports Rav Ashi by citing a Mishnah where calling a slave 'my slave' does not prevent freedom, showing 'my slaves' refers to past status.

items.text: Practical implications: damages and marriage
items.text_en: Practical implications: damages and marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a half-free slave: if gored by an ox, compensation is split. It raises a question about marriage restrictions but dismisses it as not about prohibitions. It then cites a case of a half-free slave who kills, paying half the fine to his master.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the practical halacha for a half-free slave gored by an ox: compensation goes to the master on the master's day and to the slave on his own day.
The Gemara raises a hypothetical question about marriage restrictions: on the master's day the slave should marry a maidservant, on his own day a free woman.
The Gemara dismisses the question, stating that it is not discussing prohibitions (איסורא) but rather monetary laws.
The Gemara cites a baraita about a half-free slave who kills: he pays half the fine (קנס) to his master, confirming the principle of split compensation.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about half the ransom for heirs
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about half the ransom for heirs
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah gives half the ransom to the slave's heirs, given that the slave's time is split between his master and himself. It distinguishes cases where the principal is diminished (כליא קרנא) from those where it is not, and then addresses the views of Abaye and Rava regarding the payment for lost labor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah gives half the ransom to the slave's heirs, given that the slave's time is split between master and himself.
The Gemara distinguishes this case because the principal (the slave's value) is diminished (כליא קרנא).
The Gemara provides an example where the principal is not diminished: a blow to the hand that swells but eventually heals.

sub.text: Gemara's objection regarding Abaye and Rava
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection regarding Abaye and Rava
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this works for Abaye, who distinguishes between large and small lost labor payments, but for Rava, who only pays daily lost labor, the ox pays only for damage, not lost labor.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by suggesting either that a person struck the slave (not an ox), or that the Mishnah is a statement (מימרה) that Rava does not accept.

items.text: Inquiry: Does a slave pending manumission have a fine?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Does a slave pending manumission have a fine?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question whether a slave who is מעוכב גט שחרור (pending a bill of manumission) is subject to the fine (קנס) for being gored. It considers whether he is still called 'master' (אדון) and attempts to resolve the issue from the Mishnah about a half-slave, but the resolution is inconclusive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question whether a slave who is מעוכב גט שחרור (pending a bill of manumission) is subject to the fine (קנס) for being gored.
The Gemara considers whether the slave is still called 'master' (אדון) for the purpose of the fine, since the verse says 'he shall give silver to his master'.
The Gemara attempts to bring a proof from the Mishnah about a half-slave who was gored, where he pays half the fine to his master and half the ransom to his heirs.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the Mishnah follows the first Mishnah (which holds that a half-slave is fully a slave), not the later one.

items.text: Proof from the case of tooth and eye
items.text_en: Proof from the case of tooth and eye
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a slave who loses a tooth and an eye, arguing that if the slave has a fine, the master would pay the slave himself, which is absurd. It then distinguishes between the views of Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Tarfon, and Rabbi Akiva regarding whether a slave needs a bill of manumission, and concludes with the ruling of the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a slave who loses a tooth and an eye, arguing that if the slave has a fine (קנס), the master would pay the slave himself, which is absurd.

The Gemara answers that the baraita follows the opinion that a slave does not need a bill of manumission (גט שחרור), listing the positions of Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Tarfon, and Rabbi Akiva.
The Sages who adjudicate before the Sages rule that Rabbi Tarfon's view applies to tooth and eye, while Rabbi Akiva's view applies to other limbs.
The Gemara objects to calling it a קנס (fine) since it is derived from verses, and corrects that it is a מדרש חכמים (rabbinic exposition).

items.text: Inquiry: Does a slave pending manumission eat terumah?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Does a slave pending manumission eat terumah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a slave who is מעוכב גט שחרור may eat terumah, based on the verse 'קנין כספו'. It brings a statement from Rav Mesharshiya about a mixture of a priest's child and a slave's child, but distinguishes that case because there the slave is definitely a קנין כספו, unlike here.
