sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a slave whose manumission document is delayed (מעוכב גט שחרור) may eat תרומה (priestly portion), based on the verse 'קנין כספו' (his property acquisition).

Rav Mesharshiya brings a case where a priest's child and a slave's child are mixed, and they eat תרומה (priestly portion) and share one portion on the threshing floor, and when they grow up they free each other.
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing that in Rav Mesharshiya's case the slave is definitely a קנין כספו (property acquisition) if identified, whereas here the slave is not a קנין כספו at all.

items.text: Inquiry: Can a slave be sold for the purpose of a fine?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Can a slave be sold for the purpose of a fine?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a master can sell his slave for the purpose of the fine (קנס) that might be imposed if the slave is gored. It considers the views of Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis regarding the acquisition of something not yet in existence, and raises the uncertainty of whether the goring will occur and whether payment will be made.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: if a master sells his slave specifically for the purpose of the fine (קנס) that may be imposed if the slave is gored, is the sale valid or not?
The Gemara notes that this inquiry applies both according to Rabbi Meir and according to the Rabbis, as each position raises its own difficulty.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir's principle of acquiring something not yet in existence (דבר שלא בא לעולם) applies only to items that will certainly come, like dates from a palm tree.
The Gemara raises the uncertainty: who can guarantee that the slave will be gored at all?
The Gemara further questions: even if the goring occurs, what proof is there that the owner will actually pay the fine?

items.text: Question about the Rabbis' position on selling a slave with a lien
items.text_en: Question about the Rabbis' position on selling a slave with a lien
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: according to the Rabbis who hold that one cannot transfer an object not yet in existence, would they also invalidate the sale of a slave who is already present? The question is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: according to the Rabbis who hold that one cannot transfer an object not yet in existence, would they also invalidate the sale of a slave who is already present? The question is left unresolved.

items.text: Proof from the verse 'ויליד בית' regarding acquisition
items.text_en: Proof from the verse 'ויליד בית' regarding acquisition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba brings a proof from the Torah: the extra word 'ויליד בית' teaches that even a slave without monetary value eats terumah, and the juxtaposition with 'קנין כספו' shows that a purchased slave also eats even if worthless. This implies that a slave sold with a lien is still considered a slave.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba introduces a proof from the verse 'ויליד בית' (a homeborn slave) to argue that even a slave without monetary value eats terumah.
The Gemara explains that without the extra word 'ויליד בית', one might have thought only a slave of monetary value eats terumah; the word teaches that even a worthless slave eats.

The Gemara resolves the proof: the juxtaposition of 'קנין כספו' (purchased slave) with 'ויליד בית' (homeborn slave) teaches that both eat terumah even if worthless, implying a slave sold with a lien is still a slave.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding a slave sold for a fine
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding a slave sold for a fine
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if a slave sold with a lien is considered sold, then all slaves could be sold for a fine. The answer is that there is a slave who is a treifah (mortally wounded), which cannot be sold for a fine because it is not fit for work.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if a slave sold for a fine is considered sold, then every slave would be eligible for such a sale.
The Gemara answers: there is a slave who is a טריפה (mortally wounded) and thus unfit for work, so not all slaves can be sold for a fine.
The Gemara objects: but such a slave is still fit to stand before his master (i.e., perform minimal service).
The Gemara resolves: the case involves a slave who is a מנול (maimed) or מוכה שחין (afflicted with boils), who is completely unfit for any service.

items.text: Dilemma about betrothal by a half-slave half-free man
items.text_en: Dilemma about betrothal by a half-slave half-free man
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if a half-slave half-free man betroths a free woman, is it valid? The Gemara compares it to a free man betrothing half a woman, where the issue is either she is not fit for him entirely or he left part of his acquisition. The question remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if a half-slave half-free man betroths a free woman, what is the halacha?

The Gemara considers the first possibility: if a free man betrothing half a woman is valid because she is fit for the whole man, here the woman is not fit for the whole slave, so betrothal might be invalid.

The Gemara considers the second possibility: if a free man betrothing half a woman is invalid because he left part of his acquisition, here the slave left no part of his acquisition, so betrothal might be valid.

items.text: Proof from the law of a half-slave half-free who kills
items.text_en: Proof from the law of a half-slave half-free who kills
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that betrothal is valid from the case where a half-slave half-free man kills someone: he pays half the fine to his master and half the ransom to his heirs. If betrothal were invalid, how would he have heirs? Rav Ada bar Ahava answers that the case is where he was made treifah, and 'his heirs' means himself. Rava rejects this with two objections, concluding that he is eligible to receive but does not actually get it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita as proof: a half-slave half-free man who kills pays half the fine to his master and half the ransom to his heirs, implying he has heirs, which would require valid betrothal.
Rav Ada bar Ahava answers that the case is where the slave was made a טריפה (mortally wounded animal), and 'his heirs' refers to himself, not actual heirs.
Rava raises two objections: the baraita says 'his heirs' (plural), not 'himself', and the ransom (כופר) is only paid after death, so the slave cannot receive it himself.
Rava resolves the difficulty by stating that the half-slave is merely eligible (ראוי) to receive the ransom, but in practice he does not actually get it.

items.text: Dispute about betrothal of a half-slave half-free woman
items.text_en: Dispute about betrothal of a half-slave half-free woman
items.desc_en: Rava and Rabba bar Rav Huna initially rule that a half-slave half-free woman's betrothal is invalid, like betrothing half a woman. Rav Chisda objects that the cases differ because here he did not leave part of his acquisition. Rabba bar Rav Huna then reverses his ruling, citing a principle that one only understands Torah after stumbling. Rav Sheishet agrees with the original ruling and addresses a potential objection from the term 'me'oreset' in the context of a designated slave woman.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a half-slave half-free woman's betrothal is invalid, analogizing it to betrothing half a woman.
Rabba bar Rav Huna publicly teaches the same ruling as Rava.
Rav Chisda objects that the cases are not analogous: in the half-woman case the man left part of his acquisition, but here the slave is entirely his acquisition.

Rabba bar Rav Huna retracts his ruling, citing the principle that one only understands Torah after stumbling, and now rules that the betrothal is valid because he did not leave part of his acquisition.
Rav Sheishet agrees with the original ruling that the betrothal is invalid.
A hypothetical objector argues that the term 'me'oreset' (betrothed) in the Torah regarding a designated slave woman implies that a half-slave half-free woman can be betrothed.
Rav Sheishet deflects the objection by citing Rabbi Yishmael, who interprets the verse as referring to a Canaanite slave woman betrothed to a Hebrew slave.
The Gemara objects that a Canaanite slave woman is also not capable of betrothal.
The Gemara resolves that the term 'me'oreset' in both contexts means 'designated' rather than 'betrothed', so no objection stands.

items.text: Case of levirate marriage for a half-slave half-free woman
items.text_en: Case of levirate marriage for a half-slave half-free woman
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda presents a case: a half-slave half-free woman betrothed to Reuven, then freed, then betrothed to Shimon, and both die – she must undergo yibbum with Levi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda presents a case: a half-slave half-free woman betrothed to Reuven, then freed, then betrothed to Shimon, and both die – she must undergo yibbum with Levi.

items.text: Opening dilemma about a half-slave half-free woman
items.text_en: Opening dilemma about a half-slave half-free woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a logical dilemma: if a half-slave half-free woman is betrothed to Reuven and then to Shimon, the betrothal cannot be valid for both, leading to a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a logical dilemma: if a half-slave half-free woman is betrothed to Reuven and then to Shimon, the betrothal cannot be valid for both, leading to a contradiction.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Yosef bar Chama and Rabbi Zeira
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Yosef bar Chama and Rabbi Zeira
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama quoting Rav Nachman says the first betrothal is void, while Rabbi Zeira quoting Rav Nachman says the first betrothal is completed.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute about a half-slave half-free woman who was betrothed to Reuven, freed, and then betrothed to Shimon.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Chama quoting Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama quoting Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama in the name of Rav Nachman rules that the first betrothal is void (retroactively annulled).
Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Nachman rules that the first betrothal is completed (valid and not retroactively annulled).

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's proof and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's proof and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira supports his view with a verse about a freed slave being liable for adultery. Abaye objects based on the school of Rabbi Yishmael, but resolves that the case involves freedom and re-betrothal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira argues that his view is supported by the verse 'לֹא יוּמְתוּ כִּי לֹא חוּפָּשָׁה' (they shall not be put to death because she was not freed), implying that if she were freed, she would be executed for adultery.

Abaye objects: according to the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael, who interprets the verse as referring to a Canaanite slavewoman betrothed to a Hebrew slave, would she also be executed if freed?
Abaye resolves the objection: the verse must be understood as referring to a case where she was freed and then re-betrothed, and the same applies to Rabbi Zeira's case.

items.text: Story of a half-slave woman and its interpretation
items.text_en: Story of a half-slave woman and its interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Katina quoting Rabbi Yitzchak recounts a case where the court forced the master to free a half-slave woman. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains they treated her as ownerless property.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Katina quoting Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Katina quoting Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Katina in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak recounts a case where the court forced the master to free a half-slave woman, aligning with Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's view that procreation is a universal obligation.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the alignment with Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, explaining that the court treated the woman as ownerless property (הפקר) rather than enforcing procreation.

items.text: Mishnah: Selling a slave to non-Jews
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling a slave to non-Jews
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who sells his slave to non-Jews or outside the land frees the slave.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who sells his slave to non-Jews or outside the land frees the slave.

items.text: Gemara: Details of selling to non-Jews
items.text_en: Gemara: Details of selling to non-Jews
items.desc_en: The Tosefta rules the slave goes free and needs a bill of manumission. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes whether the master wrote an 'ono' (condition). Rav Sheshet explains 'ono' as a written clause.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta rules that a slave sold to a non-Jew goes free and needs a bill of manumission from the first master, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes whether the master wrote an 'ono' (condition) which itself serves as manumission.
Rav Sheshet explains that 'ono' refers to a written clause stating that if the slave escapes from the non-Jew, the master has no further claim on him.

items.text: Borrowing on a slave from a non-Jew and the meaning of 'nimus'
items.text_en: Borrowing on a slave from a non-Jew and the meaning of 'nimus'
items.desc_en: A baraita says if a Jew borrows money from a non-Jew using the slave as collateral and the non-Jew makes a 'nimus', the slave goes free. Rav Huna bar Yehuda says 'nimus' means a lien. Rav Sheshet objects and says it means a fixed time. The Gemara resolves contradictions regarding time and produce.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that if a Jew borrows money from a non-Jew using a slave as collateral, once the non-Jew makes a 'nimus' (a certain action), the slave goes free.
The Gemara asks what the term 'nimus' means in this context.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda explains that 'nimus' means a lien (משכנתא / mortgage) on the slave.

Rav Sheshet objects by citing a baraita about sharecroppers and fields where 'nimus' is used regarding produce, arguing that a field cannot have a lien, and therefore 'nimus' must mean a fixed time (זְמַן).
The Gemara raises a contradiction between two cases involving 'nimus' as a fixed time.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when the fixed time has arrived and when it has not yet arrived.
The Gemara questions why the case of the slave, where the time has arrived, needs to be stated separately.
The Gemara resolves that both cases refer to when the time has not arrived, and the distinction is between a lien on the body of the slave versus a lien on the produce of the field.

items.text: Alternative explanation for the Mishnah
items.text_en: Alternative explanation for the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation for the Mishnah's case: where the borrower intended to give a pledge but did not actually do so.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation for the Mishnah's case: where the borrower intended to give a pledge but did not actually do so.

items.text: Contradiction from a baraita about a slave seized for debt
items.text_en: Contradiction from a baraita about a slave seized for debt
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a slave was seized for debt, he does not go free. The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about a gentile king seizing a Jew's granary, where if it was for debt, the owner must tithe. The Gemara resolves that the cases differ because in the granary case the owner retains ownership.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that if a slave was seized for debt or acquired by a סיקריקון (a royal grant), he does not go free.
The Gemara challenges: In the case of debt, does the slave not go free?
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about a gentile king seizing a Jew's granary: if for debt, the owner must tithe; if by force, he is exempt.
The Gemara resolves that the cases differ because in the granary case the owner retains ownership (the land is rooted to him), so he must tithe.

items.text: Proof from Rav's ruling about selling to a gentile's garrison
items.text_en: Proof from Rav's ruling about selling to a gentile's garrison
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings Rav's statement that selling a slave to a gentile's garrison frees the slave, and explains that the seller could have appeased the gentile but did not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings Rav's ruling that selling a slave to a gentile's garrison frees the slave, as supporting evidence for the previous discussion.
The Gemara explains that in Rav's case, the seller could have appeased the gentile but did not, distinguishing it from other cases.

items.text: Rav's statement elaborated
items.text_en: Rav's statement elaborated
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats Rav's statement and explains that the seller should have appeased the gentile but did not, so the slave goes free.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara repeats Rav's statement that selling a slave to a gentile for a permanent sale (פרהנג) results in the slave's freedom.
The Gemara explains that the seller should have appeased the gentile to prevent the sale, but failed to do so, thus the slave goes free.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's questions about partial sales and special cases
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's questions about partial sales and special cases
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about selling a slave for thirty days, or excluding his work, or excluding mitzvot, or excluding Shabbatot and festivals, or selling to a ger toshav, a Jewish apostate, or a Cuthean. The Gemara resolves that a ger toshav is like a gentile, while a Cuthean and apostate are disputed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya raises a series of questions about selling a slave for thirty days, excluding his work, excluding mitzvot, excluding Shabbatot and festivals, or selling to a ger toshav, a Jewish apostate, or a Cuthean.
The Gemara resolves that a ger toshav is like a gentile, while a Cuthean and an apostate are disputed, with some considering them like a gentile and others like a Jew.

items.text: Slave who throws himself into a gentile army
items.text_en: Slave who throws himself into a gentile army
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami asks about a slave who throws himself into a gentile army and cannot be retrieved by Jewish or gentile law. Rabbi Yirmeya tells Rabbi Zerika to check his baraita, and finds that for a house seized by a gentile, the owner may take payment. The Gemara questions whether the same applies to a slave, and Rabbi Ami sends a ruling that the slave may take payment.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami asks whether a master may take payment for a slave who threw himself into a gentile army and cannot be retrieved by any law.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zerika's discovery
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zerika's discovery
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya tells Rabbi Zerika to check his baraita, and he finds a baraita that for a house seized by a gentile, the owner may take payment because he is like one rescuing from them.

The Gemara objects that the case of a house may be different because one cannot live without a house, so he would not sell it willingly, but a slave is not essential and he might come to sell him willingly.

Rabbi Ami sends a ruling that for a slave who threw himself into a gentile army and cannot be retrieved, the master may take payment and register the sale in gentile courts because he is like one rescuing from them.

items.text: Penalty for selling a slave to a gentile
items.text_en: Penalty for selling a slave to a gentile
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the seller is fined up to one hundred times the slave's value. The Gemara questions whether this is exact, and brings a proof from Resh Lakish about selling a large animal to a gentile, where the fine is ten times. The Gemara distinguishes between a slave (who is constantly removed from mitzvot) and an animal (which returns). An alternative version reverses the fines, and the Gemara explains that the difference is due to the rarity of selling a slave.

sub.desc_en: רבי יהושע בן לוי (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) states that one who sells his slave to a gentile is penalized up to one hundred times the slave's value.
The Gemara questions whether the stated amount is exact or an exaggeration.
The Gemara brings a proof from Reish Lakish that selling a large animal to a gentile incurs a penalty of up to ten times its value.
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing a slave because each day the owner removes him from mitzvot, warranting a higher penalty.
An alternative version reverses the fines: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says ten times, and Reish Lakish says one hundred times.
The Gemara explains that a slave is different because he does not return to the master after redemption.
The Gemara objects: if the reason for the higher penalty on an animal is that it returns, then the penalty should be only one additional amount, not tenfold.
The Gemara resolves that selling a slave is an uncommon matter, and the Sages did not decree a severe penalty for uncommon matters.

items.text: Inheritance of the fine if the seller dies
items.text_en: Inheritance of the fine if the seller dies
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Assi whether if the seller dies, his son is fined. The Gemara compares it to the case of a firstborn whose ear was slit, where the son is fined because it is a Torah prohibition, but here it is only rabbinic.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Assi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Assi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Assi whether if the seller dies, the court imposes a fine (קנס) on his son after him.

Rabbi Assi distinguishes: in the case of a firstborn whose ear was slit, the son is fined because it is a Torah prohibition (איסורא דאורייתא), but here the prohibition is only rabbinic (איסורא דרבנן), so the son is not fined.

items.text: Gemara's question about penalizing the estate
items.text_en: Gemara's question about penalizing the estate
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if a person performed forbidden labor during Chol HaMoed and died, do the rabbis penalize his estate or only him? The question hinges on whether the penalty attaches to the person or to his property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if a person performed forbidden labor during Chol HaMoed and died, do the rabbis penalize his estate or only him?

items.text: Proof from the law of a field in the Sabbatical year
items.text_en: Proof from the law of a field in the Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a field that was improved during the Sabbatical year, and Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina's ruling that if the owner died, his son may sow it. This shows that the penalty applies only to the person, not to his heirs.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's ruling
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina cites a baraita about a field worked during the Sabbatical year and rules that if the owner died, his son may sow it, proving the penalty applies only to the person, not his estate.
Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina rules that if the owner improved the field and died, his son may sow it, proving that the rabbinic penalty applies only to the person, not to his heirs.

items.text: Proof from the case of one who defiled another's pure items
items.text_en: Proof from the case of one who defiled another's pure items
items.desc_en: Abaye states a tradition: if one defiled another's pure items and died, the rabbis do not penalize his son, because the damage is not perceptible and the penalty is only on the person.

sub.desc_en: Abaye adds that if one rendered a friend's pure items impure and died, the rabbis do not penalize his son, because the damage is not overt and the penalty is personal.

items.text: Baraita on selling a slave abroad and the dispute with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Baraita on selling a slave abroad and the dispute with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who sells his slave abroad goes free and requires a second writ of manumission. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between saying 'to an Antiochian' (not freed) and 'to an Antiochian in Antioch' (freed). A contradiction with another baraita is resolved by distinguishing whether the buyer has a house or just lodging in Eretz Yisrael.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who sells his slave abroad goes free and requires a second writ of manumission, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishing between saying 'to an Antiochian' (not freed) and 'to an Antiochian in Antioch' (freed).
The gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that says 'to an Antiochian' (freed) and 'to an Antiochian dwelling in Lod' (not freed), opposite of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling.
The gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing whether the buyer has a house (permanent residence) or just lodging (temporary stay) in Eretz Yisrael.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about a Babylonian who married in Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about a Babylonian who married in Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a Babylonian who married in Eretz Yisrael and brought slaves, intending to return. The Gemara explores the question from both sides of a prior dispute: whether the wife or husband has the upper hand, and whether the slaves are considered his or hers.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a Babylonian who married in Eretz Yisrael, brought slaves, and intends to return: what is the status of the slaves?
The Gemara frames the question from both sides of a prior dispute: according to the view that the wife has the upper hand, and according to the view that the husband has the upper hand.

The Gemara explores the question according to the view that the wife has the upper hand: are the slaves considered hers because the law favors her, or are they considered his because he has a right to their usufruct?

The Gemara explores the question according to the view that the husband has the upper hand: are the slaves considered his because the law favors him, or are they considered hers because he does not acquire their bodies (גופייהו)?
The Gemara concludes with תֵּיקוּ (the question stands unresolved).

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's tradition about a slave who followed his master to Syria
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's tradition about a slave who followed his master to Syria
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: a slave who followed his master to Syria and was sold there goes free. A contradiction with Rabbi Chiya's baraita is resolved by distinguishing whether the master intended to return. The Gemara then clarifies the correct version of the baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a slave who followed his master to Syria and was sold there goes free.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Chiya's baraita that the slave loses his right to freedom.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing whether the master intended to return to Eretz Yisrael.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the baraita's wording
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the baraita's wording
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the baraita's use of 'יוצא' (goes out), noting that it contradicts the Mishnah's rule that not everyone may take a slave out of Eretz Yisrael.

sub.text: Gemara's corrected version of the baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's corrected version of the baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara corrects the baraita: the slave 'went out' (not 'goes out'), and the ruling depends on the master's intent to return.

items.text: Rav Anan's tradition about Shmuel's two rulings
items.text_en: Rav Anan's tradition about Shmuel's two rulings
items.desc_en: Rav Anan heard two rulings from Shmuel: one about the slave sold abroad, and another about selling a field in the Jubilee year. Rav Yosef deduces from a baraita that the sale of a slave abroad is not reversed, and that Shmuel's ruling about the field means the sale is void and money returns.

sub.desc_en: Rav Anan reports that he heard two rulings from Mar Shmuel: one about the slave sold abroad, and another about selling a field in the Jubilee year itself, where Rav says it is sold and reverts, and Shmuel says it is not sold at all.
Rav Anan states that in one of the rulings the sale is reversed and money returns, and in the other it is not reversed, but he does not know which is which.
Rav Yosef deduces from a baraita that the sale of a slave abroad is not reversed, so Shmuel's ruling about the field means it is not sold and money returns.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rav Anan's ruling and the penalty on the buyer
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rav Anan's ruling and the penalty on the buyer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Anan's ruling about a slave sold abroad, comparing it to a case of betrothal. Abaye asks why the buyer is penalized rather than the seller, and Rav Yosef responds with a proverb. The Gemara concludes that the penalty is imposed where the prohibition lies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Anan was unaware of the baraita and compares his ruling to the dispute between Rav and Shmuel about one who betroths his sister.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef why the buyer is penalized rather than the seller.
Rav Yosef responds with a proverb about the mouse and the hole, and Abaye challenges the analogy.
The Gemara concludes that the penalty is imposed where the prohibition lies.

items.text: Case of a slave fleeing from abroad to Eretz Yisrael and the derivation from Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya
items.text_en: Case of a slave fleeing from abroad to Eretz Yisrael and the derivation from Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya
items.desc_en: A slave flees from outside the land to Eretz Yisrael. Rabbi Ammi instructs the master to write a bill of sale and a writ of manumission, citing Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya's teaching. The Gemara explains the derivation: the verse 'Do not return a slave to his master' refers to a slave who fled from abroad to Eretz Yisrael, as per Rabbi Achai's interpretation.

sub.desc_en: A slave flees from abroad to Eretz Yisrael; Rabbi Ammi instructs the master to write a bill of sale and a writ of manumission, citing Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya's teaching.
A baraita is cited, interpreting the verse 'Do not return a slave to his master' as referring to a slave who fled from abroad to Eretz Yisrael.
Rabbi Yoshiya questions the verse's wording and concludes it speaks of a master who sells his slave abroad.
Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya questions the verse's wording and resolves that it speaks of a slave who fled from abroad to Eretz Yisrael.

items.text: Another baraita: Rabbi's interpretation about a slave bought for manumission
items.text_en: Another baraita: Rabbi's interpretation about a slave bought for manumission
items.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi's view that the verse 'Do not return a slave to his master' refers to a slave bought on condition of manumission. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the condition: the buyer writes that upon acquisition, the slave is immediately self-acquired.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that the verse 'Do not return a slave to his master' is interpreted by Rabbi as referring to a slave bought on condition of manumission.
The Gemara asks: What are the circumstances of this case?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains: The buyer writes to the slave that upon acquisition, the slave is immediately self-acquired.

items.text: Rav Chisda's correspondence with the Kutim about a fugitive slave and Abaye's donkey
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's correspondence with the Kutim about a fugitive slave and Abaye's donkey
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda demands the return of his slave who fled to the Kutim, but they cite the verse 'Do not return a slave'. He counters with the verse about returning lost property, and they respond with the same verse. He then explains that verse applies only to a slave fleeing from abroad, per Rabbi Achai. The Gemara notes he cited that interpretation because it was persuasive to them. Then Abaye's donkey is held by Kutim; they demand a sign, and he provides one, but they mock him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda's slave fled to the Kutim, and he demands its return.
The Kutim cite the verse 'Do not return a slave to his master' to refuse the demand.
Rav Chisda counters with the verse about returning lost property, implying the slave is lost property.
The Kutim insist on the explicit prohibition against returning a slave.
Rav Chisda explains that the prohibition applies only to a slave fleeing from outside the Land of Israel, per Rabbi Achai bar Rabbi Yoshiya's interpretation.
The Gemara explains that Rav Chisda cited Rabbi Achai's interpretation because it was persuasive to the Kutim.
Abaye's donkey was taken by the Kutim, and he demands its return.
The Kutim ask Abaye to provide a identifying sign for the donkey.
Abaye provides the sign that the donkey's belly is white.
The Kutim mock Abaye, saying that all donkeys have white bellies, so the sign is useless, but they return it out of respect for him.

items.text: Mishnah: Limits on redeeming captives and the Gemara's inquiry into the rationale
items.text_en: Mishnah: Limits on redeeming captives and the Gemara's inquiry into the rationale
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that captives are not redeemed for more than their value, and they are not helped to escape, for the sake of tikkun haolam. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says it is for the captives' own benefit. The Gemara asks whether the reason is to avoid burdening the community or to prevent captives from being taken more often. It cites Levi bar Darga who redeemed his daughter for a large sum, but Abaye questions whether this was with rabbinic approval. The Gemara then clarifies the difference between the two opinions: when only one captive is involved.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that captives are not redeemed for more than their value, and they are not helped to escape, for the sake of tikkun haolam.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel gives an alternative reason: it is for the captives' own benefit.
The Gemara inquires whether the mishnah's reason of tikkun haolam is to avoid burdening the community or to prevent captives from being taken more often.
The Gemara cites the case of Levi bar Darga who redeemed his daughter for thirteen thousand gold dinars, as potential evidence.
Abaye objects that we do not know whether Levi bar Darga acted with rabbinic approval or against it.
The Gemara clarifies the practical difference between the two opinions: when only one captive is involved.

items.text: Story of Rav Ilish and the daughters of Rav Nachman who were captured
items.text_en: Story of Rav Ilish and the daughters of Rav Nachman who were captured
items.desc_en: Rav Ilish is troubled by a verse about finding no righteous women, given Rav Nachman's daughters. He causes them to be captured, and he is also captured. A man who understands bird language hears a raven and then a dove telling him to escape. He first doubts the raven but trusts the dove. He then checks if the daughters remain faithful; overhearing them in the latrine, he learns they want their captors to distance them so they might be redeemed. He escapes miraculously, but the bird-interpreter is killed. Upon return, he says the daughters practiced witchcraft.

sub.desc_en: The gemara narrates that Rav Nachman's daughters were cooking with their hands, troubling Rav Ilish who then caused them and himself to be captured.
A man who understood bird language interpreted a raven's call telling Rav Ilish to flee, but Rav Ilish doubted the raven as a false messenger.
A dove then called the same message, and Rav Ilish trusted it because the congregation of Israel is compared to a dove, so he decided to check on the daughters' faithfulness.
Rav Ilish overheard the daughters in the latrine saying they wanted their captors to distance them so they might be redeemed, confirming their faithfulness.
Rav Ilish escaped miraculously while the bird interpreter was killed, and upon return he said the daughters practiced witchcraft.

items.text: Mishnah: Not buying sacred scrolls from non-Jews beyond their value
items.text_en: Mishnah: Not buying sacred scrolls from non-Jews beyond their value
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one should not buy Torah scrolls, tefillin, or mezuzot from non-Jews for more than their value, to avoid encouraging theft or desecration.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah rules that one may not buy Torah scrolls, tefillin, or mezuzot from non-Jews for more than their market value.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not purchase books from non-Jews beyond their market value, due to tikkun ha'olam.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not purchase books from non-Jews beyond their market value, due to tikkun ha'olam.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Budya asks Rav Ashi if the Mishnah implies that a Torah scroll found with a non-Jew may be read, but Rav Nachman states a tradition: a scroll written by a heretic is burned, by a non-Jew is stored, and found with a non-Jew is disputed.

sub.text: Rav Budya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Budya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Budya asks Rav Ashi whether the Mishnah's rule that one may buy books from non-Jews at market price implies that a Torah scroll found with a non-Jew may be read, or whether it must be stored away.
Rav Nachman states a tradition: a Torah scroll written by a heretic is burned, by a non-Jew is stored, and one found with a non-Jew is disputed whether to store or read.

items.text: Contradictory baraitot
items.text_en: Contradictory baraitot
items.desc_en: Three contradictory baraitot are cited regarding a Torah scroll written by a non-Jew: one says burn, one says store, one says read from it.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita rules that a Torah scroll written by a non-Jew must be burned.
The second baraita rules that such a scroll must be stored away (genizah).
The third baraita permits reading from such a scroll.

items.text: Resolution of contradictions
items.text_en: Resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradictions: the baraita that says burn follows Rabbi Eliezer, who assumes a non-Jew's intent is for idolatry; the one that says store follows the baraita of Rav Hamnuna, which disqualifies scrolls written by various individuals; the one that says read follows the baraita allowing purchase of scrolls from non-Jews if written properly, citing a case with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita requiring burning follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that a non-Jew's default intent is for idolatry.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita requiring storage follows the baraita of Rav Hamnuna, which disqualifies scrolls written by various individuals based on the principle of 'וקשרתם' (and you shall bind them) and 'וכתבתם' (and you shall write them).
The Gemara resolves that the baraita permitting reading follows the baraita that allows purchasing scrolls from non-Jews if written properly, citing a case with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires the hide to be processed for the sake of the scroll but not the writing itself. It cites a baraita where he requires processing for the sake of the scroll. Rabba bar Shmuel and Rav Ashi explain that the case involves a convert who reverted due to fear, not a heretic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires processing (עיבוד) for the sake of the scroll but not the writing itself.
A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel requires processing (עיבוד) for the sake of the scroll, but does not mention writing for its sake.
Rabba bar Shmuel answers that the case involves a convert who reverted to his former ways, but the Gemara objects that such a person is certainly a heretic (מין).
Rav Ashi resolves that the convert reverted out of fear (of persecution), not out of heresy, so the writing is valid.

items.text: Maximum price and anecdote about tefillin
items.text_en: Maximum price and anecdote about tefillin
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one may pay up to a tarp'ak (an istira) for books. An anecdote is told about a non-Jewish woman who brought tefillin straps to Abaye, who treated them dismissively and later regretted it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one may raise the price paid for sacred books up to a tarp'ak.
The Gemara asks what a tarp'ak is.
Rav Sheshet answers that a tarp'ak is an istira (a coin).
An anecdote is told about a non-Jewish woman who brought tefillin straps to Abaye, who dismissed them and had them thrown into the river.
Abaye expresses regret for having treated the tefillin straps with such contempt in her presence.

items.text: Mishnah: Divorce due to bad reputation or vow
items.text_en: Mishnah: Divorce due to bad reputation or vow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a man who divorces his wife due to a bad reputation or a vow may not remarry her. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between vows known to the public and those not. Rabbi Meir distinguishes between vows requiring a sage's inquiry and those not. Rabbi Elazar explains the reason. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda cites a case where the sages permitted remarriage for tikkun ha'olam.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule: a man who divorces his wife due to a bad reputation or a vow may not remarry her.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between a vow known to the public (which forbids remarriage) and one not known (which permits it).
Rabbi Meir distinguishes between a vow requiring a sage's inquiry (forbidding remarriage) and one that does not (permitting it).
Rabbi Elazar explains the reason: the sages forbade remarriage in one case only because of the other.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda cites a case in Tzidon where the sages permitted remarriage for tikkun ha'olam (the betterment of the world).

items.text: Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman states that the Mishnah's ruling applies only if the husband explicitly said he is divorcing her due to a bad reputation.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman clarifies that the Mishnah's prohibition on remarrying a wife divorced due to a bad reputation applies only if the husband explicitly stated 'Because of a bad reputation I am divorcing you.'

items.text: Two versions of Rav Nachman's statement on the husband's declaration
items.text_en: Two versions of Rav Nachman's statement on the husband's declaration
items.desc_en: Two versions of Rav Nachman's statement are presented: one holds that the husband must say he is divorcing her because of the bad reputation or the vow, as the reason is to prevent her from causing a scandal (קלקולא); the other holds he must say it so that Jewish women will not be promiscuous in sexual matters and vows.

sub.text: First version of Rav Nachman's statement
sub.text_en: First version of Rav Nachman's statement
sub.desc_en: Presents the first version of Rav Nachman's statement: the husband must say he is divorcing her because of the vow, since the reason is to prevent her from causing a scandal (קלקולא).

sub.text: Second version of Rav Nachman's statement via Rav Yosef bar Minyomei
sub.text_en: Second version of Rav Nachman's statement via Rav Yosef bar Minyomei
sub.desc_en: Presents the second version of Rav Nachman's statement: the husband must say he is divorcing her because of the bad reputation and the vow, so that Jewish women will not be promiscuous in sexual matters and vows.

items.text: Baraitot supporting each version: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi
items.text_en: Baraitot supporting each version: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi
items.desc_en: A baraita supports the first version, citing Rabbi Meir's reasoning that the prohibition against remarrying is to prevent the get from being retroactively invalidated if she remarries and the husband claims ignorance. Another baraita supports the second version, citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's reasoning that the prohibition is to prevent promiscuity.

sub.desc_en: The gemara announces that baraitot support both versions of Rav Yosef bar Minyomei's statement.
A baraita citing Rabbi Meir explains that the prohibition against remarrying is to prevent the get from being retroactively invalidated if the husband claims ignorance after she remarries.
A baraita citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi explains that the prohibition is to prevent promiscuity in forbidden relations and vows.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's distinction and the Sages' objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's distinction and the Sages' objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between a vow known to many (which prohibits remarriage) and one not known (which permits it). Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains his source from the Gibeonites. The Sages reject this, arguing that the Gibeonites' oath was invalid because they lied, and the Israelites spared them only for the sanctification of God's name.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states a distinction: a vow known to many prohibits remarriage, but one not known permits it.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains Rabbi Yehuda's source: the Gibeonites' oath, as cited in the verse about the Israelite leaders' oath.
The Sages reject the analogy, arguing that the Gibeonites' oath was invalid because they lied, and the Israelites spared them only for the sanctification of God's name.

items.text: Dispute over the number of people constituting 'many'
items.text_en: Dispute over the number of people constituting 'many'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yitzchak dispute the minimum number for 'many' (רבים) regarding a vow: Rav Nachman says three, based on the word 'days' (two) and 'many' (three); Rabbi Yitzchak says ten, based on the word 'congregation' (עדה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the minimum number of people that constitutes 'many' (רבים) in the context of Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about a vow known to many?
Rav Nachman answers that 'many' means three people.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers that 'many' means ten people.
Rav Nachman derives three from the verse 'יָמִים' (days, implying two) and 'רַבִּים' (many, adding one more to make three).
Rabbi Yitzchak derives ten from the word 'עֵדָה' (congregation), which in the Torah refers to ten people.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar on 'a vow that requires inquiry'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar on 'a vow that requires inquiry'
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Elazar says the Sages only prohibited remarriage for a vow that 'requires' inquiry because of one that 'does not require' inquiry. The Gemara explains the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that a man wants his wife to be humiliated in court (so he will not remarry her), while Rabbi Elazar holds that a man does not want his wife to be humiliated in court.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Meir's position on vows that require inquiry and then records Rabbi Elazar's statement that the prohibition was only enacted for a vow that requires inquiry because of one that does not require inquiry.
The Gemara asks: On what principle do Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar disagree?
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir holds that a man wants his wife to be disgraced in court, so he would not remarry her after divorcing her for a vow that requires inquiry.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar holds that a man does not want his wife to be disgraced in court, so he would not remarry her after divorcing her for a vow that does not require inquiry.

items.text: The case of a husband's vow and the principle of tikkun ha'olam
items.text_en: The case of a husband's vow and the principle of tikkun ha'olam
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case is where the wife vowed, but if the husband vowed, he may remarry her. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda cites a case in Tzaydan where a man vowed to divorce his wife, divorced her, and the Sages permitted him to remarry her for the sake of tikkun ha'olam (the betterment of the world).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah taught that prompted Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda to cite the incident in Tzaydan.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is incomplete and should be read as distinguishing between the wife's vow (he may not remarry) and the husband's vow (he may remarry), and then cites Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's incident where a husband vowed to divorce, divorced, and the Sages permitted remarriage for the betterment of the world.

items.text: Definition of 'Kunam' and the leniency to remarry
items.text_en: Definition of 'Kunam' and the leniency to remarry
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that 'Kunam' refers to a vow forbidding all produce if he does not divorce her. The Gemara notes that the ruling allowing him to remarry is obvious, but it was necessary to counter Rabbi Natan's view that a vow is like building a high place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Kunam' means, and Rav Huna explains it refers to a vow forbidding all produce if he does not divorce her.
The Gemara objects that the ruling allowing him to remarry is obvious, but explains it was necessary to counter Rabbi Natan's view that a vow is like building a high place.

items.text: The reason of 'Tikkun HaOlam' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: The reason of 'Tikkun HaOlam' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that the concern for Tikkun HaOlam applies to the first clause of the Mishnah (about the vow). Ravina argues it applies to the latter clause, where the Mishnah says 'there is no concern for Tikkun HaOlam'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what concern for Tikkun HaOlam (the betterment of the world) exists in this Mishnah context.
Rav Sheshet answers that the concern applies to the first clause (רישא) of the Mishnah.
Ravina objects, arguing that the concern actually applies to the latter clause (סיפא), where the Mishnah states 'there is no concern for Tikkun HaOlam in this case'.

items.text: Mishnah: Divorce due to ailonit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Divorce due to ailonit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a man divorces his wife because she is an ailonit (incapable of bearing children), Rabbi Yehuda says he may not remarry her, while the Sages permit it. If she remarried and had children, and then claims her ketubah, Rabbi Yehuda says her silence is better than her speech.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a man divorcing his wife due to her being an ailonit (incapable of bearing children), stating Rabbi Yehuda prohibits remarriage while the Sages permit it.
The Mishnah adds that if she remarried and had children, then claims her ketubah, Rabbi Yehuda says her silence is better than her speech.

items.text: Contradiction in the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Contradiction in the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: in our Mishnah, Rabbi Yehuda is concerned about kilkula (marital misconduct) while the Rabbis are not, but in a baraita about divorce due to a bad name or a vow, the opposite is true: the Rabbis are concerned and Rabbi Yehuda is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda is concerned about kilkula (marital misconduct) while the Rabbis are not, since the opposite appears in a baraita.
The Gemara cites a baraita where the Rabbis are concerned about kilkula and Rabbi Yehuda is not, creating a contradiction with the Mishnah.

items.text: Shmuel's resolution: reverse the positions
items.text_en: Shmuel's resolution: reverse the positions
items.desc_en: Shmuel suggests reversing the opinions: in the Mishnah, Rabbi Yehuda is not concerned and the Rabbis are. The Gemara objects from the latter clause of the Mishnah, where Rabbi Yehuda's statement implies concern, so Shmuel says to reverse that as well.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel resolves the contradiction by reversing the positions: in the Mishnah, Rabbi Yehuda is not concerned about קלקול (improper consequences) and the Rabbis are.
The Gemara objects from the latter clause of the Mishnah, where Rabbi Yehuda's statement implies concern about קלקול (improper consequences).
Shmuel responds that the latter clause should also be reversed.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: no reversal, Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: no reversal, Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that no reversal is needed. Rabbi Yehuda holds like Rabbi Meir in one case and like Rabbi Elazar in another: in a case where a conditional divorce is necessary, he follows Rabbi Elazar (concerned), and where it is unnecessary, he follows Rabbi Meir (not concerned).

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that no reversal is needed; Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Meir in the case where the husband does not need her and Rabbi Elazar where he does.

items.text: Rava's resolution: Rabbi Yehuda's contradiction resolved, Rabbis are Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: Rabbi Yehuda's contradiction resolved, Rabbis are Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rava asks why only Rabbi Yehuda's contradiction is addressed. He explains that Rabbi Yehuda's contradiction is resolved as before, and the Rabbis' contradiction is resolved by identifying them as Rabbi Meir, who requires a double condition; here the condition was not doubled.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks why only Rabbi Yehuda's internal contradiction is addressed, while the contradiction among the Rabbis is ignored.
Rava resolves that Rabbi Yehuda's contradiction is settled as before, and the Rabbis are identified as Rabbi Meir, who requires a double condition (תנאי כפול), which was absent here.

items.text: Mishnah: Selling oneself to gentiles
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling oneself to gentiles
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who sells himself and his children to gentiles is not redeemed, but the children are redeemed after the father's death. Rav Asi adds that this applies only if he sold himself three times.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who sells himself and his children to gentiles is not redeemed, but the children are redeemed after the father's death.
Rav Asi adds that the Mishnah's leniency for children applies only if the father sold himself three times.

items.text: Case of tax collectors and Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Case of tax collectors and Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: Tax collectors who borrowed from gentiles and could not repay were being seized. Rav Huna initially refused to redeem them, citing the Mishnah. Rabbi Abba reminded him of Rav Asi's limitation (three times), and Rav Huna noted that these people habitually did so.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case of tax collectors who borrowed money from gentiles and could not repay.
The gentiles began to seize them, and they came before Rav Huna.
Rav Huna initially refused to redeem them, citing the Mishnah that one who sells himself to gentiles is not redeemed.
Rabbi Abba reminded Rav Huna of Rav Asi's limitation that the Mishnah applies only to one who sold himself three times.
Rav Huna responded that these tax collectors habitually sold themselves, so they are considered repeat offenders.

items.text: Case of a man who sold himself to Ludaei
items.text_en: Case of a man who sold himself to Ludaei
items.desc_en: A man who sold himself to the Ludaei (a gentile group) came before Rabbi Ammi, who began to respond.

sub.desc_en: A story begins about a man who sold himself to the Luda'im and came before Rabbi Ammi.

items.text: Story of the Jew who sold himself to gentiles and the debate over his redemption
items.text_en: Story of the Jew who sold himself to gentiles and the debate over his redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a Jew sold himself and his sons to gentiles. The rabbis argue that he should not be redeemed due to the concern of 'קלקולא' (corruption), but the sons are redeemed. Rabbi Ammi is challenged about a Jewish apostate who eats forbidden foods, and he initially excuses it as appetite-driven, but when pressed, he admits he cannot redeem him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Ammi by citing the Mishnah that a Jew who sells himself and his sons to gentiles is not redeemed due to קלקולא (corruption), and certainly not when there is danger of death.
The rabbis object that the man is a Jewish apostate (מומר) who eats נבילות וטריפות (forbidden meat), and Rabbi Ammi initially excuses it as appetite-driven.

sub.text: Rabbanan's counter-objection and Rabbi Ammi's admission
sub.text_en: Rabbanan's counter-objection and Rabbi Ammi's admission
sub.desc_en: The rabbans press that the apostate chooses forbidden food over permitted food, and Rabbi Ammi admits he cannot redeem him.

items.text: Story of Reish Lakish who sold himself to the Ludaeans and his clever escape
items.text_en: Story of Reish Lakish who sold himself to the Ludaeans and his clever escape
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish sells himself to the Ludaeans (gentiles) and brings a sword and skull. He knows that on the last day they will grant his request to soften his price. He asks to bind them and strike each with a sword, killing them all. After escaping, he eats and drinks, and his daughter asks if he needs anything to sleep on; he replies his stomach is his pillow. Upon his death, he leaves a kab of saffron, applying the verse 'and they leave their wealth to others'.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish sells himself to the Ludaeans, taking a sword and skull, relying on the tradition that on the last day they grant any request to calm his blood.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's execution of the captors
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's execution of the captors
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish requests to be bound and then kills all his captors one by one with the sword.
After escaping, Reish Lakish eats and drinks, his daughter asks about bedding, he declines, and upon his death he leaves a kab of saffron, applying the verse 'they leave their wealth to others'.
One Ludaean grinds his teeth at Reish Lakish, accusing him of mocking him, and notes that half a sword remains.
Reish Lakish kills all the Ludaeans.
After escaping, Reish Lakish eats and drinks; his daughter asks if he needs bedding, and he replies that his stomach is his pillow.
Upon his death, Reish Lakish leaves a kab of saffron, applying the verse 'and they leave their wealth to others'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Selling a field to a gentile and bringing first fruits
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Selling a field to a gentile and bringing first fruits
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who sells his field to a gentile may still buy first fruits from it and bring them, due to 'תיקון העולם' (the betterment of the world).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who sells his field to a gentile may still bring first fruits (ביכורים) from it, due to תיקון העולם (the betterment of the world).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rabbi Elazar on gentile acquisition and tithes
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rabbi Elazar on gentile acquisition and tithes
items.desc_en: Rabbah argues that a gentile has no acquisition in Israel to exempt from tithes (based on 'כי לי הארץ'), but does have acquisition for digging pits. Rabbi Elazar argues the opposite: a gentile's acquisition does exempt from tithes (based on 'דגנך' not 'דגן גוי'), but not for digging pits (based on 'לה' הארץ'). The Gemara explains their dispute: one derives from 'דגנך' (your grain) and the other from 'דיגונך' (your threshing floor).

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states that a gentile has no acquisition in Israel to exempt from tithes (based on 'כי לי הארץ'), but does have acquisition for digging pits (based on 'הארץ נתן לבני אדם').
Rabbi Elazar argues the opposite: a gentile's acquisition does exempt from tithes (based on 'דגנך' not 'דגן גוי'), but not for digging pits (based on 'לה' הארץ').
The Gemara explains their dispute: one derives from 'דגנך' (your grain) and the other from 'דיגונך' (your threshing floor).

items.text: Proof from a baraita about gleanings of a gentile
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about gleanings of a gentile
items.desc_en: Rabbah cites a baraita: gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and peah of a gentile are liable for tithes unless he declared them ownerless. The Gemara analyzes: if a Jew owned the field and a gentile gleaned, why would ownerlessness matter? It must be that a gentile owned the field and a Jew gleaned. The Gemara then rejects this, suggesting the field is owned by a Jew but the gentile gleaned, and ownerlessness is only relevant for the Jew's intent, not the gentile's.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah introduces a proof from a baraita: gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and peah of a gentile are liable for tithes unless he declared them ownerless.
The Gemara asks how to interpret the baraita: if a Jew owned the field and a gentile gleaned, why would ownerlessness matter? It must be that a gentile owned the field and a Jew gleaned.
The Gemara concludes that if the gentile did not declare ownerlessness, the produce is liable for tithes.
The Gemara rejects the interpretation, suggesting the field is owned by a Jew but the gentile gleaned, and ownerlessness is only relevant for the Jew's intent, not the gentile's.

items.text: Proof from a case of a Jew buying and reselling a field to a gentile
items.text_en: Proof from a case of a Jew buying and reselling a field to a gentile
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: a Jew who buys a field from a gentile before it has produced a third, then sells it back after it has produced a third, is liable for tithes because it already became obligated. This implies that if it had not become obligated, it would be exempt. The Gemara deflects: this deals with Syria, where individual conquest is not considered conquest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: a Jew who buys a field from a gentile before it has produced a third, then sells it back after it has produced a third, is liable for tithes because it already became obligated, implying that if it had not become obligated it would be exempt.
The Gemara deflects: this case deals with Syria, where individual conquest is not considered conquest, so the field never had full sanctity of Eretz Yisrael.

items.text: Introduction of a joint-purchase case
items.text_en: Introduction of a joint-purchase case
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new case: a Jew and a gentile who jointly purchase a field. This sets up the next stage of the argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of an Israelite and a gentile who jointly purchase a field, to further test the dispute.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding a mixture of tevel and chullin. Rabbi holds it is forbidden, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between a gentile's mixture (exempt) and a Jew's mixture (liable).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a dispute: Rabbi forbids a mixture of tevel and chullin, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between a gentile's mixture (exempt) and a Jew's mixture (liable).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute hinges on the principle of bererah: one holds yesh bererah, the other ein bererah. However, all agree that a gentile has acquisition in Eretz Yisrael to exempt from tithes. Alternatively, the case is in Syria, where conquest by an individual is not considered conquest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel hinges on the principle of בְּרֵירָה (retroactive clarification), but all agree that a gentile has acquisition in Eretz Yisrael to exempt from tithes.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the case is in Syria (סוּרְיָא), where conquest by an individual is not considered conquest, so the gentile's acquisition does not exempt from tithes.

items.text: Proof from the law of selling a field to a gentile
items.text_en: Proof from the law of selling a field to a gentile
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin brings a baraita: one who sells his field to a gentile brings bikkurim due to tikkun ha'olam, but not from the Torah. Rav Ashi explains there were two enactments: originally they brought from the Torah, then they forbade it because sellers thought the field remained in its sanctity, and finally they reinstated it to prevent the fields from becoming entrenched with gentiles.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin cites a baraita: one who sells his field to a gentile brings bikkurim only due to tikkun ha'olam, not from the Torah.
Rav Ashi explains there were two enactments: originally they brought from the Torah, then they forbade it, and finally reinstated it to prevent fields from becoming entrenched with gentiles.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on selling a field for its produce
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on selling a field for its produce
items.desc_en: An amoraic dispute is stated: one who sells his field for its produce (but retains ownership) – Rabbi Yochanan says he brings and recites, Reish Lakish says he brings but does not recite. Their reasoning is based on whether kinyan peirot is like kinyan haguf.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states an amoraic dispute: one who sells his field for its produce (retaining ownership) – Rabbi Yochanan says he brings first fruits and recites the declaration, Reish Lakish says he brings but does not recite.

The gemara explains the reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan holds that קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת (acquisition of produce rights) is equivalent to קִנְיַן הַגּוּף (acquisition of the body/ownership), while Reish Lakish holds it is not.

items.text: First objection and response
items.text_en: First objection and response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish from the verse 'u'leveitecha' which teaches that a man brings his wife's bikkurim and recites. Reish Lakish distinguishes that case because of the verse. An alternative version has Reish Lakish objecting to Rabbi Yochanan, who responds that his own reasoning is derived from there.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish by citing the verse 'וּלְבֵיתְךָ' which teaches that a man brings his wife's ביכורים (first fruits) and recites the declaration.
Reish Lakish distinguishes the case of a wife because the verse explicitly says 'וּלְבֵיתֶךָ' (to your house), implying a special rule for a wife that does not apply to a buyer of פירות (produce).
An alternative version reverses the roles: Reish Lakish objects to Rabbi Yochanan from the same verse, and Rabbi Yochanan responds that his own reasoning is derived from that very verse.

items.text: Second objection and resolution
items.text_en: Second objection and resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita: if one was bringing his wife's bikkurim and heard she died, he brings and recites – implying only if she died, but not if she is alive. The Gemara answers that the same applies even if she did not die, but the case of death was necessary to counter a possible decree due to Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's ruling about a messenger who died.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if a man was bringing his wife's bikkurim and heard she died, he brings and recites, implying only if she died, but not if she is alive.
The Gemara answers that the same rule applies even if she did not die, but the case of death was necessary to counter a possible decree due to Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's ruling.

Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina rules that if one separated bikkurim and sent them with a messenger who died on the way, the owner brings them but does not recite, because the verse requires taking and bringing by the same person; the baraita teaches that death of the wife does not create a similar problem.

items.text: Continuation of the dispute's reasoning
items.text_en: Continuation of the dispute's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish follow their own reasoning, as stated in a parallel dispute about selling a field for its produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish follow their own reasoning, as stated in a parallel dispute about selling a field for its produce.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on bringing firstfruits when the Jubilee is in effect
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on bringing firstfruits when the Jubilee is in effect
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds that one brings and recites, because acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body; Reish Lakish holds one brings but does not recite, because it is not. The Gemara explains why both cases of dispute are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says one brings firstfruits and recites the declaration even when the Jubilee is in effect, while Reish Lakish says one brings but does not recite.
The Gemara explains the reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan holds that acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body (קניין פירות כקניין הגוף דמי), while Reish Lakish holds it is not.
The Gemara explains why both cases of dispute (firstfruits and the other case) are necessary, showing that each sage might concede in the other case.

items.text: Attempted proofs from mishnayot about buying trees
items.text_en: Attempted proofs from mishnayot about buying trees
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from the Mishna that one who buys a tree with its land brings and recites, but deflects that this is when the Jubilee is not in effect. Similarly, buying two trees brings without reciting, but three trees brings and recites, again deflected as when the Jubilee is not in effect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishna that one who buys a tree with its land brings first fruits and recites the declaration.
The Gemara deflects the proof by explaining that the Mishna deals with a time when the Jubilee is not in effect.
The Gemara attempts another proof from the Mishna: one who buys two trees brings without reciting, but three trees brings and recites.
The Gemara again deflects, stating that this case too is when the Jubilee is not in effect.

items.text: Resolution with Rav Chisda's distinction between first and second Jubilee
items.text_en: Resolution with Rav Chisda's distinction between first and second Jubilee
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the dispute applies only to the second Jubilee, but in the first Jubilee everyone agrees one brings and recites because the buyers have not yet relied on the land. The earlier proofs are thus reconciled.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the first Jubilee (everyone agrees one brings and recites) and the second Jubilee (the dispute applies).

items.text: Support from a Tannaitic dispute about a field bought from one's father
items.text_en: Support from a Tannaitic dispute about a field bought from one's father
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon debate whether a field bought from one's father that is later consecrated is considered ancestral land. The Gemara suggests they argue over whether acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish aligns with a Tannaitic dispute about a field bought from one's father and later consecrated, citing the baraita's positions.
Rabbi Meir requires a verse for a field consecrated after the father's death, implying it is not automatically ancestral land.

The Gemara analyzes the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body, so the field is not inherited until consecration, requiring a verse; Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon hold the opposite, so no verse is needed for post-death consecration.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that for Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, the verse is only needed when the field was consecrated before the father's death, not after.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation of the Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation of the Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak argues that even Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon hold that acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body, but they derive their ruling from a different exegesis of the verse.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak argues that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon actually hold that acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body (קניין פירות כקניין הגוף), but they derive their ruling from a different exegesis of the verse, reading the extra letter מ

items.text: Rav Yosef's statement that without Rabbi Yochanan's principle one could not find a basis for firstfruits
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's statement that without Rabbi Yochanan's principle one could not find a basis for firstfruits
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says that if not for Rabbi Yochanan's view that acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body, one would not be able to find anyone who brings firstfruits with a declaration except for a single chain from Joshua bin Nun.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef declares that without Rabbi Yochanan's principle that acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body, he would be at a loss in the study hall.
Rabbi Asi cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that brothers who divided an inheritance are considered purchasers and return land to each other in the Jubilee year.
Rav Yosef concludes that without the principle, one would find only a single uninterrupted chain of firstfruit bringers from Joshua bin Nun onward.

items.text: Rava's support for Reish Lakish from a verse and a Mishna
items.text_en: Rava's support for Reish Lakish from a verse and a Mishna
items.desc_en: Rava states that a verse and a Mishna support Reish Lakish's position, beginning to cite the verse.

sub.desc_en: Rava announces that a verse and a Mishna support Reish Lakish's position, beginning to cite the verse.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that damages are assessed from the best quality land, while a creditor collects from intermediate land, and a woman's ketubah from the worst land. It also lists cases where collection is not made from encumbered property due to tikkun ha'olam.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a verse citation about selling by number of crops.

items.text: Gemara's preliminary discussion and Abaye's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's preliminary discussion and Abaye's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a firstborn taking a double portion in a field that returns in the Jubilee. Abaye states a principle: a husband managing his wife's property needs authorization, but if he has already taken the produce, the court can adjudicate the produce and thereby the land itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that a firstborn takes a double portion in a field that returns to his father in the Jubilee year.
Abaye states a general principle: a husband managing his wife's property needs authorization from the court.
Abaye qualifies: the need for authorization applies only if the husband has not yet taken the produce; if he has, the court can adjudicate the produce and thereby the land itself.

items.text: Return to the Mishnah
items.text_en: Return to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the Mishnah with the phrase 'We return to you, the one who sends' (a standard formula for resuming study of the Mishnah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the Mishnah with the standard formula 'We return to you, the one who sends'.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of collection and tikkun ha'olam
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of collection and tikkun ha'olam
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details that damages are collected from the best land, debts from intermediate, and ketubah from the worst. Rabbi Meir says ketubah is also from intermediate. It then lists cases where collection is not made from encumbered property or from orphans' property except from the worst, and where certain claims are not made from encumbered property due to tikkun ha'olam.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: damages are collected from the best land, debts from intermediate, and ketubah from the worst; Rabbi Meir adds that ketubah is also from intermediate.
The Mishnah rules that one does not collect from encumbered property when there is free property, even if the free property is of inferior quality.
The Mishnah rules that collection from orphans' property is only from the worst land.
The Mishnah states that one does not appropriate encumbered property for produce consumption, land enhancement, or sustenance of wife and daughters, due to tikkun ha'olam.
The Mishnah rules that a finder of a lost item is not required to swear, due to tikkun ha'olam.

items.text: Gemara's question on tikkun ha'olam
items.text_en: Gemara's question on tikkun ha'olam
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why is the rule that damages are collected from the best land attributed to tikkun ha'olam? It is a Torah law, as it says 'the best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why is the rule that damages are collected from the best land attributed to tikkun ha'olam? It is a Torah law, as it says 'the best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay'.

items.text: Abaye's answer and the dispute of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Abaye's answer and the dispute of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah is necessary according to Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that Torah law requires assessing damages from the best land of the injured party; the Mishnah teaches that due to tikkun ha'olam, we assess from the best land of the injurer. A baraita elaborates: Rabbi Yishmael says 'the best of his field' refers to the injured party's best, while Rabbi Akiva says the verse is only to collect damages from the best land, and a fortiori for consecrated property.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah's ruling that damages are assessed from the best land of the injurer is necessary only according to Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that Torah law would assess from the best land of the injured party, so the Mishnah teaches that due to תיקון העולם (the betterment of the world) we assess from the injurer's best land.
