A baraita is cited to clarify Rabbi Yishmael's position: he interprets 'the best of his field' as the best of the injured party's field, while Rabbi Akiva argues the verse only serves to collect damages from the best land, and a fortiori for consecrated property.

items.text: Rava's objection and Rav Acha bar Yaakov's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection and Rav Acha bar Yaakov's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: According to Rabbi Yishmael, if an animal ate a fat plant, it pays for a fat plant; if it ate a lean one, does it pay for a fat one? Rav Idi bar Avin explains the case is where the animal ate from a bed between beds and we don't know if it was lean or fat, so it pays from the best. Rava objects: If we knew it ate a lean one, it would pay for a lean one; now that we don't know, should it pay for a fat one? The burden of proof is on the claimant. Rav Acha bar Yaakov begins to offer an alternative explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yishmael's position: if the animal ate a fat plant, it pays for a fat one; if it ate a lean one, does it also pay for a fat one?
Rav Idi bar Avin explains the case is where the animal ate from a bed between beds and we don't know if it was lean or fat, so it pays from the best.
Rava objects: if we knew it ate a lean one, it would pay for a lean one; now that we don't know, should it pay for a fat one? The burden of proof is on the claimant.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's beginning of an alternative explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's beginning of an alternative explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov begins to offer an alternative explanation, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Setting the case for the dispute
items.text_en: Setting the case for the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva concerns a scenario where the victim's best land is equivalent to the tortfeasor's inferior land. Rabbi Yishmael assesses based on the victim's land, Rabbi Akiva based on the tortfeasor's land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets the case: the victim's best land equals the tortfeasor's inferior land, and states the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael (assess by victim's land) and Rabbi Akiva (assess by tortfeasor's land).

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning and Rabbi Akiva's counter
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning and Rabbi Akiva's counter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael uses a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'field' to argue that assessment follows the victim's land. Rabbi Akiva cites the verse 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ יְשַׁלֵּם' to argue it follows the payer's land. Rabbi Yishmael responds that both the גזירה שווה and the verse apply: the verse ensures payment from the tortfeasor's best land if his inferior land is worth less than the victim's best.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning and explains his use of a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'field' to assess damages based on the victim's land.
Rabbi Akiva cites the verse 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ יְשַׁלֵּם' (the best of his field he shall pay) to argue that assessment follows the payer's land.

Rabbi Yishmael resolves the apparent contradiction by applying both the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) and the verse: the גזירה שווה sets the assessment standard, while the verse ensures payment from the tortfeasor's best land if his inferior land is worth less than the victim's best.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's statement about consecrated property
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's statement about consecrated property
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva states that the verse only comes to collect damages from the best land, and applies a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) to consecrated property.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva states that the verse comes only to collect damages from the best land, and a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) applies to consecrated property.

items.text: Clarifying the קל וחומר for consecrated property
items.text_en: Clarifying the קל וחומר for consecrated property
items.desc_en: The Gemara first rejects the possibility that the קל וחומר refers to an ox of consecrated property goring an ordinary ox, since the Torah says 'שׁוֹר רֵעֵהוּ' (the ox of one's fellow), excluding consecrated property. Instead, it explains the case as someone who pledges a sum to the Temple treasury, where the treasurer collects from the best land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) for consecrated property mentioned by Rabbi Akiva.

The Gemara rejects the possibility that the קל וחומר refers to an ox of consecrated property goring an ordinary ox, because the Torah says 'שׁוֹר רֵעֵהוּ' (the ox of one's fellow), excluding consecrated property.
The Gemara explains the case as someone who pledges a sum to the Temple treasury (בדק הבית), where the treasurer collects from the best land.

items.text: Objection to the קל וחומר based on creditor law
items.text_en: Objection to the קל וחומר based on creditor law
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: even if consecrated property is like a creditor, a creditor collects from intermediate land, not best land. If Rabbi Akiva holds that a creditor collects from best land like a victim, one can refute: a creditor's power is strong regarding victims, but consecrated property's power is weak regarding victims.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: even if it were like a creditor, a creditor collects from intermediate land, and one could refute the קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) because creditors have stronger power in damages, while consecrated property has weaker power.

items.text: Alternative explanation: the case of an ox goring consecrated property
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: the case of an ox goring consecrated property
items.desc_en: The Gemara reverts to the case of an ordinary ox goring a consecrated ox, and explains that Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, who rules that a consecrated ox that gores is exempt, but an ordinary ox that gores a consecrated ox pays full damages whether tam or mu'ad.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case is indeed about our ox goring a consecrated ox, and Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's opinion that a consecrated ox goring a common ox is exempt, but a common ox goring a consecrated ox pays full damages.

items.text: Reframing the dispute: is it about assessment or about Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya?
items.text_en: Reframing the dispute: is it about assessment or about Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the dispute is actually about the assessment method or about the opinion of Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya. If Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya and Rabbi Yishmael follows the Rabbis, then the original framing is problematic. The Gemara raises three difficulties: the phrase 'לֹא בָּא הַכָּתוּב', the 'קַל וָחוֹמֶר', and a statement by Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the dispute is actually about assessment method or about the opinion of Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, suggesting both sides might agree on assessment but differ on the halacha of consecrated property.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's view on consecrated property, while Rabbi Yishmael follows the Rabbis.
The Gemara raises three difficulties with this reframing: the phrase 'לֹא בָּא הַכָּתוּב', the 'קַל וָחוֹמֶר', and a statement by Rav Ashi.

items.text: Opening Tannaitic dispute on the source of 'meitav'
items.text_en: Opening Tannaitic dispute on the source of 'meitav'
items.desc_en: A baraita cites a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva regarding the interpretation of 'meitav sadehu' – whether it refers to the best land of the victim or the best land of the injurer.

sub.desc_en: A baraita opens with the verse 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם' and presents Rabbi Yishmael's position that it refers to the best land of the victim.
Rabbi Akiva counters that the verse refers to the best land of the injurer, not the victim.

items.text: Ravina's resolution and Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution and Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the mishnah aligns with Rabbi Akiva (who says evaluation is from the injurer's property) and with Rabbi Shimon, who derives the reason for the rule: damages claimants collect from the best land as a tikkun ha'olam to deter robbers and oppressors.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves that the mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva (evaluation from the injurer's property) and Rabbi Shimon (who derives the reason for the rule as a tikkun ha'olam).
Rabbi Shimon explains that damages claimants collect from the best land to deter robbers and oppressors, citing the verse 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם'.

items.text: Reason for ordinary creditor in intermediate land
items.text_en: Reason for ordinary creditor in intermediate land
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why a creditor collects from intermediate land: to prevent people from lending only to seize a nice field. It then asks why not from the worst land, and answers that would close the door on borrowers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why an ordinary creditor collects from intermediate land, and the answer is given: to prevent people from lending only to seize a nice field.
The Gemara objects: if so, let the creditor collect from the worst land; the answer is that this would close the door on borrowers.

items.text: Ketubah collected from the worst land: reasons
items.text_en: Ketubah collected from the worst land: reasons
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir dispute whether a ketubah is collected from the worst or intermediate land. Rabbi Shimon explains the reason: a woman is more eager to marry than a man, and she can be divorced against her will, so the rabbis did not need to incentivize her.

sub.text: Tannaic statement (Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir)
sub.text_en: Tannaic statement (Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda rules that a ketubah is collected from the worst land (זיבורית), while Rabbi Meir rules it is collected from intermediate land (בינונית).
Rabbi Shimon explains that the ketubah is collected from the worst land because a woman is more eager to marry than a man, so no incentive is needed for her.
A second reason is given: a woman can be divorced against her will, but a man only divorces willingly, so the rabbis did not need to incentivize her with better land.
The Gemara asks: what does the second reason add? If the concern is that when she leaves willingly she should also pay, why not institute a ketubah from her?
The Gemara answers: the second reason teaches that since a man can delay the divorce (משהה לה בגיטא), he has leverage, so the rabbis did not need to give her a ketubah from her own property.

items.text: Mar Zutra's distinction: from orphans vs. from himself
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's distinction: from orphans vs. from himself
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman rules that the ketubah is collected from the worst land only from orphans, but from the husband himself it is from intermediate land. The Gemara questions why this is specific to ketubah, and answers that one might have thought the rabbis were lenient due to charm, so the ruling is necessary.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman rules that the ketubah is collected from the worst land only from orphans, but from the husband himself it is from intermediate land.
The Gemara questions why Mar Zutra specifies ketubah from orphans, since all debts from orphans are collected from the worst land, implying the ruling must be about the husband himself.

The Gemara answers that the ruling indeed refers to orphans, but the specification for ketubah is necessary because one might have thought the rabbis were lenient due to the woman's charm (חינא), so Mar Zutra teaches that this leniency does not apply.

items.text: Rava's challenge from Rabbi Meir's opinion
items.text_en: Rava's challenge from Rabbi Meir's opinion
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Mar Zutra from Rabbi Meir's ruling that ketubah is from intermediate land, arguing that if it were from orphans, Rabbi Meir would contradict the general rule. The Gemara deflects by saying ketubah is different due to charm.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Mar Zutra by citing Rabbi Meir's ruling that ketubah is collected from intermediate land, arguing that if it were from orphans, Rabbi Meir would contradict the rule that orphans pay only from inferior land, implying the ruling is from the husband himself.
The Gemara deflects Rava's challenge by asserting that Rabbi Meir's ruling indeed applies to orphans, and the ketubah is different because of the special consideration of charm (חינא).

items.text: Abaye's challenge and Rav Acha bar Yaakov's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge and Rav Acha bar Yaakov's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges from a baraita listing all three categories, implying they are from the same debtor. Rav Acha bar Yaakov resolves that the case is where a father became a guarantor for his son's damages, debts, and his daughter-in-law's ketubah, and the distinction follows the timing of collection.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges by citing a baraita listing the three collection categories (עידית, בינונית, זיבורית) and argues that since they are listed together, they must all refer to collection from the debtor himself, not from orphans.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov resolves that the baraita deals with a case where a father became a guarantor for his son's damages, debts, and his daughter-in-law's ketubah, and the distinction follows the timing of collection: damages and debts are collected during the son's lifetime (so the father collects as if from the living), while the ketubah is collected after the son's death (so the father collects as if from orphans).

items.text: Discussion on the guarantor's liability for ketubah
items.text_en: Discussion on the guarantor's liability for ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a guarantor for a ketubah is liable, given that a guarantor for a ketubah is generally not obligated. It resolves that the case is a 'kablan' (a type of guarantor), and offers alternative answers: either the father had assets that were lost, or a father is considered to have obligated himself for his son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the guarantor is liable, since a guarantor for a ketubah is generally not obligated.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a 'kablan' (a type of guarantor who accepts full responsibility).
The Gemara objects that this answer works only for the opinion that a 'kablan' is bound even without the debtor's assets, but not for the opinion that he is bound only if the debtor has assets.
An alternative answer: the father had assets that were subsequently lost (flooded), so the 'kablan' is liable.
Another alternative answer: a father is considered to have obligated himself for his son, so the guarantor is bound.
The Gemara concludes that a guarantor for a ketubah is universally not obligated.

items.text: Dispute about guarantors for a ketubah
items.text_en: Dispute about guarantors for a ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute regarding a guarantor for a ketubah: some say he is liable even if the borrower has no assets, while others say he is liable only if the borrower has assets. The halakha is that all guarantors are liable even without assets, except for a guarantor for a ketubah, who is not liable even if the borrower has assets, because he performed a mitzvah and did not cause her any loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute about guarantors: a guarantor for a debt is universally liable, but for a ketubah there is disagreement whether liability depends on the borrower's assets.
The halakhic ruling is stated: all guarantors are liable even without assets, except for a guarantor for a ketubah, who is not liable even if the borrower has assets.
The Gemara explains the reason: the guarantor for a ketubah performed a מצוה (commandment) and did not cause the woman any loss.

items.text: Ravina's refutation of Mar Zutra
items.text_en: Ravina's refutation of Mar Zutra
items.desc_en: Ravina brings a proof from the original enactment that a woman prefers to be married more than a man desires to marry, implying that the concern is for the woman, not for orphans. This refutes Mar Zutra's position that the enactment was for orphans.

sub.desc_en: Ravina refutes Mar Zutra by citing the original enactment that a woman prefers to be married more than a man desires to marry, showing the concern is for the woman, not for orphans.

items.text: Mar Zutra's ruling on collecting from orphans
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's ruling on collecting from orphans
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman states in the name of Rav Nachman that a debt document that comes against orphans, even if it includes a clause of appreciation (shevach), is collected only from inferior land (zibburit). Abaye supports this by noting that a creditor normally collects from intermediate land, but from orphans he collects from inferior land.

sub.text: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman rules in the name of Rav Nachman that a debt document against orphans, even with a clause of appreciation (שבח), is collected only from inferior land (זיבורית).
Abaye supports Mar Zutra's ruling by noting that a creditor normally collects from intermediate land (בינונית), but from orphans he collects from inferior land (זיבורית).

items.text: Rava's objection and alternative reasoning
items.text_en: Rava's objection and alternative reasoning
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's comparison, arguing that by Torah law a creditor collects from inferior land, and the rabbis instituted intermediate land only to encourage lending. For orphans, the rabbis restored the Torah law. But for a creditor with a lien on superior land (iddit), even from orphans he should collect from superior land.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's comparison, arguing that by Torah law a creditor collects from inferior land (זיבורית), and the rabbis instituted intermediate land (בינונית) only to encourage lending; for orphans, the rabbis restored the Torah law.
Rava concludes that for a creditor with a lien on superior land (עידית), even from orphans he should collect from superior land, since that is the Torah law.

items.text: Reconciling Rava with the baraita of Avram the Seer
items.text_en: Reconciling Rava with the baraita of Avram the Seer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava from a baraita that says even for damages (where Torah law mandates superior land), collection from orphans is only from inferior land. The answer is that the case involves a situation where the damaged party's superior land is equivalent to the damager's inferior land, and it follows Rabbi Yishmael's view that Torah law assesses based on the damaged party's land, but the rabbis instituted assessment based on the damager's land for the sake of social order; for orphans, the rabbis restored the Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava by citing a baraita from Avram the Seer that even for damages (where Torah law mandates superior land), collection from orphans is only from inferior land.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a situation where the damaged party's superior land is equivalent to the damager's inferior land.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows Rabbi Yishmael's view that Torah law assesses based on the damaged party's land, but the rabbis instituted assessment based on the damager's land for social order; for orphans, the rabbis restored the Torah law.

items.text: Clarifying the baraita of Rabbi Eliezer the Dyer
items.text_en: Clarifying the baraita of Rabbi Eliezer the Dyer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the previous answer with a baraita from Rabbi Eliezer the Dyer that says collection from orphans is only from inferior land, even if it is 'iddit'. The Gemara explains that 'iddit' here means 'surplus superior land' (shif'ei iddit), as per Rava's rule: if one damages inferior land, he pays from superior land; if one damages surplus superior land, he pays from intermediate land. For orphans, the rabbis restored the Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the previous answer by citing a baraita of Rabbi Eliezer the Dyer that collection from orphans is only from inferior land, even if the debt document specifies superior land.
The Gemara answers that 'iddit' in the baraita means 'surplus superior land' (shif'ei iddit), not actual superior land.
Rava's rule is cited: if one damages inferior land, he pays from superior land; if one damages surplus superior land, he pays from intermediate land; for orphans, the rabbis restored the Torah law.

items.text: Question about the definition of 'orphans'
items.text_en: Question about the definition of 'orphans'
items.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami asks whether 'orphans' in the ruling refers only to minors or even to adults. The Gemara considers two possibilities: it might be a special enactment for minors, or it might be due to the creditor not anticipating the debtor's death, which would discourage lending, so it applies even to adults. A baraita from Abaye the Elder states that 'orphans' means adults, and certainly minors. The Gemara questions whether this applies only to oaths (where an adult is like a minor regarding his father's matters) but not to the law of inferior land. The Gemara concludes with the halakha.

sub.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami asks whether 'orphans' in the ruling refers only to minors or even to adults, considering the possibility that the enactment was only for minors.
The Gemara raises an alternative possibility: the enactment applies even to adults because the creditor does not anticipate the debtor's death, which would discourage lending.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Abaye the Elder
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Abaye the Elder
sub.desc_en: A baraita from Abaye the Elder is cited, stating that 'orphans' means adults, and certainly minors.
The Gemara objects that the baraita might apply only to oaths (where an adult is like a minor regarding his father's matters) but not to the law of inferior land.
The Gemara concludes with the halakha, though the ruling is not explicitly stated here.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that orphans who said they are adults (and certainly minors) cannot have their debts collected from liened property when there is free property available, whether for an oath or for inferior land.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that orphans who claim to be adults (and certainly minors) cannot collect debts from liened property when free property is available, whether for an oath or for inferior land.

items.text: Gemara's question about gifts
items.text_en: Gemara's question about gifts
items.desc_en: Rav Ahadbui bar Ami raises a dilemma: does the rabbinic enactment protecting orphans apply only to sales (due to loss to buyers) or also to gifts, since the recipient benefits the giver?

sub.desc_en: Rav Ahadbui bar Ami raises a dilemma: does the rabbinic enactment protecting orphans apply to gifts as well as sales?
The Gemara presents two sides: the enactment was only for loss to buyers, but a gift may also involve benefit to the giver, making it similar to a sale.

items.text: Proof from a dying man's gift
items.text_en: Proof from a dying man's gift
items.desc_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda cites a case of a dying man who allocated sums to multiple recipients; the rule that a creditor collects from the last recipient shows that the rabbinic enactment applies even to gifts.

sub.text: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda cites a case of a dying man who allocated sums to multiple recipients without priority, where a creditor collects from all, to prove the rabbinic enactment applies to gifts.
Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda contrasts the case where the dying man specified sequential priority, so the creditor collects only from the last recipient.

Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda concludes that even if the first recipient received medium-quality land and the last received poor-quality land, the creditor collects from the poor-quality land, proving that the rabbinic enactment (תקנתא) applies to gifts as well.

items.text: Rejection: the case is about a debt
items.text_en: Rejection: the case is about a debt
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the case involves a debt (not a gift), and the phrase 'first in the document' refers to a document of appointment, not a deed of gift.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by explaining that the case involves a debt (not a gift), and the phrase 'first in the document' refers to a document of appointment (שטר פקדתא), not a deed of gift.

items.text: Alternative answers
items.text_en: Alternative answers
items.desc_en: Two alternative explanations are offered: either the case is indeed a gift but 'collects from the last' means only the last is harmed, or all recipients are equal in value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a first alternative: even if the case is a gift, the phrase 'collects from the last' means only the last recipient is harmed, so the creditor collects from him alone.
The Gemara offers a second alternative: all recipients are equal in value, so the creditor collects from any of them without special priority.

items.text: Mishnah: no collection for produce
items.text_en: Mishnah: no collection for produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one cannot collect for the consumption of produce from liened property. Ulla cites Resh Lakish: because they are not written.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one cannot collect for the consumption of produce from liened property.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind the Mishnah's ruling.
Ulla cites Resh Lakish that the reason is because these obligations are not written in the liened property document.

items.text: Objection from sustenance
items.text_en: Objection from sustenance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects that sustenance for wife and daughters is considered as if written, yet it cannot be collected from liened property. Ulla answers that it was instituted as written regarding free property but not regarding liened property.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects to Ulla's explanation that sustenance is not collected from liened property because it is not written, pointing out that the sustenance of wife and daughters is considered as if written, yet the Mishnah still rules that it is not collected from liened property.
Ulla answers that the sustenance was originally instituted as written regarding free property but not regarding liened property, resolving the objection.

items.text: Parallel objection and answer
items.text_en: Parallel objection and answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises the same objection to Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan, and receives the same answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Asi said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the reason is because they are not written.
Rabbi Zeira objects to Rabbi Asi that the allowance for a wife and daughters, which is as if written, still cannot be collected from liened property.
Rabbi Asi answers that from the outset the ordinance was established that they are considered written regarding free property but not regarding liened property.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's alternative reason
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's alternative reason
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina says the reason is that they are not fixed amounts. The Gemara then asks whether Rabbi Chanina requires both fixed and written amounts.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina provides an alternative reason for the mishnah's rule: because the amounts are not fixed (קצובין).
The Gemara raises a question: according to Rabbi Chanina, does he require both fixed amounts (קצובין) and written amounts (כתובין) for collection from liened property?

items.text: Gemara's concluding question on the previous sugya
items.text_en: Gemara's concluding question on the previous sugya
items.desc_en: The Gemara poses a final dilemma: is the reason that daughters' sustenance is not collected from encumbered property because the obligation is fixed (קצובין) even if not written, or perhaps because it is not fixed?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses a final dilemma: is the reason that daughters' sustenance is not collected from encumbered property because the obligation is fixed (קצובין) even if not written, or perhaps because it is not fixed?

items.text: Proof from a case of two daughters and a son
items.text_en: Proof from a case of two daughters and a son
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case where a man died leaving two daughters and a son; the first daughter took her tenth, then the son died. Rabbi Yochanan says the second daughter forfeited her sustenance, but Rabbi Chanina objects: they even collect for sustenance (פרנסה) which is fixed but not written, so surely sustenance (מזונות) should be collected? The Gemara answers that sustenance has publicity (קלא) and is considered as written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case: a man died leaving two daughters and a son; the first daughter took her tenth, then the son died before the second daughter could collect.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and Rabbi Chanina's objection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and Rabbi Chanina's objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says the second daughter forfeited her sustenance; Rabbi Chanina objects, arguing that if they even collect for פרנסה (sustenance for a daughter's dowry) which is fixed but not written, surely sustenance (מזונות) should be collected.
The Gemara emphasizes the strength of Rabbi Chanina's objection: פרנסה is fixed but unwritten, yet the court collects it, so all the more so should מזונות be collected.
The Gemara resolves: פרנסה is different because it has publicity (קלא) and is therefore considered as written, unlike ordinary מזונות.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution with a purchase
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution with a purchase
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach objects from the Mishnah that daughters of deceased are sustained from free property, but a wife from encumbered property because she is a creditor. The Gemara answers that the case involves a purchase (קנו מידו). It then explains the difference: if the purchase was made for one but not the other, the daughter of his wife benefits from the purchase, but his own daughter does not because she was not present at the time of the purchase.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach objects from the Mishnah: daughters of deceased are sustained from free property, but a wife from encumbered property because she is a creditor.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a purchase (קנו מידו) from the husband.
The Gemara objects: if so, daughters should also benefit from the purchase; it answers that the purchase was made for one but not the other.
The Gemara explains the difference: the daughter of his wife, who was present at the time of the purchase, benefits from it, but his own daughter, who was not present, does not.

items.text: Refinement: both present at the purchase, but distinction by תנאי בית דין
items.text_en: Refinement: both present at the purchase, but distinction by תנאי בית דין
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what if both were present at the purchase (e.g., he divorced and remarried)? It answers that his daughter eats by virtue of the court's condition (תנאי בית דין), so the purchase does not benefit her; but his wife's daughter does not eat by that condition, so the purchase does benefit her. The Gemara then refines: perhaps the daughter is not diminished; rather, since she eats by the court's condition, we say he might have mentally tied her to the purchase (צררי אתפסה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what if both women were present at the time of the purchase, e.g., he divorced and remarried?

The Gemara answers: his daughter eats by virtue of the court's condition (תנאי בית דין), so the purchase does not benefit her; but his wife's daughter does not eat by that condition, so the purchase does benefit her.
The Gemara refines: the daughter is not diminished; rather, since she eats by the court's condition, we say he might have mentally tied her to the purchase (צררי אתפסה).

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Natan's statement
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Natan's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a statement of Rabbi Natan: when does a prior lienholder collect from encumbered property? Only if the second purchaser's purchase preceded the first's improvement; otherwise, the first collects from encumbered property. This implies that the reason is that the obligation is not prior (קדים), supporting the view that lack of writing is the issue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Natan's statement that a prior lienholder collects from encumbered property only when the second purchase preceded the first's improvement, concluding that the reason is that the obligation is not prior (קָדֵים), supporting the view that lack of writing is the issue.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: reason for not collecting from encumbered property
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: reason for not collecting from encumbered property
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this is a dispute among Tannaim: one Tanna says that sustenance for wife and daughters is not collected from encumbered property because they are not written (אין כתובין). Rabbi Yosei objects: what repair of the world is there? Rather, because they are not fixed (אין קצובין).

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that sustenance for wife and daughters is not collected from encumbered property because these obligations are not written (אין כתובין) in a contract.
Rabbi Yosei objects: what repair of the world is there in this reason? Rather, the true reason is that these obligations are not fixed (אין קצובין) in amount.

items.text: Mishnah's rule: finder does not swear, and Rabbi Yitzchak's examples
items.text_en: Mishnah's rule: finder does not swear, and Rabbi Yitzchak's examples
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah: one who finds a lost object does not swear. Rabbi Yitzchak gives examples: if one claims two tied purses and the other admits to one, he swears; but for two tied oxgoads, he does not swear because they can be separated. The Gemara then asks: does Rabbi Yitzchak not accept the Mishnah's reason of תיקון העולם?

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who finds a lost object does not swear.
Rabbi Yitzchak provides examples: for two tied purses, the finder swears; for two tied oxgoads, he does not swear because they can be separated.
The Gemara explains the reason: oxgoads can be separated from each other, but purses cannot.
Rabbi Yitzchak adds: if one claims two tied oxgoads and the other admits to finding one and returning it, the finder swears.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yitzchak rejects the Mishnah's reason of תיקון העולם (the betterment of the world) for exempting the finder from swearing.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov vs. Sages
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov vs. Sages
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that one can swear on his own claim, as in the case where someone says 'I have a maneh of your father's in my hand, and I fed him pras' – he swears. The Sages say this is merely a returner of a lost object and he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute by citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that one can swear on his own claim, as in the case of someone who says 'I have a maneh of your father's in my hand, and I fed him pras'.
The Sages object that this case is merely a returner of a lost object, and the defendant is exempt from swearing.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Does Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov not accept the principle of 'returner of a lost object is exempt'? Rav answers: The case is with a minor claimant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rejects the principle that a returner of a lost object is exempt from an oath.
Rav answers that the case involves a minor claimant, which explains the exemption.

items.text: Objection and resolution: 'Minor' means adult in relation to father
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: 'Minor' means adult in relation to father
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: A minor has no tangible claim, as we learned that one does not swear on the claim of a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor. Rav explains: 'Minor' here means an adult, but he is called 'minor' because relative to his father's matters he is considered a minor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a minor has no tangible claim, citing the mishnah that one does not swear on the claim of a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor.
Rav resolves that 'minor' here means an adult, but he is called 'minor' because relative to his father's matters he is considered a minor.

items.text: Further objection: It's a claim of others, not his own
items.text_en: Further objection: It's a claim of others, not his own
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: If so, it is a claim of others, not his own claim! The response: It is a claim of others and an admission of his own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how this can be a claim of his own, and answers that it is a claim of others combined with his own admission.
The Gemara answers that it is a claim of others combined with an admission of his own.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: The dispute is based on Rabbah's principle
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: The dispute is based on Rabbah's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that all claims are claims of others and admissions of one's own. Rather, the dispute is based on Rabbah's reasoning: The Torah says a partial admitter swears because a person is not brazen-faced before his creditor. The defendant wants to deny everything but cannot due to shame, and wants to admit everything but delays. The Torah imposes an oath to force full admission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why all claims are not similarly considered claims of others with self-admission, and introduces Rabba's explanation for the Torah's law of partial admission.
Rabba explains that the Torah imposes an oath on a partial admitter because a person does not have the audacity to deny entirely in front of his creditor, and the partial denial is a stalling tactic.

The Gemara explains Rabbah's full reasoning: the defendant wants to deny everything but cannot due to shame, and wants to admit everything but delays, so the Torah imposes an oath to force full admission.

items.text: Conclusion: The dispute over brazenness toward the son
items.text_en: Conclusion: The dispute over brazenness toward the son
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that one is not brazen-faced whether before the creditor or his son, so it is not a returner of a lost object. The Sages hold that one is brazen-faced only before the creditor, but before his son he is brazen-faced, and since he is not brazen-faced, it is a returner of a lost object.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that one does not have audacity toward either the creditor or his son, so the defendant is not a returner of a lost object, while the Sages hold that audacity applies only toward the creditor himself, not his son, so the defendant is a returner of a lost object.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Guardians' obligations and oath requirements
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Guardians' obligations and oath requirements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that orphans who live with a householder or whose father appointed a guardian require the guardian to tithe their produce. A guardian appointed by the father must take an oath, but one appointed by the court does not; Abba Shaul reverses this.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that orphans living with a householder or whose father appointed a guardian require the guardian to tithe their produce.
The Mishnah rules that a guardian appointed by the father must take an oath, but one appointed by the court does not.
Abba Shaul reverses the ruling: a court-appointed guardian must take an oath, while a father-appointed one does not.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction and Rav Chisda's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction and Rav Chisda's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that excludes partners, sharecroppers, and guardians from tithing. Rav Chisda resolves it by distinguishing between tithing to feed (leha'achil) and tithing to store (lehaniach).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that excludes partners, sharecroppers, and guardians from tithing, implying they cannot tithe others' produce.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between tithing to feed (leha'achil) the orphans immediately and tithing to store (lehaniach) for later.

items.text: Baraita detailing guardians' powers and restrictions
items.text_en: Baraita detailing guardians' powers and restrictions
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates: guardians may tithe to feed but not to store; they may sell movable property for feeding but not for storage; they may acquire items with a fixed limit (lulav, shofar, etc.) but not charity or redeeming captives; they cannot sell at a distance or exchange fields for slaves; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi offer dissenting opinions; guardians must account at the end; women, slaves, and minors cannot be guardians unless appointed by the father.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that guardians may tithe and sell produce only for immediate feeding, not for storage.
The baraita lists items with a fixed limit (lulav, shofar, etc.) that guardians may acquire for orphans.
The baraita prohibits guardians from pledging charity or redeeming captives, as these have no fixed limit.
The baraita restricts guardians from litigating on behalf of orphans in a way that might incur a loss even if it could later bring a gain.
The baraita forbids selling distant fields to redeem nearby ones, lest the orphans' property be ruined.
The Tanna Kamma rules that guardians may not sell fields to buy slaves, but may sell slaves to buy fields.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel objects that even selling slaves for fields is forbidden, lest the slaves not be fit for work.
The Tanna Kamma rules that guardians may not free slaves directly, but may sell them to others who may free them.
Rabbi objects that the guardian himself may allow the slave to pay his own value and go free, since it is like selling to him.
The Tanna Kamma requires the guardian to account at the end; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees.
The baraita concludes that women, slaves, and minors may not be appointed guardians unless the father appointed them.

items.text: Stories of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi with guardians
items.text_en: Stories of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi with guardians
items.desc_en: Two anecdotes: Rabbi Meir prevented a guardian from selling land and buying slaves, despite a dream; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi did not intervene when a guardian sold land and bought oxen, following Rabbi Yose's principle of not calling one's property by another's name.

sub.desc_en: A guardian in Rabbi Meir's neighborhood was selling land and buying slaves, and Rabbi Meir prevented him.
A dream rebuked Rabbi Meir for interfering, but he dismissed dreams as inconsequential.
Rabbi Meir made peace between two quarreling neighbors, but one later regretted the peacemaking.

sub.text: Narrator (story about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi)
sub.text_en: Narrator (story about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi did not intervene when a guardian sold land and bought oxen, following Rabbi Yose's principle of not calling one's property by another's name.

items.text: Case of the old woman selling orphans' cow and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Case of the old woman selling orphans' cow and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: Orphans living with an old woman had their cow sold; relatives challenged the sale. Rav Nachman ruled that the sale is valid under the Mishnah's principle, but since the cow appreciated and no money was taken, the sale is void per Shmuel's rule that orphans' property is like hekdesh and only acquired with cash.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: orphans living with an old woman had their cow sold by her.
Relatives came before Rav Nachman and challenged the old woman's authority to sell the cow.
Rav Nachman initially rules that the sale is valid, citing the Mishnah's principle that orphans living with a householder are under the householder's authority.
The Gemara objects: the cow appreciated in value, and the buyers have not yet paid, so the sale should be invalid.
Rav Nachman reverses his ruling, applying Shmuel's principle that orphans' property is like הקדש (consecrated property) and is only acquired with cash, so since no money was taken, the sale is void.

items.text: Cases of price fluctuations and the application of Shmuel's rule
items.text_en: Cases of price fluctuations and the application of Shmuel's rule
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman applies Shmuel's rule to cases where wine or produce was drawn but prices changed: if the price rose, the sale is void (like hekdesh); if it fell, the buyer benefits (no stronger than a commoner). Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi adds that if orphans paid money, the sale is valid even if prices rise, as otherwise they would be unable to buy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates a case: the wine of Rabbana Ukva the orphan was drawn at four dinars per barrel, then increased to six.
Rav Nachman rules that this is the case of Rav Chanilai bar Idi citing Shmuel: orphans' property is like hekdesh and is acquired only with money, so the buyers must pay the higher price.

The Gemara states a general rule: if a buyer drew produce from orphans and the price rose, Shmuel's rule applies; if it fell, the buyer cannot renege because the power of a commoner is not greater than hekdesh.
The Gemara states the reverse: if the steward drew produce for the orphans and the price rose, the orphans benefit; if it fell, the students thought Shmuel's rule applies and the steward can cancel.
Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi objects that this would harm the orphans, as sellers would refuse to give them produce until they pay cash.
The Gemara states another case: if orphans paid money for produce and the price fell, they can renege; if it rose, the students thought Shmuel's rule applies and they acquire at the lower price.
Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi objects again that this would harm the orphans, as sellers would not sell to them without payment.

items.text: Opening scenario: selling land for taxes without proclamation
items.text_en: Opening scenario: selling land for taxes without proclamation
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where people come to say that the orphans' wheat was burned in the upper story. The guardians gave the orphans money for fruit; if it was expensive, they argue that the power of a commoner should not be stricter than that of consecrated property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where people inform guardians that the orphans' wheat was burned, and the guardians gave the orphans money for fruit.

The Gemara rules that if fruit became expensive, the guardians are not liable, as the power of a commoner should not be stricter than that of consecrated property, and this aligns with Rav Chanilai bar Idi's principle.

items.text: Rav Shisha bar Idi's objection
items.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Idi's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Idi argues that this practice is harmful to the orphans because sometimes they need money and no one will give them any until they give fruit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi objects that giving orphans money for fruit is harmful because sometimes they need money and no one will give them any until they give fruit.

items.text: Rav Ashi's testimony about selling land for taxes
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's testimony about selling land for taxes
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi recounts that he and Rav Kahana signed a document for the mother of Ze'eira the orphan, who sold land for the tax without proclamation, citing the Nehardeans' ruling that for tax, sustenance, and burial, one may sell without proclamation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi recounts that he and Rav Kahana signed a document for the mother of Ze'eira the orphan, who sold land for the tax without proclamation, citing the Nehardeans' ruling that for tax, sustenance, and burial, one may sell without proclamation.

items.text: Case of Amram the dyer and the guardian's liability
items.text_en: Case of Amram the dyer and the guardian's liability
items.desc_en: Amram the dyer was a guardian for orphans. Relatives complained to Rav Nachman that he was wearing clothes and eating from their property. Rav Nachman responded that he needs to be heard, and that if he causes loss, they should bring witnesses and he will remove him, citing Rav Huna's ruling that a guardian who causes loss is removed.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the case of Amram the dyer, who was a guardian for orphans, and relatives complained to Rav Nachman that he was wearing clothes from the orphans' property.
Rav Nachman responds that the guardian needs to be heard, and regarding his eating and drinking, perhaps he found a lost item.

Rav Nachman tells the relatives to bring witnesses that he causes loss, and he will remove him, citing Rav Huna's ruling that a guardian who causes loss is removed, and the halacha is that we remove him.

items.text: Dispute about oath for guardian appointed by father vs. court
items.text_en: Dispute about oath for guardian appointed by father vs. court
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the oath requirement: a guardian appointed by the father swears because he benefits, while one appointed by the court does not swear. Abba Shaul reverses the rulings, and Rav Chanan bar Ami says the halakha follows Abba Shaul.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states the rule: a guardian appointed by the father swears an oath, but one appointed by the court does not swear.

The Gemara asks the rationale for the Tanna Kamma's ruling and provides the reason: the father-appointed guardian benefits, so he does not refrain from taking the oath; the court-appointed guardian does not benefit, so imposing an oath would deter him.

Abba Shaul reverses the rulings: the court-appointed guardian swears because he gains a reputation as trustworthy, while the father-appointed guardian does not swear because he acts as a favor between friends and would be deterred by an oath.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Ami citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Ami citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Ami reports in the name of Shmuel that the halakha (binding law) follows Abba Shaul.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion and Rav Tachlifa's baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion and Rav Tachlifa's baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says both types of guardians swear, and the halakha follows him. Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva taught that a guardian appointed by the father swears because he is like a paid bailee, but Rabbi Avahu corrects him to say 'like a paid bailee'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says both types of guardians swear, and the halakha follows him.
Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva taught before Rabbi Avahu that a guardian appointed by the father swears because he is a paid bailee, but Rabbi Avahu corrects him to say 'like a paid bailee'.

items.text: Mishnah: One who causes impurity, mixes, or libates
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who causes impurity, mixes, or libates
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who causes impurity, mixes terumah with non-sacred produce, or libates wine for idolatry is exempt if unintentional but liable if intentional.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who causes impurity, mixes terumah with non-sacred produce, or libates wine for idolatry is exempt if unintentional but liable if intentional.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on 'menasech'
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on 'menasech'
items.desc_en: Rav says 'menasech' means actual libation, while Shmuel says it means mixing. The Gemara explains each position: Shmuel holds that an actual libator is liable for a more severe penalty, while Rav holds that one is not liable for capital punishment until the act of libation, citing Rabbi Yirmeya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by reporting a dispute: Rav says 'menasech' means actual libation, while Shmuel says it means mixing.
The Gemara asks: why does the one who says 'me'arev' (mixing) not say 'menasech' (actual libation)?
Shmuel's position is that an actual libator (מנסך) would be liable for a more severe penalty (capital punishment), so the Mishnah's context of monetary liability must refer to mixing.

sub.text: Rav's answer (via Gemara and Rabbi Yirmeya)
sub.text_en: Rav's answer (via Gemara and Rabbi Yirmeya)
sub.desc_en: Rav, citing Rabbi Yirmeya, holds that one is not liable for capital punishment until the actual act of libation (ניסוך), so the Mishnah can refer to actual libation even in a monetary context.
The Gemara asks: why does the one who says 'menasech' (actual libation) not say 'me'arev' (mixing)?
Rav's position is that the term 'me'arev' (mixing) would imply a lesser act, but the Mishnah's context requires the more severe act of actual libation.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's three cases
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's three cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists three separate cases (מטמא, מנסך, מדמע) if they all involve the same principle of causing damage that is not immediately noticeable. It explains that each case is necessary to teach a unique aspect: for מטמא, the concern is causing impurity to terumah; for מנסך, it is a penalty and not learned from other penalties; for מדמע, it is a common occurrence. The Gemara concludes that all three are needed to cover different scenarios.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists three cases (מטמא, מנסך, מדמע) when they seem to be the same principle.
The Gemara answers that the case of מנסך is a penalty (קנסא) and one cannot derive other penalties from it.

sub.text: Gemara's question (for those who derive penalties)
sub.text_en: Gemara's question (for those who derive penalties)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the one who does derive penalties from other penalties, why are all three cases needed?

The Gemara explains that all three are necessary: if only מטמא were taught, one might think it applies only to terumah (complete loss) but not to hullin; if only מדמע were taught, one might think it applies only because it is common, but not מטמא.
The Gemara continues: if only מדמע were taught, one might think it applies only because it is common, but not מטמא which is uncommon.

The Gemara explains that if only מטמא and מדמע were taught, one might think they apply only because the damage is not certain (לא קים ליה בדרבה מיניה), but for מנסך where it is certain, one might exempt; therefore the Mishnah teaches the case of מנסך, in accordance with Rabbi Yirmeya's principle.

items.text: Alternative version of the Mishnah's cases
items.text_en: Alternative version of the Mishnah's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita from the father of Rabbi Avin that initially only listed מטמא and מנסך, and later added מדמע. It then explains why all three are still necessary: each case teaches a different reason for liability, such as lack of awareness of the greater prohibition (מטמא), complete loss (מנסך), or significant loss (מטמא and מנסך together), while מדמע involves a minor loss.

sub.text: Baraita from the father of Rabbi Avin
sub.text_en: Baraita from the father of Rabbi Avin
sub.desc_en: The baraita presents an earlier version of the Mishnah's cases, initially only listing מטמא and מנסך, and later adding מדמע.
The Gemara asks why all three cases are necessary, given that they seem redundant.

The Gemara begins to explain that each case is needed: מטמא alone might be thought to apply only because of complete loss or because of the prohibition of causing טומאה to חולין in Eretz Yisrael, but מדמע might not be included.
The Gemara continues: if only מדמע were taught, one might think it applies because it is common, but מטמא, which is uncommon, might not be included.

The Gemara concludes: if only מטמא and מדמע were taught, one might think they apply because the perpetrator is not aware of the greater prohibition, but מנסך, where he is aware, might not be included; therefore all three are necessary.

items.text: Chizkiyah's view on damage that is not noticeable
items.text_en: Chizkiyah's view on damage that is not noticeable
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah states that by Torah law, both an unintentional and intentional actor are liable for damage that is not noticeable (הזיק שאינו ניכר), because it is considered actual damage. The reason the Sages exempted the unintentional actor is to encourage him to inform the victim. The Gemara questions why this reasoning would not also apply to the intentional actor, and answers that since he intends to cause damage, he will not inform.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiyah states that by Torah law, both an unintentional and intentional actor are liable for damage that is not noticeable (הזיק שאינו ניכר), because it is considered actual damage.
Chizkiyah explains that the Sages exempted the unintentional actor to encourage him to inform the victim.
The Gemara questions why the same reasoning would not apply to the intentional actor, and answers that since he intends to cause damage, he will not inform.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's opposing view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's opposing view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that by Torah law, both unintentional and intentional actors are exempt for damage that is not noticeable, because it is not considered actual damage. The Sages imposed liability on the intentional actor to prevent people from deliberately causing such damage and claiming exemption.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that by Torah law both unintentional and intentional actors are exempt for damage that is not noticeable, because it is not considered actual damage, and explains that the Sages imposed liability on the intentional actor to prevent people from deliberately causing such damage and claiming exemption.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yochanan from a Mishnah about priests
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yochanan from a Mishnah about priests
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where priests who intentionally commit piggul in the Temple are liable, and the explanation is 'for the betterment of the world.' If Chizkiyah were correct, the Mishnah should have also mentioned that unintentional actors are exempt for the betterment of the world. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah indeed implies that unintentional actors are exempt for the betterment of the world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that priests who intentionally commit פיגול (improper intention) in the Temple are liable, and a baraita explains this is for the betterment of the world.

The Gemara objects that if Chizkiyah were correct that damage not evident is considered damage, the Mishnah should have explicitly stated that unintentional actors are exempt for the betterment of the world.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah indeed implies that unintentional actors are exempt for the betterment of the world, as it states only intentional actors are liable.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar raises an objection from a case where one performs work with the water of the red heifer or the heifer itself, which is exempt from human courts but liable in heavenly courts. If damage that is not noticeable were considered actual damage, one should be liable in human courts as well. Rabbi Elazar himself resolves the objection by explaining that the case involves using the heifer for nursing and treading, and the water for weighing, which are not typical uses that cause damage.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar raises an objection: if damage that is not noticeable is considered actual damage, then one who performs work with the water of the red heifer or the heifer itself should be liable in human courts, not only in heavenly courts.

Rabbi Elazar resolves his own objection by explaining that the cases involve atypical uses: the heifer was placed to nurse and tread, and the water was used for weighing, which are not standard acts of damage.
The Gemara begins to cite Rava's statement about the water of purification, likely to challenge or clarify the resolution.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction about coins used for weights
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction about coins used for weights
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction about coins used for weights: one case involves using the coins themselves (בגופן), which is an actual act of damage, while the other involves using them as a counterweight (בכנגדן). The distinction is whether the owner had abandoned hope of recovery (אסח דעתיה) or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if coins used for weights are valid, how can this be reconciled with the principle of damage?

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between using the coins themselves (בגופן), which is actual damage, and using them as a counterweight (בכנגדן), which is not; further, the owner's abandonment of hope (אסח דעתיה) determines liability.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection from the Mishnah of damaged coins
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection from the Mishnah of damaged coins
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites a Mishnah where one who steals a coin that later becomes invalid, or terumah that becomes impure, or chametz that passes Passover, can simply return the item. If damage that is not apparent is considered damage, the thief would have to pay full value. This is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites a Mishnah where one who steals a coin that becomes invalid, terumah that becomes impure, or chametz that passes Passover can simply return the item, implying that damage that is not apparent is not considered damage.
The Gemara concludes that if damage that is not apparent were considered damage, the thief would have to pay full value, making this a refutation of that position.

items.text: Attempt to resolve from the Tannaitic dispute about rendering terumah impure
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve from the Tannaitic dispute about rendering terumah impure
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about one who renders terumah impure, mixes it with hullin, or pours libation to idolatry, is about whether damage that is not apparent is considered damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about one who renders terumah impure, mixes it with hullin, or pours libation to idolatry, is about whether damage that is not apparent (היזק שאינו ניכר) is considered damage.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that all agree damage that is not apparent is not considered damage; the dispute is about whether the Sages penalized an unintentional offender because of an intentional one (קנסו שוגג אטו מזיד).

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the dispute by asserting that all agree damage that is not apparent is not considered damage, and the disagreement is about whether the Sages penalized an unintentional offender because of an intentional one (קנסו שוגג אטו מזיד).

items.text: Contradictions within Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's positions
items.text_en: Contradictions within Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises contradictions between Rabbi Meir's ruling here and his ruling about cooking on Shabbat, and similarly for Rabbi Yehuda. It resolves them by distinguishing between rabbinic and biblical laws, and by noting the special stringency of idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rabbi Meir's ruling here (about one who renders wine libation) and his ruling about cooking on Shabbat, and similarly for Rabbi Yehuda, citing a baraita with three opinions.
The baraita presents the positions of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar regarding eating food cooked on Shabbat by a shogeg (unintentional) or mezid (intentional) cook.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction for Rabbi Meir by distinguishing between rabbinic laws (דרבנן), where he penalizes, and biblical laws (דאורייתא), where he does not.
The Gemara objects that the case of rendering wine libation (מנסך) is a biblical prohibition, yet Rabbi Meir penalizes the shogeg, contradicting the proposed distinction.
The Gemara resolves that the penalty for idolatry (עבודה זרה) is an exception due to its special stringency, overriding the general rule.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction for Rabbi Yehuda by reversing the distinction: he does not penalize for rabbinic laws but does for biblical ones, with idolatry again being an exceptional stringency.

items.text: Further contradiction regarding planting on Shabbat and Shemittah
items.text_en: Further contradiction regarding planting on Shabbat and Shemittah
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another contradiction within Rabbi Meir's rulings about planting on Shabbat and during the Sabbatical year. It resolves by citing Rabbi Meir's own reasoning: Israel counts years to the Shemittah, so the prohibition is more severe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction within Rabbi Meir's rulings regarding planting on Shabbat and during the Sabbatical year, both of which are Torah prohibitions.
The Gemara objects that the contradiction is inherent: both Shabbat and Shemittah are Torah laws, so why should Rabbi Meir distinguish between them?
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by citing Rabbi Meir's own reasoning: Israel counts years to the Shemittah, so the prohibition is more severe and applies even to an unintentional act.

items.text: Opening statement: Israel not suspected regarding Shabbat
items.text_en: Opening statement: Israel not suspected regarding Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not count years from Shabbatot, and a second reason: Israel was suspected regarding shemittah but not regarding Shabbatot.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not count years from Shabbatot, and adds that Israel was suspected regarding shemittah but not regarding Shabbatot.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of 'davar acher'
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of 'davar acher'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'davar acher' addresses a potential concern: if the thirtieth day falls on Shabbat, planting that day might not count as a full year. The second statement confirms that Israel was not suspected regarding Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'דבר אחר' (another matter) means, and explains that it addresses a hypothetical: if the thirtieth day falls on Shabbat, planting that day might not count as a full year.
The Gemara answers by citing the second statement: 'דבר אחר' teaches that Israel was suspected regarding the Sabbatical year but not regarding Shabbat.

items.text: Resolution of Rabbi Yehuda's apparent contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of Rabbi Yehuda's apparent contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's views: in his locale, shemittah was treated stringently, as illustrated by a story where one rebukes another for eating shemittah produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's views by explaining that in his locale, shemittah was treated stringently.
A story is cited where one rebukes another for eating shemittah produce, illustrating the local stringency.

items.text: Baraita on paying for impure terumah
items.text_en: Baraita on paying for impure terumah
items.desc_en: A baraita states: one who ate impure terumah pays pure hullin. If he paid impure hullin, Sumchos in the name of Rabbi Meir says: if unintentional, payment is valid; if intentional, invalid. The Gemara questions why intentional payment is invalid, noting the offender benefits by paying something he could use.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the case of one who ate impure terumah and pays pure hullin, and the dispute between Sumchos in the name of Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding payment with impure hullin.
The Gemara questions why intentional payment is invalid, noting that the offender benefits by paying something he could use during his impurity.

items.text: Rava's emendation and Rav Acha's explanation
items.text_en: Rava's emendation and Rav Acha's explanation
items.desc_en: Rava emends the baraita: one who ate impure terumah pays any amount; one who ate pure terumah pays pure hullin. Rav Acha bar Rav Ika explains the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that the Sages did not penalize an unintentional offender to deter intentional transgression, while the Sages hold they did.

sub.desc_en: Rava emends the baraita: one who ate impure terumah pays any amount; one who ate pure terumah pays pure hullin; the dispute about paying impure hullin remains as before.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages is whether the Sages penalized an unintentional offender (שוגג) to deter intentional transgression (מזיד).

items.text: Objection to penalizing the unintentional offender
items.text_en: Objection to penalizing the unintentional offender
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: in the case of payment, the offender intends to pay, so why penalize him?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that since the offender intends to pay, there is no basis to penalize him.

items.text: Supporting cases and their rejection
items.text_en: Supporting cases and their rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings cases of blood, tithing on Shabbat, and immersing vessels on Shabbat, where intentional acts are penalized. Rabbi Meir rejects each: in those cases, the person intends for atonement, improvement, or purification, so penalizing is inappropriate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about blood that became impure and was sprinkled: unintentionally it is accepted, intentionally it is not, suggesting a penalty for unintentional acts.
Rabbi Meir rejects the proof: there the person intends for atonement, so we do not penalize him.
The Gemara brings a mishna about one who tithes on Shabbat: unintentionally he may eat, intentionally he may not, again suggesting a penalty.
Rabbi Meir rejects again: there the person intends to repair the produce, so we do not penalize him.
The Gemara brings a mishna about one who immerses vessels on Shabbat: unintentionally he may use them, intentionally he may not.
Rabbi Meir rejects: there the person intends to purify the vessels, so we do not penalize him.

items.text: Introduction of a contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's views
items.text_en: Introduction of a contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's views
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Yehuda regarding rabbinic laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Yehuda regarding rabbinic laws, citing a baraita.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Priests who piggul in the Temple
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Priests who piggul in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that priests who intentionally commit piggul (disqualification of a sacrifice by improper intent) in the Temple are liable. This sets the stage for the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that priests who intentionally commit piggul (disqualification of a sacrifice by improper intent) in the Temple are liable.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita on trustworthiness of a priest's statement
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita on trustworthiness of a priest's statement
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a priest says he made pure items or sacrifices with someone and they became impure or piggul, he is believed. But if he specifies a particular day, he is not believed. The Gemara questions the distinction.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a priest is believed when he says that pure items or sacrifices he prepared with someone became impure or piggul, but not when he specifies a particular day.

items.text: Abaye and Rava explain the baraita
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava explain the baraita
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the priest is believed only when the matter is still in his hands (i.e., he can still affect it). Rava explains that the case is where the priest was found and said nothing initially, but later made the claim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the first case of the baraita from the second case.
Abaye explains that the priest is believed only when the matter is still in his hands (i.e., he can still affect it).
Rava explains that the case is where the priest was found and said nothing initially, but later made the claim.

items.text: Story with Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi: Source for priest's credibility
items.text_en: Story with Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi: Source for priest's credibility
items.desc_en: A man comes before Rabbi Ami claiming his pure items became impure on a specific day. Rabbi Ami rules he is not believed. Rabbi Asi challenges this, citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei that the Torah believed him. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna proves this from the High Priest on Yom Kippur, who is believed about piggul even though no one else is in the Tent of Meeting. The Gemara raises and rejects objections.

sub.desc_en: A man comes before Rabbi Ami claiming that pure items he prepared with a colleague became impure on a specific day, and Rabbi Ami rules that he is not believed.
Rabbi Asi challenges Rabbi Ami, citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei that the Torah believed the priest.
The Gemara asks where the Torah believed the priest.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna proves the principle from the High Priest on Yom Kippur, who is believed about piggul even though no one else is in the Tent of Meeting.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the High Priest was heard declaring piggul, but the Gemara rejects this because even if heard, he might be lying after the fact.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the High Priest was seen through a window, but this objection is left unresolved as a difficulty.

items.text: Story of a Torah scroll with improperly written divine names
items.text_en: Story of a Torah scroll with improperly written divine names
items.desc_en: A man comes before Rabbi Ami claiming he wrote a Torah scroll for someone but did not write the divine names with proper intent. Rabbi Ami rules he is believed to lose his own wages but not to invalidate the scroll. Rabbi Yirmeya questions this, and Rabbi Ami explains that a scroll without properly written divine names is worthless.

sub.desc_en: A man comes before Rabbi Ami and claims that the divine names (אזכרות) in the Torah scroll he wrote for a buyer were not written with proper intent (לשמן).
Rabbi Ami asks who currently holds the scroll, and the man replies that it is in the buyer's possession.
Rabbi Ami rules that the scribe is believed to forfeit his own wages but not to invalidate the Torah scroll.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects: even if the scribe loses the wages for the divine names, why should he lose the entire wage for the whole scroll?
Rabbi Ami answers that indeed the entire scroll is worthless, because any Torah scroll whose divine names were not written with proper intent (לשמן) has no value.

items.text: Discussion of fixing the scroll and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Discussion of fixing the scroll and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the divine names could be fixed by scraping and re-sanctifying. It questions whether this follows Rabbi Yehuda's view that such correction is valid. The Gemara explains that even Rabbi Yehuda would not allow this for an entire scroll, as it would appear spotted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the scribe cannot simply scrape the divine names and re-sanctify them, implying this would follow Rabbi Yehuda's view.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda permits scraping and re-sanctifying a single divine name, while the Sages forbid it.
The Gemara resolves that even Rabbi Yehuda would not permit scraping the entire scroll, because it would appear spotted (like a patchwork).

items.text: Second story: Torah scroll with improperly processed parchment
items.text_en: Second story: Torah scroll with improperly processed parchment
items.desc_en: A man comes before Rabbi Avahu claiming he wrote a Torah scroll for someone but did not process the parchment for the sake of the scroll. Rabbi Avahu rules that since he is believed to lose his own wages, he is also believed to invalidate the scroll.

sub.desc_en: A man comes before Rabbi Avahu claiming he wrote a Torah scroll for someone but did not process the parchment for the sake of the scroll; Rabbi Avahu rules that since he is believed to lose his own wages, he is also believed to invalidate the scroll.

items.text: Transition from previous sugya: distinguishing Rabbi Ammi's case
items.text_en: Transition from previous sugya: distinguishing Rabbi Ammi's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the current case from Rabbi Ammi's ruling, answering that here the husband loses his entire wage and says 'I mean truth' to ensure the get is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the current case from Rabbi Ammi's ruling, where the husband might have been mistaken about Rabbi Yirmeya's teaching.
The Gemara answers that here the husband loses his entire wage, so he is presumed to be truthful when he says 'I mean truth' to validate the get.

items.text: Mishnah: Testimony of Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgda
items.text_en: Mishnah: Testimony of Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgda
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records four testimonies: a deaf woman whose father married her off goes out with a get; a minor Israelite girl married to a kohen eats terumah and the husband inherits; a stolen brick built into a palace is compensated with money due to takkanat hashavim; a stolen chatat unknown to the public atones due to tikkun hamizbe'ach.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgda's testimony about a deaf woman married off by her father, who goes out with a גט (bill of divorce).
The Mishnah continues with the testimony about a minor Israelite girl married to a kohen, who eats תרומה (priestly portion) and whose husband inherits her.
The Mishnah adds the testimony about a stolen brick built into a palace, where the thief receives its value due to תקנת השבים (the enactment for penitents).
