The Mishnah concludes with the testimony about a stolen sin-offering unknown to the public, which atones due to תיקון המזבח (the improvement of the altar).

items.text: Rava's deduction from the deaf woman's case
items.text_en: Rava's deduction from the deaf woman's case
items.desc_en: Rava infers from Rabbi Yochanan's testimony that if a husband says to witnesses 'see this get' and then tells his wife 'collect this document', she is divorced, because no awareness is required — just as the deaf woman needs no understanding. The Gemara clarifies this is not obvious and addresses a potential challenge about nullification.

sub.desc_en: Rava infers from Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada's testimony that if a husband tells witnesses 'see this get' and then tells his wife 'collect this document', she is divorced, because no awareness is required, just as the deaf woman needs no understanding.
The Gemara objects that Rava's deduction is obvious, and suggests that one might think the husband nullified the get by calling it a 'document of debt'.
The Gemara resolves that the case teaches that if the husband truly intended to nullify the get, he would have told the witnesses, not his wife; his statement to her was merely out of embarrassment.

items.text: Why a deaf woman does not eat terumah
items.text_en: Why a deaf woman does not eat terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts the minor girl who eats terumah with a deaf woman who does not. It offers several reasons: a decree lest a deaf man feed a deaf woman; the minor is like one eating neveilot; a decree lest a deaf man feed a hearing woman; a concern about ascending from rabbinic terumah to Torah terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah permits a minor girl married to a priest to eat terumah, but a deaf woman (who is an adult) does not, and asks why.
The Gemara answers that it is a decree lest a deaf man (her husband) feed a deaf woman (herself) terumah, since a deaf person lacks understanding of the prohibition.
The Gemara objects: let the deaf woman eat terumah anyway, because a minor who eats neveilot (non-kosher meat) is not culpable, so why worry about the deaf man feeding her?
The Gemara answers that the decree is lest a deaf man feed a hearing woman (who is obligated in the prohibition), which would be a Torah violation.
The Gemara objects: let the deaf woman eat at least rabbinic terumah (תרומה דרבנן), which is less stringent.
The Gemara answers that it is a decree lest one come to feed her Torah terumah (תרומה דאורייתא), since the distinction between rabbinic and Torah terumah might be confused.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on stolen brick
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on stolen brick
items.desc_en: A baraitha records that Beit Shammai require dismantling the entire palace to return the brick, while Beit Hillel rule the thief only pays its value due to takkanat hashavim.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the case of a stolen brick built into a palace, with Beit Shammai ruling that the thief must dismantle the entire palace to return the brick.
Beit Hillel rules that the thief only pays the value of the brick, due to תקנת השבין (the enactment for penitents).

items.text: Dispute on why stolen chatat atones
items.text_en: Dispute on why stolen chatat atones
items.desc_en: Ulla states that by Torah law a stolen chatat never atones unless unknown to the public, due to tikkun hamizbe'ach — otherwise priests would be distressed and neglect the altar. Rav Yehuda holds that Torah law itself permits atonement because despair effects acquisition.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that by Torah law a stolen chatat never atones, but the rabbis decreed that if unknown to the public it atones, to prevent priests from becoming distressed and neglecting the altar.
The rabbis object to Ulla, noting that the Mishnah explicitly says the reason is 'for the sake of tikkun hamizbe'ach (repair of the altar),' not 'so that priests not be distressed.'
Ulla answers that since distressed priests would neglect the altar, the result is the same as tikkun hamizbe'ach.
Rav Yehuda states that by Torah law a stolen chatat always atones, because יאוש (despair of the owner) effects acquisition.

items.text: Reason for stolen sin-offering not atoning
items.text_en: Reason for stolen sin-offering not atoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why a stolen sin-offering whose theft is known does not atone: to prevent people from saying the altar consumes stolen goods.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a stolen sin-offering whose theft is known does not atone.
The Gemara answers that the reason is to prevent people from saying the altar consumes stolen goods.

items.text: Reconciling Ulla and Rav Yehuda on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Reconciling Ulla and Rav Yehuda on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifically mentions a sin-offering, given Rav Yehuda's view that even a burnt-offering is disqualified. It answers that the Mishnah is not exclusive, but even a sin-offering, which is partially consumed by priests, is included in the decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies a sin-offering (חטאת) given Rav Yehuda's view that even a burnt-offering (עולה) would be disqualified.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is not exclusive but uses a 'not to mention' (לא מיבעיא) formulation: even a sin-offering, partially consumed by priests, is included in the decree.

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah's ruling on unknown theft
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah's ruling on unknown theft
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a contradiction: the Mishnah says a stolen sin-offering whose theft is unknown atones, but according to Rav Yehuda, it should be the opposite. It resolves that the Mishnah means the opposite: unknown theft atones, known theft does not, due to the repair of the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishna: a stolen sin-offering whose theft is unknown to the public atones, for the benefit of the altar.
The Gemara asks: according to Ulla it works, but according to Rav Yehuda the opposite should have been stated.
The Gemara resolves: the mishna means the opposite — unknown theft atones, known theft does not, for the benefit of the altar.

items.text: Rava's objection from the law of theft and consecration
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the law of theft and consecration
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection: if one steals, consecrates, then slaughters or sells, he pays double but not four or five. A baraita adds that if done outside, he is liable for karet. If despair does not acquire, why is there karet?

sub.desc_en: Rava objects: if one steals, consecrates, then slaughters or sells, he pays double but not four or five; a baraita adds that if done outside he is liable for karet, but if despair does not acquire, why is there karet?

items.text: Rav Sheizvi's answer and Rava's defense
items.text_en: Rav Sheizvi's answer and Rava's defense
items.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi answers that the karet is rabbinic. When challenged, Rava defends him, explaining that the rabbis placed the animal in his domain to impose liability, so the karet comes through their enactment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi answers that the karet penalty in the baraita is rabbinic (מדבריהם), not biblical.
The Gemara objects: is there such a thing as a rabbinic karet penalty?
Rava defends Rav Sheizvi, explaining that the rabbis placed the animal in the thief's domain to impose liability, so the karet penalty comes through their enactment.

items.text: Rava's inquiry about the timing of rabbinic ownership
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry about the timing of rabbinic ownership
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether the rabbis placed the animal in his domain from the time of theft or from consecration, with practical implications for shearings and offspring. He concludes it is from consecration, so the sinner does not profit.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether the rabbis placed the animal in his domain from the time of theft or from consecration, with practical implications for shearings and offspring.
Rava concludes it is from consecration, so the sinner does not profit.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of Sicaricon in Judea
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of Sicaricon in Judea
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that there was no Sicaricon in Judea for those killed in war, but after the war there was. It details cases where purchases from a Sicaricon are void or valid, and later courts added that the buyer gives a quarter to the original owners, with priority if they can buy. Rabbi instituted a twelve-month waiting period.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the general rule about Sicaricon in Judea and gives the first case: buying from the Sicaricon and then from the owner voids the purchase, but the reverse is valid.
The Mishnah adds a second case: buying from the husband and then from the wife voids the purchase, but the reverse is valid, and notes this is the first Mishnah.
The later court rules that a buyer from a Sicaricon must give a quarter to the original owners, but only when the owners cannot afford to buy; if they can, they have priority.
Rabbi institutes a twelve-month waiting period after which any buyer acquires the property, but still must give a quarter to the original owners.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's wording: if there was no Sicaricon during the war, how could there be after? Rav Yehuda explains it means they did not judge Sicaricon cases. Rabbi Assi details three decrees: in the first, anyone who didn't kill was killed; in the second, a killer paid four zuz; in the third, a killer was killed. In the first two, the coercion caused the seller to transfer ownership; in the third, the buyer could be sued later.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's contradiction: if there was no Sicaricon during the war, how could there be after?
Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah means they did not judge Sicaricon cases during the war.

Rabbi Assi details three decrees: in the first, anyone who didn't kill was killed; in the second, a killer paid four zuz; in the third, a killer was killed, explaining that in the first two the coercion caused the seller to transfer ownership, while in the third the buyer could be sued later.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's aggadic explanation of Jerusalem's destruction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's aggadic explanation of Jerusalem's destruction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains the verse about fearing constantly, attributing the destruction of Jerusalem to the story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, where a man mistakenly invited his enemy Bar Kamtza to a feast, leading to humiliation and ultimately the destruction.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by citing the verse 'אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם מְפַחֵד תָּמִיד וּמַקְשֶׁה לִבּוֹ יִפּוֹל בְּרָעָה' (Happy is the man who fears always, but he who hardens his heart will fall into evil).

Rabbi Yochanan answers that the verse applies to three historical calamities: the destruction of Jerusalem due to the story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, the destruction of the king's mountain due to a rooster and a hen, and the destruction of Beitar due to a shaft of a carriage.

The Gemara elaborates the story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza: a man who loved Kamtza but hated Bar Kamtza sent his servant to invite Kamtza, but the servant mistakenly brought Bar Kamtza; the host found Bar Kamtza seated and demanded he leave, but Bar Kamtza pleaded to stay and offered to pay for his food and drink.

items.text: Bar Kamtza's humiliation and revenge
items.text_en: Bar Kamtza's humiliation and revenge
items.desc_en: Bar Kamtza is publicly humiliated at a feast when the host refuses to let him stay, even after offering to pay for the entire meal. In anger, he decides to inform on the Jews to the Roman emperor.

sub.desc_en: The host refuses Bar Kamtza's escalating offers to pay for the feast and physically removes him.

items.text: Bar Kamtza's plot and the sages' inaction
items.text_en: Bar Kamtza's plot and the sages' inaction
items.desc_en: Bar Kamtza goes to the emperor and claims the Jews are rebelling. He suggests sending a sacrifice to test them. The emperor sends a calf with a blemish, which the sages consider offering for the sake of peace with the empire, but Rabbi Zecharya ben Avkulas prevents it, fearing it would set a precedent. He also prevents killing Bar Kamtza to silence him.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kamtza concludes that the sages' silence at his humiliation indicates their approval, so he decides to inform against them to the emperor.
Bar Kamtza tells the emperor that the Jews are rebelling, and the emperor asks for proof.
Bar Kamtza suggests sending a sacrifice to test whether the Jews will offer it.
The emperor sends a three-year-old calf, and Bar Kamtza places a blemish on its lip (or eye) that is a defect for Jews but not for Romans.
The sages consider offering the blemished sacrifice for the sake of peace with the empire.
Rabbi Zecharya ben Avkulas objects that offering a blemished sacrifice would set a precedent that blemished animals may be offered on the altar.
The sages consider killing Bar Kamtza to prevent him from reporting back to the emperor.

sub.text: Rabbi Zecharya ben Avkulas' second objection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zecharya ben Avkulas' second objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zecharya ben Avkulas objects that killing Bar Kamtza would set a precedent that one who places a blemish on consecrated animals is executed.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's lament
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's lament
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan laments that the excessive humility of Rabbi Zecharya ben Avkulas led to the destruction of the Temple and the exile of the Jewish people.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan declares that the excessive humility of Rabbi Zecharya ben Avkulas destroyed the Temple, burned the Sanctuary, and exiled the Jews from their land.

items.text: Nero's campaign and conversion
items.text_en: Nero's campaign and conversion
items.desc_en: The emperor sends Nero Caesar against the Jews. Nero tests the direction of his arrows and finds they all point toward Jerusalem, interpreting this as divine will. He then asks a child for a verse, which speaks of God taking vengeance on Edom through Israel. Nero concludes that God wants to destroy the Temple but will punish him, so he flees, converts to Judaism, and becomes the ancestor of Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The emperor sends Nero Caesar against the Jews; Nero tests his arrows and they all fall toward Jerusalem, indicating divine will.
Nero asks a child to recite a verse for him.
The child recites the verse about God taking vengeance on Edom through Israel.
Nero concludes that God wants to destroy the Temple but will punish him, so he flees, converts to Judaism, and becomes the ancestor of Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Vespasian's siege and the city's wealthy benefactors
items.text_en: Vespasian's siege and the city's wealthy benefactors
items.desc_en: Vespasian besieges Jerusalem for three years. Three wealthy men—Nakdimon ben Guryon, Ben Kalba Savua, and Ben Tzitzit Hakeset—offer to supply the city with provisions. They have enough to sustain the city for twenty-one years.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces Vespasian's siege of Jerusalem for three years and the three wealthy benefactors who could supply the city.
Each benefactor offers to supply different provisions, and the sages praise the wood supplier, citing Rav Chisda's teaching that grain requires sixty times its volume in wood for cooking.

items.text: The biryoni's destruction and the famine
items.text_en: The biryoni's destruction and the famine
items.desc_en: The biryoni (zealots) prevent the sages from making peace with the Romans and also prevent them from fighting. They burn the storehouses of grain, causing a famine. The wealthy Marta bat Baytus dies from eating a dried fig of Rabbi Tzadok, and she throws her gold into the street.

sub.desc_en: The biryoni (zealots) prevent the sages from making peace with the Romans and also prevent them from fighting, then burn the storehouses of grain, causing a famine.
The wealthy Marta bat Baytus dies from starvation after her servant fails to find any flour to buy, and she steps outside barefoot.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai applies the verse about the delicate woman to Marta, and some say she died from eating a dried fig of Rabbi Tzadok, who had fasted for forty years.
As Marta dies, she throws all her gold and silver into the street, fulfilling the verse 'They shall cast their silver into the streets.'

items.text: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's escape plan
items.text_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's escape plan
items.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, through his nephew Abba Sikra (the head of the biryoni), devises a plan to escape the city. He feigns death and is carried out in a coffin by his students, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, while the biryoni are tricked into not stabbing or pushing the coffin.

sub.desc_en: Introduces Abba Sikra as the head of the biryoni and nephew of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai summons Abba Sikra and asks him how long they will continue killing the world through famine.
Abba Sikra replies that he can do nothing, as the biryoni would kill him if he spoke against them.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asks Abba Sikra to devise a plan for his own escape, hoping it might bring some salvation.
Abba Sikra instructs Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai to feign illness, then death, and be carried out only by his students to avoid detection.
The plan is executed: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua carry the coffin, and the biryoni are dissuaded from stabbing or pushing it, allowing Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai to escape.

items.text: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai before Vespasian
items.text_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai before Vespasian
items.desc_en: Upon arriving at the Roman camp, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai greets Vespasian as 'king.' Vespasian questions why he did not come earlier and threatens him with death for the false title.

sub.desc_en: When Rabban Yochanan arrives before Vespasian, he greets him as 'king'; Vespasian objects that he is not king and asks why, if he were king, Rabban Yochanan did not come earlier.
Vespasian questions why Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai did not come earlier and threatens him with death for calling him 'king' when he is not.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's encounter with Vespasian
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's encounter with Vespasian
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan greets Vespasian as 'emperor' and explains why he did not come earlier due to the zealots. Vespasian responds with a parable about a barrel of honey and a snake, and Rabbi Yochanan is criticized for not offering a better solution.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai greets Vespasian as emperor, citing a verse to prove Jerusalem's fall is divinely ordained, and explains that zealots prevented him from coming earlier.
Vespasian responds with a parable about a barrel of honey and a snake, implying the zealots must be destroyed to save the city, and Rabbi Yochanan is criticized for not suggesting a better solution.

items.text: Vespasian becomes emperor and Rabbi Yochanan's shoe incident
items.text_en: Vespasian becomes emperor and Rabbi Yochanan's shoe incident
items.desc_en: A messenger arrives announcing the death of the emperor and that Vespasian is to be appointed. Vespasian struggles with his shoe, and Rabbi Yochanan interprets this as a good omen, advising him to have someone he dislikes pass before him to relieve the swelling.

sub.desc_en: A messenger arrives from Rome announcing the emperor's death and Vespasian's appointment, but Vespasian struggles to put on his second shoe.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the shoe difficulty as a good omen and advises Vespasian to have someone he dislikes pass before him to relieve the swelling, which works.
Vespasian asks why Rabbi Yochanan and the sages did not come to him earlier, and Rabbi Yochanan responds that the biryoni (rebels) prevented them, to which Vespasian retorts that he too said so.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's three requests
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's three requests
items.desc_en: Vespasian offers to grant Rabbi Yochanan a request before leaving. Rabbi Yochanan asks for Yavneh and its sages, the chain of Rabban Gamliel, and healers for Rabbi Tzadok. Rav Yosef or Rabbi Akiva criticizes him for not asking to spare Jerusalem entirely, but Rabbi Yochanan feared even that would not be granted.

sub.desc_en: Vespasian announces he is leaving and will send someone else, but offers Rabbi Yochanan a request.
Rabbi Yochanan asks for Yavneh and its sages, the chain of Rabban Gamliel, and healers for Rabbi Tzadok.
Rav Yosef or Rabbi Akiva criticizes Rabbi Yochanan for not asking to spare Jerusalem entirely.
The gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan feared Vespasian would not grant even that much, so he settled for partial salvation.

items.text: The healing treatment for Rabbi Tzadok
items.text_en: The healing treatment for Rabbi Tzadok
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the healing process for Rabbi Tzadok, who had fasted for many years: he was given water with bran, then water with coarse flour, then water with fine flour, gradually expanding his stomach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what was the healing treatment administered to Rabbi Tzadok.
The Gemara describes the gradual process: first bran water, then coarse flour water, then fine flour water, until his stomach expanded little by little.

items.text: Titus's desecration of the Temple and his blasphemy
items.text_en: Titus's desecration of the Temple and his blasphemy
items.desc_en: Vespasian sends Titus to Jerusalem. Titus enters the Holy of Holies with a prostitute, desecrates the Torah, and cuts the curtain, causing blood to flow. Abba Chanan and the school of Rabbi Yishmael comment on God's silence. Titus then takes the Temple vessels and boasts in Rome.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces Titus's mission to Jerusalem and cites the verse applied to his blasphemy.
Titus enters the Holy of Holies with a prostitute, desecrates the Torah, and cuts the curtain, causing blood to flow.
Abba Chanan interprets the verse to highlight God's silence in the face of Titus's blasphemy.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael interprets the verse to mean 'who is like You among the mute ones,' emphasizing God's restraint.
Titus takes the Temple vessels and the curtain, boards a ship to boast in Rome, with a homiletic reading of the verse.
Some say the verse refers literally to buried things being revealed to the wicked.

items.text: Titus's punishment by a gnat
items.text_en: Titus's punishment by a gnat
items.desc_en: A wave threatens to drown Titus, but he challenges God to fight on dry land. A bat kol tells him to fight a gnat, which enters his nose and gnaws at his brain for seven years. Titus tries to silence it with a blacksmith's hammer, but the gnat eventually becomes accustomed.

sub.desc_en: A wave threatens to drown Titus, who challenges God to fight on dry land, claiming God's power is only in water.
A bat kol (heavenly voice) tells Titus to fight a gnat, a lowly creature.
The gemara explains why the gnat is called a 'lowly creature': it has an entrance but no exit.
Titus goes to dry land, a gnat enters his nose and gnaws at his brain for seven years; he tries to silence it with a blacksmith's hammer, but the gnat becomes accustomed.

items.text: The gnat's size and Titus's final command
items.text_en: The gnat's size and Titus's final command
items.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Aruva testifies that after Titus's death, a bird-like object weighing two selas was found in his brain. A baraita says it was like a one-year-old bird weighing two litrin. Abaye describes the gnat's beak and claws. Titus orders his body to be burned and ashes scattered to avoid judgment.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Aruva testifies that after Titus's death, a bird-like object weighing two selas was found in his brain.
A baraita describes the object as like a one-year-old bird weighing two litrin.
Abaye describes the gnat's beak as copper and its claws as iron.
Titus orders his body to be burned and his ashes scattered on the sea to prevent the God of the Jews from finding him and bringing him to judgment.

items.text: Onkelos's consultation with Titus about conversion
items.text_en: Onkelos's consultation with Titus about conversion
items.desc_en: Onkelos, Titus's nephew, seeks to convert. He raises Titus from the dead and asks who is important in the next world. Titus says Israel, but warns that their commandments are many. He advises Onkelos to oppose Israel to become a leader, and describes his own punishment.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Onkelos, Titus's nephew, who seeks to convert and raises Titus from the dead to ask who is important in the next world.
Titus answers that Israel is most important in the next world, but warns that their commandments are many and difficult to fulfill.
Titus advises Onkelos to oppose Israel in this world to become a leader, citing a verse that those who afflict Israel become heads.
Onkelos asks Titus what his own judgment is in the next world.

items.text: Onkelos raises Balaam and Jesus to inquire about the fate of Jewish sinners and gentile prophets
items.text_en: Onkelos raises Balaam and Jesus to inquire about the fate of Jewish sinners and gentile prophets
items.desc_en: Onkelos uses necromancy to summon Balaam and Jesus, asking who is important in the next world. Balaam says Israel, but warns not to attach to them; his punishment is boiling semen. Jesus says to seek their good but not their harm; his punishment is boiling excrement, as per the rule for those who mock the sages.

sub.desc_en: The gemara describes the ongoing punishment of a certain individual whose ashes are gathered, judged, burned, and scattered daily.
Onkelos raises Balaam through necromancy and asks who is important in the next world.
Balaam answers that Israel is important, but warns Onkelos not to attach to them, citing the verse 'do not seek their peace or welfare all the days'.
Onkelos asks Balaam what his own punishment is in the next world.
Balaam replies that his punishment is boiling semen.
Onkelos raises Jesus through necromancy and asks who is important in the next world.
Jesus answers that Israel is important, and advises to seek their good but not their harm, as touching them is like touching the apple of God's eye.
Onkelos asks Jesus what his own punishment is in the next world.
Jesus replies that his punishment is boiling excrement, citing the rule that one who mocks the sages is punished with boiling excrement.
The gemara concludes by contrasting the fate of Jewish sinners with that of gentile prophets.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar extols the power of shame
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar extols the power of shame
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that the power of shame is so great that God assisted Bar Kamtza, leading to the destruction of the Temple and the burning of the Sanctuary.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar declares that the power of shame is so great that God assisted Bar Kamtza, leading to the destruction of the Temple and the burning of the Sanctuary.

items.text: The destruction of Tur Malka due to a rooster and hen incident
items.text_en: The destruction of Tur Malka due to a rooster and hen incident
items.desc_en: A custom of bringing a rooster and hen before a bride and groom led to a conflict with Roman soldiers, escalating to a rebellion. Bar Daroma, a mighty warrior, was killed due to a misquoted verse, and the Romans eventually destroyed Tur Malka after a three-day battle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the destruction of Tur Malka, explaining the custom of bringing a rooster and hen before a bride and groom as a blessing for fertility.
The narrative describes how Roman soldiers seized the rooster and hen, leading to a conflict, and how the mighty warrior Bar Daroma fought the Romans, prompting Caesar to pray for his downfall.
Bar Daroma's mouth caused his downfall when he misquoted a verse from Psalms, which was actually an expression of wonder by David, not a complaint.
Bar Daroma died in the latrine when a dragon removed his hip, and Caesar, seeing a miracle, initially withdrew, but returned when he saw the Jews celebrating.
Rabbi Asi reports that 300,000 sword-wielding Romans entered Tur Malka and killed for three days and nights, while on the other side there was celebration and they were unaware of each other.

items.text: The sixty myriad cities of King Yannai and the nature of the Land of Israel
items.text_en: The sixty myriad cities of King Yannai and the nature of the Land of Israel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Yehuda describe the sixty myriad cities of King Yannai on the mountain, each populous. Ulla testifies to the smallness of the site, and a heretic challenges the claim. Rabbi Chanina explains that the Land of Israel expands when inhabited, like a deer's skin.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse as referring to the sixty myriad cities of King Yannai on the mountain.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi confirms the sixty myriad cities, each with a population like the Exodus, except three with double.
The gemara lists the three exceptional cities and explains the etymology of each name.
Ulla testifies that he saw the site and it could not even hold sixty myriad reeds, challenging the claim.
A heretic accuses the rabbis of lying about the size of the Land of Israel.
Rabbi Chanina resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Land of Israel expands when inhabited, like a deer's skin.

items.text: Three stories from Kfar Sekhanya and the reason for the sages' suffering
items.text_en: Three stories from Kfar Sekhanya and the reason for the sages' suffering
items.desc_en: Three sages share stories of righteousness: a betrothed couple who refrained from intimacy, a father and son stoned for a sin that restored market prices, and a man who falsely accused his wife. Abaye asks why such righteous people suffered, and Rav Yosef answers it was because they did not mourn for Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: Three sages sit together and invite anyone who knows a story from Kfar Sekhanya of Egypt to share it.

A sage tells the story of a betrothed couple captured by gentiles who were married but refrained from intimacy because the wife lacked a כתובה (marriage contract), and she praised him after his death as greater than Joseph.
A second sage tells how market prices dropped, and investigation revealed a father and son who committed a sin on Yom Kippur were stoned by the court, restoring prices.

A third sage tells how a man tried to frame his wife for adultery using egg white, but Bava ben Buta exposed the fraud by citing a tradition from Shammai the Elder that egg white congeals from fire while semen repels from fire, leading to the man being flogged and forced to pay the כתובה (marriage contract).
Abaye asks Rav Yosef why these righteous people suffered.
Rav Yosef answers that they suffered because they did not mourn for Jerusalem, citing the verse that those who mourn for her will rejoice with her.

items.text: The destruction of Beitar and the extent of the massacre
items.text_en: The destruction of Beitar and the extent of the massacre
items.desc_en: A custom of planting trees for newborns led to a conflict with the Caesar's daughter, resulting in the destruction of Beitar. Rabbi Zeira reports 80,000 battle horns entered Beitar, and the blood flowed to the sea. Rabbi Eliezer and a baraisa describe the vast amount of blood, which fertilized vineyards for seven years.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts the destruction of Beitar due to a custom of planting trees for newborns, which led to a conflict with the Caesar's daughter.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that 80,000 battle horns entered Beitar, and the blood flowed to the Great Sea, a mile away.
Rabbi Eliezer the Great describes two streams in the valley of Yadayim, where the ratio of water to blood was measured as two parts water to one part blood.
A baraisa adds that for seven years, gentiles fertilized their vineyards with the blood of Israel without needing manure.

items.text: The murder of Zechariah and Nebuzaradan's repentance
items.text_en: The murder of Zechariah and Nebuzaradan's repentance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin reports an elder's account of Nebuzaradan's slaughter in the valley and Jerusalem, and his discovery of Zechariah's unceasing blood. After failing to appease the blood with various executions, Nebuzaradan addresses Zechariah directly, and the blood settles. This leads Nebuzaradan to repent, convert, and send a deed of gift to his home.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: An elder from Jerusalem reports that Nebuzaradan killed vast numbers in the valley and Jerusalem, and their blood touched the blood of Zechariah.
Nebuzaradan finds Zechariah's blood boiling and asks what it is; the people falsely claim it is spilled sacrificial blood, but a test fails.
Under threat of torture, the people confess that they killed a prophet who rebuked them, and his blood has not rested for years.
Nebuzaradan attempts to appease the blood by executing various groups, and finally succeeds when he addresses Zechariah directly and offers to destroy all the people.
Nebuzaradan repents, converts, and sends a deed of gift to his home.

items.text: Descendants of enemies who converted and taught Torah
items.text_en: Descendants of enemies who converted and taught Torah
items.desc_en: A baraita lists converts: Naaman was a ger toshav, Nebuzaradan a ger tzedek. Descendants of Haman, Sisera, and Sennacherib taught Torah or children, with Shemayah and Avtalyon identified as descendants of Sennacherib.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna opens by listing two converts: Naaman as a ger toshav (resident alien) and Nebuzaradan as a ger tzedek (righteous convert).
The Tanna adds that descendants of Haman, Sisera, and Sennacherib taught Torah or children, identifying Shemayah and Avtalyon as descendants of Sennacherib.

items.text: Interpretation of verses about blood and the voice of Jacob
items.text_en: Interpretation of verses about blood and the voice of Jacob
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about blood on a rock, then interprets "the voice is the voice of Jacob and the hands are the hands of Esau" in two ways: first, referring to Hadrian and Vespasian's massacres, and the evil kingdom's destruction; second, that no prayer is effective without Jacob's seed, and no war is won without Esau's seed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'I placed her blood on a bare rock so that it would not be covered' as a prooftext for the bloodshed described.
The Gemara interprets 'the voice is the voice of Jacob and the hands are the hands of Esau' as referring to the massacres by Hadrian and Vespasian, and the destruction by the evil kingdom.
An alternative interpretation: no prayer is effective without Jacob's seed, and no war is won without Esau's seed.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rav Yehuda on hiding and David's vision
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rav Yehuda on hiding and David's vision
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says one should hide from slander. Rav Yehuda says Rav taught that God showed David the destruction of both Temples, citing verses from Psalms.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse 'בשוט לשון תחבא' (by a scourge of the tongue one shall be hidden) to mean one should hide from the incitements of slander.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that God showed David the destruction of both Temples, citing Psalms 137:1 for the first Temple and Psalms 137:7 for the second.

items.text: The story of 400 children who drowned themselves
items.text_en: The story of 400 children who drowned themselves
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda or Shmuel or Rabbi Ami relates that 400 captured children, realizing they were destined for shame, asked if drowning brings them to the World to Come. The eldest taught a verse, and the girls jumped into the sea. The boys then reasoned a fortiori and also jumped. The verse "For Your sake we are killed all day long" applies to them.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel (or Rabbi Ami, or a baraita)
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel (or Rabbi Ami, or a baraita)
sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a story of 400 captured children who, realizing their fate, ask whether drowning in the sea grants them entry to the World to Come.

The eldest child interprets the verse 'מִבָּשָׁן אָשִׁיב, אָשִׁיב מִמְּצוּלוֹת יָם' (from Bashan I will return, from the depths of the sea) to mean that those who drown in the sea will be brought back.
The girls jump into the sea, and the boys, reasoning a fortiori (קל וחומר) from the girls' action, also jump.
The verse 'כִּי עָלֶיךָ הֹרַגְנוּ כׇל הַיּוֹם, נֶחְשַׁבְנוּ כְּצֹאן טִבְחָה' (For Your sake we are killed all day long, we are considered as sheep for the slaughter) is applied to these children.

items.text: The woman and her seven sons
items.text_en: The woman and her seven sons
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda tells of a woman and her seven sons brought before the emperor, each refusing to worship idols, citing different Torah verses. They are executed one by one. The youngest refuses to bow to the emperor, and the mother asks to kiss him, then tells him to tell Abraham she bound seven altars. She then jumps off a roof, and a bat kol declares the mother of children is happy.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda introduces the story of a woman and her seven sons, and the first son is brought before the emperor, refuses to worship idols citing 'אָנֹכִי ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ', and is executed.
The second son is brought, refuses to worship idols citing 'לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים', and is executed.
The third son is brought, refuses to worship idols citing 'זוֹבֵחַ לֵאלֹהִים יׇחֳרָם', and is executed.
The fourth son is brought, refuses to worship idols citing 'לֹא תִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה לְאֵל אַחֵר', and is executed.
The fifth son is brought, refuses to worship idols citing 'שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל', and is executed.
The sixth son is brought, refuses to worship idols citing 'וְיָדַעְתָּ הַיּוֹם... אֵין עוֹד', and is executed.
The seventh son is brought, refuses to worship idols citing 'אֶת ה׳ הֶאֱמַרְתָּ' and the mutual oath between Israel and God.

The emperor offers the youngest son a compromise: bow to pick up a signet ring, but the son rebukes him, arguing that if the emperor cares about his own honor, how much more should God's honor be respected.

sub.text: Mother's final act and bat kol
sub.text_en: Mother's final act and bat kol
sub.desc_en: The mother asks to kiss her son, then tells him to tell Abraham that she bound seven altars; she then jumps off a roof and dies, and a bat kol (heavenly voice) declares 'אֵם הַבָּנִים שְׂמֵחָה' (the mother of children is happy).

items.text: Interpretations of the bat kol's verse
items.text_en: Interpretations of the bat kol's verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the verse refers to circumcision on the eighth day. Reish Lakish says it refers to Torah scholars who demonstrate slaughtering laws on themselves, as Rava said one should not practice slaughtering on oneself. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it refers to scholars who kill themselves over Torah, citing Reish Lakish's teaching that Torah only endures through one who kills himself over it, and Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan about forty se'ah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets the bat kol's verse as referring to circumcision (מילה) performed on the eighth day.

Reish Lakish interprets the verse as referring to Torah scholars who demonstrate the laws of slaughtering (שחיטה) on themselves, citing Rava's ruling that one should not practice slaughtering on oneself.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak interprets the verse as referring to Torah scholars who kill themselves over Torah, citing Reish Lakish's teaching that Torah only endures through one who kills himself over it, and Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan about forty se'ah.

items.text: Tefillin straps found on Betar victims
items.text_en: Tefillin straps found on Betar victims
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the quantity of tefillin straps found on the heads of the slain of Betar, with a dispute between Rabbi Yannai and a baraita, and resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between head and arm tefillin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that tefillin straps were found on the heads of the slain of Betar.
Rabbi Yannai bar Rabbi Yishmael states that three baskets of forty se'ah each were found.
A baraita teaches that forty baskets of three se'ah each were found, contradicting Rabbi Yannai's measure.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between head tefillin (רֵישָׁא) and arm tefillin (דִּדְרָעָא), so both measures refer to different types.

items.text: Brains found on a stone
items.text_en: Brains found on a stone
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi and Ulla dispute the amount of brain matter found on a single stone after the massacre, and Rav Kahana cites a verse from Psalms to describe the vengeance.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi reports that four kav of brain matter were found on a single stone after the massacre.
Ulla disputes Rabbi Asi's measure, claiming nine kav of brain matter were found.
Rav Kahana (or alternatively Sheila bar Mari) cites the verse from Psalms (137:8-9) to describe the vengeance of dashing infants against the rock.

items.text: The precious children of Zion and Roman degradation
items.text_en: The precious children of Zion and Roman degradation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse about the precious children of Zion, describing how they were more beautiful than gold, and then recounts how the Romans initially used luxurious linens but later degraded Israelite captives by using them as footstools.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse means by 'the precious children of Zion, who are comparable to fine gold'.

The Gemara objects that if the verse meant they were literally covered in gold, that would be impossible because there is only a limited amount of gold in the world, as stated by the school of Rabbi Sheila.

The Gemara answers that the verse means they were so beautiful that they made gold appear ugly by comparison, and then recounts how the Romans initially used luxurious linens but later degraded Israelite captives by using them as footstools.

items.text: Dialogue about a verse and distance
items.text_en: Dialogue about a verse and distance
items.desc_en: Two people discuss where a verse is written, and one asks how far he is from a certain place, receiving a measurement in parasangs.

sub.desc_en: One person asks another where a certain verse is written, and the second answers by citing the verse 'גם כל חלי וכל מכה אשר לא כתוב בספר התורה הזאת' (Deuteronomy 28:61).
The first speaker asks how far he is from a certain place, and the second answers that the distance is a parasang and a half.
The first speaker says that if he had reached that place, he would not have needed the second speaker's help.

items.text: Four hundred synagogues in Betar
items.text_en: Four hundred synagogues in Betar
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel describes the immense number of synagogues, teachers, and students in Betar, and how the enemy killed them and burned them wrapped in their scrolls.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel introduces the verse and describes the four hundred synagogues in Betar, each with four hundred teachers and four hundred students.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The narrative continues describing how the enemy entered, stabbed the children with rods, and when they captured them, wrapped them in their scrolls and burned them.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya redeems a child
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya redeems a child
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya goes to a prison in Rome, recites a verse, and a child responds with the continuation. He vows to redeem him at any cost, and the child grows up to be Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya went to a large city in Rome, was told about a beautiful child imprisoned there, and the child responded to his biblical verse with the continuation.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya declares he is certain the child will teach halacha in Israel, redeems him at great cost, and the child grows up to be Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.

items.text: The son and daughter of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
items.text_en: The son and daughter of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav tells how Rabbi Yishmael's son and daughter were captured by two masters who planned to marry them, but they recognized each other as brother and sister, mourned, and died in each other's arms.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav introduces the story of Rabbi Yishmael's son and daughter who were captured by two masters, each boasting about the beauty of their slave.
The masters decide to marry the two slaves, but each refuses out of priestly dignity, and they weep all night.
At dawn they recognize each other as brother and sister, embrace, weep, and die, with Jeremiah lamenting over them.

items.text: The story of Tzofnat bat Peniel
items.text_en: The story of Tzofnat bat Peniel
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish tells the story of a beautiful woman, Tzofnat bat Peniel, who was abused by a captor and then displayed for sale. A repulsive man insisted on seeing her, and she tore her clothes, rolled in ashes, and prayed, prompting Jeremiah's lament.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish introduces the story of Tzofnat bat Peniel, explaining her name as 'all gaze at her beauty' and 'daughter of the High Priest who served in the Holy of Holies'.
Reish Lakish describes how a captor abused her all night, then dressed her in seven garments and brought her to market, where a repulsive man insisted on seeing her beauty.

The repulsive man persisted, so the captor stripped her to the last garment, which she tore; she then rolled in ashes and prayed to God, asking why He does not spare His great name even if He does not spare them.
Reish Lakish cites Jeremiah's lament over her, noting that the verse says 'upon us' rather than 'upon you', implying that God Himself, as it were, shares in the tragedy.

items.text: The story of the man who coveted his master's wife
items.text_en: The story of the man who coveted his master's wife
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav relates a story of a carpenter's apprentice who coveted his master's wife, tricked him into divorcing her, married her, and then enslaved the master, leading to tears falling into cups and the sealing of the decree.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav introduces a story about a carpenter's apprentice who coveted his master's wife, citing the verse 'וְעָשְׁקוּ גֶּבֶר וּבֵיתוֹ' (they oppress a man and his house).
The apprentice tricks the master into sending his wife to him under the pretense of a loan, and he detains her for three days.
When the master asks about his wife, the apprentice falsely claims he sent her away and that children abused her on the road.
The apprentice advises the master to divorce his wife, offers to lend him the money for her כתובה (marriage contract), and then marries her himself.
When the apprentice cannot repay the loan, the master enslaves him, and as the master serves them, his tears fall into their cups, sealing the decree of destruction.
Some say the decree was sealed because of two wicks in one lamp, alluding to a separate sin.

items.text: Dispute on purchasing from a sikarikon
items.text_en: Dispute on purchasing from a sikarikon
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute the law of purchasing from a sikarikon: Rav says the Mishnah only applies when the seller says 'go, take possession and acquire', but with a document he acquires; Shmuel says even with a document he does not acquire unless the seller writes him a guarantee.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's opening phrase about purchasing from a sikarikon.
Rav limits the Mishnah's restriction to cases where the seller says 'go, take possession and acquire', but with a document the buyer acquires.
Shmuel disagrees, ruling that even with a document the buyer does not acquire unless the seller writes him a guarantee.

items.text: Baraita supporting Shmuel and Rav's response
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Shmuel and Rav's response
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Shmuel's view: if one buys from a woman and then from the man, the purchase stands; if from the man and then the woman, it is void unless she writes him a guarantee. The Gemara suggests this is a refutation of Rav, but Rav explains that 'guarantee' here means a document.

sub.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is cited that supports Shmuel's ruling: buying from a woman then the man is valid, but buying from the man then the woman is void unless she writes a guarantee.
The Gemara suggests that this baraita is a refutation of Rav's position.
Rav responds that the 'guarantee' mentioned in the baraita refers to a document, not a verbal guarantee, thus reconciling the baraita with his view.

items.text: Baraita on a purchase from a sikarikon and the principle of claiming for an heir
items.text_en: Baraita on a purchase from a sikarikon and the principle of claiming for an heir
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if one buys from a sikarikon and possesses it for three years in the owners' presence, then sells it to another, the owners have no claim against the second purchaser. The Gemara questions the scenario, and Rav Sheshet explains that it is a case where the second purchaser does not claim, and we claim for an heir or purchaser. The Gemara distinguishes between when the second purchaser claims and when he does not.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that if one buys from a sikarikon and possesses the land for three years in the owners' presence, then sells it to another, the owners have no claim against the second purchaser.
The Gemara questions the scenario: if the second purchaser claims he bought from the first, even the first should be protected; if he does not claim, even the second should not be protected.
Rav Sheshet explains that the case is where the second purchaser does not claim, and we claim for an heir or purchaser.
The Gemara concludes that if the second purchaser claims, he is protected; if he does not claim, he is not.

items.text: Baraita on anparut and its clarification
items.text_en: Baraita on anparut and its clarification
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who comes due to debt or anparut (a form of confiscation) is not subject to the law of sikarikon, but anparut itself requires a waiting period of twelve months. The Gemara questions the apparent contradiction and clarifies that the baraita means that the sikarikon itself requires twelve months.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who comes due to debt or anparut (confiscation) is not subject to the law of sikarikon, but anparut itself requires a twelve-month waiting period.
The Gemara questions the apparent contradiction: the baraita first says anparut has no sikarikon status, then says it requires twelve months.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by clarifying that the baraita means the sikarikon itself requires twelve months, not that anparut is exempt.

items.text: Rav Yosef's ruling on anparut in Babylonia
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's ruling on anparut in Babylonia
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that there is no anparut in Babylonia. The Gemara questions this, noting that anparut is observed, so Rav Yosef clarifies that there is no legal validity of anparut in Babylonia because the owner can go to the government (bei davar) and protest, so his silence is considered acquiescence.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states a tradition that there is no anparut (confiscation) in Babylonia.
The Gemara objects that anparut is visibly practiced in Babylonia.
Rav Yosef clarifies that there is no legal validity of anparut in Babylonia, because the owner can go to the government (bei davar) and protest, so his silence is considered acquiescence.

items.text: Story of Giddul bar Re'ilai and Rav Pappa's ruling
items.text_en: Story of Giddul bar Re'ilai and Rav Pappa's ruling
items.desc_en: Giddul bar Re'ilai leased land from the Bnei Baga and paid three years' rent in advance. The original owners later came and claimed the land. They came before Rav Pappa, who considered writing a deed of seizure against the Bnei Baga. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objected, saying that would be like sikarikon, and instead ruled that Giddul's money is lost (like placing money on a deer's horn).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of Giddul bar Re'ilai, who leased land from the Bnei Baga and paid three years' rent in advance, and then the original owners came and claimed the land.
Rav Pappa considered writing a deed of seizure (טירפא) against the Bnei Baga to recover Giddul's money.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objected that writing such a deed would be like the law of sikarikon (which protects original owners).
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua ruled that Giddul's money is lost, like one who places money on a deer's horn (i.e., he has no recourse).

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the quarter payment
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the quarter payment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the later court ruled that a purchaser from a sikarikon gives the owners a quarter. Rav says a quarter of the land or a quarter in money, while Shmuel says a quarter of the land, which is a third in money. The Gemara explains their dispute: one holds the sikarikon sold at a discount of a quarter, the other at a discount of a fifth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that the later court ruled the purchaser from a sikarikon gives the owners a quarter.
Rav states that the quarter is either a quarter of the land or a quarter in money.
Shmuel states that the quarter is a quarter of the land, which equals a third in money.
The Gemara asks what is the basis of the dispute between Rav and Shmuel.
The Gemara explains that one holds the sikarikon sold at a discount of a quarter, the other at a discount of a fifth.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that seems to contradict Rav and Shmuel, stating that the owners have the upper hand and can choose land or money, and that if they have the means they are first to buy. It also mentions a ruling by Rabbi Hoshaya that after twelve months, any purchaser acquires the land but gives a quarter. Rav Ashi resolves that the baraita refers to after the money has come into the purchaser's hand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav and Shmuel by citing a baraita that states the owners have the upper hand and can choose land or money.
The baraita continues with Rabbi Hoshaya's ruling that after twelve months any purchaser acquires the land but gives a quarter.
Rav Ashi resolves that the baraita refers to after the money has come into the purchaser's hand.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi's counting method
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi's counting method
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi could have been counted first in the court's vote, given the Mishnah's rule that monetary cases begin with the greatest. Rabba bar Rava (or Rabbi Hillel) answers that in Rabbi's court, all votes began from the side, not from the greatest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi could have been counted first in the court's vote, given the Mishnah's rule that monetary cases begin with the greatest.
Rabba bar Rava (or Rabbi Hillel) answers that in Rabbi's court, all votes began from the side, not from the greatest.

items.text: Claim that Torah and greatness were never together until Rabbi
items.text_en: Claim that Torah and greatness were never together until Rabbi
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rava (or Rabbi Hillel) asserts that from Moses until Rabbi, Torah and greatness were never found in one place. The Gemara challenges this with examples like Joshua and Eleazar, Saul and Samuel, David and Ira, Solomon and Shimei, Hezekiah and Shebna, Ezra and Nehemiah, but each is refuted because the Torah scholar died before the leader or was killed.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rava (or Rabbi Hillel) asserts that from Moses until Rabbi, Torah and greatness were never found together in one place.
The Gemara objects by listing Joshua and Eleazar, then Eleazar and Phinehas, then Phinehas and the elders, as counterexamples.
The Gemara continues objecting with Saul and Samuel, then David and Ira the Jairite.
The Gemara objects with Solomon and Shimei ben Gera, noting that Shimei was killed.
The Gemara objects with Hezekiah and Shebna, then Ezra and Nehemiah ben Hachaliah.

items.text: Extension of the claim to Rav Ashi's time
items.text_en: Extension of the claim to Rav Ashi's time
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava extends the claim from Rabbi to Rav Ashi, stating that Torah and greatness were not together. The Gemara objects with Huna bar Natan, but answers that Huna bar Natan was subservient to Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava extends the claim that Torah and greatness were not found together from Rabbi's time to Rav Ashi's time.
The Gemara objects that Huna bar Natan was a counterexample of Torah and greatness together.
The Gemara answers that Huna bar Natan was subservient to Rav Ashi, so he did not possess independent greatness.

items.text: Mishnah on deaf-mute and dispute about its scope
items.text_en: Mishnah on deaf-mute and dispute about its scope
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a deaf-mute can gesture and be gestured to, and Ben Betera says they can jump and be jumped to, regarding movable property. The Gemara cites Rav Nachman's two versions: one limits the dispute to movable property, but all agree on gittin (divorce documents) via gestures; the other extends the dispute to gittin as well.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a deaf-mute communicates by gestures and Ben Betera says by jumping, regarding movable property.
Rav Nachman says the dispute is limited to movable property, but regarding gittin (divorce documents) all agree gestures suffice.

The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'regarding movable property,' so Rav Nachman's limitation is obvious, and resolves that the Mishnah might have meant 'even regarding movable property.'

An alternative version reports Rav Nachman saying the dispute extends to gittin as well, and the Gemara explains that the Mishnah's wording 'regarding movable property' should be read as 'even regarding movable property.'

items.text: Age for minors' transactions and reason
items.text_en: Age for minors' transactions and reason
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that minors' purchases and sales are valid for movable property. The Gemara debates the age: Rav Yehuda says six or seven, Rav Kahana says seven or eight, a baraita says nine or ten. They do not disagree; each depends on the child's sharpness. Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov cites Rabbi Yochanan: the reason is for the child's livelihood.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that minors' purchases and sales are valid for movable property, and the Gemara cites different opinions on the age threshold: Rav Yehuda says six or seven, Rav Kahana says seven or eight, and a baraita says nine or ten.

The Gemara resolves that the opinions do not dispute; each age threshold depends on the child's sharpness, and Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov quoting Rabbi Yochanan explains the reason is for the child's livelihood.
Rav Yehuda demonstrated to his son Rav Yitzchak that the age is six or seven.
Rav Kahana says the age is seven or eight.
A baraita teaches that the age is nine or ten.
The Gemara resolves that the opinions do not disagree; each age depends on the child's sharpness.
The Gemara asks what is the reason for this rule.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov cites Rabbi Yochanan that the reason is for the child's livelihood.

items.text: Etymology of 'meltachah' and related terms
items.text_en: Etymology of 'meltachah' and related terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the word 'meltachah' from the verse about Jehu, defining it as something that is spoken and stretched. Rav Dimi reports that Bunyaim ben Nunyaim sent Rabbi various fruits, and 'malmala' is also defined as something spoken and stretched.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'meltachah' means in the verse about Jehu.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan defines 'meltachah' as something that can be compressed and stretched.
Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Bonyam ben Nunyam sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a gift of special linen fabrics: sivni, chomes, salsela, and malmala.
The Gemara explains that sivni and chomes could be compressed to the size of a nut and half a nut, while salsela and malmala could be compressed to the size of a pistachio and half a pistachio.
The Gemara asks what the term 'malmala' means.
The Gemara answers that 'malmala' is something that can be compressed and stretched, echoing the definition of 'meltachah'.

items.text: Error in valuation and gift of a deaf-mute
items.text_en: Error in valuation and gift of a deaf-mute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yona cites Rabbi Zeira on the limit of error in valuation: up to one-sixth of the greater value. Abaye questions whether a deaf-mute's gift is valid. Rav Yeimar says no, Mar bar Rav Ashi says yes. The story is sent to Rav Mordechai, who clarifies that Mar bar Rav Ashi ruled that a gift is valid, whether from a sick or healthy person, large or small.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks up to what amount of error in valuation is a child's transaction valid.
Rabbi Yona says in the name of Rabbi Zeira that the error limit is up to one-sixth, like an adult.
Abaye raises a dilemma about whether a young child's gift is valid.
Rav Yeimar rules that a child's gift is not valid.
Mar bar Rav Ashi rules that a child's gift is valid.
Rav Mordechai clarifies that Mar bar Rav Ashi actually ruled the gift is valid, whether from a sick or healthy person, large or small.

items.text: Mishnah on darkhei shalom
items.text_en: Mishnah on darkhei shalom
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists things instituted for darkhei shalom (ways of peace): a priest reads first in the Torah, then a Levite, then an Israelite; and they may use an old house for an eruv (to avoid conflict).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists things instituted for the sake of peace: a priest reads first, then a Levite, then an Israelite; and they may use an old building for an eruv (עירוב) for the sake of peace.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Cases of darkhei shalom
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Cases of darkhei shalom
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists several situations—a cistern near a channel, traps for animals, finding lost property of a deaf-mute, etc.—where the law is enforced only for the sake of peace, though Rabbi Yosei considers them outright theft.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a cistern nearest the channel is filled first, on account of the ways of peace.
The Mishnah states that taking from traps is robbery only on account of the ways of peace, while Rabbi Yosei considers it full-fledged robbery.
The Mishnah rules that taking a lost item found by a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor is robbery only on account of the ways of peace, while Rabbi Yosei calls it full-fledged robbery.

The Mishnah states that taking olives that fall beneath a poor person gleaning at the top of an olive tree is robbery only on account of the ways of peace, while Rabbi Yosei considers it full-fledged robbery.
The Mishnah concludes that one does not protest against poor gentiles taking gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'a, on account of the ways of peace.

items.text: Biblical sources for kohen precedence
items.text_en: Biblical sources for kohen precedence
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the rule that a kohen is honored before a Levi. Rav Mattanah, Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, Rav Ashi, and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba each cite verses showing that kohanim are mentioned before Leviim, and the Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael adds that a kohen is to be first in opening, blessing, and taking a good portion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the rule that a kohen reads first from the Torah.
Rav Mattanah cites the verse 'וַיִּכְתּוֹב מֹשֶׁה... אֶל הַכֹּהֲנִים בְּנֵי לֵוִי' (Deuteronomy 31:9) to prove that a kohen is mentioned before a Levi, establishing the order.
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha derives the same rule from the verse 'וְנִגְּשׁוּ הַכֹּהֲנִים בְּנֵי לֵוִי' (Deuteronomy 21:5).

Rav Ashi cites the verse 'בְּנֵי עַמְרָם אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה, וַיִּבָּדֵל אַהֲרֹן לְהַקְדִּישׁוֹ קֹדֶשׁ קֳדָשִׁים' (I Chronicles 23:13) to show that Aaron (a kohen) is separated for holiness, implying precedence.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba derives the rule from the verse 'וְקִדַּשְׁתּוֹ' (Leviticus 21:8), which commands sanctifying the kohen for every matter of sanctity.
The Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael elaborates on the verse 'וְקִדַּשְׁתּוֹ', specifying that a kohen is to be first in opening the discussion, blessing, and taking a fine portion.

items.text: Abaye's question: Is darkhei shalom Torah law?
items.text_en: Abaye's question: Is darkhei shalom Torah law?
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef why the Mishnah says 'for the sake of peace' if the laws are from the Torah. Rav Yosef answers that even Torah laws are for the sake of peace, as Proverbs says 'its ways are ways of pleasantness and all its paths are peace.'

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef why the Mishnah attributes certain laws to 'darkhei shalom' (ways of peace) if they are actually Torah law.
Rav Yosef answers that even Torah laws are taught under the rubric of 'darkhei shalom' because the entire Torah is for the sake of peace.
The gemara cites the verse from Proverbs (3:17) that the Torah's ways are pleasant and its paths are peace, supporting Rav Yosef's answer.

items.text: Rules of precedence in breaking bread and synagogue
items.text_en: Rules of precedence in breaking bread and synagogue
items.desc_en: Abaye clarifies that the Mishnah's rule about the one who breaks bread extending his hand first applies only at a meal, not in the synagogue, lest it cause contention. Rav Mattanah adds that this restriction applies only on Shabbat and festivals when many are present, but not on Mondays and Thursdays.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the earlier difficulty by citing a baraita about the one who breaks bread extending his hand first, with an option to honor a greater person.
Mar restricts the rule to a meal, not the synagogue, to avoid contention.
Rav Mattanah adds that the synagogue restriction applies only on Shabbat and festivals when many are present, not on Mondays and Thursdays.

items.text: Challenge from Rav Huna's practice
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Huna's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Mattanah's distinction, noting that Rav Huna would call a kohen to read even on Shabbat and festivals. The Gemara answers that Rav Huna was exceptional, as even the great kohanim Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi would defer to him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Mattanah's distinction by citing Rav Huna's practice of calling a kohen to read even on Shabbat and festivals.
The Gemara answers that Rav Huna was exceptional, as even the great kohanim Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi would defer to him.

items.text: Rules for when there is no kohen or Levi
items.text_en: Rules for when there is no kohen or Levi
items.desc_en: Abaye states traditions: if there is no kohen, a Levi reads in his place; if there is no Levi, a kohen reads again. The Gemara questions this based on Rabbi Yochanan's rule that a kohen after a kohen is not called due to the first's blemish, and a Levi after a Levi due to both's blemish. The discussion explores the reasoning and concludes that the concern is only for those leaving, not those sitting.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states two traditions: if there is no kohen, a Levi reads in his place; if there is no Levi, a kohen reads again.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yochanan's rule that a kohen after a kohen is not called due to the first's blemish, and a Levi after a Levi due to both's blemish.
The Gemara answers that Abaye's case refers to the same kohen reading again, not a different kohen.
The Gemara questions why the concern for blemish applies to a Levi after a Levi but not to a kohen after a kohen, since both could raise suspicion.
The Gemara answers that the second kohen is known from his father to be a kohen, so there is no suspicion.
The Gemara objects that the same reasoning should apply to a Levi, but people might say the second Levi's mother was a mamzeret or netinah, disqualifying his lineage.
The Gemara further objects that the same suspicion could apply to a kohen, that he married a divorcee or a חלוצה (a woman who performed חליצה), disqualifying his offspring.
The Gemara asks: ultimately, does a Levi even exist in this scenario (since the second is suspected of being a non-Levi)?
The Gemara resolves that the concern is only for those leaving the synagogue, not for those sitting who see the person.

items.text: Inquiry from the Galileans to Rabbi Chelbo
items.text_en: Inquiry from the Galileans to Rabbi Chelbo
items.desc_en: The daf ends with the Galileans sending a question to Rabbi Chelbo about the order after the kohen and Levi, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Galileans send a question to Rabbi Chelbo about the order after the kohen and Levi, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Order of who reads from the Torah
items.text_en: Order of who reads from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing the order of who is called to read from the Torah: first a kohen, then a Levite, then an Israelite, then scholars who are appointed as community leaders, then those worthy of appointment, then their sons, then synagogue heads, and then any person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who reads from the Torah, and reports that the answer was not known.

Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha answers that after the kohen and Levite, the order is: Torah scholars who are appointed community leaders, those worthy of appointment, their sons, synagogue heads, and then any person.

items.text: Question about reading from chumashim in synagogue
items.text_en: Question about reading from chumashim in synagogue
items.desc_en: The people of Galilee sent a query to Rabbi Chelbo: may one read from chumashim (individual books of the Torah) in the synagogue in public? He did not know, so he asked Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, who also did not know. They then asked in the study hall and resolved it from a statement of Rabbi Yochanan: a Torah scroll missing even one sheet may not be read from.

sub.text: People of Galilee's query to Rabbi Chelbo
sub.text_en: People of Galilee's query to Rabbi Chelbo
sub.desc_en: The people of Galilee ask Rabbi Chelbo whether one may read from chumashim (individual Torah books) in the synagogue in public, but he does not have an answer.

sub.text: Rabbi Chelbo's inquiry to Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chelbo's inquiry to Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo asks Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha the same question, but he also does not have an answer.

sub.text: Study hall's resolution via Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Study hall's resolution via Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: They ask in the study hall and resolve the question from a statement of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yochanan: a Torah scroll missing even one sheet may not be read from, implying chumashim are also invalid for public reading.

items.text: Distinction and ruling of Rabbah and Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Distinction and ruling of Rabbah and Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof: there the scroll is lacking in its content (a missing sheet), but here the chumash is not lacking in its content (it is complete). Rabbah and Rav Yosef both say: one may not read from chumashim in the synagogue because of the honor of the congregation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by distinguishing between a Torah scroll missing a sheet (content lacking) and a chumash that is complete in content.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef both rule that one may not read from chumashim in the synagogue because of the honor of the congregation.

items.text: Haftarah book is forbidden to read on Shabbat
items.text_en: Haftarah book is forbidden to read on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef both also say: this book of haftarot (prophetic readings) is forbidden to read from on Shabbat. What is the reason? Because it was not given to be written (i.e., it is not a sacred scroll).

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef both rule that the book of haftarot (prophetic readings) is forbidden to read from on Shabbat.
The gemara asks for the reason behind this prohibition.
They answer that the reason is because the haftarah book was not given to be written (i.e., it lacks the sanctity of a sacred scroll).

items.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's stringency and the counter-proof from Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's stringency and the counter-proof from Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi adds that it is even forbidden to move the haftarah book on Shabbat, since it is not fit for reading. The Gemara rejects this: it is permitted both to move and to read from it, as Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish would study from an aggadah book on Shabbat, even though it was not given to be written, because 'it is time to act for the Lord; they have nullified Your Torah.'

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi adds a stringency: it is even forbidden to move the haftarah book on Shabbat.
The Gemara rejects Mar bar Rav Ashi's stringency, stating that it is permitted both to move and to read from the haftarah book.

sub.text: Supporting evidence from Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Supporting evidence from Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports its ruling by citing that Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish would study from an aggadah book on Shabbat, invoking the principle 'it is time to act for the Lord; they have nullified Your Torah' to override the prohibition against writing.

items.text: Abaye's question about writing a scroll for a child
items.text_en: Abaye's question about writing a scroll for a child
items.desc_en: Abaye asked Rabbah: may one write a scroll (megillah) for a child to learn from? The question depends on whether the Torah was given scroll by scroll or as a sealed whole. If scroll by scroll, perhaps it is permitted, but perhaps once it was completed it became a single unit. If sealed, perhaps it is forbidden, but perhaps since it is impossible (to have a full scroll for a child), we write. Rabbah answered: one may not write, and the reason is simply that one may not write.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether one may write a scroll (מגילה) for a child to learn from.
The Gemara analyzes the question according to the view that the Torah was given scroll by scroll (מגילה מגילה ניתנה), raising the possibility that once completed it became a single unit.

The Gemara analyzes the question according to the view that the Torah was given sealed (חתומה ניתנה), raising the possibility that since it is impossible to have a full scroll for a child, one may write.
Rabbah answers that one may not write, and the reason is simply that one may not write.

items.text: Objections from the sotah tablet and the golden plate
items.text_en: Objections from the sotah tablet and the golden plate
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises objections: the sotah tablet had the sotah passage written on it, and the high priest's golden plate had writing. The Gemara deflects: the tablet was written in alphabetical order (not as a scroll), and regarding the plate, the scribe saw and wrote 'like' what was written, not from it. A further objection about the plate's writing of 'if he lay' and 'if he did not lay' is answered by saying it was written in sections (serugin).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the sotah tablet, which had the sotah passage written on it, implying that writing Torah portions for children should be permitted.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish answers that the tablet was written in alphabetical order (אלף בית), not as a continuous scroll, so it is not a precedent for writing a Torah scroll for a child.
The Gemara objects further: the scribe of the golden plate saw and wrote what was written on the tablet, implying direct copying from a written source.
The Gemara deflects by reinterpreting the phrase: the scribe wrote 'like' what was written on the tablet, not from it, meaning he wrote from memory in the style of the tablet.

The Gemara objects again with a more precise version: the scribe saw the tablet and wrote what was written on it, specifically the phrases 'if he lay' and 'if he did not lay', implying direct copying.
The Gemara answers that the plate was written in sections (סירוגין), meaning the phrases were written in a non-continuous, broken order, not as a full scroll, so it does not serve as a precedent.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about writing a scroll for a child
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about writing a scroll for a child
items.desc_en: A baraita states: one may not write a scroll for a child to learn from, but if one intends to complete it (into a full Torah scroll), it is permitted. Rabbi Yehuda says: for Genesis up to the generation of the flood, and for Leviticus up to 'And it was on the eighth day'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general rule: one may not write a scroll for a child to learn from, but if one intends to complete it into a full Torah scroll, it is permitted.
Rabbi Yehuda adds a dissenting opinion specifying the permissible scope: for Genesis up to the generation of the flood, and for Leviticus up to 'And it was on the eighth day'.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on how Torah was given
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on how Torah was given
