items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Benaiah says the Torah was given scroll by scroll, as it says 'in the scroll of the book it is written of me.' Resh Lakish says it was given sealed, as it says 'take this book of the Torah.' The Gemara reconciles the verses: the latter refers to after it was completed, and the former refers to the entire Torah being called a scroll, as in Zechariah. Alternatively, it is for the teaching of Rabbi Levi about eight sections said on the day the Tabernacle was erected.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Benaiah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Benaiah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the Torah was given scroll by scroll (מגילה מגילה), citing the verse 'אז אמרתי הנה באתי במגילת ספר כתוב עלי'.
Resh Lakish argues that the Torah was given sealed (חתומה), citing the verse 'לקח את ספר התורה הזאת'.
The Gemara objects that Resh Lakish's verse also appears in the Torah, and resolves that it refers to after the Torah was completed (sealed).
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan's verse also appears, and resolves that the entire Torah is called a scroll, as in Zechariah's vision of a flying scroll.
Alternatively, the verse is explained by Rabbi Levi's teaching that eight sections were said on the day the Tabernacle was erected, including the section of 'אחרי מות'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists several enactments instituted for darkhei shalom, including the section on the drunkards, the section on lamps, and the section on the red heifer.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three Torah portions read for darkhei shalom: the drunkards, the lamps, and the red heifer.

items.text: Dispute on the majority of Torah: Written vs. Oral
items.text_en: Dispute on the majority of Torah: Written vs. Oral
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan argue whether most of the Torah is written or oral, each citing a verse. The Gemara then explains the opposing verses: the verse 'I would write for him the majority of My Torah' is an expression of astonishment, and the verse 'for according to these words' indicates that oral matters are difficult to learn.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar opens by asserting that most of the Torah is written and a minority is oral, citing the verse 'I would write for him the majority of My Torah; they are considered like a stranger'.
Rabbi Yochanan counters that most of the Torah is oral and a minority is written, citing the verse 'for according to these words'.
The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yochanan's position can be reconciled with the verse 'I would write for him the majority of My Torah'.
The Gemara explains that the verse is an expression of astonishment: 'I would write for him the majority of My Torah?! They are considered like a stranger!'
The Gemara questions how Rabbi Elazar's position can be reconciled with the verse 'for according to these words'.
The Gemara explains that the verse indicates that oral matters are difficult to learn, not that they constitute the majority.

items.text: Derasha on writing and reciting Torah
items.text_en: Derasha on writing and reciting Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Nachmani, the interpreter of Reish Lakish, derives from verses that written matters may not be recited orally and oral matters may not be written. The school of Rabbi Yishmael similarly teaches that 'these' words you may write, but not halakhot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Nachmani derives from the verses 'כתוב לך את הדברים האלה' and 'כי על פי הדברים האלה' that written matters may not be recited orally and oral matters may not be written.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the word 'אלה' (these) restricts writing to these matters, but you may not write halakhot (oral traditions).

items.text: The covenant was for the Oral Torah
items.text_en: The covenant was for the Oral Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that God made a covenant with Israel only for the sake of the Oral Torah, citing the verse 'for according to these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that God made a covenant with Israel only for the sake of the Oral Torah, citing the verse 'כי על פי הדברים האלה כרתי אתך ברית ואת ישראל' (for according to these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel).

items.text: Reason for mixing in an old house
items.text_en: Reason for mixing in an old house
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah allows mixing in an old house for darkhei shalom. It rejects the explanation of honor, citing the example of a shofar that moved through several houses, and concludes it is due to suspicion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah permits mixing in an old house for darkhei shalom.
The Gemara rejects the explanation of honor, citing the example of a shofar that moved through several houses.
The Gemara concludes that the reason is due to suspicion (חשדא).

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on water rights
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on water rights
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel argue about who draws water first from a river: Rav says the lower ones drink first, Shmuel says the upper ones drink first. The Gemara clarifies that when the water flows, all agree; the dispute is when the water is dammed. Shmuel interprets the Mishnah's 'a cistern near a channel' in accordance with Rav's view. Rav Huna bar Tachlifa concludes that since no halakha was stated, whoever is stronger prevails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding which residents of a river draw water first: Rav says the lower ones drink first, Shmuel says the upper ones drink first.

The Gemara clarifies that when the water flows freely, all agree; the dispute is only when the water is dammed, with Shmuel's reasoning being proximity and Rav's reasoning being that the river should flow naturally.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah about a cistern near a channel, and notes that Shmuel interprets it in accordance with Rav's view, referring to a channel that flows directly into the cistern.

The Gemara questions what novel point the Mishnah teaches if it refers to a channel flowing into the cistern, and answers that it precludes the claim that the upper residents could dam and divert the water.
Rav Huna bar Tachlifa concludes that since no halakha was stated for either opinion, whoever is stronger prevails.

items.text: Story of Rav Shimi bar Ashi and Abaye
items.text_en: Story of Rav Shimi bar Ashi and Abaye
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi asks Abaye to sit in judgment, but Abaye is busy watering. Rav Shimi offers to water for him, then deceitfully tells the upper and lower residents each that the other side drinks first, causing a delay. Abaye rebukes him and does not taste fruit that year.

sub.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's request to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's request to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi comes before Abaye and asks him to sit in judgment, first during the day and then at night.
Abaye explains he must water his fields, and Rav Shimi offers to water for him during the day so Abaye can judge at night; Abaye agrees.
Rav Shimi goes to the upper residents and tells them the lower residents drink first, then goes to the lower residents and tells them the upper residents drink first, thereby delaying the watering.
When Rav Shimi returns, Abaye rebukes him for acting like two people, and Abaye does not taste fruit from that year's harvest.

items.text: Case of the people of Bei Charma
items.text_en: Case of the people of Bei Charma
items.desc_en: People from Bei Charma dug a canal at the head of a river and diverted it, causing the upper residents to complain of reduced flow. Abaye tells them to dig a bit more alongside, and when they complain of drying fruit, he tells them to remove themselves from there.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where people from Bei Charma dug a canal at the head of a river and diverted it into river channels.
The upper residents come before Abaye and complain that the canal is weighing down (reducing flow in) their river.
Abaye tells them to dig a bit more alongside the canal to alleviate the problem.
The upper residents object that their fruit trees are drying up due to the reduced water flow.
Abaye tells them to remove themselves from there, effectively dismissing their complaint.

items.text: Introduction to the dispute about the cheek and the kukrei
items.text_en: Introduction to the dispute about the cheek and the kukrei
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that everyone agrees on the basic law, and the dispute is specifically about the cheek and the kukrei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that everyone agrees on the basic law, and the dispute is specifically about the cheek and the kukrei.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's ruling on the find of a deaf-mute, etc.
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's ruling on the find of a deaf-mute, etc.
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says it is outright robbery, and Rav Chisda explains that this is outright robbery according to rabbinic law. The Gemara asks what practical difference this makes, and answers that it is to remove it through judges.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the case of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor's found object, and Rabbi Yosei says it is outright theft.
Rav Chisda explains that 'outright theft' means by rabbinic decree, and the practical difference is that the court can force its return.
The Gemara asks what practical difference this classification makes.
The Gemara answers that the difference is that the item can be recovered through judges (דיינין).

items.text: The poor person knocking olives from a tree
items.text_en: The poor person knocking olives from a tree
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if the poor person gathered and put the olives in his hand, it is outright robbery.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a poor person gleaning olives collects them by hand, it is outright theft.

items.text: Story of Rav Kahana and the dates
items.text_en: Story of Rav Kahana and the dates
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana saw a man throwing branches and dates falling, so he gathered and ate them. The man claimed they were his, and Rav Kahana responded that he must be from the school of Rabbi Yoshiya, citing the verse about a righteous person being the foundation of the world.

sub.desc_en: A story about Rav Kahana illustrates the principle of not taking fallen dates from a man who threw them, citing Rabbi Yoshiya's teaching.
Rav Kahana gathered and ate the fallen dates.
The man objected that he had thrown the branches himself, implying the dates were his.
Rav Kahana responded that the man must be from the school of Rabbi Yoshiya, citing the verse 'and a righteous person is the foundation of the world' (Proverbs 10:25).

items.text: Supporting non-Jewish poor for darkhei shalom
items.text_en: Supporting non-Jewish poor for darkhei shalom
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that we do not prevent non-Jewish poor from gleaning, and the Gemara adds that we support them along with Jewish poor, visit their sick, and bury their dead, all for darkhei shalom.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that we do not prevent gentile poor from taking gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah, for the sake of peace.
A baraita expands the principle: we support gentile poor, visit their sick, and bury their dead together with Jews, for the sake of peace.

items.text: Mishnah: Borrowing utensils from a woman suspected of violating sheviit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Borrowing utensils from a woman suspected of violating sheviit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses what a woman may borrow from a friend suspected of violating sheviit, and the distinctions between a chaver's wife and an am ha'aretz's wife, concluding that all these allowances are only for darkhei shalom.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman may lend certain utensils to a friend suspected of violating sheviit, but may not actively assist in selecting or grinding.
The Mishnah adds that the wife of a chaver may lend utensils and even assist the wife of an am ha'aretz, except after water is added, due to impurity concerns, all for darkhei shalom.
The Mishnah concludes that one may assist gentiles during sheviit but not Jews, and may greet them, all for darkhei shalom.

items.text: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between the first and last cases. Abaye answers that most amei ha'aretz tithe their produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between the first and last cases.
Abaye answers that most amei ha'aretz tithe their produce.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah deals with the am ha'aretz of Rabbi Meir, who is defined by not eating non-sacred food in purity, and the Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between impurity of non-sacred food and impurity of challah.

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes that the Mishnah deals with the am ha'aretz (ignoramus) as defined by Rabbi Meir, who is one who does not eat non-sacred food in purity, and that the issue involves rabbinic impurity and purity.
The Gemara objects: from the latter clause which says 'once she pours water she may not touch it', it implies that the entire Mishnah deals with impurity and purity, contradicting Rava's distinction.

Rava resolves: both the first and latter clauses deal with impurity and purity, but the first clause concerns impurity of non-sacred food (חולין), while the latter clause concerns impurity of challah (חלה).

items.text: Introduction of a contradiction
items.text_en: Introduction of a contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a contradiction with another source, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a contradiction by citing another source.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may grind and deposit produce with those who eat Sabbatical produce or those who eat their produce in a state of impurity, but not for them (i.e., on their behalf).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may grind and deposit produce with those who eat Sabbatical produce or those who eat their produce in a state of impurity, but not on their behalf.

items.text: Abaye's explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah deals with a priest suspected of eating terumah in impurity, which is a biblical impurity.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah deals with a priest suspected of eating תרומה (priestly portion) in טומאה (ritual impurity) of biblical severity.

items.text: Gemara's question and objection
items.text_en: Gemara's question and objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Abaye: if so, how can one deposit terumah with such a priest? It cites a baraita that one may deposit terumah with an Israelite am ha'aretz but not with a priest am ha'aretz, because he is brazen with it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Abaye's explanation: if so, how can one deposit terumah with such a priest? It then cites a contradictory baraita.
The baraita states that one may deposit terumah with an Israelite am ha'aretz but not with a priest am ha'aretz, because the priest is brazen with it.

items.text: Rabbi Ila'a's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a answers that the case involves a clay vessel sealed with a tight lid (צמיד פתיל), which prevents impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a answers that the case involves a clay vessel sealed with a tight lid (צמיד פתיל), which prevents impurity.

items.text: Gemara's objection
items.text_en: Gemara's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: one should still be concerned that his menstruating wife might move the vessel (causing impurity).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one should still be concerned that his menstruating wife might move the vessel, causing impurity.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the difficulty: the Mishnah deals with produce that has been made susceptible to impurity (הוכשרו), while the baraita deals with produce that has not been made susceptible.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between produce that has been made susceptible to impurity (הוכשרו) and produce that has not.

items.text: Further challenge and resolution regarding suspicion of exchange
items.text_en: Further challenge and resolution regarding suspicion of exchange
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita about taking wheat to a Samaritan or am ha'aretz miller, which is trusted for tithes and Sabbatical but not for purity. The Gemara initially dismisses the challenge based on the previous distinction, but then notes that the baraita also implies no concern for exchange (חלופי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita about taking wheat to a Samaritan or am ha'aretz miller, which is trusted for tithes and Sabbatical but not for purity, challenging the previous resolution.
The Gemara objects that the baraita is not a challenge, since it was already established that the case involves fruits that were not made susceptible to impurity.
The Gemara explains that the baraita was raised not as a challenge to the purity ruling but to highlight that it implies no concern for exchange (חלופי).

items.text: Cases where suspicion of exchange is raised
items.text_en: Cases where suspicion of exchange is raised
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings cases where exchange is suspected: a man giving to his mother-in-law (suspected of exchanging spoiled produce), and a woman innkeeper (suspected of exchanging for hot food). It also cites a baraita about a wife of a ḥaver grinding with a wife of an am ha'aretz, where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar prohibits even when she is impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita: a man giving produce to his mother-in-law must tithe both what he gives and what he receives, because she is suspected of exchanging spoiled produce.
Rabbi Yehuda explains the case: the mother-in-law wants to protect her daughter's marriage and is embarrassed before her son-in-law, so the suspicion is specific, not general.
The Gemara challenges: is there no general concern for exchange? It cites a baraita about a woman innkeeper who must tithe both what she gives and receives because she exchanges produce for hot food.
The Gemara explains the innkeeper case: she says 'Let the scholar's son eat hot food while I eat cold,' so her exchange is motivated by self-interest, not general suspicion.
The Gemara challenges again: is there still no general concern? It cites a baraita about a wife of a ḥaver grinding with a wife of an am ha'aretz, which restricts the practice.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that even when the ḥaver's wife is impure, she should not grind, because her friend (the am ha'aretz wife) might exchange impure for pure produce.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a woman can be trusted not to swap the food she is given, given that she could steal. Rav Yosef answers by citing a proverb that implies she will not swap because she benefits from the arrangement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can trust a woman not to swap the food she is given, given that she could steal it outright.
Rav Yosef answers with a proverb: the woman will not swap because she benefits from the arrangement, like an ox that eats from its own trough.

items.text: Baraita on preparing ḥallah and terumah for an am ha'aretz
items.text_en: Baraita on preparing ḥallah and terumah for an am ha'aretz
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshulam cites a tradition from Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar ben Chasma that one may not prepare ḥallah of an am ha'aretz in purity, but may prepare his ordinary dough in purity, setting aside the ḥallah portion in a basket or container. Similarly, one may not prepare terumah from his olives in purity, but may prepare his ordinary olives in purity, setting aside the terumah portion in a vessel of a ḥaver.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the tradition that one may not prepare ḥallah of an am ha'aretz in purity, but may prepare his ordinary dough in purity, setting aside the ḥallah portion in a basket or container, and the am ha'aretz may take both without concern.

The baraita adds a parallel ruling for olives: one may not prepare terumah from an am ha'aretz's olives in purity, but may prepare his ordinary olives in purity, setting aside the terumah portion in a vessel of a ḥaver, and the am ha'aretz may take both without concern.

items.text: Reason for the leniency and necessity of both cases
items.text_en: Reason for the leniency and necessity of both cases
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the leniency is due to the livelihood of the baker and the olive presser. The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: for the baker, because his wage is small, but for the olive presser, whose wage is large, one might think it is not permitted; and for the olive presser, because he is not readily available, but for the baker, who is readily available, one might think it is not permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason for the leniency in the baraita.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the leniency is for the sake of the kneader's livelihood and the olive presser's livelihood.
The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary to teach the leniency, because each case alone might have been insufficient to extend the leniency to the other.

items.text: Gemara's challenge on the ḥallah case
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge on the ḥallah case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's ruling that the am ha'aretz takes both portions without concern: why not worry that he might touch the ḥallah? The answer is that he is told that if he touches it, it reverts to being untithed. The Gemara further asks: what if he does not care? The response is that since he intends to fix the dough, he certainly cares.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita's ruling: why not worry that the am ha'aretz might touch the ḥallah portion?
The Gemara answers that the am ha'aretz is warned that touching the ḥallah would revert the dough to its untithed state.
The Gemara raises a further concern: what if the am ha'aretz does not care about the warning?
The Gemara rejects the concern, arguing that since the am ha'aretz intends to fix the dough, he certainly cares about the outcome.

items.text: Gemara's challenge on the terumah case
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge on the terumah case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's ruling for terumah: why not worry that the am ha'aretz might touch it? The answer is that there is a distinguishing mark, as the terumah is placed in vessels of dung, stone, or earth, which are not susceptible to impurity. The Gemara then asks why the baraita specifies a vessel of a ḥaver; even a vessel of an am ha'aretz would suffice. The answer is that the baraita means vessels of an am ha'aretz that are fit for use by a ḥaver.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita's ruling for terumah: why not worry that the am ha'aretz might touch the terumah vessel?
The Gemara answers that there is a distinguishing mark: the terumah is placed in vessels of dung, stone, or earth, which are not susceptible to impurity.
The Gemara asks why the baraita specifies a vessel of a ḥaver; even a vessel of an am ha'aretz would suffice.
The Gemara answers that the baraita means vessels of an am ha'aretz that are fit for use by a ḥaver.

items.text: Mishnah on supporting gentiles in the Sabbatical year
items.text_en: Mishnah on supporting gentiles in the Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's ruling that we support gentiles during the Sabbatical year. It questions how this is allowed, given Rav Dimi's statement that one may not work with a gentile in the Sabbatical year nor greet them with a double 'peace'. The Gemara explains that the Mishnah only means saying 'strengthen yourselves' in a general sense, as Rav Yehuda and Rav Sheshet did. It then discusses the prohibition of doubling 'peace' to a gentile, with examples from Rav Chisda and Rav Kahana.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that we support gentiles during the Sabbatical year.

The Gemara questions how supporting gentiles is allowed, given Rav Dimi bar Shishna's statement in Rav's name that one may not work with a gentile in the Sabbatical year nor greet them with a double 'peace'.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah only means saying 'strengthen yourselves' in a general sense, as exemplified by Rav Yehuda and Rav Sheshet.
The Gemara discusses the prohibition of doubling 'peace' to a gentile, noting that Rav Chisda would greet them first and Rav Kahana would say 'peace to the master'.

items.text: Clarification on greeting gentiles on their festival day
items.text_en: Clarification on greeting gentiles on their festival day
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since we support them, surely we may inquire about their welfare? Rav Yeiva explains that the Mishnah's ruling is only needed for their festival day, as a baraita teaches that one should not enter a gentile's home on his festival to greet him, and if meeting in the market, one should greet with a subdued tone and bowed head.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one may inquire about a gentile's welfare, given that we already support them economically.
Rav Yeiva explains that the Mishnah's leniency is needed only for their festival day, citing a baraita that restricts greeting a gentile on his festival to a subdued tone and bowed head.

items.text: Story of Geniva and the rabbis about greeting kings
items.text_en: Story of Geniva and the rabbis about greeting kings
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story where Rav Huna and Rav Chisda debate whether to stand before Geniva, who is a Torah scholar. Geniva approaches and greets them with a double 'peace', calling them kings. When asked how he knows rabbis are called kings, he cites a verse. He then proves from a verse that one doubles 'peace' to a king. Finally, when invited to eat, he cites a verse that one must feed his animal before eating himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets the scene: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda are sitting; Geniva passes by, and one suggests standing before him because he is a Torah scholar.
Rav Chisda objects: should we stand before a disputant (one who argues with rabbis)?
Geniva approaches and greets them with a double 'peace', calling them kings.

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's question
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's question
sub.desc_en: They ask Geniva: from where do you know that rabbis are called kings?
Geniva answers by citing the verse 'By me kings reign' (Proverbs 8:15), implying that Torah scholars, through whom the Torah is transmitted, are the true kings.

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's question
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's question
sub.desc_en: They ask Geniva: from where do you know that we double 'peace' to a king?
Geniva answers by citing a tradition from Rav Yehuda quoting Rav, who derives from the verse about Amasai (I Chronicles 12:18) that one doubles 'peace' to a king.
They invite Geniva to taste something (to eat).

Geniva declines, citing a tradition from Rav Yehuda quoting Rav that one must not taste anything until feeding his animal, based on the verse order: first 'I will give grass in your field for your cattle' and then 'you shall eat and be satisfied' (Deuteronomy 11:15).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a husband says 'accept this get for my wife' or 'bring this get to my wife', he may retract. If the wife says 'accept my get for me', the messenger cannot retract. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that if she says 'take my get for me', the messenger also cannot retract.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma rules that a husband who says 'accept this get for my wife' or 'deliver this get to my wife' may retract, but if the wife says 'accept my get for me', the agent cannot retract.
The Tanna Kamma adds that if the husband says 'I do not want you to receive it for her, but deliver and give it to her', he may retract.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that even if the wife says 'take my get for me', the agent cannot retract.

items.text: Gemara's first inference and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's first inference and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya infers from the Mishnah that if the wife appointed the messenger, 'bring' is like 'acquire on behalf of', so the husband cannot retract. The Gemara rejects this, explaining that the Mishnah's case is needed to counter the assumption that since a husband cannot appoint a messenger for receipt, the get would be invalid even if it reaches her hand; the Mishnah teaches that 'accept and bring' is said.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya infers from the Mishnah that if the wife appointed the messenger, 'bring' is like 'acquire on behalf of', so the husband cannot retract.
The Gemara rejects the inference, stating that 'bring' is not like 'acquire on behalf of', and the Mishnah's case of 'accept a get for my wife' was necessary.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case counters the assumption that since a husband cannot appoint a messenger for receipt, the get would be invalid even if it reaches her hand; the Mishnah teaches that 'accept and bring' is said.

items.text: Question on the wife's case
items.text_en: Question on the wife's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that the wife's messenger cannot retract applies equally to receipt and delivery. It answers that it applies only to receipt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that the wife's messenger cannot retract applies equally to receipt and to delivery (הוֹלָכָה).
The Gemara answers that the ruling applies only to receipt (קַּבָּלָה), not to delivery.

items.text: Second inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Second inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the husband's statement 'I do not want you to accept for her' that if he did not say this, the husband cannot retract, implying 'bring' is like 'acquire on behalf of'. It deflects by suggesting the case involves 'take' (הֵילָךְ).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's case where the husband says 'I do not want you to accept for her' that if he did not say this, the husband cannot retract, implying that 'bring' (הוֹלֵךְ) is equivalent to 'acquire on behalf of' (זְכִי).
The Gemara deflects the inference by suggesting that the case involves the term 'take' (הֵילָךְ), not 'bring' (הוֹלֵךְ).

items.text: Inquiry about gender and agency
items.text_en: Inquiry about gender and agency
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a man can be a messenger for receipt and a woman for delivery. It attempts to prove from the Mishnah that one messenger is fit for both, but the proof is rejected as possibly involving two messengers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a man can be an agent for receipt and a woman for delivery, since the basic cases are obvious.
The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that one agent is fit for both receipt and delivery.
The Gemara rejects the proof, suggesting the Mishnah may refer to two different agents.
The Gemara attempts another proof from the Mishnah's case of one agent whose designation is changed, suggesting the same agent is fit for both roles.

items.text: Proofs for gender and agency
items.text_en: Proofs for gender and agency
items.desc_en: Rav Mari proves that a man can be a messenger for receipt from the father receiving for his minor daughter. Rav Ashi proves that a woman can be a messenger for delivery from the Mishnah's ruling that women are trusted to bring a get, which involves delivery.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that a man can be an agent for receipt, citing the father who receives a גט (bill of divorce) for his minor daughter, but leaves the question of a woman as an agent for delivery unresolved.

Rav Mari brings evidence from the Mishnah that women who are not credible to say their husband died are credible to bring a גט (bill of divorce), which is an act of delivery, proving a woman can be an agent for delivery.

Rav Ashi adds proof from the latter clause of the Mishnah, where a woman brings her own גט (bill of divorce) and must testify about its writing and signing, which is established as a case of delivery, confirming a woman can be an agent for delivery.

items.text: Case of conflicting instructions
items.text_en: Case of conflicting instructions
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where the wife says 'accept my get' and the husband says 'take it as she said'. Rav Nachman in the name of Rav rules that even if the get reaches her hand, she is not divorced, because the husband relies on his own words. Rav Ashi questions this conclusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where the wife says 'bring me my get' or 'accept my get', and the husband says 'take it as she said'.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rav rules that even if the get reaches her hand, she is not divorced, because the husband relies on his own words (not hers).
Rav Ashi objects, questioning how this conclusion can stand given the earlier Mishnah.

items.text: Gemara's initial analysis of Rav Nachman's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's initial analysis of Rav Nachman's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies Rav Nachman's ruling: if the wife said 'accept my get' and the husband said 'take it as she said', the get takes effect when it reaches the husband's hand because he relies on her words; but if she said 'bring my get', he relies on his own words. Here, the messenger revoked his agency, claiming he was only a receiver, not a deliverer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Nachman's ruling distinguishes between the wife saying 'accept my get' (relying on her words) and 'bring my get' (relying on his words).
The Gemara concludes that here the messenger revoked his agency, claiming he was only a receiver, not a deliverer.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Chiyya's attempted proof from a mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya's attempted proof from a mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya cites a mishnah: one who says 'accept this get for my wife' or 'take this get to my wife' may retract. This implies that if he does not retract, it is a valid get. The Gemara questions why, since a husband cannot appoint a receiver, and answers that since he set his mind to divorce her, he intends that she be divorced in any valid manner.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya cites a mishnah: one who says 'accept this get for my wife' or 'take this get to my wife' may retract, implying that if he does not retract, it is a valid get.
The Gemara questions why the mishnah's case would be valid, since a husband cannot appoint a receiver for the get.
The Gemara answers that since the husband set his mind to divorce her, he intends that she be divorced in any valid manner.

items.text: Rejection of the proof
items.text_en: Rejection of the proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof: there, the husband knows there is no agency for receiving, so he gives it for delivery; here, the messenger mistakenly thought he was appointed as a receiver.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: there, the husband knows there is no agency for receipt and gives for delivery; here, he mistakenly thinks the messenger is a receiver.

items.text: Rava's attempted proof from a minor
items.text_en: Rava's attempted proof from a minor
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita: a minor who says 'accept my get' is not divorced until the get reaches her hand. The Gemara questions why, since she did not appoint him for delivery, and answers again with the principle that the husband intends any valid divorce.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita: a minor who says 'accept my get' is not divorced until the get reaches her hand.
The Gemara questions why the divorce is valid, since the minor did not appoint him as an agent for delivery.
The Gemara answers with the principle that the husband, having set his mind on divorce, intends any valid divorce.

items.text: Rejection of Rava's proof
items.text_en: Rejection of Rava's proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this proof as well: there, the husband knows a minor cannot appoint an agent, so he gives it for his own delivery; here, the messenger errs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: there, the husband knows there is no agency for a minor and gives for his own delivery; here, he mistakenly thinks the minor can receive.

items.text: Analysis of a baraita with mixed formulations
items.text_en: Analysis of a baraita with mixed formulations
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a baraita listing cases where the wife says 'bring my get' and the husband says 'accept', or vice versa, and the husband says 'take and give', 'acquire for her', or 'accept for her'. The Gemara questions whether the baraita pairs reception with reception and delivery with delivery, or cross-references them, and concludes that the husband relies on his own words only when he says 'take it as she said'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing cases where the wife says 'bring my get' or 'accept my get' and the husband says 'take and give', 'acquire for her', or 'accept for her', ruling that if the husband wishes to retract he may, but once the get reaches her hand she is divorced.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita pairs reception with reception and delivery with delivery.
The Gemara answers that the baraita cross-references reception with delivery and delivery with reception.
The Gemara objects that if reception is paired with delivery, the get should take effect immediately upon reaching the husband's hand, implying he relies on his own words.
The Gemara rejects the objection, distinguishing that in the earlier case the husband said 'take it as she said', whereas here he did not.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about retraction
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about retraction
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma rules that in all cases the husband may not retract; Rabbi Nathan distinguishes between 'take and give' (may retract) and 'acquire for her'/'accept for her' (may not); Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that in all cases he may not retract unless he explicitly says 'I do not want you to accept for her, but take and give'. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view is identical to the Tanna Kamma, and resolves that he teaches the case of 'I do not want' or that the Tanna Kamma is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states: if the wife says 'accept my get' and the husband says 'take', 'give', 'acquire for her', or 'accept for her', he may not retract.
Rabbi Natan distinguishes: 'take and give' allows retraction; 'acquire for her' and 'accept for her' do not.
Rabbi rules that in all cases he may not retract, unless he explicitly says 'I do not want you to accept for her, but take and give'.
The Gemara asks: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling is identical to the Tanna Kamma — why is it stated separately?
The Gemara resolves: either Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi teaches the case of 'I do not want' (אִי אֶיפְשִׁי) as a novel detail, or he informs us that the Tanna Kamma is actually Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi himself.

items.text: Unresolved inquiry about 'take it' according to Rabbi Nathan
items.text_en: Unresolved inquiry about 'take it' according to Rabbi Nathan
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: according to Rabbi Nathan, does the term 'take it' (הֵילָךְ) have the same status as 'acquire for her' (זְכֵי) or not? It attempts to resolve this from a baraita where the husband says 'accept this get for my wife' or 'take this get to my wife' – he may retract; but if the wife says 'accept my get', he may not retract. The implication for Rabbi Nathan's view is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires: according to Rabbi Natan, is the term 'הֵילָךְ' (take) like 'זְכֵי' (acquire) or not?

The Gemara attempts to resolve the inquiry by citing a baraita: if a husband says 'accept this get for my wife' or 'take this get to my wife' he may retract, but if the wife says 'accept my get' he may not retract, leaving the implication for Rabbi Nathan's view unresolved.

items.text: First attempt to resolve the dispute about הוֹלֵךְ vs. הֵילָךְ
items.text_en: First attempt to resolve the dispute about הוֹלֵךְ vs. הֵילָךְ
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a baraita using 'הֵילָךְ' implies the ruling follows Rabbi Natan, who holds that the husband cannot retract. It answers that the baraita actually uses 'הוֹלֵךְ' and follows Rabbi, who permits retraction.

items.text: Second attempt: a baraita about 'אי אפשי'
items.text_en: Second attempt: a baraita about 'אי אפשי'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where the husband says 'אי אפשי שתקבל לה' and uses 'הוֹלֵךְ ותן לה'. It infers that without 'אי אפשי' the husband cannot retract, suggesting the case uses 'הֵילָךְ' and follows Rabbi Natan. The Gemara again deflects, saying it uses 'הוֹלֵךְ' and follows Rabbi.

items.text: Conclusive proof from a direct teaching
items.text_en: Conclusive proof from a direct teaching
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states: for 'הוֹלֵךְ' the husband may retract (Rabbi Natan's view), for 'הֵילָךְ' he may not. This proves that 'הֵילָךְ' is like 'זְכֵי' (acquisition), and the Gemara concludes definitively.

items.text: Rav's ruling on a mixed agency formulation
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a mixed agency formulation
items.desc_en: Rav rules that when the wife says 'התקבל לי גיטי' and the husband says 'הוֹלֵךְ ותן לה', the agent becomes an agent of both, and the woman must undergo חליצה (levirate release) due to uncertainty. The Gemara questions Rav's consistency, since elsewhere he holds 'הוֹלֵךְ' is irrevocable in monetary cases. It resolves the contradiction: monetary doubt is lenient, but ritual doubt is stringent.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Chanina about a woman's agent
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Chanina about a woman's agent
items.desc_en: Rav holds that a woman cannot appoint an agent to receive her get from the husband's agent, while Rabbi Chanina permits it. Two reasons are given for Rav's position: due to the husband's dignity, or because the agent's agency is a 'later courtyard' (not effective retroactively). The difference between the reasons is whether the woman appointed the agent initially.

items.text: Case of the woman who said 'להוי בידך'
items.text_en: Case of the woman who said 'להוי בידך'
items.desc_en: A messenger gave a get to a woman who was grinding, and she said 'להוי בידך'. Rav Nachman initially thought to rule based on Rabbi Chanina, but Rava objected because the agency had not returned to the husband. The case was sent to Rabbi Ami, who ruled that the agency had not returned. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba initially hesitated, then ruled that since it is a matter of ערוה (forbidden relations), she must undergo חליצה.

items.text: Rav Yitzchak's ruling: get and chalitzah
items.text_en: Rav Yitzchak's ruling: get and chalitzah
items.desc_en: In a practical case, Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta required both a get (during the husband's lifetime) and chalitzah (after his death). The Gemara clarifies: the get is given while the husband is alive, and chalitzah after his death.

items.text: Dispute about witnesses who wrote the wrong name
items.text_en: Dispute about witnesses who wrote the wrong name
items.desc_en: A woman called 'נפאתה' but witnesses wrote 'תפאתה'. Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta said in Rav's name that the witnesses fulfilled their agency. Rabba objected because they were not told to write a defective get. Rabba then said that if the witnesses wrote a valid get and it was lost, they fulfilled their agency. Rav Nachman objected further, and ruled that witnesses may write and give a get even a hundred times.

items.text: Questions about the scope of the agent's instructions
items.text_en: Questions about the scope of the agent's instructions
items.desc_en: Rava asked Rav Nachman: if the husband says 'כתבו ותנו לשליח', does that remove the witnesses from further involvement or just consider their convenience? Ravina asked Rav Ashi about the phrase 'ויוליך לה' – the answer is תיקו (undecided).

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement about 'טול לי'
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement about 'טול לי'
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that if a woman says 'טול לי גיטי', the husband cannot retract. The Tanna Kamma adds that 'טול לי', 'שא לי', and 'יהי לי בידך' are all terms of acceptance.

items.text: Mishnah: requirement of two sets of witnesses
items.text_en: Mishnah: requirement of two sets of witnesses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when a woman says 'התקבל לי גיטי', she needs two sets of witnesses: one set to testify that she said it, and another to testify that the agent received and tore the get. Even if the first set is the same as the second, it is valid.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman says 'Receive my get for me,' she needs two sets of witnesses: two to testify that she said so, and two to testify that the agent received and tore the get.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a woman says 'Receive my get for me,' she needs two sets of witnesses: two to testify that she said so, and two to testify that the agent received and tore the get.

items.text: Gemara's dispute: Who is believed when husband and third party disagree?
items.text_en: Gemara's dispute: Who is believed when husband and third party disagree?
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda: if the husband says he gave the deposit for a pledge and the third party says for a get, Rav Huna says the husband is believed, while Rav Chisda says the third party is believed, each with their reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: if the husband says he gave the deposit for a pledge and the third party says for a get, who is believed?
Rav Huna rules that the husband is believed.
Rav Chisda rules that the third party is believed.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba raises an objection from a baraita that a third party is believed over both parties in monetary matters. The Gemara distinguishes monetary cases from get cases, but further baraitot mention 'and similarly for gittin' and 'and similarly for shtarot'. The Gemara questions whether these were taught together, implying they are not a single source.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba raises an objection from a baraita that a third party is believed over both parties in monetary matters, implying the same should apply to gittin.
The Gemara distinguishes monetary cases from gittin because monetary matters can be forgiven (מחילה), so the third party's testimony is more reliable.
The Gemara objects that baraitot explicitly state 'and similarly for gittin' and 'and similarly for shtarot', suggesting the rule applies to gittin as well.
The Gemara rejects the objection by questioning whether these baraitot were actually taught together as a single source, implying they are separate and not a unified tradition.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah and response
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah and response
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from the Mishnah: why does a woman need two sets of witnesses? Let the third party (agent) be believed! The Gemara answers: the get is not in the agent's possession to be believed about it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from the Mishnah: why does a woman who says 'accept my get' need two sets of witnesses? Let the third party (the agent) be believed!
The Gemara answers: the get is not in the agent's possession to be believed about it.

items.text: Explaining the need for witnesses of receipt and tearing
items.text_en: Explaining the need for witnesses of receipt and tearing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why witnesses of receipt are needed, and Rabba explains the Mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar who holds that witnesses of delivery are essential. For the tearing, Rav Yehuda says it was taught during a time of persecution to prevent the agent from using the get again.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why witnesses of receipt (קבלה) are needed, given that the woman's statement about the agent's appointment is already verified.
Rabba answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar, who holds that witnesses of delivery (עדי מסירה) are the essential ones, so witnesses of receipt are needed to establish the agent's status.
The Gemara asks why witnesses of tearing (קריעה) are needed.
Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that the requirement for witnesses of tearing was taught during a time of persecution (שעת השמד), to prevent the agent from reusing the get.

items.text: Rav Huna's concession and the wife's claim
items.text_en: Rav Huna's concession and the wife's claim
items.desc_en: Rabba says Rav Huna concedes that if the wife herself says the third party told her the deposit was for a get, she is believed. The Gemara questions this, then clarifies: she is believed if she says 'in my presence he gave it for a get,' due to the principle of מִיגּוֹ (since she could have claimed the husband gave it to her directly).

sub.desc_en: Rabba states that Rav Huna concedes: if the wife herself says the third party told her the deposit was for a get, she is believed.
The Gemara objects: is there anything that the third party himself is not believed, yet she is believed?
The Gemara resolves: rather, she is believed if she says 'in my presence he gave it for a get,' due to the principle of מִיגּוֹ (since she could have claimed the husband gave it to her directly).

items.text: Case where husband and third party both say 'for a get' and wife claims loss
items.text_en: Case where husband and third party both say 'for a get' and wife claims loss
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that when both husband and third party say the deposit was for a get, and the wife says she received it but lost it, it is a matter of איסור (prohibition) requiring two witnesses. The Gemara questions why the third party is not believed, and why the husband is not believed (citing a principle that a husband who says 'I divorced my wife' is believed), and why the principle that an agent fulfills his mission is not applied.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that when both husband and third party say the deposit was for a get, and the wife says she received it but lost it, it is a matter of איסור (prohibition) requiring two witnesses.
The Gemara questions why the third party is not believed, given that the get is not in his possession.
The Gemara questions why the husband is not believed, citing the principle that a husband who says 'I divorced my wife' is believed, but notes that here he did not say he divorced her.

The Gemara questions why the principle that an agent fulfills his mission (חזקה שליח עושה שליחותו) is not applied, citing Rabbi Yitzchak's ruling about a man who sends an agent to betroth a woman and the agent dies.

items.text: Limitation on Rav Hamnuna's principle
items.text_en: Limitation on Rav Hamnuna's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara qualifies Rav Hamnuna's ruling that a woman who says 'You divorced me' is believed because she would not be brazen before her husband. This applies only when there is no supporting evidence; if there is supporting evidence, she might be brazen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that Rav Hamnuna's principle applies only for stringency (לחומרא), not for leniency (לקולא).
The Gemara cites Rav Hamnuna's ruling that a woman who says 'You divorced me' is believed because a woman is not brazen before her husband.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Hamnuna's principle applies only when there is no supporting evidence; if there is supporting evidence, she might be brazen.

items.text: Mishnah: Who receives the get of a betrothed minor girl
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who receives the get of a betrothed minor girl
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a betrothed minor girl and her father both may receive her get. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, saying only the father receives it, and any girl who cannot guard her get cannot be divorced.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a betrothed minor girl and her father both may receive her get, while Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, saying only the father receives it, and any girl who cannot guard her get cannot be divorced.

items.text: Gemara: The dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara: The dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: the Sages hold that the Torah granted the girl an additional hand (ability to receive her get), while Rabbi Yehuda holds that in the presence of her father, her hand is null.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what basis do the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda dispute?
The Gemara explains: The Sages hold that the Torah granted the girl an additional hand (ability to receive her get), while Rabbi Yehuda holds that in the presence of her father, her hand is null.

items.text: Definition of a minor who can guard her get
items.text_en: Definition of a minor who can guard her get
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a minor who knows how to guard her get can be divorced. Rabbi Yochanan defines this as one who guards another object because of her get. Rav Huna bar Manoach objects that this describes a fool, and instead defines it as one who distinguishes between her get and another object.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a minor who knows how to guard her get can be divorced, and defines such a minor as one who guards her get and another object.
The gemara asks what the baraita means by 'guards her get and another object.'
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the minor guards another object because of her get, i.e., she guards it due to the get's presence.
Rav Huna bar Manoach objects that Rabbi Yochanan's definition describes a fool, not a capable minor.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach, citing Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika, redefines the minor as one who distinguishes between her get and another object.

items.text: Acquisition for oneself vs. others
items.text_en: Acquisition for oneself vs. others
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rabbi Asi rules: if a child throws a pebble and takes a nut, he acquires for himself but not for others; if he takes an object and returns it later, he acquires for both himself and others. Shmuel disagrees, saying both cases are the same: he acquires only for himself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rabbi Asi's ruling distinguishing two stages of a minor's capacity: one who throws a pebble and takes a nut acquires for himself but not for others; one who returns an object after an hour acquires for both himself and others.
Shmuel objects to Rabbi Asi's distinction, stating that both cases are the same.
The Gemara asks what Shmuel means by 'this and that are one'.
Rav Chisda explains that Shmuel means both stages are the same: the minor acquires for himself but not for others.

items.text: Challenge from the law of joining alleyways
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of joining alleyways
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana Vardan challenges Shmuel's view from a baraita about joining alleyways, where a minor girl who has not reached puberty can acquire for others. The Gemara answers that the laws of joining alleyways are rabbinic, so the rules differ.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana Vardan challenges Shmuel's view by citing a baraita about joining alleyways, where a minor maidservant who has not reached puberty can acquire for others.
The Gemara answers that the laws of joining alleyways are rabbinic, so the rules differ and a minor can acquire for others in that context.
Rav Chisda notes that Rav Chinana Vardan was silent, and the Gemara suggests he could have responded that all rabbinic ordinances follow a lenient principle.

items.text: Distinction between Torah-level and rabbinic enactments
items.text_en: Distinction between Torah-level and rabbinic enactments
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the principle 'all rabbinic enactments are modeled on Torah law' applies only to matters with a Torah foundation, not to purely rabbinic matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that rabbinic enactments are modeled on Torah law.
The Gemara clarifies that this principle applies only to matters with a Torah foundation, not to purely rabbinic matters.

items.text: Rav Avya's challenge from ma'aser sheni
items.text_en: Rav Avya's challenge from ma'aser sheni
items.desc_en: Rav Avya challenges the distinction by citing a mishnah where one can use a minor Hebrew maidservant to redeem ma'aser sheni without the added fifth. The Gemara resolves that this case involves rabbinic-level ma'aser (in the present era) and a planter without a hole, both rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avya challenges the previous distinction by citing a mishnah that one may use a minor Hebrew maidservant to redeem ma'aser sheni without the added fifth.
The Gemara analyzes the case of the maidservant, concluding she must be a minor who has not yet grown two pubic hairs.
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah deals with ma'aser sheni in the present era, which is only rabbinic in status.
The Gemara objects that a Hebrew maidservant does not exist in the present era, citing a baraita that the law of a Hebrew slave applies only when the Jubilee year is observed.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves a planter without a hole, which is also rabbinic, so both elements are rabbinic and the challenge is deflected.

items.text: Rava's three categories of a minor
items.text_en: Rava's three categories of a minor
items.desc_en: Rava delineates three stages of a minor's legal capacity: a very young child (who acquires only for himself), a child who can transact in movables (whose sales are valid), and one who has reached the age of vows (whose vows are binding). Corresponding rules for a minor girl are given.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that there are three categories of a minor, beginning with the youngest stage: a child who picks up a pebble and throws it, or a nut and takes it, acquires only for himself and not for others, and the parallel for a minor girl is that she can be betrothed only for the purpose of מיאון (refusal).

Rava states the second category: children who have reached the stage of 'פעוטות' (young children) — their purchases and sales of movable property are valid, and the parallel for a minor girl is that she can be divorced through her father's betrothal.

Rava states the third category: when they reach the age of vows, their vows are binding and their dedications are valid, and the parallel for a minor girl is that she performs חליצה (the levirate release ceremony), and a minor may sell his father's property only after reaching twenty years of age.

items.text: Mishnah: Minor girl's agency for get
items.text_en: Mishnah: Minor girl's agency for get
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if a minor girl says 'accept my get for me,' it is not a get until it reaches her hand, and the husband may retract. But if her father says 'go accept my daughter's get,' the husband cannot retract.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that if a minor girl says 'accept my get for me,' it is not a valid get until it reaches her hand, and the husband may retract, because a minor cannot appoint an agent.
The mishnah adds that if the father says 'go accept my daughter's get,' the husband cannot retract, because the father can act as an agent for his minor daughter.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional delivery and agency
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional delivery and agency
items.desc_en: The mishnah discusses cases where the husband specifies a place for delivery or the wife specifies a place for receipt, and the agent deviates. Rabbi Elazar distinguishes between the husband's and wife's specifications.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that if a husband says 'Give this get to my wife in place X' and the agent gives it elsewhere, the get is invalid.
The mishnah states that if the husband says 'She is in place X' and the agent gives it elsewhere, the get is valid.
The mishnah states that if the wife says 'Receive my get in place X' and the agent receives it elsewhere, the get is invalid.
Rabbi Elazar validates the get in the wife's case of 'Receive my get in place X' even if received elsewhere.
The mishnah states that if the wife says 'Bring my get from place X' and the agent brings it from elsewhere, the get is valid.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Elazar's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Elazar's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Elazar disagrees only in the second case (wife's specification) but not the first (husband's). The answer: the husband, divorcing willingly, is particular about the place; the wife, being divorced against her will, is merely showing a preference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Elazar disagrees only in the second case (wife's specification) but not the first (husband's).
The Gemara answers: the husband, divorcing willingly, is particular about the place; the wife, being divorced against her will, is merely showing a preference.

items.text: Mishnah: When is she forbidden to eat terumah?
items.text_en: Mishnah: When is she forbidden to eat terumah?
items.desc_en: The mishnah rules that if she says 'bring my get,' she may eat terumah until it reaches her hand; if 'accept my get,' she is forbidden immediately. Rabbi Elazar forbids immediately even if she specifies a place.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah rules that a woman who says 'bring my get' may eat terumah until the get reaches her hand, but if she says 'accept my get' she is forbidden immediately; Rabbi Elazar forbids immediately even if she specifies a place.

items.text: Gemara: Reconciling the mishnayot
items.text_en: Gemara: Reconciling the mishnayot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the second mishnah can call it a get at all, given the first mishnah says it is not a get. It resolves that the case is where she said 'accept my get in Mata Mechasya, and sometimes you find him in Babylon,' meaning she instructs him to take it wherever he finds him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the second mishnah can call it a valid get (גט) at all, given the first mishnah explicitly says it is not a get.

The Gemara resolves that the case is where she said 'accept my get in Mata Mechasya, and sometimes you find him in Babylon,' meaning she instructs him to take it wherever he finds him, so the get is valid.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Elazar's ruling on a get delivered outside the specified location
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Elazar's ruling on a get delivered outside the specified location
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Elazar forbids the get immediately, assuming it is obvious that specifying a location is a condition. It explains that the case is where the husband said 'go east' but the agent went west, and the Gemara teaches that perhaps the husband might encounter the agent and give the get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Elazar forbids the get immediately, since specifying a location is merely showing a place, not a condition.
The Gemara explains that the case is where the husband said 'go east' but the agent went west, and the teaching is that perhaps the husband might encounter the agent and give the get.

items.text: Baraita on eruv with different fruit types
items.text_en: Baraita on eruv with different fruit types
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a contradiction: if one says to his agent 'mix an eruv for me with dates' and he mixed with raisins, or vice versa, one source says it is valid and another says it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the case of an agent instructed to mix an eruv with one fruit type who used another.
The baraita cites two conflicting tannaitic sources: one validates the eruv and the other invalidates it.

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef resolve the contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef resolve the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the contradiction by attributing one view to the Rabbis (who require precision) and the other to Rabbi Elazar (who holds that specifying a location is not a condition). Rav Yosef says both views are the Rabbis, but one case involves the agent's own property and the other involves another's property.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the contradiction by attributing one baraita to the Rabbis (who require precise compliance) and the other to Rabbi Elazar (who holds that specifying a location is merely a suggestion).

Rav Yosef offers an alternative resolution: both baraitot reflect the Rabbis' view, but one case involves the agent's own property (where he is precise) and the other involves another's property (where he is lenient).

items.text: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef with a similar case
items.text_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef with a similar case
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef by citing a baraita about an eruv with a tower and a dovecote, where there is no distinction of one's own or another's property. The Gemara answers that there are fruits of the tower and fruits of the dovecote.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects: in the case of 'tower' vs. 'dovecote', where there is no distinction of ownership, what can Rav Yosef say?
The Gemara answers that even there, there is a distinction between the fruits of the tower and the fruits of the dovecote, which can be owned by different people.

items.text: Mishnah on explicit vs. ambiguous divorce language
items.text_en: Mishnah on explicit vs. ambiguous divorce language
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if a husband says 'write a get and give it to my wife', 'divorce her', or 'write a letter and give it to her', the agents write and give. But if he says 'release her', 'support her', 'act for her according to law', or 'act for her appropriately', he has said nothing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'write a get and give it to my wife', 'divorce her', or 'write a letter and give it to her', the court writes and gives it.
The Mishnah states that if one says 'release her', 'support her', 'act for her according to custom', or 'act for her appropriately', he has said nothing.

items.text: Gemara expands on the Mishnah and Rabbi Nathan's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara expands on the Mishnah and Rabbi Nathan's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that adds more terms. Rabbi Nathan distinguishes between 'patruha' (release her) and 'pitruha' (with a different vowelization), saying the former is valid. Rava explains that Rabbi Nathan, a Babylonian, is precise about the language, while the Tanna of our Mishnah, from Eretz Yisrael, is not.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that lists terms for divorce: 'שלחוה' (send her), 'שבקוה' (leave her), 'תרכוה' (divorce her) are valid; 'פטרוה' (release her), 'פרנסוה' (support her), 'עשו לה כנימוס' (act according to custom), 'עשו לה כראוי' (act appropriately) are invalid.
Rabbi Nathan distinguishes between 'פטרוה' (release her) with a patach vowel, which is valid, and 'פיטרוה' with a chirik vowel, which is invalid.

Rava explains that Rabbi Nathan, being a Babylonian, is precise about the vowelization of 'פטרוה' vs. 'פיטרוה', while the Tanna of our Mishnah, from Eretz Yisrael, is not precise about such linguistic distinctions.

items.text: Unresolved questions about other terms
items.text_en: Unresolved questions about other terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises unresolved questions about terms like 'hutzihu' (take her out), 'izvuha' (leave her), 'hatiruha' (permit her), etc. It resolves one: 'asu la kadas' (act for her according to law) is like 'asu la kenimus' and 'asu la kara'ui', which are invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises questions about the validity of terms like 'hocuha' (bring her out), 'izvuha' (leave her), 'hatiruha' (permit her), 'hannichuha' (let her go), 'ho'ilu lah' (benefit her), and 'asu lah kadat' (act for her according to law).
The Gemara resolves one question: a baraita states that 'asu lah kadat' (act for her according to law) is invalid, like the other terms.

items.text: Mishnah on a person in danger writing a get
items.text_en: Mishnah on a person in danger writing a get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that originally, if someone going out to be executed said 'write a get for my wife', the agents write and give. Later they ruled that even one going on a sea voyage or caravan, and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says even one who is dangerously ill. The Gemara begins a story about Geniva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires: 'Take her out', what is it? 'Leave her', what? 'Permit her', what? 'Set her aside', what? 'Benefit her', what? 'Act for her according to law', what?

items.text: Rav Huna's analogy between a gift and a get
items.text_en: Rav Huna's analogy between a gift and a get
items.desc_en: Rav Huna draws an analogy between a gift and a get: just as a gift given by a dangerously ill person can be retracted if he recovers, so too a get ordered in such a state can be retracted. He extends the analogy to the requirement of explicit wording: just as a get requires the word 'write' but not 'give', a gift requires 'give' but not a formal acquisition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avina goes to Rav Huna, who states that a get (bill of divorce) follows the same rule as a gift: if the giver recovers, both can be retracted.
Rav Huna extends the analogy: just as a get requires the word 'write' but not 'give', a gift requires 'give' but not a formal acquisition (קניין).

items.text: Rabbi Abba's objection to the analogy
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's objection to the analogy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects: a gift can take effect after death, but a get cannot, so the analogy fails. He argues that the comparison is invalid because a get has no effect posthumously.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects: if the analogy is strict, then just as a gift can be given after death, so too a get could be given after death, which is impossible.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's real difficulty: partial gift requires acquisition
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's real difficulty: partial gift requires acquisition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba's true challenge is that a gift of part of one's property by a dangerously ill person requires a formal act of acquisition, but Rav Huna seems to hold it does not. The Gemara distinguishes this case because the person is 'commanding due to death' (מצוה מחמת מיתה).

sub.text: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Abba's real difficulty
sub.text_en: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Abba's real difficulty
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Abba's real difficulty is that a partial gift of a dangerously ill person requires a formal acquisition (קניין), but Rav Huna's analogy implies it does not; the Gemara resolves that this case is different because the person is commanding due to impending death (מצווה מחמת מיתה).
The Gemara distinguishes this case because the person is 'commanding due to death' (מצוה מחמת מיתה), which exempts from the usual requirement of acquisition.

items.text: Objection to Rabbi Abba's assumption about מצוה מחמת מיתה
items.text_en: Objection to Rabbi Abba's assumption about מצוה מחמת מיתה
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Abba really hold that a 'commander due to death' requires acquisition? The established rule is that such a person does not need a formal acquisition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Abba hold that a person commanding due to death requires a formal acquisition? But we know it does not.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's final difficulty: ambiguous wording 'מחמרא'
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's final difficulty: ambiguous wording 'מחמרא'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba's real issue is the ambiguous language: the person said 'from wine' (מחמרא), not 'wine' or 'the value of wine'. The Gemara resolves that 'from wine' is meant to enhance his power, and this is the ruling sent from the academy.

sub.text: Gemara's final clarification of Rabbi Abba's difficulty
sub.text_en: Gemara's final clarification of Rabbi Abba's difficulty
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Abba's real difficulty is about the wording: the donor said 'from wine' (מחמרא) not 'wine' or 'the value of wine', and the resolution is that 'from wine' is meant to enhance his power; this is confirmed by a message from there.
The Gemara resolves that 'מחמרא' is meant to enhance the recipient's power, and this is the ruling sent from the academy.

items.text: Mishnah: person thrown into a pit
items.text_en: Mishnah: person thrown into a pit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a person thrown into a pit says 'whoever hears my voice shall write a get for my wife', they should write and give it. The Gemara raises concerns about a demon, but resolves by requiring they saw his image and a shadow of a shadow. Another concern about a rival wife is dismissed because in a time of danger, we write and give even without identification.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a person thrown into a pit says 'whoever hears my voice shall write a get for my wife', they should write and give it.
The Gemara raises a concern that the voice might be from a demon, not a person.
Rav Yehuda answers that the concern is resolved when they saw his human form.
The Gemara objects that demons can also appear in human form, so seeing a shadow is required.
The Gemara answers that they saw a shadow of a shadow, which demons lack.
The Gemara objects that perhaps demons also have a shadow of a shadow.
Rabbi Chanina resolves that his son Yonatan taught him that demons have a shadow but not a shadow of a shadow.
The Gemara raises a concern that the voice might be from a rival wife (צרה) trying to harm the wife.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael resolves that in a time of danger, we write and give even without identification.

items.text: Mishnah: healthy person who orders a get and dies
items.text_en: Mishnah: healthy person who orders a get and dies
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says a healthy person who orders a get is assumed to be joking. A story follows: a healthy man ordered a get, climbed a roof, fell and died. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules: if he fell by himself, it is a get; if the wind pushed him, it is not. The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction by explaining the Mishnah is missing a clause: if his end proves his beginning, it is a get.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a healthy person who says 'write a גט (bill of divorce) for my wife' is assumed to be joking.

The Mishnah relates a story of a healthy man who ordered a גט (bill of divorce), climbed a roof, fell and died; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that if he fell by himself it is a valid גט (bill of divorce), but if the wind pushed him it is not.
The Gemara asks whether the story contradicts the Mishnah's ruling.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is incomplete and should include a clause: if his end proves his beginning, it is a valid גט (bill of divorce); the story illustrates this principle.

items.text: Case of ambiguous agency: son as agent in place of father
items.text_en: Case of ambiguous agency: son as agent in place of father
items.desc_en: A man entered a synagogue and found a teacher of children, his son, and another person. He said two of you should write a get for my wife. Later the teacher died. The question: can people appoint a son as an agent in place of his father? Rav Nachman says no, Rav Pappi says yes, and Rava rules in favor of the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates a case: a man entered a synagogue, found a teacher of children, his son, and another person, and said two of you should write a גט (bill of divorce) for my wife; later the teacher died, raising the question of whether people appoint a son as an agent in place of his father.
Rav Nachman rules that people do not appoint a son as an agent in the presence of his father.
Rav Pappi rules that people do appoint a son as an agent in the presence of his father.
Rava rules that the הלכה (binding law) is that people do appoint a son as an agent in the presence of his father.

items.text: Beginning of next Mishnah: 'Give a get to my wife'
items.text_en: Beginning of next Mishnah: 'Give a get to my wife'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a new case: if a man says to two people 'give a get to my wife'...

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins: if one said to two people 'give a get to my wife'...

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Instructions to write and deliver a get
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Instructions to write and deliver a get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between a husband telling three people 'write and give a get to my wife' (they write and give) versus 'give a get to my wife' (they tell others to write, because they are a court). Rabbi Chanina from Ono confirms this tradition, and Rabbi Yosei adds that even the Great Court of Jerusalem, if told 'give a get to my wife,' would learn, write, and give. The Mishnah also rules that if a husband tells ten people 'write and give,' one writes and two sign; if he says 'all of you write,' one writes and all sign, and if one dies the get is void.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that if a husband tells three people 'write and give a get to my wife,' they write and give; if he says 'give a get to my wife,' they tell others to write because they are a court.
Rabbi Chanina from Ono confirms from prison that he received a tradition that when one tells three 'give a get to my wife,' they tell others to write because they are a court.
Rabbi Yosei adds that they said to the messenger: we too are recipients of a tradition that even if one tells the Great Court of Jerusalem 'give a get to my wife,' they learn, write, and give.

The Mishnah concludes with the rule that if a husband tells ten people 'write and give,' one writes and two sign; if he says 'all of you write,' one writes and all sign, and if one dies the get is void.

items.text: Gemara's opening question: Sending to Shmuel about two people instructing a scribe
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question: Sending to Shmuel about two people instructing a scribe
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba reports that the academy of Rav sent to Shmuel asking: if a husband told two people 'write and give a get to my wife,' and they told a scribe who wrote, and they signed, what is the law? Shmuel replied that the woman may leave her husband (the get is valid), but the matter requires further study.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba reporting the academy of Rav's question to Shmuel
