sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba reporting the academy of Rav's question to Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba reports that the academy of Rav sent to Shmuel asking about the validity of a get when the husband told two people to write and give it, and they told a scribe who wrote and they signed.
Shmuel replies that the woman may leave her husband (the get is valid), but the matter requires further study.

items.text: First attempt to explain Shmuel's doubt: delegation of verbal instructions
items.text_en: First attempt to explain Shmuel's doubt: delegation of verbal instructions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Shmuel's doubt was. If it was whether verbal instructions can be delegated to an agent (since the two told a scribe), that is already settled: Shmuel himself ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yosei, who says verbal instructions cannot be delegated to an agent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Shmuel's doubt was, suggesting it might be whether verbal instructions (מילי) can be delegated to an agent.
The Gemara rejects this possibility, noting that Shmuel himself ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that verbal instructions cannot be delegated to an agent.

items.text: Second explanation: Shmuel's doubt about the meaning of 'write'
items.text_en: Second explanation: Shmuel's doubt about the meaning of 'write'
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Shmuel's doubt was about the meaning of 'write' (כתובו) in the husband's instruction: does it mean the witnesses must write the get themselves (כתב ידן), or does it mean they must have the get written (כתב הגט)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's doubt was whether 'כתובו' (write) means the witnesses must write the get in their own handwriting (כתב ידן) or have the get written by a scribe (כתב הגט).

items.text: Attempt to resolve from the Mishnah: 'write' means the get's writing
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve from the Mishnah: 'write' means the get's writing
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests resolving Shmuel's doubt from the Mishnah, which says that if a husband tells two 'give' or three 'write and give,' they write and give. But the Gemara notes that the Mishnah itself is ambiguous. It then argues that the Mishnah's continuation (Rabbi Yosei's statement about the Great Court) implies 'write' means the get's writing, because otherwise the court would need to know how to sign, which is not always the case for a new court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to resolve Shmuel's doubt from the Mishnah, which states that if a husband says 'write and give,' the addressees write and give.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah itself is ambiguous about whether 'write' means their own handwriting or the get's writing.

The Gemara argues that it is obvious that 'write' means the get's writing, because the Mishnah's continuation (Rabbi Yosei's statement) implies that even the Great Court must learn to write the get, which would be unnecessary if 'write' meant their own handwriting.
The Gemara elaborates: if 'write' meant their own handwriting, why would the court need to learn to write? Surely every court knows how to sign their own names.
The Gemara rejects the argument by noting that there is indeed a new court that might not know how to sign.

items.text: Objection and resolution: Rabbi Yosei's position on 'say'
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: Rabbi Yosei's position on 'say'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if 'write' means the witnesses' own handwriting, then having a scribe write would be like saying 'say' (imru), and Rabbi Yosei agrees that 'say' can be delegated. But the Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei invalidates a get written by a scribe and signed by the scribe as a witness, showing he does not agree. The Gemara concludes that if Rabbi Yosei agreed, it would lead to a breach, as sometimes the two might tell others to write.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if 'כתובו' means the witnesses' own handwriting, then having a scribe write the get would be like saying 'אמרו' (say), and Rabbi Yosei agrees that 'אמרו' can be delegated, but this contradicts the established halacha that Rabbi Yosei holds 'מילי לא מימסרן לשליח' (verbal instructions cannot be delegated to an agent).
The Gemara suggests: if we hold that 'כתובו' means their own handwriting, then the scribe's writing the get is treated like saying 'אמרו', and Rabbi Yosei concedes that 'אמרו' can be delegated.

The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Yosei actually concede regarding 'אמרו'? It cites a Mishnah where a scribe wrote and a witness signed is valid, and Rabbi Yirmeya clarifies that the Mishnah means 'the scribe signed' (as a witness), implying Rabbi Yosei invalidates such a get.

Rav Chisda confirms that the Mishnah's ruling (invalidating a get where the scribe signed as a witness) follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds 'מילי לא מימסרן לשליח' (verbal instructions cannot be delegated).

The Gemara concludes: if Rabbi Yosei conceded regarding 'אמרו', it would lead to a breach (חורבה), because sometimes the two witnesses might tell others to write, undermining the requirement that the witnesses themselves write the get.

items.text: Opening statement and initial reasoning
items.text_en: Opening statement and initial reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the case where a husband says 'Tell the scribe to write and so-and-so to sign.' It explains that due to concern for the scribe's embarrassment, the witnesses might have the scribe sign along with one of them, even though the husband did not say so. The Gemara then notes that since the master said it is 'valid but not to be done in Israel,' such a case is uncommon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the case where a husband says 'Tell the scribe to write and so-and-so to sign,' and explains that due to concern for the scribe's embarrassment, the witnesses might have the scribe sign along with one of them, even though the husband did not say so.
The Gemara concludes that since the master said it is 'valid but not to be done in Israel,' such a case is uncommon.

items.text: Second scenario and its resolution
items.text_en: Second scenario and its resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: what if the husband told two people 'Tell the scribe to write and you sign,' and due to the scribe's embarrassment, they have the scribe sign with one of them, even though the husband did not say so? The Gemara answers that this too is 'valid but not to be done.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: what if the husband told two people 'Tell the scribe to write and you sign,' and due to the scribe's embarrassment, they have the scribe sign with one of them, even though the husband did not say so?
The Gemara answers that this too is 'valid but not to be done.'

items.text: Challenge from the 'valid and permitted' view
items.text_en: Challenge from the 'valid and permitted' view
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: this works for the one who says 'valid but not to be done,' but for the one who says 'valid and permitted,' what can be said? It then explains that Rabbi Yosei said two things, and Shmuel agrees with him on one and disagrees on the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this explanation works for the one who says 'valid but not to be done,' but for the one who says 'valid and permitted,' what can be said?
The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yosei said two things, and Shmuel agrees with him on one and disagrees on the other.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling and Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi's question
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling and Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel quoting Rabbi: the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei who says that verbal instructions cannot be given to an agent. Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi questions why Rabbi rules like Rabbi Yosei when Rabbi Meir and Chanina Ish Ono disagree. Rabbi responds: 'Be quiet, my son, you have not seen Rabbi Yosei; if you had seen him, his reasoning is with him.'

sub.desc_en: Shmuel reports in the name of Rabbi that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that verbal instructions cannot be given to an agent.
Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi questions why Rabbi rules like Rabbi Yosei when Rabbi Meir and Chanina Ish Ono disagree with him.
Rabbi tells his son to be quiet, explaining that if he had seen Rabbi Yosei, he would understand that his reasoning accompanies him.

items.text: Baraita praising the sages
items.text_en: Baraita praising the sages
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Isi ben Yehudah enumerates the praises of the sages: Rabbi Meir is wise and a scribe; Rabbi Yehudah is wise when he wants; Rabbi Tarfon is a heap of nuts; Rabbi Yishmael is a well-stocked store; Rabbi Akiva is a full treasure; Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri is a peddler's basket; Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah is a spice basket; the mishnah of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is a small but clean measure; Rabbi Yosei – his reasoning is with him; Rabbi Shimon grinds much and produces little. The Gemara adds that he forgets a little, and what he produces is only bran. Rabbi Shimon told his students to learn his measures, as they are choice selections from Rabbi Akiva's measures.

sub.desc_en: The baraita enumerates the praises of each sage, from Rabbi Meir to Rabbi Shimon, with metaphorical descriptions.
A Tanna adds that Rabbi Shimon forgets a little and produces only bran.
Rabbi Shimon tells his students to learn his measures, as they are choice selections from Rabbi Akiva's measures.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling and Ulla's question
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling and Ulla's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the case: if one said to two 'Tell the scribe to write and so-and-so to sign,' Rav Huna said in the name of Rav: it is valid but not to be done in Israel. Ulla asked Rav Nachman: since it is valid, why not do it? Rav Nachman answered: we are concerned that he might hire witnesses. The Gemara objects: are we concerned? But a baraita says that witnesses who sign on a field purchase or a woman's get – the sages were not concerned about this matter; they do not do an action, they only speak.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Huna's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Huna's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the case: if one said to two 'Tell the scribe to write and so-and-so to sign,' Rav Huna said in the name of Rav: it is valid but not to be done in Israel.
Ulla asked Rav Nachman: since it is valid, why not do it?
Rav Nachman answered: we are concerned that he might hire witnesses.

The Gemara objects: are we concerned? But a baraita says that witnesses who sign on a field purchase or a woman's get – the sages were not concerned about this matter; they do not do an action, they only speak.

items.text: Dispute among Amoraim on the second scenario
items.text_en: Dispute among Amoraim on the second scenario
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute regarding the case where the husband said to two 'Tell the scribe to write and you sign.' Rav Chisda says: valid but not to be done; Rabbah bar bar Chanah says: valid and permitted; Rav Nachman says: valid but not to be done; Rav Sheshet says: valid and permitted; Rabbah says: valid but not to be done; Rav Yosef says: valid and permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the second scenario: the husband said to two people 'Tell the scribe to write and you sign.'
Rav Chisda rules that the get is valid (כשר) but should not be done (ולא תיעשה).
Rabbah bar bar Chanah rules that the get is valid and may be performed (כשר ותיעשה).
Rav Nachman rules that the get is valid but should not be done.
Rav Sheshet rules that the get is valid and may be performed.
Rabbah rules that the get is valid but should not be done.
Rav Yosef rules that the get is valid and may be performed.

items.text: Alternative version of the earlier dispute
items.text_en: Alternative version of the earlier dispute
items.desc_en: Some reverse the opinions of Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan regarding whether counting the group is like saying 'all of you'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that some reverse the opinions of Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan regarding the dispute about counting the group.

items.text: Baraita on instructions to a group
items.text_en: Baraita on instructions to a group
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a husband tells ten people 'write a get and give it to my wife', one writes on behalf of all; if he says 'all of you write', one writes in the presence of all. Similarly for delivery.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the rules for a husband instructing ten people to write or deliver a get, distinguishing between general instructions and the phrase 'all of you'.

items.text: Dispute: Does counting the group equal 'all of you'?
items.text_en: Dispute: Does counting the group equal 'all of you'?
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if the husband counted the ten people, does that have the same effect as saying 'all of you'? Rav Huna says it does not, while Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar of Rome says it does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if the husband counted the ten people (rather than saying 'all of you'), what is the halacha (הלכה)?
Rav Huna rules that counting the group is not equivalent to saying 'all of you'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's answer in the name of Rabbi Elazar of Rome
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's answer in the name of Rabbi Elazar of Rome
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Elazar of Rome, rules that counting the group is equivalent to saying 'all of you'.

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says they do not disagree: one case is where he counted all of them, the other where he counted only some, and they refer to different sides of the dispute.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the dispute by distinguishing between counting all of them and counting only some, each referring to a different side.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's enactment and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's enactment and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda instituted a formula for a 'all of you' get: write – either all of you or each one; sign – either all of you or any two; deliver – either all of you or each one. Rava objects that sometimes the husband might cut short and say only 'all of you', leading to invalidation. Rava instead proposes a different formula: write – each one; sign – any two; deliver – each one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda instituted a formula for a 'all of you' get: write – either all of you or each one; sign – either all of you or any two; deliver – either all of you or each one.
Rava objects that sometimes the husband might cut short and say only 'all of you', leading to invalidation.
Rava instead proposes a different formula: write – each one; sign – any two; deliver – each one.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The mishnah of the chapter is cited: 'He who says...'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'We return to you, O one who says...'

items.text: Mishnah: One seized by kurdiyakos
items.text_en: Mishnah: One seized by kurdiyakos
items.desc_en: The mishnah states: If one was seized by kurdiyakos and said 'write a get for my wife', he said nothing. If he said 'write a get' and was then seized and retracted, his latter words are void. If he became mute and nodded in response to questions, we test him three times and if consistent, they write and give.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case of one seized by kurdiyakos who said 'write a get for my wife' — his words are void.
The mishnah adds: if he said 'write a get' and was then seized and retracted, his latter words are void.
The mishnah concludes: if he became mute and nodded consistently in response to questions, they write and give the get.

items.text: Gemara on kurdiyakos and remedies
items.text_en: Gemara on kurdiyakos and remedies
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that kurdiyakos is a fever from new wine from the press. It discusses remedies: red meat on coals and diluted wine for sun-related ailments, and various cures including a black chicken, leeks, and immersion. A story is told about Rav Amram the Pious and Yalta's intervention.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'kurdiyakos' means.
Shmuel explains that kurdiyakos is a fever caused by new wine from the press.
The Gemara objects: why not simply say 'one who was bitten by new wine'?
The Gemara answers that the term teaches that this specific type of fever is called 'kurdiyakos'.
The Gemara asks what practical difference this definition makes.
The Gemara answers that the distinction matters for writing an amulet (קמיע) specifically for this condition.
The Gemara states the remedy: red meat on coals and diluted wine.
Abaye reports his mother's remedies for sun-related ailments of different durations, including immersion and leeks.
The Gemara lists remedies for sun and snow ailments: red meat on coals with diluted wine for sun, and fatty meat on coals with undiluted wine for snow.

sub.text: Story about Rav Amram the Pious
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Amram the Pious
sub.desc_en: A story is told about Rav Amram the Pious being mistreated by the Exilarch's household, who deliberately gave him the wrong remedy.
Yalta intervenes by immersing Rav Amram in a bathhouse until the water turns to blood)Skip and his flesh becomes smooth.

items.text: Stories about Rav Yosef, Rav Sheshet, and the Exilarch
items.text_en: Stories about Rav Yosef, Rav Sheshet, and the Exilarch
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef engaged in grinding, Rav Sheshet in weaving, praising work that warms the body. The Exilarch asks Rav Sheshet why he does not attend his feasts; Rav Sheshet demonstrates that the servants are suspected of serving forbidden meat. A humorous exchange follows with a multi-legged animal and a dish of bread and a jar of wine.

sub.desc_en: The narrator reports that Rav Yosef engaged in grinding and Rav Sheshet in weaving, with Rav Sheshet praising work that warms the body.
The Exilarch asks Rav Sheshet why he does not attend his feasts, and Rav Sheshet answers that the servants are suspected of serving אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי (a limb from a living animal).
The Exilarch objects, asking who says so, and Rav Sheshet responds by instructing his attendant to bring a leg from a living animal to prove the point.
Rav Sheshet demonstrates the servants' dishonesty by having them bring legs of an animal, showing they brought a three-legged and then a five-legged creature, exposing their deceit.

sub.text: Exilarch's proposal and Rav Sheshet's acceptance
sub.text_en: Exilarch's proposal and Rav Sheshet's acceptance
sub.desc_en: The Exilarch proposes that Rav Sheshet's attendant prepare food before him, and Rav Sheshet agrees; they bring bread and a jar of wine, and Rav Sheshet wraps the bread in his scarf.
After eating, they said to him, setting up the next exchange (which continues beyond the section).

items.text: The silver cup incident and Rav Chisda's escape
items.text_en: The silver cup incident and Rav Chisda's escape
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda is tricked by demons who steal his silver cup, but he discovers it wrapped in his cloak. He insists he will eat the food offered, tasting a white substance, and instructs them to check the place, citing Rav Chisda's principle about black on white being a sign of leprosy. As he leaves, they dig a pit and cover it with a mat, but Rav Chisda is warned by a child's verse and his servant's observation, and he avoids the trap. Afterwards, he explains how he knew of the plot.

sub.desc_en: The demons complain that their silver cup was stolen, and they find it wrapped in Rav Chisda's cloak.
The demons ask Rav Chisda to see that he does not eat their food, suggesting it is only to torment them.
Rav Chisda insists he will eat and tastes a white substance in the food.
The demons object that white substance is not currently produced for them.
Rav Chisda instructs them to check the place, citing his principle that black on white or white on black is a sign of leprosy.
They check and find the leprous spot, confirming Rav Chisda's diagnosis.
As Rav Chisda leaves, the demons dig a pit, cover it with a mat, and invite him to rest.
Rav Chisda snorts from behind, signaling his awareness.
Rav Chisda asks a child to recite his verse.
The child recites the verse 'Incline to your right or to your left,' warning Rav Chisda to avoid the trap.
Rav Chisda asks his servant what he sees.
The servant reports seeing a mat spread over the pit.
Rav Chisda tells the servant to turn back from the trap.
After escaping, the demons ask Rav Chisda how he knew of the plot.
Rav Chisda explains he knew from three signs: his own snort, the child's verse, and the fact that servants are suspected of being dishonest.

items.text: Interpretation of 'shidah veshidot' and Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'shidah veshidot' and Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'I made for myself male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of man, shidah veshidot' from Ecclesiastes. It explains 'sharim vesharon' as types of music, 'ta'anugot' as pools and bathhouses, and 'shidah veshidot' as male and female demons. In the West they say 'shidta'. Rabbi Yochanan then states that there were three hundred types of demons in Shichin, but he does not know what a female demon herself is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse from Ecclesiastes, explaining 'sharim vesharon' as types of music, 'ta'anugot' as pools and bathhouses, and 'shidah veshidot' as male and female demons, with a Western alternative term 'shidta'.
Rabbi Yochanan states that there were three hundred types of demons in Shichin, but he does not know what a female demon herself is.

items.text: Solomon's inquiry about the shamir and the advice to capture demons
items.text_en: Solomon's inquiry about the shamir and the advice to capture demons
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Solomon needed male and female demons, and explains that when building the Temple, he asked the Sages how to cut the stones without iron. They told him about the shamir worm that Moses used for the stones of the ephod. When he asked where to find it, they advised him to bring male and female demons and subdue them together, as they might know and reveal the location. The demons said they did not know, but suggested that Ashmedai, the king of demons, might know.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Solomon needed male and female demons (שֵׁדָה וְשֵׁידְתִין).
The Gemara explains that when building the Temple, Solomon asked the Sages how to cut stones without iron, and they told him about the shamir worm that Moses used for the stones of the ephod.

The Sages advised Solomon to bring male and female demons and subdue them together, as they might know and reveal the location of the shamir; the demons said they did not know, but suggested that Ashmedai, the king of demons, might know.

items.text: Ashmedai's location and Benaiah's preparation
items.text_en: Ashmedai's location and Benaiah's preparation
items.desc_en: The demons tell Solomon that Ashmedai is on a certain mountain, where he has dug a pit, filled it with water, covered it with a rock, and sealed it with his seal. Every day he ascends to heaven to study, descends to earth to study, then returns to check his seal, drink, and reseal it. Solomon sends Benaiah ben Yehoyada with a chain engraved with the Name, a ring engraved with the Name, tufts of wool, and skins of wine. Benaiah digs a pit below, drains the water, plugs it with wool, digs a pit above, pours in wine, and covers it, then sits in a tree.

sub.desc_en: Solomon asks the demons where Ashmedai is, and they reply that he is on a certain mountain.
The demons describe Ashmedai's daily routine: he ascends to heaven to study, descends to earth to study, then returns to check his seal, drink, and reseal it.

Solomon sends Benaiah ben Yehoyada with a chain engraved with the Name, a ring engraved with the Name, tufts of wool, and skins of wine; Benaiah digs a pit below, drains the water, plugs it with wool, digs a pit above, pours in wine, and covers it, then sits in a tree.

items.text: Ashmedai's capture
items.text_en: Ashmedai's capture
items.desc_en: Ashmedai comes, finds wine instead of water, quotes verses against wine, but eventually drinks due to thirst, becomes drunk, and falls asleep. Benaiah descends, puts the chain on him, and seals it. When Ashmedai awakens and struggles, Benaiah tells him the Name of his Master is upon him.

sub.desc_en: Ashmedai arrives, finds wine instead of water, and refuses to drink, citing verses against wine.
Ashmedai becomes thirsty, drinks, falls asleep; Benaiah descends, chains him, and seals the chain with the Name.

items.text: Ashmedai's violent journey
items.text_en: Ashmedai's violent journey
items.desc_en: As Benaiah leads Ashmedai, the demon violently uproots a palm tree, destroys a house, and when they reach a certain widow's hut, she comes out and begs him not to destroy it.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes Ashmedai's violent journey as Benaiah leads him, uprooting a palm tree and destroying a house, until a widow comes out to beg him not to destroy her hut.

items.text: Ashmedai's initial encounter and the breaking of the bone
items.text_en: Ashmedai's initial encounter and the breaking of the bone
items.desc_en: Ashmedai breaks a bone in Solomon's body, citing the verse about a soft tongue breaking a bone.

sub.desc_en: Ashmedai breaks a bone in Solomon's body, citing the verse about a soft tongue breaking a bone.

items.text: Ashmedai's observations on the road
items.text_en: Ashmedai's observations on the road
items.desc_en: Ashmedai observes a blind man, a drunkard, a joyous woman, a man ordering shoes for seven years, and a sorcerer, and reacts to each.

sub.desc_en: Ashmedai observes a blind man, a drunkard, a joyous woman, a man ordering shoes for seven years, and a sorcerer, and reacts to each.

items.text: Solomon's tests of Ashmedai's wisdom
items.text_en: Solomon's tests of Ashmedai's wisdom
items.desc_en: Solomon tests Ashmedai by withholding drink and food, and Ashmedai responds with symbolic actions that Solomon interprets correctly.

sub.desc_en: Ashmedai asks why King Solomon has not summoned him, and is told that Solomon forgot to drink.
Ashmedai places one brick on top of another, which Solomon interprets as a sign that they should give him drink.
Ashmedai again asks why he is not summoned, and is told that Solomon forgot to eat.
Ashmedai removes the top brick and places it on the ground, which Solomon interprets as a sign to withhold food from him.

items.text: Ashmedai's rebuke of Solomon
items.text_en: Ashmedai's rebuke of Solomon
items.desc_en: Ashmedai measures four cubits and rebukes Solomon for conquering the whole world but not being satisfied.

sub.desc_en: Ashmedai measures four cubits and rebukes Solomon for conquering the whole world but not being satisfied.

items.text: Acquiring the shamir worm
items.text_en: Acquiring the shamir worm
items.desc_en: Solomon asks for the shamir worm to build the Temple. Ashmedai explains it is entrusted to a wild rooster, and they trick the rooster into bringing it.

sub.desc_en: Solomon tells Ashmedai he wants nothing for himself but needs the shamir worm to build the Temple.
Ashmedai explains that the shamir is not entrusted to him but to the Prince of the Sea, who gives it only to a wild rooster that is trusted with its oath.
The gemara describes how the wild rooster uses the shamir to split mountains and create fertile land, explaining the Aramaic translation 'נגר טורא' (mountain cleaver).

Solomon's agents find the wild rooster's nest, cover it with glass, and trick the rooster into bringing the shamir to break the glass; they take the shamir, and the rooster kills itself over its broken oath.

items.text: Explanations of Ashmedai's reactions
items.text_en: Explanations of Ashmedai's reactions
items.desc_en: Benaiah asks Ashmedai to explain his earlier reactions to the blind man, drunkard, joyous woman, shoe order, and sorcerer, and Ashmedai provides reasons.

sub.desc_en: Benaiah asks Ashmedai why he helped the blind man who was lost.
Ashmedai explains that the blind man was a complete righteous person, and helping him earns a share in the World to Come.
Benaiah asks Ashmedai why he helped the drunkard who was lost.
Ashmedai explains that the drunkard was a complete wicked person, and helping him allows him to enjoy this world before his punishment.
Benaiah asks Ashmedai why he cried when he saw the joyous woman.
Ashmedai explains that the woman's husband will die within thirty days, and she will have to wait for a young brother-in-law for thirteen years.
Benaiah asks Ashmedai why he laughed when he heard the man ordering shoes for seven years.
Ashmedai explains that the man does not have even seven days to live, yet he orders shoes for seven years.
Benaiah asks Ashmedai why he laughed when he saw the sorcerer performing magic.
Ashmedai explains that the sorcerer was sitting over the king's treasure, and should have used his magic to uncover what was beneath him instead of trivial tricks.

items.text: Solomon's downfall and Ashmedai's usurpation
items.text_en: Solomon's downfall and Ashmedai's usurpation
items.desc_en: Solomon asks about the superiority of angels over demons. Ashmedai tricks Solomon into giving him his ring, swallows him, and casts him far away, leading Solomon to lament.

sub.desc_en: Solomon asks Ashmedai what makes angels superior to demons, citing the verse about 'תועפות ראם' (the horns of the wild ox).
Ashmedai tricks Solomon into giving him his ring, swallows him, and casts him far away, leading Solomon to lament his loss.

items.text: Solomon's wandering and restoration
items.text_en: Solomon's wandering and restoration
items.desc_en: Solomon wanders as a beggar, is recognized by the Sanhedrin, and is restored to his throne through the efforts of Benaiah and the queens.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the verse and dispute
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the verse and dispute
sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse 'וְזֶה הָיָה חֶלְקִי מִכׇּל עֲמָלִי' and records a dispute between Rav and Shmuel over what 'וְזֶה' refers to: one says his staff, the other says his garment.

The gemara describes how Solomon, reduced to begging, would declare his former kingship, and when he reaches the Sanhedrin, the rabbis question his sanity because a madman does not fixate on a single claim.
The Sanhedrin asks Benaiah if the king is summoning him, and Benaiah replies no.
The Sanhedrin sends word to the queens to verify if Solomon is coming; the queens confirm he is coming on foot, so they check his feet.
Solomon demands the queens' submission and also his mother Bathsheba; they bring him the ring and chain with the divine name, and when he enters, Ashmedai sees him and flees.
The gemara notes that despite Ashmedai's flight, Solomon still feared him, and cites the verse about sixty guards around his bed 'מִפַּחַד בַּלֵּילוֹת' (from fear of the night).

items.text: Debate about Solomon's status
items.text_en: Debate about Solomon's status
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether Solomon was a king and a commoner, or a king, commoner, and king again.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether Solomon was a king and a commoner, or a king, commoner, and king again.

items.text: Medical remedies for headaches and migraines
items.text_en: Medical remedies for headaches and migraines
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides remedies for headaches and migraines using various herbs and a wild rooster.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a remedy for headaches: boil together shurbina, willow, myrtle, olive, chalfa, sea-chalfa, and yavla, and apply 300 cups to each side of the head.
If the first remedy fails, the Gemara offers an alternative: boil a white rose from a single row and apply 60 cups to each side of the head.

For migraines, the Gemara prescribes slaughtering a wild rooster with a white knife on the painful side, being careful of its blood, and hanging it on the doorpost so the patient rubs against it when entering and exiting.

items.text: Remedy for ברוקתא (a type of eye ailment)
items.text_en: Remedy for ברוקתא (a type of eye ailment)
items.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a specific treatment for ברוקתא, involving a scorpion, kohl, and precise application to the eyes, warning against overfilling to avoid eye damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a remedy for ברוקתא (an eye ailment) using a scorpion, kohl, and precise application to the eyes, warning against overfilling.

items.text: Remedy for night-time שַׁבְרִירֵי (cataracts or vision impairment)
items.text_en: Remedy for night-time שַׁבְרִירֵי (cataracts or vision impairment)
items.desc_en: A complex ritual involving a dog, children, and specific incantations is described to cure night-time vision problems, followed by a final act of releasing the dog.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a complex remedy for לילית (night blindness), involving a black snake, a dog, children, and incantations.

items.text: Remedy for daytime שַׁבְרִירֵי
items.text_en: Remedy for daytime שַׁבְרִירֵי
items.desc_en: A different cure for daytime vision problems involves seven red items from a חיוותא, a potter's shard, and a dialogue between a blind person and another, with a warning to break the shard afterward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a remedy for daytime blindness, involving seven red insects, a potter's shard, and a ritual exchange with a blind person.

items.text: Remedies for nosebleed (דְּמָא דְּאָתֵי מִנְּחִירָא)
items.text_en: Remedies for nosebleed (דְּמָא דְּאָתֵי מִנְּחִירָא)
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides a series of escalating remedies for nosebleeds, starting with writing the name 'Levi' backwards by a priest named Levi, then other names and incantations, followed by herbal mixtures and a ritual involving water flowing from east to west, and finally a simpler water ritual.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes the first remedy for a nosebleed: a priest named Levi writes the name 'Levi' backwards.
The Gemara offers a second remedy: any person writes the incantation 'אנא פפי שילא בר סומקי' backwards.
The Gemara provides a third remedy: writing the phrase 'טעם דלי במי כסף, טעם דלי במי פגם'.
The Gemara prescribes a fourth remedy: a mixture of herbs, old bed straw, and other ingredients burned together, then applied as a wick to the nostril.
The Gemara prescribes a fifth remedy: a ritual involving standing over a stream flowing east to west, taking mud from under each foot, and inserting it as a wick into the nostril.
The Gemara prescribes a sixth and final remedy: sitting under a drainpipe while water is poured over him, and reciting an incantation that the blood should stop like the water.

items.text: Diagnosis for blood from the mouth (דְּמָא דְּאָתֵי מִפּוּמָּא)
items.text_en: Diagnosis for blood from the mouth (דְּמָא דְּאָתֵי מִפּוּמָּא)
items.desc_en: A diagnostic test using wheat flour determines if blood from the mouth originates from the lungs (curable) or the liver (incurable). Rav Ami challenges Rav Ashi with a contradictory Mishnah, and Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that the blood from the mouth is absorbed from the lungs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a diagnostic test for blood from the mouth: if it sticks to wheat flour, it comes from the lungs and is curable; if not, it comes from the liver and is incurable.
Rav Ami challenges Rav Ashi by citing a Mishnah that states the opposite: a missing liver renders an animal kosher, while a punctured or missing lung renders it a neveila.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that since the blood comes from the mouth, it is absorbed from the lungs, so the lung is effectively punctured, making the animal a neveila.

items.text: Cure for blood from the lungs
items.text_en: Cure for blood from the lungs
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides a specific remedy for blood originating from the lungs, involving seven measures of various vegetables and spices, cooked and eaten with beer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the remedy for bleeding from the lungs?
The Gemara prescribes a remedy involving seven measures of various vegetables and spices, cooked and eaten, followed by strong beer.

The Gemara prescribes a remedy: take seven measures of beet stalks, seven of leek stalks, five of peeled beans, three of fenugreek, a measure of cumin, a measure of spices, and an equal amount of unleavened bread, cook and eat them, then drink strong beer of Tevet.

items.text: Remedy for כאכא (a type of skin condition)
items.text_en: Remedy for כאכא (a type of skin condition)
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna prescribes a treatment for כאכא using garlic, oil, and salt applied to the nail, with a warning to avoid contact with the skin as it is harmful to white skin.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna prescribes a remedy for כאכא (a type of skin ailment) using garlic, oil, and salt applied to the thumbnail, with a warning about its danger to white skin.

items.text: Remedies for חינכי (gums or mouth ailments)
items.text_en: Remedies for חינכי (gums or mouth ailments)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan discusses remedies for חינכי, including using חומתי and ממרא, and then provides separate treatments for swelling, opening, and raising the gums, involving various herbs and substances.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by stating that for חינכי (gums or mouth ailments), חומתי (a plant) is like ממרא (another plant), and the root of חומתי is superior; one should hold it in the mouth.
The Gemara provides a remedy for swelling gums: take various herbs and hold them like a nut in the mouth.
The Gemara gives a remedy for opening the gums: a friend should blow white תחלי (a substance) into the mouth through a reed of wheat.
The Gemara gives a remedy for raising the gums: take dust from the shade of a toilet, mix with honey, and eat, as it is beneficial.

items.text: Remedy for ברסם (a type of skin condition or inflammation)
items.text_en: Remedy for ברסם (a type of skin condition or inflammation)
items.desc_en: A remedy for ברסם is described, involving pistachio, helbenita, honey, and wine, cooked together, with an alternative using goat's milk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a remedy for ברסם (a type of skin condition), involving pistachio, galbanum, honey, and wine, or alternatively, a quarter-log of white goat's milk.
An alternative remedy is provided using a quarter-log of white goat's milk.

items.text: Remedy for fever
items.text_en: Remedy for fever
items.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a treatment for fever involving a specific procedure with a gourd, and if that fails, a mixture of white dog feces and tar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a treatment for fever: applying a gourd to three palm branches, and if that fails, mixing white dog feces with tar, warning not to eat the feces as it is dangerous.

items.text: Remedies for arrow-wound, uncovered water, and morisa
items.text_en: Remedies for arrow-wound, uncovered water, and morisa
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides remedies for an arrow-wound (gira), uncovered water (giluya), and morisa, each with specific ingredients and precautions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a remedy for an arrow-wound (gira): take a pebble from a lilith, invert it, pour water over it, and drink.
The Gemara offers an alternative: take water from which a dog drank at night, and warns to guard against uncovered water (giluya).
The Gemara prescribes a remedy for uncovered water (giluya): the excrement of live wine (lees).
The Gemara prescribes a remedy for morisa (a skin condition): the excrement of wine, hung in a tent.

items.text: Remedy for heart disease (pirkha d'libba) – first version
items.text_en: Remedy for heart disease (pirkha d'libba) – first version
items.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes eating three barley heads with a certain condiment and drinking diluted wine. Rav Acha from Difti questions Ravina, who clarifies he meant for heart heaviness, not heart disease.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a remedy for heart disease (פירחא דליבא): take three barley heads, tie them with a condiment that has not passed forty days, eat them, and then drink diluted wine.
Rav Acha from Difti objects to Ravina: this remedy would exacerbate the condition, as it would cause the heart to 'fly away' even more.
Ravina clarifies that his prescription was intended for heart heaviness (יוקרא דליבא), not for heart disease (פירחא דליבא), resolving the objection.

items.text: Remedy for heart disease – second version
items.text_en: Remedy for heart disease – second version
items.desc_en: An alternative remedy for heart disease: eating three wheat heads with honey and drinking fresh wine.

sub.desc_en: The gemara prescribes an alternative remedy for heart disease: eating three wheat heads with honey and drinking fresh wine afterward.

items.text: Remedy for heart pain (tzircha d'libba)
items.text_en: Remedy for heart pain (tzircha d'libba)
items.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes eating three eggs of niniya, an egg of cumin, and an egg of sesame.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes eating three eggs of niniya, an egg of cumin, and an egg of sesame as a remedy for heart pain (צירחא דליבא).

items.text: Remedy for stomach pain and anecdote
items.text_en: Remedy for stomach pain and anecdote
items.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes drinking 100 long peppers in wine daily. Ravin from Naresh treated Rav Ashi's daughter with 150 of their peppers, and she was healed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes drinking 100 long peppers in wine daily for stomach pain.
Ravin from Naresh treated Rav Ashi's daughter with 150 of their peppers, and she was healed.

items.text: Remedies for kirtza and white kirtza
items.text_en: Remedies for kirtza and white kirtza
items.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a remedy for kirtza using wine and a leaf, and for white kirtza using a specific seed prepared with water, with a warning about binta.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a remedy for kirtza (a type of skin ailment) using wine sediment on a leaf of a certain plant.
The Gemara prescribes a remedy for white kirtza using a specific seed prepared with water.
The Gemara warns to be careful about binta, because otherwise it will perforate the patient's intestine.

items.text: Remedies for constipation and diarrhea
items.text_en: Remedies for constipation and diarrhea
items.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes moist sisin in water for constipation and dry sisin in water for diarrhea, with a mnemonic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes moist sisin in water for constipation and dry sisin in water for diarrhea, with a mnemonic.

items.text: Remedies for spleen ailments
items.text_en: Remedies for spleen ailments
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides multiple remedies for spleen problems, including drinking dried binei in wine, using a spleen from an unopened bird, placing a hand from a corpse, eating a binit from a smithy, and opening a wine barrel. Rav Acha bar Rava questions Rav Ashi, who suggests a morning bread roll instead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a remedy for spleen ailments: take seven dried binei (a type of fish) in wine, or alternatively, use the spleen of an unopened bird, dry it in an oven, and recite an incantation.
The Gemara offers another alternative: dry the spleen between the rafters of a new house with a similar incantation, or use the hand of a corpse placed on the spleen.
The Gemara suggests eating a binit (a type of fish) roasted at a smithy and drinking the smithy's water, citing a story of a goat that drank such water and was found without a spleen.
Rav Acha bar Rava questions Rav Ashi: if one has a barrel of wine, he would not come to the master for a remedy, implying the remedy is impractical.
Rav Ashi responds that the real remedy is a morning bread roll (פת שחרית), which is beneficial for the entire body.

items.text: Remedy for rash (rushchata)
items.text_en: Remedy for rash (rushchata)
items.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a mixture of various minerals and a cloth, with seasonal variations, or alternatively, diluted beer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a mixture of minerals and cloth for rash (רושחתא), with seasonal variations, or alternatively, diluted beer.

items.text: Remedy for shigrona
items.text_en: Remedy for shigrona
items.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes rolling a patya of moninei sixty times on each temple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes rolling a patya of moninei sixty times on each temple as a remedy for shigrona.

items.text: Remedies for tzimeret (gonorrhea)
items.text_en: Remedies for tzimeret (gonorrhea)
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides several remedies for tzimeret, including an oil mixture applied to the male organ or female place, hanging a bladder, a red thread from Dumah, and a male and female louse, with a final instruction about urinating on a dry assisana.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes an oil mixture of three drops of tar, leek juice, and strained wine applied to the male organ or female place for tzimeret.
If the first remedy fails, the Gemara suggests hanging a bladder on the male organ or on the woman's breasts.
If still unsuccessful, the Gemara prescribes a red thread from the fields of Dumah, daughter of Dumah, hung on the male organ or on the woman's breasts.
If still not cured, the Gemara suggests hanging a male and female louse on the male organ or on the female place.
The Gemara concludes with a final instruction: when urinating, urinate on a dry assisana in the door hinge, and examine the thick substance that emerges, which is effective for all types of tzimeret.

items.text: Remedy for external tzimeret
items.text_en: Remedy for external tzimeret
items.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a steam treatment using three griva of sufli and three griva of adara leaves, with instructions for bathing and drinking only adara water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a steam treatment for external tzimeret using three griva of sufli and three griva of adara leaves, with instructions for bathing and drinking only adara water.

items.text: Remedy for internal tzimeret
items.text_en: Remedy for internal tzimeret
items.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes eating seven bundles of beets from seven beds with their earth, and drinking adara leaf in beer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes eating seven bundles of beets from seven beds with their earth, and drinking adara leaf in beer, as a remedy for internal tzimeret.

items.text: Remedies for specific ailments
items.text_en: Remedies for specific ailments
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a remedy for a certain condition using grapes of a wild vine and water, then provides a cure for חזזית using wheat and oil. It concludes with a story about Rav Shimi bar Ashi who performed a similar cure for a gentile for a different purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a remedy using wild vine grapes and water.
The Gemara provides a cure for חזזית (a skin condition) using wheat and oil.

sub.text: Story about Rav Shimi bar Ashi
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Shimi bar Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi performed the same cure for a gentile for a different purpose, and he was healed.

items.text: Treatments for those struck by Persians or stung by a hornet
items.text_en: Treatments for those struck by Persians or stung by a hornet
items.desc_en: Shmuel teaches that one struck by Persian clubs will not survive, but one should give him fatty meat on coals and live wine so he might live long enough to instruct his household. Rav Idi bar Avin adds that one who swallows a hornet will not survive, but should be given a quarter-log of vinegar so he might live long enough to instruct his household.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel teaches that one struck by Persian clubs will not survive, but one should give him fatty meat on coals and live wine so he might live long enough to instruct his household.
Rav Idi bar Avin adds that one who swallows a hornet will not survive, but should be given a quarter-log of vinegar so he might live long enough to instruct his household.

items.text: Causes of אחילו (fever)
items.text_en: Causes of אחילו (fever)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that eating beef with turnip and sleeping in the moonlight during the summer solstice causes אחילו. A baraisa adds that filling one's stomach with anything causes it, and Rav Pappa specifies that even dates can cause it, despite their benefits.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that eating beef with turnip and sleeping in the moonlight during the summer solstice causes אחילו (fever).
A baraisa adds that filling one's stomach with anything causes אחילו.
Rav Pappa specifies that even dates can cause it, despite their benefits, countering a potential assumption.

items.text: Definition and cure for אחילו
items.text_en: Definition and cure for אחילו
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines אחילו as a fire of bones, explained by Abaye as a fire of bones. It then provides a detailed cure involving drinking three, seven, or twelve cups, followed by a specific regimen after eating and using the bathroom, including a mixture of flour and old wine, wrapping in a sheet, and sleeping until one wakes naturally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'אחילו' means.
Rabbi Elazar defines 'אחילו' as a fire of bones.
The Gemara asks what 'fire of bones' means.
Abaye explains that 'fire of bones' means a burning sensation in the bones.
The Gemara asks what the cure for 'אחילו' is.
Abaye reports his mother's general rule that all drink-based cures involve three, seven, or twelve cups, but this one requires drinking until cured.

Abaye details the full cure regimen: drink after eating and using the bathroom, then consume a mixture of flour and old wine, wrap in a sheet, sleep until waking naturally, and remove the sheet immediately to prevent relapse.

items.text: Advice from Elijah and Rabbi Chiyya for health
items.text_en: Advice from Elijah and Rabbi Chiyya for health
items.desc_en: Elijah told Rabbi Natan to eat a third, drink a third, and leave a third, so that when angry he will be full. Rabbi Chiyya teaches that one who wants to avoid intestinal illness should be regular with dipping, withdraw from a meal when it is enjoyable, and not delay when needing to relieve oneself.

sub.desc_en: Elijah instructs Rabbi Natan to eat a third, drink a third, and leave a third so that when angry he will be full.
Rabbi Chiyya teaches three practices to avoid intestinal illness: regular dipping, withdrawing from a meal while enjoyable, and not delaying when needing to relieve oneself.

items.text: Dangers of white wine and sitting by fire in Nisan
items.text_en: Dangers of white wine and sitting by fire in Nisan
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva says that one who drinks white wine will be seized with ויתיק. Rav Chisda explains that among sixty types of wine, the best is red and fragrant, the worst is white wine. Rav Yehuda adds that one who sits by the fire in the mornings of Nisan, anoints with oil, and then goes out into the sun will be seized with ויתיק.

sub.desc_en: Mar Ukva states that one who drinks white wine will be seized with ויתיק (weakness).
Rav Chisda explains that among sixty types of wine, the best is red and fragrant, while the worst is white wine.
Rav Yehuda adds that one who sits by the fire in the mornings of Nisan, anoints with oil, and then goes out into the sun will be seized with ויתיק (weakness).

items.text: Dangers of marital relations after bloodletting or travel
items.text_en: Dangers of marital relations after bloodletting or travel
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that if one bleeds and then engages in relations, the children will be epileptic; if both do so, the children will have skin disease. Rav Pappa limits this to when they have not tasted anything. Rabbah bar Rav Huna adds that one who returns from a journey and engages in relations will have epileptic children. Another baraisa warns against relations after using the bathroom until waiting half a mil, due to a demon accompanying the person.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach that bloodletting followed by marital relations produces weak children, and if both spouses do so, the children will have skin disease.
Rav Pappa limits the ruling to cases where the person has not tasted anything after bloodletting.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna adds that one who returns from a journey and engages in relations will have weak children.
Another baraita warns against relations after using the bathroom until waiting half a mil, due to a demon accompanying the person, resulting in epileptic children.

items.text: Improper positions for relations and remedies
items.text_en: Improper positions for relations and remedies
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that relations while standing causes עוית, sitting causes דלריא, and if she is above and he below, also דלריא. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains דלריא as דרדרא, which Abaye identifies as מוריקא דחוחי. Rav Pappa and Rav Pappi demonstrate different methods of consuming it. Abaye then provides a remedy for one unfamiliar with proper conduct: three measures of thorn berries boiled in wine.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach that improper positions for relations cause specific ailments: standing causes עוית, sitting causes דלריא, and if she is above and he below, also דלריא.
The gemara asks what the term דלריא means.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that דלריא refers to דרדרא (thorn berries).
The gemara asks what דרדרא means.
Abaye identifies דרדרא as מוריקא דחוחי (the juice of thorn berries).

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Pappi's practices
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Pappi's practices
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa chews and swallows the thorn berries, while Rav Pappi chews and spits them out.
Abaye prescribes a remedy of three measures of thorn berries boiled in wine for one unfamiliar with proper conduct, and Rabbi Yochanan attests that this restored his youth.

items.text: Lists of things that weaken, harm, or benefit the body
items.text_en: Lists of things that weaken, harm, or benefit the body
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents several lists: three things that weaken a person (fear, travel, sin), three that jolt the body (eating, drinking, relations while standing), five close to death (eating, drinking, bloodletting, sleeping, relations and then standing), six that cause immediate death if done in order (with a story about a maidservant), eight that are mostly harmful but partially beneficial (travel, etc.), and eight that diminish seed (salt, hunger, etc.). A baraisa notes that bloodletting below is doubly harmful, above doubly beneficial.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a list of three things that weaken a person: fear, travel, and sin, each supported by a biblical verse.
The Gemara presents a second list: three things that jolt the body — eating, drinking, and relations while standing.
The Gemara lists five things that bring a person close to death: eating, drinking, bloodletting, sleeping, and relations followed by standing.
The Gemara lists six actions that cause immediate death if done in order, and Rabbi Yochanan adds the condition that they must be performed in sequence.

Abaye clarifies that doing them in order causes death, but out of order merely weakens; he then objects with a story of a maidservant who died after only three, and resolves that she was already weak.
The Gemara lists eight things that are mostly harmful but partially beneficial: travel, intercourse, wealth, work, wine, sleep, hot water, and bloodletting.
The Gemara lists eight things that diminish seed: salt, hunger, skin eruption, crying, sleeping on the ground, etc., with bloodletting below being doubly harmful.
A baraita states that just as bloodletting below is doubly harmful, so too above it is doubly beneficial, and Rav Pappa begins to comment.

items.text: Opening discussion: definitions of 'below' and 'above' in the context of eggs, and the seasons for cucumbers
items.text_en: Opening discussion: definitions of 'below' and 'above' in the context of eggs, and the seasons for cucumbers
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the terms 'below' and 'above' relative to eggs, and discusses the cucumber that is out of season. A baraisa states that an out-of-season cucumber is as harmful as an in-season one is beneficial. Rav Papa specifies that the season is Tammuz, out of season is Tevet, and Nisan and Tishrei are neither good nor bad.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara defines the terms 'below' and 'above' relative to eggs.
A baraisa teaches that an out-of-season cucumber is as harmful as an in-season one is beneficial.
Rav Papa specifies the seasons: Tammuz is in-season, Tevet is out-of-season, and Nisan and Tishrei are neither good nor bad.

items.text: The case of a man seized by קורדייקוס who retracts his instruction to write a get
items.text_en: The case of a man seized by קורדייקוס who retracts his instruction to write a get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a man said 'Write a get for my wife' and was then seized by a fit (קורדייקוס) and said 'Do not write', his latter words are void. Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether the get may be written immediately or only after he recovers.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a man who instructed to write a get, was seized by קורדייקוס (a fit), and retracted; his latter words are void.
Reish Lakish rules that the get may be written and given immediately (לכתחילה).
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the get may only be written after he recovers (לכתחילה).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning behind each opinion. Reish Lakish compares the man to a sleeper, whose retraction is meaningless, while Rabbi Yochanan compares him to a madman, whose retraction is also meaningless but who cannot act coherently. The Gemara then questions why Rabbi Yochanan does not compare him to a sleeper (because a sleeper requires no action, while this man requires an action to recover), and why Reish Lakish does not compare him to a madman (because a madman cannot be cured, while this man can be cured with red meat and wine).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of Reish Lakish.
The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish compares the man to a sleeper, while Rabbi Yochanan compares him to a madman.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan should also compare him to a sleeper, and answers that a sleeper requires no action, while this man requires an action to recover.
The Gemara objects that Reish Lakish should also compare him to a madman, and answers that a madman cannot be cured, while this man can be cured with red meat and wine.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from a baraita about a man who slaughtered an animal and nodded
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from a baraita about a man who slaughtered an animal and nodded
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position from a statement of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: if a man slaughtered two or the majority of two (an animal) and nodded to write a get, they may write and give it. A baraita similarly states that if one saw a man wounded or crucified who nodded, they may write and give. The Gemara distinguishes: there the man's mind is clear but he is weak, while here (in the case of קורדייקוס) his mind is confused.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position by citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: if a man slaughtered two or the majority of two (an animal) and nodded to write a get, they may write and give it.
A baraita similarly states that if one saw a man wounded or crucified who nodded, they may write and give a get.
The Gemara distinguishes: there the man's mind is clear but he is weak, while here (in the case of קורדייקוס) his mind is confused.

items.text: Challenge to Shmuel from the case of a man who slaughtered an animal and fled
items.text_en: Challenge to Shmuel from the case of a man who slaughtered an animal and fled
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's statement that a man who slaughtered two or the majority of two (an animal) and fled may be testified about (to his death). If he is considered alive, why may they testify? The Gemara answers that he is alive but will eventually die. It then raises a contradiction: if so, he should be exiled for manslaughter, but a baraita says he is not exiled. The Gemara resolves with Rabbi Hoshaya's explanation: we suspect the wind confused him, or he hastened his own death. The difference between these explanations is whether the slaughter was in a house of marble (where he might have been confused by echoes) or outside (where he did not convulse).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel's statement that a man who slaughtered two or the majority of two (an animal) and fled may be testified about (to his death), asking: if he is considered alive, why may they testify?
The Gemara answers that he is alive but will eventually die, so testimony is permitted.
The Gemara objects: if he is alive, he should be exiled for manslaughter, but a baraita says he is not exiled.
Rabbi Hoshaya resolves the contradiction by explaining that we suspect the wind confused him, or he hastened his own death.
The Gemara notes the practical difference between the two explanations: whether the slaughter was in a house of marble (where echoes might confuse) or outside (where he did not convulse).

items.text: The case of a mute person who nods regarding writing a get
items.text_en: The case of a mute person who nods regarding writing a get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a mute person who is asked 'Shall we write a get for your wife?' and nods. The Gemara raises a concern: perhaps he is merely affected by a seizure of 'no no' or 'yes yes'. Rav Yosef bar Minyomi citing Rav Nachman says we ask him in stages. The Gemara then worries that he might have a seizure of stages (e.g., one 'no' and two 'yes', etc.). The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that we ask him about matters of summer in winter and vice versa. The Gemara questions what these matters are: if it is about cloaks and sheets, we might worry that cold or heat affected him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern about the Mishnah's case of a mute person who nods: perhaps he is seized by a fit of repeating 'no no' or 'yes yes'.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Nachman answers that we ask the mute person in stages (סֵירוּגִין) to verify his intent.
The Gemara objects: perhaps he is seized by a fit of stages (e.g., one 'no' and two 'yes', or two 'no' and one 'yes'), so the staged questioning is unreliable.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught a baraita: we ask him about matters of summer in winter and vice versa, to test his coherence.
The Gemara questions what these seasonal matters are: if they are cloaks and sheets, we might worry that cold or heat affected his responses.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The segment quotes the Mishnah's conclusion: 'אֶלָּא בְּפֵירֵי' (but only for produce), setting the context for the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes that a deaf person's gestures are only valid for produce transactions, not for divorces.

items.text: Rav Kahana's ruling and the distinction between deaf and mute
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's ruling and the distinction between deaf and mute
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules that a deaf person who can speak through writing may write a get. Rav Yosef objects, citing a baraita about a mute person. Rabbi Zeira clarifies that a deaf person (who cannot hear) is different from a mute (who cannot speak), and supports this with a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules in the name of Rav that a deaf person who can speak through writing may write and deliver a get.
Rav Yosef objects, citing a baraita about a mute person who is tested by nodding, implying that writing is not sufficient for a get.
Rabbi Zeira distinguishes between a deaf person (who cannot hear) and a mute person (who cannot speak), citing a baraita that defines each and treats both as fully competent.
Rabbi Zeira supports the distinction with a verse from Psalms and a folk saying, showing that a deaf person is one who cannot hear and a mute person is one who cannot speak.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's difficulty and Abaye's resolution regarding testimony
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's difficulty and Abaye's resolution regarding testimony
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises a contradiction from a baraita that excludes a mute from testimony, even though he can communicate in writing. Abaye answers that testimony requires oral testimony ('מִפִּיהֶם'), not written.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises a difficulty: a baraita excludes a mute from testimony even though he can communicate in writing.
Abaye answers that testimony requires oral testimony ('מִפִּיהֶם'), not written communication.

items.text: Objection from a baraita listing 'testimonies' and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita listing 'testimonies' and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that includes 'testimonies' among matters for which a mute is examined. Rav Yosef bar Minyomi limits this to testimony about a woman (which is lenient). Rabbi Avahu limits 'inheritances' to the inheritance of a firstborn. The Gemara then limits 'business and gifts' to the mute's own benefit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that includes 'testimonies' (עדויות) among matters for which a mute is examined, contradicting the earlier limitation.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Sheishet
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Sheishet
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Sheishet answers that the baraita refers specifically to testimony about a woman (עדות אשה), which the rabbis treated leniently.
The Gemara objects that the baraita also lists 'inheritances' (ירושות), which cannot be limited to testimony about a woman.
Rabbi Avahu answers that 'inheritances' refers specifically to the inheritance of a firstborn son (ירושת בנו הבכור), which is a lenient matter.
The Gemara objects that the baraita also lists 'business and gifts' (משאות ומתנות), which seem to be general matters, not limited to the mute's own benefit.
The Gemara resolves that 'business and gifts' refers only to transactions for the mute's own benefit (לדידיה), not general matters.

items.text: Another objection regarding a deaf person's writing
items.text_en: Another objection regarding a deaf person's writing
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a deaf person's writing is not followed for gittin, only for movables. This contradicts Rav Kahana's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita that a deaf person's gestures are not followed for divorces, only for movable property.

items.text: Resolution: Tannaitic dispute and distinction between congenital and acquired deafness
items.text_en: Resolution: Tannaitic dispute and distinction between congenital and acquired deafness
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by citing a Tannaitic dispute: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between a congenital deaf person (who cannot write a get) and one who became deaf (who can). The Gemara then questions this, and explains that the case involves a yevamah from a hearing brother, or a decree lest one confuse a deaf brother with a hearing brother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute, citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel who distinguishes between a congenital deaf person (חֵרֵשׁ מֵעִיקָּרוֹ) and one who became deaf (פִּיקֵּחַ וְנִתְחָרֵשׁ), allowing the latter to write a get.
The Gemara objects: for a congenital deaf person, just as he married her by hint (רְמִיזָה), he should also divorce her by hint — so why does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel forbid it?
The Gemara answers: if it were his own wife, indeed he could divorce her by hint; but here the case involves a yevamah (יבִמְתּוֹ) from a hearing brother.
The Gemara asks: from which brother did the yevamah fall to him? If from a deaf brother, then just as her entry was by hint, so too her exit should be by hint.
The Gemara clarifies: the case is where she fell to him from a hearing brother, so the deaf brother cannot divorce her by hint because the marriage was not by hint.
Alternatively, the Gemara says: even if she fell from a deaf brother, there is a decree (גְּזֵירָה) lest one confuse a deaf brother with a hearing brother.

The Gemara objects: if so, the same decree should apply to his own wife (אִשְׁתּוֹ) as well; the answer is that a yevamah might be confused with another yevamah, but a wife is not confused with a yevamah.

items.text: Final question on the decree
items.text_en: Final question on the decree
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we indeed decree a deaf person on account of a hearing person, leaving the issue unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we indeed decree a deaf person's case because of a hearing person's case.

items.text: Contradiction from a Mishnah about deaf-mute brothers and sisters-in-law
items.text_en: Contradiction from a Mishnah about deaf-mute brothers and sisters-in-law
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that two deaf-mute brothers married to two hearing sisters, or similar cases, are exempt from halitzah and yibbum. If the women were unrelated, they may enter into marriage, and if they wish to divorce, they may do so. This seems to contradict the earlier assumption about deaf-mutes' legal capacity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about deaf-mute brothers and sisters-in-law that seems to contradict the earlier assumption about deaf-mutes' legal capacity.

items.text: Resolution: The contradiction is resolved by the earlier established principle
items.text_en: Resolution: The contradiction is resolved by the earlier established principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that the earlier ruling (about the deaf-mute's ability to divorce) was already established from the beginning, so the Mishnah cited does not pose a problem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that the earlier ruling was already established from the beginning, so the cited Mishnah does not pose a problem.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's colleagues disagree
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's colleagues disagree
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asserts that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's colleagues disagree with his ruling, indicating that the earlier dispute is not universally accepted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asserts that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's colleagues disagree with his ruling.

items.text: Abaye's support: A Mishnah about a deaf-mute husband who cannot divorce
items.text_en: Abaye's support: A Mishnah about a deaf-mute husband who cannot divorce
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a Mishnah stating that if a husband becomes a deaf-mute or insane, he cannot divorce his wife permanently. He asks what "permanently" means, implying that even if he can communicate through writing, he cannot divorce, supporting the view that a deaf-mute cannot divorce.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a Mishnah about a deaf-mute husband who cannot divorce, and asks what 'עולמית' (permanently) means, implying that even if he can communicate through writing, he cannot divorce.

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative interpretation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains the first Tanna
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative interpretation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains the first Tanna
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa suggests that without Rabbi Yochanan's statement, he would have thought Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was merely explaining the first Tanna's reasoning, and "permanently" means even if the husband is sharp-witted (but still deaf-mute).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that without Rabbi Yochanan's statement, he would have thought Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was merely explaining the first Tanna's reasoning, and 'עולמית' (permanently) means even if the husband is sharp-witted.

items.text: Alternative explanation based on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle about a shoteh
items.text_en: Alternative explanation based on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle about a shoteh
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another explanation: according to Rabbi Yitzchak, by Torah law a shoteh (insane woman) can be divorced, just as a hearing woman can be divorced against her will. The reason the Sages said she cannot be divorced is to prevent people from treating her licentiously.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation based on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that by Torah law a shoteh (insane woman) can be divorced, just as a hearing woman can be divorced against her will.
The Gemara explains that the Sages ruled she cannot be divorced to prevent people from treating her licentiously.

items.text: Mishnah: A husband who tells others to write a get but does not say "give"
items.text_en: Mishnah: A husband who tells others to write a get but does not say "give"
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a husband is asked "Should we write a get for your wife?" and he says "Write," and they write and sign it and give it to him, and he then gives it to her, the get is invalid unless he explicitly tells the scribe "Write" and the witnesses "Sign."

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a husband merely says 'write' without specifying 'give', the get is invalid unless he explicitly instructs the scribe and witnesses.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Which Tanna holds that saying "write" without "give" invalidates?
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Which Tanna holds that saying "write" without "give" invalidates?
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if the husband had said "Give" (instead of just "Write"), the get would be valid, aligning with Rabbi Meir who holds that verbal instructions are transferable to an agent. However, the Mishnah's requirement to say "Write" and "Sign" seems to follow Rabbi Yossi, who holds that verbal instructions are not transferable. The Gemara explores various resolutions: Abaye suggests the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Meir, but the case is where he did not say "Give"; the Gemara objects that the Mishnah should then say "until he says 'Give.'" Another attempt: the case is where he did not say to three people; again an objection. Then the Gemara suggests the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yossi, but the case is where he did not say "Say" (to the scribe and witnesses); an objection follows, and the Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yossi even agrees with the validity of saying "Say," citing a Mishnah and Rabbi Yirmeya's and Rav Chisda's comments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if the husband had said 'תנו' (give), the get would be valid, and identifies this as the view of Rabbi Meir, who holds that verbal instructions are transferable to an agent.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's requirement to say 'כתוב' (write) and 'חתומו' (sign) aligns with Rabbi Yossi, who holds that verbal instructions are not transferable to an agent.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is split: the first clause follows Rabbi Meir and the latter clause follows Rabbi Yossi.
Abaye argues that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Meir, and the case is where the husband did not say 'תנו' (give).
The Gemara objects that if so, the Mishnah should have said 'עד שיאמר תנו' (until he says 'give').
The Gemara suggests that the case is where the husband did not say to three people (a court).
The Gemara objects that if so, the Mishnah should have said 'עד שיאמר לשלשה' (until he says to three).
The Gemara suggests that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yossi, and the case is where the husband did not say 'אמרו' (say).
The Gemara objects that if so, the Mishnah should have said 'עד שיאמר אמרו' (until he says 'say').
The Gemara objects further that Rabbi Yossi may not even agree with the validity of saying 'אמרו' (say), citing a Mishnah and the comments of Rabbi Yirmeya and Rav Chisda.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah: Rabbi Yossi's view
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah: Rabbi Yossi's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests the Mishnah is entirely Rabbi Yossi, but then questions whether he would agree in the case of 'imru'. It concludes that the first clause is Rabbi Meir and the latter clause is Rabbi Yossi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah is entirely Rabbi Yossi, who holds that verbal instructions (מילי) cannot be entrusted to an agent.
The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yossi would agree in the case of 'imru' (say), a destructive loophole would emerge where the scribe might be signed out of embarrassment.
The Gemara concludes that the first clause of the Mishnah is Rabbi Meir and the latter clause is Rabbi Yossi.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation and a supporting baraita
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation and a supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yossi, using a 'not only... but even' structure. A baraita supports him, requiring the husband's direct command to the scribe and witnesses, and the Gemara explains the baraita's wording to exclude other opinions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yossi, using a 'לא מיבעיא' (not only) structure to include all cases, even 'imru'.
A baraita supports Rav Ashi, stating that a get is invalid unless the husband personally instructs the scribe and witnesses.
The Gemara explains that 'ישמעו' excludes the view that Rabbi Yossi agrees in 'imru', and 'קולו' excludes a statement of Rav Kahana in the name of Rav.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional divorce formulations
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional divorce formulations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents various conditional divorce formulations: 'if I die' alone is invalid; 'from today if I die' or 'from now if I die' is valid; 'from today and after death' is a valid but uncertain get; and a case where the husband recovers then dies requires assessment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of conditional gittin: 'if I die', 'from this illness', 'after death' are invalid; 'from today if I die' or 'from now if I die' are valid; 'from today and after death' is a ספק (doubtful) get.
The Mishnah states that 'from today and after death' is a valid but uncertain get, requiring חליצה (release from levirate marriage) but not יבום (levirate marriage).
The Mishnah presents a case where the husband recovers then dies, requiring assessment of whether death was from the original illness.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'if I die' and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'if I die' and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the first clause treats 'if I die' like 'after death', but the second clause treats it differently. Abaye resolves this by explaining that 'if I die' is ambiguous; adding 'from today' clarifies it means 'from now', while without it, it means 'after death'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the contradiction: the first clause treats 'if I die' like 'after death', but the second clause treats 'if I die' differently when combined with 'from today'.
