Abaye resolves that 'if I die' has two meanings: when said with 'from today' it means 'from now', and without it means 'after death'.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on 'if I die' and the dispute with the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on 'if I die' and the dispute with the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a woman given a get with 'if I die' must perform חליצה, contradicting the Mishnah's 'lo amar klum'. The Gemara explains the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, while Rav Huna follows Rabbi Yossi, who holds that the date of the document clarifies intent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna adds that even though the get is invalid, the woman must perform חליצה (release from levirate marriage).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah says 'lo amar klum' (it says nothing), implying she is forbidden to everyone, including the yavam.
The Gemara further objects that from the latter clause requiring חליצה, the first clause would imply יבום (levirate marriage) is permitted, contradicting Rav Huna.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, while Rav Huna follows Rabbi Yossi, who holds that the date of the document proves its intent.
The Gemara objects further: from the later clause (סיפא) which requires חליצה, it implies that the first clause (רישא) would permit יבום (levirate marriage), contradicting Rav Huna's interpretation.
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah follows the Rabbis (who hold that the condition is entirely ineffective), while Rav Huna's ruling follows Rabbi Yossi.
The Gemara explains that Rav Huna follows Rabbi Yossi, who holds that the date of the document (זמן השטר) clarifies the husband's intent, making the get effective from the date written.

items.text: Rav Huna's uncertainty about the halakha like Rabbi Yossi
items.text_en: Rav Huna's uncertainty about the halakha like Rabbi Yossi
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav Huna requires חליצה if he follows Rabbi Yossi, suggesting he is uncertain about the halakha. A story about Rav Huna and Rav Nachman asking Rabbah bar Avuha reveals that Rav Huna knew the reasoning but was unsure of the ruling, until Rabbah confirmed the halakha follows Rabbi Yossi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Yossi, even חליצה should not be required, and questions whether Rav Huna was uncertain about the הלכה (binding law).

sub.text: Story about Rav Huna and Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Huna and Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: A story is told: when Rabbah bar Avuha was ill, Rav Huna asked Rav Nachman to inquire about the הלכה (binding law) regarding Rabbi Yossi, but Rav Nachman deferred, saying he didn't know the reasoning.
Rabbah bar Avuha inquired and reported that Rav ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yossi, and then explained the reasoning: the date of the document proves its intent.
The Gemara concludes that Rav Huna was uncertain about the matter, hence he required חליצה (release) as a stringency.

items.text: Rav Huna's uncertainty about Rabbi Yosi's oral principle
items.text_en: Rav Huna's uncertainty about Rabbi Yosi's oral principle
items.desc_en: Rav Huna is uncertain whether Rabbi Yosi holds his principle (that the time of the document proves its validity) only for written documents or also for oral statements.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna questions whether Rabbi Yosi applies his principle of the document's time proving its validity also to oral statements.

items.text: Gemara's objection from a mishnah and the resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's objection from a mishnah and the resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav Huna should not be uncertain, citing a mishnah where the Sages permitted a woman to remarry, implying they follow Rabbi Yosi's principle. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that the court of Shro Misha holds like Rabbi Yosi, resolving the objection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav Huna should not be uncertain, citing a mishnah where the Sages permitted a woman to remarry after a conditional get, implying they follow Rabbi Yosi's principle.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that the court of Shro Misha holds like Rabbi Yosi, resolving the objection.

items.text: Refined uncertainty: halakha like Rabbi Yosi orally or not
items.text_en: Refined uncertainty: halakha like Rabbi Yosi orally or not
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rav Huna's uncertainty is specifically whether the halakha follows Rabbi Yosi's oral application or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rav Huna's uncertainty is specifically whether the halakha follows Rabbi Yosi's oral application or not.

items.text: Rava's statement proves halakha like Rabbi Yosi
items.text_en: Rava's statement proves halakha like Rabbi Yosi
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects again, citing Rava's ruling that 'if I die' and 'that I die' are valid gittin, implying that the time is not specified, which aligns with Rabbi Yosi. The Gemara concludes that this proves the halakha is like Rabbi Yosi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: is Rava uncertain about Rabbi Yosi's position? It cites Rava's ruling on conditional gittin.
Rava rules that 'if I die' and 'that I die' are valid gittin, while 'when I die' and 'after death' are not.
The Gemara concludes that Rava's ruling proves the halakha follows Rabbi Yosi, since the time is not specified.

items.text: Distinction between Rava and Rav Huna
items.text_en: Distinction between Rava and Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: Rava is certain about Rabbi Yosi's oral principle, while Rav Huna is uncertain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing that Rava is certain about Rabbi Yosi's oral principle, while Rav Huna is uncertain.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Rava's statement is about terminology
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Rava's statement is about terminology
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: Rava's statement is about the specific phrases, not about Rabbi Yosi, and it is needed to distinguish between similar expressions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: Rava's statement is about the specific phrases, not about Rabbi Yosi, and it is needed to distinguish between similar expressions.

items.text: Rav Huna's statement about Rabbi Yosi and the need for chalitza
items.text_en: Rav Huna's statement about Rabbi Yosi and the need for chalitza
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that according to Rabbi Yosi, a woman who receives a get 'after death' must perform chalitza. The Gemara questions this, and explains that it teaches that Rabbi and Rabbi Yosi do not agree with each other's positions, citing their respective disputes.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Huna's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Huna's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version teaches that Rav Huna's statement applies to the latter clause of the mishna: if a husband says 'this is your get after my death', it is invalid, but according to Rabbi Yosi she must perform chalitza.
The Gemara questions: this is obvious, since in the latter clause according to the Rabbis she performs chalitza, so in the first clause according to Rabbi Yosi she also performs chalitza.
The Gemara answers: lest you say that Rabbi Yosi holds like Rabbi, that it is a proper get and no chalitza is needed, so Rav Huna teaches that Rabbi and Rabbi Yosi do not agree with each other.

The Gemara explains: Rabbi does not hold like Rabbi Yosi, as he says 'like this is a get' to exclude Rabbi Yosi's opinion; and Rabbi Yosi does not hold like Rabbi, as he says 'like this is a get' to exclude Rabbi's opinion.
The Gemara cites a baraita: if a husband says 'from today and after my death', the Sages say it is a get and not a get, but Rabbi says 'like this is a get'.

sub.text: Supporting mishna for Rabbi Yosi's opinion
sub.text_en: Supporting mishna for Rabbi Yosi's opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna: if one says 'write and give a get if I do not come within twelve months', and they wrote it within twelve months and gave it after twelve months, it is not a get; Rabbi Yosi says 'like this is a get'.
The Gemara begins citing the next mishna: 'This is your get from today if I die from this illness', and he arose and walked in the market, etc.

items.text: Rav Huna's comparison of get to a gift and the objection from the mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Huna's comparison of get to a gift and the objection from the mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna compares a conditional get to a gift: if the husband recovers, the get is void. The Gemara objects from a mishnah that requires an assessment of the cause of death, implying the get is not automatically void upon recovery. Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava explains that the case is where the husband recovered from one illness but fell into another.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the halakhot of a conditional גט (bill of divorce) given by a dying man are the same as those of his gift: if he recovers, both are retracted.

Rav Huna extends the analogy: just as a dying man's instruction to write a גט (bill of divorce) implies giving it even without explicit 'give', so too his instruction to give a gift suffices without formal acquisition.

The Gemara objects from a mishnah: if the husband recovered and later died, an assessment is needed to determine if the גט (bill of divorce) is valid; this contradicts Rav Huna's claim that recovery automatically voids the גט.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava answers that the mishnah's case is where the husband went from one illness directly to another, not a full recovery.

The Gemara rejects the answer by noting that the mishnah says 'arose' and 'walked in the market', implying full recovery; the Gemara resolves that 'arose' means from one illness to another, and 'walked' means with a cane, not fully healed.

items.text: Clarification of Rav Huna's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav Huna's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Huna's earlier statement teaches that only when the husband walks with his cane do we need an assessment of his condition, but in the other case no assessment is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rav Huna's statement teaches that only when the husband walks with his cane do we require an assessment of his condition, but in the other case no assessment is needed.

items.text: Inference about a deathly ill person who recovers and falls ill again
items.text_en: Inference about a deathly ill person who recovers and falls ill again
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rav Huna's statement that a deathly ill person who passes from one illness to another, his gift is valid, citing Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rav Huna's statement that a deathly ill person who passes from one illness to another, his gift is valid, and confirms this with a citation from Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav.

items.text: Rabbah and Rava's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rava's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rava reject Rav Huna's reasoning due to a decree lest people say there is a get after death. The Gemara objects that we cannot permit a married woman based on a decree if the get is invalid by Torah law. The Gemara answers that one who betroths does so subject to rabbinic approval, and the rabbis retroactively annul the betrothal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rava reject Rav Huna's reasoning, citing a decree lest people say there is a get after death.
The Gemara objects: how can we permit a married woman based on a decree if the get is invalid by Torah law?
The Gemara answers that one who betroths does so subject to rabbinic approval, and the rabbis retroactively annul the betrothal.

items.text: Ravina's question about betrothal through intercourse
items.text_en: Ravina's question about betrothal through intercourse
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if the betrothal was through intercourse, what can be said? Rav Ashi answers that the rabbis made his intercourse an act of licentiousness.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if the betrothal was through intercourse (ביאה), what can be said?
Rav Ashi answers that the rabbis made his intercourse an act of licentiousness (בעילת זנות).

items.text: Baraita about conditional get and the distinction between cases
items.text_en: Baraita about conditional get and the distinction between cases
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if a man says 'This is your get from today if I die from this illness' and a house falls on him or a snake bites him, it is not a get. But if he says 'if I do not rise from this illness' and such happens, it is a get. The Gemara asks what is the difference, and the answer from the academy is: 'a lion ate him – we have no [ruling]'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents two cases of a conditional get: one where the condition is 'if I die from this illness' and an accident occurs, the get is invalid; the other where the condition is 'if I do not rise from this illness' and an accident occurs, the get is valid.
The Gemara asks what distinguishes the first case from the second case in the baraita.

The academy in Eretz Yisrael responds that the case of a lion eating him is not comparable, implying that the distinction lies in whether the accident is a common occurrence (like a house falling) or an uncommon one (like a lion attack), which affects the validity of the conditional get.

items.text: Story of the land sale and the principle of uncommon circumstances
items.text_en: Story of the land sale and the principle of uncommon circumstances
items.desc_en: A man sold land and accepted all arising circumstances. A river was later diverted through it. Ravina ruled he must compensate, but Rav Acha bar Tachlifa objected that it is an uncommon circumstance. The case reached Rava who agreed it is uncommon. Ravina challenged Rava from the baraita about the get, but Rava noted the first clause also poses a difficulty. Rav Acha from Difti said that since the first clause contradicts the second, the baraita is a scribal error and one should follow logic.

sub.desc_en: A man sold land to another and accepted all arising circumstances; later a river was diverted through the land.
Ravina ruled that the seller must compensate because he accepted all arising circumstances.
Rav Acha bar Tachlifa objected that a river diversion is an uncommon circumstance.
The case reached Rava, who agreed that it is an uncommon circumstance.
Ravina challenged Rava by citing the baraita about the get where uncommon circumstances still validate the get.
Rava noted that the first clause of the baraita also poses a difficulty, implying the baraita is inconsistent.
Rav Acha from Difti objected that the inconsistency between clauses does not invalidate the challenge from the baraita.
Ravina resolved that since the baraita is internally contradictory, it is a scribal error and one should follow logic.

items.text: Second story about sesame transport and uncommon circumstances
items.text_en: Second story about sesame transport and uncommon circumstances
items.desc_en: Rav Papa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua bought sesame and hired boatmen who accepted all circumstances. The river dried up, and the boatmen demanded compensation. Rava ruled that white storks stripping people of their cloaks is an uncommon circumstance.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua bought sesame on the bank of the King's Canal and hired boatmen who accepted all possible circumstances.
The river dried up, and the boatmen demanded that the rabbis hire donkeys to transport the sesame, citing the boatmen's acceptance of all circumstances.
Rava ruled that white storks stripping people of their cloaks is an uncommon circumstance (אונסא דלא שכיח), so the boatmen are not liable.

items.text: Mishnah about seclusion and the question of the days
items.text_en: Mishnah about seclusion and the question of the days
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman should not be secluded with the agent unless witnesses are present, even a slave or maidservant, except for her own maidservant. Rabbi Yehuda asks: what is the law regarding those days?

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman may not be secluded with the agent unless witnesses are present, even a slave or maidservant, except for her own maidservant because her heart is bold with her.
Rabbi Yehuda asks: what is the law regarding those days (when she is in her niddah period)?

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who received a conditional get is like a married woman in all respects, but Rabbi Yosei says she is both divorced and not divorced.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who received a conditional get is like a married woman in all respects, but Rabbi Yosei says she is both divorced and not divorced.

items.text: Baraita on Seclusion
items.text_en: Baraita on Seclusion
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a woman was seen secluded with a man or sleeping near him, we do not suspect they engaged in intercourse; we suspect zenut but not kiddushin. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda adds that we also suspect kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that seclusion or sleeping near a man raises suspicion of zenut but not kiddushin; Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda adds suspicion of kiddushin.

items.text: Rav Nachman's Explanation of the Baraita
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's Explanation of the Baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Avuh explains the baraita: if she was seen being intimate, we suspect kiddushin; if he gave her money, we suspect zenut, not kiddushin. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda disagrees and suspects kiddushin even with money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita means.
Rav Nachman bar Avuh explains the baraita: if she was seen being intimate, we suspect קידושין (betrothal); if he gave her money, we suspect זנות (promiscuity), not קידושין.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda disagrees and suspects קידושין even with money.

items.text: First Attempt to Identify the Tanna of Rabbi Yochanan's Statement
items.text_en: First Attempt to Identify the Tanna of Rabbi Yochanan's Statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which authority holds the view of Rabbi Yochanan that the dispute is only when she was seen being intimate, but otherwise all agree she needs no second get. It concludes that this aligns with everyone (דברי הכל).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds the view of Rabbi Yochanan that the dispute is only when she was seen being intimate, but otherwise all agree she needs no second get.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan's statement aligns with everyone (דברי הכל).

items.text: Abaye's Objection and Alternative Explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's Objection and Alternative Explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that the baraita does not mention money. He reinterprets: if she was seen being intimate, we suspect zenut, not kiddushin; Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda suspects kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the baraita does not mention money, undermining Rav Nachman's interpretation.

Abaye reinterprets the baraita: if she was seen being intimate, we suspect זנות (zenut, promiscuity), not קידושין (kiddushin, betrothal); Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda suspects קידושין (kiddushin, betrothal).

items.text: Second Attempt to Identify the Tanna
items.text_en: Second Attempt to Identify the Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara again asks which authority holds Rabbi Yochanan's view, and now concludes it aligns with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna's view aligns with the statement of Rabba bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan regarding the dispute.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan's view aligns with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Rava's Objection and Final Explanation
items.text_en: Rava's Objection and Final Explanation
items.desc_en: Rava objects that if so, the word 'even' (אף) is problematic. He explains that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says: even if she was not seen being intimate, we suspect kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that if Abaye's explanation were correct, the word 'אף' (even) in the baraita is problematic.
Rava explains that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says: even if she was not seen being intimate, we suspect kiddushin.

items.text: Third Attempt to Identify the Tanna
items.text_en: Third Attempt to Identify the Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks again which authority holds Rabbi Yochanan's view, and concludes it aligns with neither (דלא כחד).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna's position aligns with the statement of Rabba bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan's view aligns with neither of the two Tannaic positions (דלא כחד).

items.text: Mishnah on the Intermediate Days
items.text_en: Mishnah on the Intermediate Days
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses the status of the woman during the intermediate days between the conditional get and the condition's fulfillment: Rabbi Yehuda says she is like a married woman, Rabbi Yosei says she is divorced and not divorced.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks about the woman's status during the intermediate days between the conditional get and the condition's fulfillment.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that she is like a fully married woman (אשת איש) in all respects.
Rabbi Yosei rules that she is in an intermediate status: divorced and not divorced (מגורשת ואינה מגורשת).

items.text: Gemara on the Condition of Death
items.text_en: Gemara on the Condition of Death
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the condition requires the husband's death, but questions how a get can take effect after death. Rabba explains that he said 'from now while I am alive' (מעתה שאני בעולם).

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states that the condition requires the husband's death.
The Gemara questions how a get can take effect after death.
The Gemara objects that it is established that no get takes effect after death.
Rabba answers that the husband said 'from now while I am alive' (מעתה שאני בעולם), so the get takes effect before death.

items.text: Baraita on the Husband's Rights During the Intermediate Days
items.text_en: Baraita on the Husband's Rights During the Intermediate Days
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that during the intermediate days, the husband is entitled to her findings, her handiwork, and the annulment of her vows, and he inherits from her.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that during the intermediate days (between the giving of the get and the husband's death), the husband retains rights to her findings, her handiwork, the annulment of her vows, and inheritance from her.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about the status of a woman whose husband gave a get on condition
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about the status of a woman whose husband gave a get on condition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yosei, and the Sages regarding the status of a woman whose husband gave her a get on condition that she not marry someone else. Rabbi Yehuda says she is like his wife in all respects except she does not need a second get; Rabbi Meir says her intercourse is תלויה (pending); Rabbi Yosei says it is ספק (doubtful); the Sages say she is מגורשת ואינה מגורשת (divorced and not divorced) provided he dies.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Yehuda's position: a woman whose husband gave a conditional get is like his wife in all respects except she does not need a second get.
The Mishnah records Rabbi Meir's position: her intercourse is תלויה (pending).
The Mishnah records Rabbi Yosei's position: her intercourse is ספק (doubtful).
The Mishnah records the Sages' position: she is מגורשת ואינה מגורשת (divorced and not divorced) provided he dies.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the difference between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei, and the Sages' position
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the difference between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei, and the Sages' position
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the difference between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Yochanan answers that the difference is the אשם תלוי (suspensive guilt-offering): Rabbi Meir does not bring it, Rabbi Yosei does. Then it questions the Sages' statement, noting it seems identical to Rabbi Yosei, and introduces Rabbi Zeira's teaching that wherever the Sages say 'מגורשת ואינה מגורשת', the husband is obligated for her sustenance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei in the Mishnah.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the difference is the אשם תלוי (suspensive guilt-offering): Rabbi Meir does not bring it, Rabbi Yosei does.
The Gemara questions why the Sages' statement seems identical to Rabbi Yosei's position.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira quoting Rabbah bar Yirmiyah quoting Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira quoting Rabbah bar Yirmiyah quoting Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the difference is Rabbi Zeira's teaching: wherever the Sages say 'מגורשת ואינה מגורשת', the husband is obligated for her sustenance.

items.text: Mishnah: Get on condition of payment
items.text_en: Mishnah: Get on condition of payment
items.desc_en: A new Mishnah states that if a man says to his wife 'This is your get on condition that you give me 200 zuz', she is divorced and must give. If he says 'on condition that you give me within 30 days', if she gives within 30 days she is divorced, otherwise not. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel relates a case in Tzidan where a man said 'on condition that you give me my cloak', and it was lost, and the Sages said she gives its value.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a get given on condition that the wife pays 200 zuz, ruling that she is divorced and must pay.
The Mishnah adds a second case: if the condition is payment within 30 days, the divorce is retroactive only if she pays in time.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel cites a precedent from Tzidan where a man conditioned the get on receiving his cloak, and when it was lost the Sages ruled she pays its value.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda on the meaning of 'ותתן'
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda on the meaning of 'ותתן'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'ותתן' means. Rav Huna says 'והיא תתן' (she gives, implying immediate divorce), Rav Yehuda says 'לכשתתן' (when she gives, implying divorce is contingent on payment). The difference is if the get is torn or lost: according to Rav Huna she does not need a second get, according to Rav Yehuda she does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the meaning of 'ותתן' (and she shall give) is in the Mishnah.
Rav Huna explains that 'ותתן' means 'והיא תתן' (she gives immediately), implying the divorce takes effect at once.
Rav Yehuda explains that 'ותתן' means 'לכשתתן' (when she gives), making the divorce contingent on future payment.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two interpretations.
The difference is when the get is torn or lost: according to Rav Huna she does not need a second get, but according to Rav Yehuda she does.

items.text: Parallel in Kiddushin and necessity of both cases
items.text_en: Parallel in Kiddushin and necessity of both cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a parallel case in Kiddushin where a man says 'You are betrothed to me on condition that I give you 200 zuz', with the same dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda. The difference there is if she accepted kiddushin from another. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: in each case, one might think the other Amora would concede, so both are taught.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a parallel Mishnah in Kiddushin with a similar condition, and notes the same dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda over the meaning of 'וְיִתֵּן' (and he shall give).

The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda in the Kiddushin case, and explains: if she accepted kiddushin from another man, Rav Huna holds the condition is merely a stipulation and the kiddushin are retroactive, while Rav Yehuda holds the kiddushin are not effective until he gives the money.
The Gemara explains why both cases (Gittin and Kiddushin) are necessary: in each case, one might think the other Amora would concede, so both are taught to show the full scope of the dispute.

items.text: Objection to Rav Yehuda from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection to Rav Yehuda from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if a man says 'This is your get on condition that you give me 200 zuz', even if the get is torn or lost, she is divorced, but she cannot marry another until she gives. Another baraita says if he died, if she gave she is not required to undergo yibbum, if not she is. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says she gives to his father or brothers. The Gemara concludes that all agree it is a condition, which is a refutation of Rav Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if a man says 'This is your get on condition that you give me 200 zuz', even if the get is torn or lost, she is divorced, but she cannot marry another until she gives.
Another baraita is cited: if he died, if she gave she is not required to undergo yibbum, if not she is; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says she gives to his father or brothers.
The Gemara concludes that all agree it is a condition, which is a refutation of Rav Yehuda.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's defense and Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's defense and Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda defends himself by saying the baraita follows Rabbi's opinion that 'על מנת' is like 'מעכשיו', and the Rabbis disagree with him, and Rav Yehuda follows the Rabbis. Rabbi Zeira reports that in Babylonia they said the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi, but when he went up to Eretz Yisrael he found Rabbi Assi saying in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that everyone agrees 'על מנת' is like 'מעכשיו', and the only dispute is about 'מהיום ולאחר מיתה'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda defends himself against the objection by identifying the baraita as Rabbi's opinion, who holds that 'על מנת' (on condition) is like 'מעכשיו' (from now), while the Rabbis disagree, and Rav Yehuda follows the Rabbis.

Rabbi Zeira reports that in Babylonia they said the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi, but when he went up to Eretz Yisrael he found Rabbi Assi saying in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that everyone agrees 'על מנת' is like 'מעכשיו', and the only dispute is about 'מהיום ולאחר מיתה' (from today and after death).

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi and the Sages about "from today and after death"
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi and the Sages about "from today and after death"
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah presents the dispute using the phrase "from today and after death" rather than "on condition that..." according to Rav Yehuda's view. It explains that the Mishnah chose this formulation to highlight Rabbi's lenient position, and the Sages' position is not highlighted because the power of leniency is preferred.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting the dispute between Rabbi and the Sages regarding a get written 'from today and after death'.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the phrase 'from today and after death' instead of 'on condition that' according to Rav Yehuda's view that the dispute is about conditional clauses.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah chose this formulation to highlight Rabbi's lenient position, and the Sages' position is not highlighted because the power of leniency (כֹּחַ דְּהֶיתֵּירָא) is preferred.

items.text: The Mishnah's case of "on condition that you give me within thirty days"
items.text_en: The Mishnah's case of "on condition that you give me within thirty days"
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling about a conditional get with a time limit is obvious, but it is taught to counter the possibility that the condition was only meant to hurry her, not to be a real condition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state the case of 'on condition that you give me from now until thirty days' since it seems obvious.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches us that the husband's stipulation is not merely to urge her on but is a genuine condition.

items.text: The case of the lost cloak and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
items.text_en: The case of the lost cloak and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause: if the husband said "on condition that you give me my cloak" and the cloak was lost, he meant specifically that cloak. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says she may give him its value, and he brought a supporting story from Sidon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Tanna is cited by the story of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel about the incident in Tzidon.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause: it first states the dispute about 'on condition that you give me my cloak' and then Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds the story from Tzidon as support.

items.text: Rabbi Assi's inquiry about waiving the condition
items.text_en: Rabbi Assi's inquiry about waiving the condition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Assi asks Rabbi Yochanan: if a husband says "this is your get on condition that you give me 200 zuz" and then says "they are forgiven to you," what is the law? The Gemara considers whether this case differs from the cloak case for the Sages or for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rabbi Yochanan answers that she is not divorced.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Assi asks Rabbi Yochanan: if a husband says 'this is your get on condition that you give me 200 zuz' and then says 'they are forgiven to you', what is the law?
The Gemara notes that the question applies both according to the Sages and according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that she is not divorced, explaining that the Sages' leniency only applies when she appeases him with money, not when he completely forgives the debt.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that she is not divorced.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about vows and the distinction
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about vows and the distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where one can release a vow by saying "I consider myself as if I received," which seems to allow waiving a condition. The Gemara distinguishes: there the intent was to cause pain, and she was not pained, so the condition is void; here the intent was for benefit, and he did not need it, so the condition remains.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita about a vow: Rabbi Meir says the vow remains until the condition is fulfilled, but the Sages say the person can release himself by saying 'I consider it as if I received'.
The Gemara rejects the objection, distinguishing that there the intent was to cause pain and she was not pained, while here the intent was for benefit and he did not need it.

items.text: The case of the sharecropper and the dispute between Rav Yosef and Rabbah
items.text_en: The case of the sharecropper and the dispute between Rav Yosef and Rabbah
items.desc_en: A man told his sharecropper: everyone draws three buckets and eats a quarter; you draw four and eat a third. Later it rained. Rav Yosef says: he did not draw, so he does not get the extra. Rabbah says: he did not need to draw. The Gemara initially suggests they follow the dispute between the Sages and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but rejects this because the halakha follows Rabbah yet not Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. It concludes that both follow the Sages, but Rabbah distinguishes: there the intent was to cause pain, here it was for benefit and not needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a man told his sharecropper that everyone draws three buckets and eats a quarter, but you draw four and eat a third; later it rained.
Rav Yosef rules that since the sharecropper did not draw the extra bucket, he does not get the extra portion; Rabbah rules that he did not need to draw because the rain made it unnecessary.
The Gemara suggests that Rav Yosef follows the Sages and Rabbah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
The Gemara rejects this because the halakha follows Rabbah but not Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
The Gemara concludes that both follow the Sages, but Rabbah distinguishes: there the intent was to cause pain, here it was for benefit and not needed.

items.text: Rava's inference from Hillel's enactment about conditional gifts
items.text_en: Rava's inference from Hillel's enactment about conditional gifts
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about Hillel's enactment regarding the removal of a house from the seller's control. Rava infers: if a man says "this is your get on condition that you give me 200 zuz" and she gives it willingly, she is divorced; if against his will, she is not divorced. This is derived from the fact that Hillel needed to institute a method of giving against the seller's will, implying that a forced gift is not a valid gift.

sub.desc_en: A Mishnah is cited about Hillel's enactment regarding the prosbul and the deposit of money.
Rava infers from Hillel's enactment that if a husband says 'this is your get on condition that you give me 200 zuz' and she gives willingly, she is divorced; if against his will, she is not divorced.
Rava explains that Hillel's enactment was necessary because giving against his will is still considered a valid giving.

items.text: Inference from Hillel's enactment
items.text_en: Inference from Hillel's enactment
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Hillel's enactment that generally, giving a get against the husband's will is not considered valid giving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Hillel's enactment that generally, giving a get against the husband's will is not considered valid giving.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge: distinction between presence and absence
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge: distinction between presence and absence
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or Rav Shimi bar Ashi) challenges the inference, suggesting that Hillel's enactment only applied when the husband was not present, but when he is present, even coercion constitutes valid giving.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the inference, suggesting that Hillel's enactment only applied when the husband was not present, but when he is present, even coercion constitutes valid giving.

items.text: Rava's alternative version: Hillel's enactment about conditional get
items.text_en: Rava's alternative version: Hillel's enactment about conditional get
items.desc_en: Rava presents a different version: Hillel's enactment concerned a conditional get where the wife must give the husband 200 zuz, and giving in his presence is valid even under coercion.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents an alternative version of Hillel's enactment: in a conditional get where the wife must give 200 zuz, giving in the husband's presence is valid even under coercion.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge to Rava's version
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge to Rava's version
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or Rav Shimi bar Ashi) challenges Rava's version, arguing that even in the husband's presence, only willing giving is valid, and Hillel only enacted what was necessary.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or Rav Shimi bar Ashi) challenges Rava's version, arguing that even in the husband's presence, only willing giving is valid, and Hillel only enacted what was necessary.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's rule about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's rule about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan's principle that wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states a ruling in the Mishnah, the halakha follows him, except for three cases: Eruv, Tzidon, and the later proof.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports Rabbi Yochanan's principle that wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states a ruling in the Mishnah, the halakha follows him, except for three cases: Eruv, Tzidon, and the later proof.

items.text: Baraita: conditional get with paper
items.text_en: Baraita: conditional get with paper
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if a husband says 'This is your get and the paper is mine,' she is not divorced; but if he says 'on condition that you return the paper to me,' she is divorced.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches the law of a conditional get involving paper, distinguishing between a statement that retains ownership of the paper and a condition to return it.

items.text: Rav Chisda's explanation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's explanation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains the baraita according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that the wife can pay the value of the paper, so the condition is possible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita distinguishes between the first case (not divorced) and the second case (divorced).
Rav Chisda explains that the baraita follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that the wife can appease him with money (the value of the paper), making the condition possible.

items.text: Abaye's objection to Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel only said that when the item is not in its original state, but here the paper is still intact, so his ruling does not apply.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling only applies when the item is not intact (ליתיה בעיניה), but here the paper is intact (איתיה בעיניה), so his ruling does not apply.

items.text: Abaye's alternative: Rabbi Meir and double condition
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative: Rabbi Meir and double condition
items.desc_en: Abaye instead attributes the baraita to Rabbi Meir, who requires a double condition; here the condition was not doubled, so the get is invalid in the first clause.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the baraita by attributing it to Rabbi Meir, who requires a double condition (תנאי כפול), and here the condition was not doubled, so the get is invalid in the first clause.

items.text: Rava's objection: condition must precede action
items.text_en: Rava's objection: condition must precede action
items.desc_en: Rava objects that even if the condition were doubled, the get would still be invalid because the action (giving the get) precedes the condition, unlike the paradigm of the tribes of Gad and Reuven.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that even if the condition were doubled, the get would still be invalid because the action (giving the get) precedes the condition, unlike the paradigm of the tribes of Gad and Reuven.

items.text: Rava's conclusion: action precedes condition
items.text_en: Rava's conclusion: action precedes condition
items.desc_en: Rava concludes that the reason the get is invalid is because the action precedes the condition, not because of the lack of a double condition.

sub.desc_en: Rava concludes that the get is invalid because the action (giving the get) precedes the condition (the wife's payment), not because of the lack of a double condition.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's objection: condition must be in a separate matter
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's objection: condition must be in a separate matter
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that even if the condition preceded the action, the get would still be invalid because the condition and action must involve separate matters, but here the paper is the same object.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that even if the condition preceded the action, the get would still be invalid because the condition and action must involve separate matters, but here the paper is the same object.

items.text: Rejection of Rav Ada bar Ahava's earlier answer
items.text_en: Rejection of Rav Ada bar Ahava's earlier answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous suggestion that the Mishnah's case involves a condition and an action in one thing, and Rav Ada bar Ahava instead attributes the Mishnah to the fact that the condition and action are one thing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous answer by pointing out that the condition and action are one thing, and then cites Rav Ada bar Ahava's alternative explanation that the Mishnah's case is because the condition and action are one thing.

items.text: Rav Ashi's attribution to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's attribution to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who holds that saying 'on condition' is like saying 'from now'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who holds that saying 'על מנת' (on condition) is equivalent to saying 'מעכשיו' (from now).

items.text: Shmuel's enactment for a deathbed get and its analysis
items.text_en: Shmuel's enactment for a deathbed get and its analysis
items.desc_en: Shmuel instituted a formula for a deathbed get: 'If I do not die, it shall not be a get, and if I die, it shall be a get.' The Gemara questions why the positive condition does not precede the negative, and why the condition is not stated before the action.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel instituted a formula for a deathbed get: 'If I do not die, it shall not be a get, and if I die, it shall be a get.'
The Gemara asks why the positive condition ('if I die') does not precede the negative, and answers that one does not mention calamity first.
The Gemara asks why the condition is not stated before the action, and answers that the condition must precede the action.

items.text: Rava's objection and alternative formulation
items.text_en: Rava's objection and alternative formulation
items.desc_en: Rava objects that the condition must follow the pattern of the condition of the tribes of Gad and Reuben, where the positive precedes the negative. He therefore proposes a three-part formula that satisfies both the concern for not bringing calamity and the requirement that the positive condition precedes the negative.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that all conditions are derived from the condition of the tribes of Gad and Reuben, where the positive (הן) precedes the negative (לאו), so the same must apply here.

Rava proposes a three-part formula that begins with the negative condition to avoid calamity, then repeats the positive before the negative to satisfy the requirement that the positive precedes the negative.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditions of service and nursing
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditions of service and nursing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a get is given on condition that the wife serves her father or nurses her son. The duration of nursing is debated: two years or eighteen months. If the beneficiary dies or the father declines without being particular, the get is valid. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a general principle: any impediment not from her side renders the get valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with cases of a get given on condition of service or nursing, and states the default nursing duration as two years, with Rabbi Yehuda disputing it as eighteen months.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the nursing period is eighteen months, and the Mishnah adds that if the son or father dies, the get is valid.
The Mishnah presents a second case where a specific duration is stipulated; if the son dies or the father declines without being particular, the get is not valid.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that in such a case the get is valid, and states a general principle: any impediment not from her side renders the get valid.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction and resolution via Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction and resolution via Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah requires two years of nursing, but a baraita says one day suffices. Rav Chisda resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, while the baraita follows the Rabbis. However, the Gemara points out that the latter part of the Mishnah is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, implying the first part is not; so the baraita is actually Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who is lenient with conditions, and the Mishnah is the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah requires two years of nursing, but a baraita says one day suffices.
Rav Chisda resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, while the baraita follows the Rabbis.
The Gemara elaborates: the Mishnah is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the baraita is the Rabbis.
The Gemara objects: since the latter clause of the Mishnah is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the first clause cannot be his.
The Gemara resolves: the baraita is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who is lenient with conditions, and the Mishnah is the Rabbis.

items.text: Rava and Rav Ashi's alternative resolutions
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Ashi's alternative resolutions
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between an unspecified condition (which requires the full term) and a specified condition (where one day suffices). Rav Ashi counters that even an unspecified condition is like specifying 'one day'.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between an unspecified condition (סתם), which requires the full term, and a specified condition (מפרש), where one day suffices.
Rav Ashi counters that even an unspecified condition (סתם) is like specifying 'one day', thus rejecting Rava's distinction.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Ashi from the Mishnah's durations
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Ashi from the Mishnah's durations
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Ashi: if an unspecified condition is like specifying one day, why does the Mishnah specify two years or eighteen months? The Gemara explains that the Mishnah means one day within two years or within eighteen months, excluding after that period.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Ashi: if an unspecified condition is like specifying one day, why does the Mishnah specify durations of two years or eighteen months, when one day should suffice?
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah means one day within the two-year or eighteen-month period, excluding after that period.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah's second clause
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah's second clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the Mishnah's second clause, which states that if the father says he does not want to be served without being particular, the get is not valid, implying that the condition is taken seriously.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the Mishnah's second clause, which states that if the father says he does not want to be served without being particular, the get is not valid, implying that the condition is taken seriously.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rava and Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rava and Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the consistency of the Mishnah's logic according to Rava and Rav Ashi. According to Rava, the first clause deals with an unspecified condition and the latter with a specified one, but according to Rav Ashi, the distinction is unclear, leading to a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the consistency of the Mishnah's logic according to Rava and Rav Ashi, noting that according to Rava the first clause deals with an unspecified condition and the latter with a specified one, but according to Rav Ashi the distinction is unclear, leading to a difficulty.

items.text: Baraita on conditional service and nursing
items.text_en: Baraita on conditional service and nursing
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting a dispute about a get given on condition of serving the father or nursing the son for two years. Rabbi Meir rules the get is valid even if the condition is not fulfilled, because the condition was not phrased as 'if... if not'. The Sages require fulfillment, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that no condition in the Torah is not doubled.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting the case of a conditional get with service or nursing, where Rabbi Meir rules that even if the condition is not fulfilled, the get is valid because the condition was not phrased as 'if… if not'.
The baraita continues: the Sages rule that the get is valid only if the condition is fulfilled, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that there is no condition in the Torah that is not doubled.

sub.text: Baraita's continuation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Baraita's continuation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that no condition in the Torah is not doubled, implying a general rule about conditional formulations.

items.text: Two interpretations of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement
items.text_en: Two interpretations of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two versions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's intent. One version holds he spoke to Rabbi Meir, arguing that since all conditions in the Torah are doubled, these two cases are two verses that come as one and do not teach. The other version holds he spoke to the Sages, arguing that since conditions are doubled, we learn from them that a condition must be doubled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the first version of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement, that he spoke to Rabbi Meir.
According to the first version, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel argued that since all conditions in the Torah are doubled, these two cases are two verses that come as one and do not teach.
The Gemara introduces the second version, that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel spoke to the Sages.
According to the second version, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel argued that since conditions in the Torah are doubled, we learn from them that a condition must be doubled.

items.text: Contradiction between baraitot on Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Contradiction between baraitot on Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: A second baraita is cited where Rabbi Meir rules that if the father or son dies, the get is invalid, contradicting his earlier ruling. The Sages rule it is valid, contradicting their earlier ruling. The Gemara declares a contradiction between Rabbi Meir's statements and between the Sages' statements.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a second baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that if the father or son dies, the get is invalid, contradicting his earlier ruling.

sub.text: Sages' position in the second baraita
sub.text_en: Sages' position in the second baraita
sub.desc_en: The Sages rule that even if the condition was not fulfilled, the get is valid because the woman can claim she would have served or nursed if the person were alive.
The Gemara declares a contradiction between Rabbi Meir's two statements and between the Sages' two statements.

items.text: Resolution of the contradictions
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradictions. For Rabbi Meir, the first baraita is where he did not double the condition, while the second is where he did double it. For the Sages, the Sages in the second baraita are actually Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that any impediment not from her side renders the get valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction in Rabbi Meir's positions: the first baraita (segments 2-3) is where he did not double the condition, while the second baraita (segments 6-7) is where he did double it.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction in the Sages' positions: the Sages in the second baraita are actually Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that any impediment not from her side renders the get valid.

items.text: Baraita on sequential conditions and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Baraita on sequential conditions and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a case where a husband gives a get on condition of service, then later on condition of payment. The later condition does not nullify the earlier; she may choose which to fulfill. But if the later condition is a different amount, it nullifies the earlier, and witnesses from each condition cannot combine. The Gemara questions which clause this applies to and clarifies that the ruling is necessary to prevent the assumption that witnesses combine to fulfill the condition.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the first case: a husband gives a get on condition of service, then later on condition of payment; the later condition does not nullify the earlier, and she may choose which to fulfill.
The baraita presents the second case: if the later condition is a different amount, it nullifies the earlier, and witnesses from each condition cannot combine.
The Gemara asks which clause the ruling about witnesses not combining applies to, rejecting the possibility that it refers to the second case where the later condition clearly nullifies the earlier.
The Gemara answers that the ruling applies to the first case, and it is necessary to prevent the assumption that witnesses from each condition combine to fulfill the condition.

items.text: Mishnah on conditional get with travel and Gemara's geographical question
items.text_en: Mishnah on conditional get with travel and Gemara's geographical question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a get is conditional on not returning within thirty days, and the husband turns back before reaching his destination, voiding the condition. The Gemara questions the geography, noting that Antipatris is in Judah and Kfar Otnai in Galilee, and rules that between them the woman is in doubt and treated as possibly divorced.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: a conditional get (גט) based on not returning within thirty days, where the husband travels from Judah to the Galilee, reaches Antipatris, and returns, voiding the condition.
The Mishnah presents the second case: a similar conditional get (גט) where the husband travels from the Galilee to Judah, reaches Kfar Otnai (כפר עותנאי), and returns, voiding the condition.
The Mishnah presents the third case: a conditional get (גט) where the husband travels to a country overseas (מדינת הים), reaches Acco (עכו), and returns, voiding the condition.

The Mishnah presents the fourth case: a conditional get (גט) based on the husband not being opposite her face for thirty days, where he comes and goes but does not seclude himself with her, so the get (גט) is valid.

The Gemara questions the geography: does the Mishnah imply that Antipatris (אנטיפרס) is in the Galilee, and cites a contradiction that Antipatris is in Judah and Kfar Otnai (כפר עותנאי) is in the Galilee.
The Gemara resolves that between the two locations (Antipatris and Kfar Otnai), the woman is treated with stringency (לחומרא) and is considered possibly divorced (מגורשת).

items.text: Gemara's question on the first Mishnah case
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the first Mishnah case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that if a husband says 'if I do not come within 30 days' and he reaches Antipatris and returns, she is not divorced. Abaye explains that the husband made two conditions: immediate divorce upon reaching the Galilee, or divorce after 30 days if delayed. Since he neither reached the Galilee nor delayed 30 days, the condition is void.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that she is not divorced.
Abaye explains that the husband made two conditions, and since neither was fulfilled, the condition is void.

items.text: Gemara's question on the second Mishnah case
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the second Mishnah case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case of 'if I do not come from here until 30 days' and he goes to Akko, implying Akko is outside the Land. Rav Safra notes that rabbis would part in Akko because leaving the Land is forbidden. Abaye again explains that the husband made two conditions: immediate divorce upon reaching the diaspora, or divorce after 30 days if delayed. Since he neither reached the diaspora nor delayed 30 days, the condition is void.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Akko is considered outside the land, citing Rav Safra's practice of parting there.
Abaye again explains that the husband made two conditions, and since neither was fulfilled, the condition is void.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan on 'panayich'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan on 'panayich'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says 'all the time that I pass from before your face' – but he didn't pass! Rav Huna explains 'face' means sexual relations, a euphemism. Rabbi Yochanan says 'face' literally, but the Mishnah doesn't say 'she is divorced' but 'this is a get' – meaning it is not an old get, and after 30 days it becomes a get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that he did not pass before her face.
Rav Huna explains that 'face' here is a euphemism for marital relations.
Rabbi Yochanan insists 'face' is literal, and the get is not a 'get yashan' but becomes valid after 30 days.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan and concern for appeasement
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan and concern for appeasement
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan: if the husband goes back and forth but does not seclude himself, it is a valid get and not an old get. The Gemara asks: shouldn't we worry he appeased her? Rabba bar Rav Huna says in the name of Rav: when he says 'she is believed to say that I did not come'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan: if the husband goes back and forth but does not seclude himself, the get is valid and not considered an old get.
The Gemara objects: shouldn't we worry that the husband appeased his wife during the back-and-forth, invalidating the get?

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna says in the name of Rav that the case is where the husband says 'she is believed to say that I did not come,' so there is no concern for appeasement.

items.text: Alternative version of the concern for appeasement
items.text_en: Alternative version of the concern for appeasement
items.desc_en: Some teach the concern for appeasement on the Mishnah: 'from now, if I do not come within 12 months' and he dies within 12 months – it is a get. The same answer is given. The Gemara notes that one who teaches it on the Mishnah certainly applies it to the baraita, but one who teaches it on the baraita does not apply it to the Mishnah because the husband did not come.

sub.desc_en: Some teach the concern for appeasement on the Mishnah's case of 'from now, if I do not come within 12 months' and he dies within 12 months – it is a get.
The Gemara raises the same concern: should we worry that the husband appeased his wife after the get was written?

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna answers in the name of Rav that the husband said: 'She is believed upon me to say that I did not come.'
The Gemara notes that one who teaches the concern on the Mishnah certainly applies it to the baraita as well.
One who teaches it on the baraita does not apply it to the Mishnah because the husband did not come.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional gittin with 12-month deadline
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional gittin with 12-month deadline
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases: if the husband says 'if I do not come within 12 months' and dies within 12 months – it is not a get. If he says 'from now, if I do not come' – it is a get. If he instructs 'write and give a get if I do not come' and they write within 12 months but give after – it is not a get. Rabbi Yosei says in such a case it is a get. If they write and give after 12 months and he dies, if the get precedes death it is a get, if death precedes the get it is not, and if unknown she is in the status of 'divorced and not divorced'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: if the husband says 'this is your get if I do not come within 12 months' and dies within 12 months, it is not a get.
The Mishnah states the second case: if he says 'from now, if I do not come within 12 months' and dies within 12 months, it is a get.
The Mishnah states the third case: if he instructs 'write and give a get if I do not come' and they write within 12 months but give after 12 months, it is not a get.
The Mishnah presents a parallel case with reversed word order, and Rabbi Yosei rules that in such a case it is a get.

The Mishnah concludes with the case where the get is written and given after 12 months and the husband dies: if the get precedes death it is a get, if death precedes the get it is not, and if unknown she is in the status of 'divorced and not divorced'.

items.text: Gemara: Who permitted her to marry?
items.text_en: Gemara: Who permitted her to marry?
items.desc_en: A baraita says 'our rabbis permitted her to marry'. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel identifies them as the court of 'Sharo Mishcha' who hold like Rabbi Yosei that the time of the document proves it. Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah ruled but his colleagues did not agree, and some say 'all his time'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that 'our rabbis' permitted the woman to marry.
The gemara asks who these 'our rabbis' are.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel identifies them as the court of 'Sharo Mishcha', who hold like Rabbi Yosei that the time of the document proves it.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah ruled but his colleagues did not agree.
Some say the ruling was 'all his time' (a different interpretation of the condition).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's question and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks an elder: did they permit her immediately or after 12 months? The Mishnah suggests it is a get from now, but perhaps after 12 months when the condition is fulfilled. The Gemara says yes, and that was the case. Abaye states that all agree that if he says 'when the sun comes out of its sheath' – the get takes effect immediately.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's question to the elder
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question to the elder
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks the elder whether the court permitted the woman to remarry immediately upon the husband's death or only after twelve months when the condition was fulfilled.
The Gemara raises the same question from the Mishnah: does the get take effect immediately or after twelve months?
The Gemara answers that indeed the get takes effect immediately, and that was the case in that incident.
Abaye states that all agree that if the husband said 'when the sun comes out of its sheath' (a fixed future event), the get takes effect immediately.

items.text: Distinguishing 'al menat' from 'im' in conditional gittin
items.text_en: Distinguishing 'al menat' from 'im' in conditional gittin
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that when a husband says 'al menat sheteitzei chammah min nartikah' (on condition that the sun comes out of its sheath), it is effective immediately because 'al menat' is like 'me'akhshav'. The dispute between the two opinions in the Mishnah is only regarding 'im teitzei' (if the sun comes out), where one follows Rabbi Yosei that the time of the document testifies for it, making it like 'me'hayom im mati', and the other does not follow Rabbi Yosei, making it like a plain 'im mati'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case of 'im teitzei' (if the sun comes out), suggesting it means 'when it comes out' and thus would be a posthumous get.
The Gemara distinguishes that 'al menat' (on condition that) is like saying 'me'akhshav' (from now), citing Rav Huna citing Rav, so the get takes effect immediately.

The Gemara resolves that the dispute in the Mishnah is only about 'im teitzei' (if the sun comes out), where one opinion follows Rabbi Yosei that the document's date testifies for it, making it like 'me'hayom im mati' (from today if I die), and the other does not, making it like a plain 'im mati' (if I die).

items.text: The case of 'if I do not come within twelve months'
items.text_en: The case of 'if I do not come within twelve months'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's case of 'kitvu utnu get l'ishti im lo bati mikan v'ad shneim asar chodesh' is analyzed. Rav Yemar asks Rav Ashi if this implies Rabbi Yosei holds that writing a get on a condition is valid. Rav Ashi rejects this, explaining that here the husband's wording 'kitvu utnu im lo bati' implies 'kitvu me'akhshav utnu im lo bati', so it is different. The Rabbis hold that both formulations are the same (and invalid).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a husband saying 'write and give a get to my wife if I do not come within twelve months'.

sub.text: Rav Yemar's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Yemar's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Yemar asks Rav Ashi whether this implies Rabbi Yosei holds that writing a get on a condition is valid.
Rav Ashi rejects the inference, explaining that here the husband's wording 'kitvu utnu im lo bati' implies 'write now and give if I do not come', so it is different from a standard conditional get.
The Gemara concludes that the Rabbis hold both formulations are the same (and invalid).

items.text: Interpretation of 'achar shavua', 'achar shanah', etc.
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'achar shavua', 'achar shanah', etc.
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'achar shavua' means a year, 'achar shanah' means a month, 'achar chodesh' means a week. Regarding 'achar shabbat', Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Assi (or Rabbi Assi asks Rabbi Yochanan) and explains that 'achar shabbat' refers to the days after Shabbat (Sunday, Monday, Tuesday) or before Shabbat (Wednesday, Thursday, Friday).

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches the interpretive sequence: 'after a week' means a year, 'after a year' means a month, 'after a month' means a week.
The Gemara asks what 'after Shabbat' means in this context.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira before Rabbi Assi (or Rabbi Assi before Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira before Rabbi Assi (or Rabbi Assi before Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Assi) explains that 'after Shabbat' refers to Sunday, Monday, Tuesday (after Shabbat) or Wednesday, Thursday, Friday (before Shabbat).

items.text: Rabbi's statement on 'achar haregel'
items.text_en: Rabbi's statement on 'achar haregel'
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi says 'achar haregel' means thirty days. Rabbi Chiyya taught this in Rabbi's name and was praised, but when he taught it in the name of the Rabbis he was not praised, indicating that the halakhah does not follow Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi's statement that 'achar haregel' (after the festival) means thirty days.
The gemara reports that Rabbi Chiyya taught this ruling in Rabbi's name and was praised.
The gemara notes that when Rabbi Chiyya taught the same ruling in the name of the Rabbis, he was not praised.
The gemara concludes that the halakhah does not follow Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi's opinion.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard formula 'Hadran alach mi she'achazo' marks the end of the previous chapter and the transition to the next.

sub.desc_en: The standard concluding formula 'Hadran alach' marks the end of the previous chapter.

items.text: Opening Mishnah of 'HaZorek'
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah of 'HaZorek'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a husband throws a get to his wife while she is in her house or courtyard, she is divorced. If he throws it into his own house or courtyard, even if he is with her in bed, she is not divorced. If he throws it into her lap or basket, she is divorced.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule of throwing a get into the wife's domain versus the husband's domain.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of a woman's courtyard acquiring her get
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of a woman's courtyard acquiring her get
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of these laws. A baraita derives from 'venatan beyadah' that her hand acquires, and from 'venatan' that her roof, courtyard, and enclosure also acquire. A similar derivation is made for a thief's acquisition. The Gemara explains that both derivations are necessary: for get, one might think only her hand works because it is against her will, and for a thief, one might think only his hand works because it is a penalty; the extra verses teach otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's ruling that a woman's courtyard acquires her get.
A baraita derives from the verse 'ונתן בידה' (and place in her hand) that her hand acquires, and from the extra 'ונתן' (and he shall give) that her roof, courtyard, and enclosure also acquire.
A parallel baraita derives the same rule for a thief's acquisition from the verse 'המצא תמצא' (found shall be found).

The Gemara explains that both derivations are necessary: for a get, one might think only her hand works because it is against her will, and for a thief, one might think only his hand works because it is a penalty; the extra verses teach otherwise.

items.text: Problem and solutions: How can a married woman's courtyard acquire?
items.text_en: Problem and solutions: How can a married woman's courtyard acquire?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: a married woman's courtyard is acquired by her husband (he has rights to it). Rabbi Elazar answers that the case is where he writes her 'din udvarim ein li b'nikhsayich' (I have no claim to your property). But a baraita says such a statement is ineffective. The school of Rabbi Yannai answers that the case is when he writes this while she is still an arusah (betrothed), and it follows Rav Kahana's principle that a person can stipulate not to inherit property that comes from elsewhere, and Rava's statement about one who says...

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: how can a married woman's courtyard acquire the get for her, since whatever she acquires, her husband acquires?
Rabbi Elazar answers that the case is where he writes to her 'din udvarim ein li b'nikhsayich' (I have no claim to your property).
The Gemara objects: even if he writes such a statement, what good is it? A baraita teaches that one who says 'I have no claim to this field' has said nothing.

The school of Rabbi Yannai answers that the case is when he writes this while she is still an arusah (betrothed), and it follows Rav Kahana's principle that a person can stipulate not to inherit property that comes from elsewhere.
The Gemara adds that this also aligns with Rava's statement about one who says...

items.text: Opening statement and definition of 'such a rabbinic enactment'
items.text_en: Opening statement and definition of 'such a rabbinic enactment'
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by stating that if a woman says she cannot abide by a particular rabbinic enactment, we listen to her. It then clarifies what 'such an enactment' refers to, citing Rav Huna citing Rav that a woman can say to her husband, 'I am not sustained and I do not work.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that if a woman says she cannot abide by a rabbinic enactment of this sort, we listen to her.
The Gemara asks what 'such an enactment' refers to.
Rav Huna citing Rav answers that a woman can say to her husband, 'I am not sustained and I do not work.'

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution regarding the courtyard acquiring the get
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution regarding the courtyard acquiring the get
items.desc_en: Rava objects: does the husband not acquire his wife's hand? He explains that the get and her hand come simultaneously, and similarly the get and her courtyard come simultaneously. Ravina questions Rava's difficulty with the woman's hand, and Rav Ashi explains Rava's difficulty is with the slave's hand, concluding that the get and his hand come simultaneously, and similarly the get and her courtyard come simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects: does the husband not acquire his wife's hand (i.e., her labor)?
Rava resolves: the get and her hand come simultaneously, and similarly the get and her courtyard come simultaneously.
Ravina questions Rav Ashi: is Rava's difficulty with the woman's hand itself, which the husband does not acquire?
Rav Ashi explains: Rava's difficulty is with the slave's hand, and he resolves that the get and the slave's hand come simultaneously, and similarly the get and her courtyard come simultaneously.

items.text: Case of a dying man who wrote a get on Friday afternoon
items.text_en: Case of a dying man who wrote a get on Friday afternoon
items.desc_en: A story is told of a dying man who wrote a get for his wife on Friday afternoon but did not give it to her. The next day he became very ill. Rava instructed them to tell him to acquire the place where the get was located for her, and she would go, lock, open, and take possession of it, citing a mishnah about chazakah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story of a dying man who wrote a get for his wife on Friday afternoon but could not give it to her, and Rava instructed them to tell him to acquire the place where the get was located for her so she could take possession of it.
The Gemara cites a mishnah that locking, fencing, or breaching any amount constitutes a chazakah (act of possession), supporting Rava's ruling.

items.text: Rav Ilish's objection and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ilish's objection and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ilish objects: what a woman acquires, her husband acquires! Rava was embarrassed. Later it was revealed that she was an arusah (betrothed). Rava initially said that if they said this for a nesuah, would they say it for an arusah? Then he retracted, saying both are the same: the get and her courtyard come simultaneously. The Gemara notes that Rava had already said this earlier, but he said it regarding this case.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ilish objects to Rava's ruling, arguing that whatever a woman acquires, her husband acquires, so the courtyard acquisition is invalid; Rava is embarrassed.

It is revealed that the woman was an arusah (betrothed), not a nesuah (married); Rava first distinguishes between the two, then retracts and rules that both are the same: the get and her courtyard come simultaneously.
The Gemara notes that Rava had already stated this principle earlier, but he said it specifically regarding this case.

items.text: Dispute about the woman's proximity to the courtyard
items.text_en: Dispute about the woman's proximity to the courtyard
