sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya argues that the word 'כריתות' implies a complete severance between husband and wife, which is lacking in a conditional divorce.
The Gemara asks how the Rabbis interpret the word 'כריתות' that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya used.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from 'כריתות' that a conditional divorce with a permanent condition ('לעולם') is not a valid severance, but one with a temporary condition ('שלושים יום') is.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive the law of conditional divorces from the double expression 'כרת-כריתות', while Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya does not derive from this double expression.

items.text: Rava's distinction regarding time-based conditions
items.text_en: Rava's distinction regarding time-based conditions
items.desc_en: Rava discusses the validity of a get conditioned on the husband's lifetime versus another's lifetime. The Gemara questions the distinction and Rava clarifies that a condition tied to the wife's own lifetime ('כל ימי חייכי') invalidates the get, while 'כל ימי חיי' or 'חיי פלוני' is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that a conditional divorce 'on condition that you never drink wine' for the husband's lifetime is not a valid severance, but for the lifetime of another person it is.
The Gemara questions why the husband's own lifetime is different, since he too might die and fulfill the condition.
The Gemara corrects Rava's statement: a condition for the wife's lifetime is not a valid severance, but for the husband's lifetime or another's lifetime it is.

items.text: Rava's inquiry about a split-day divorce
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry about a split-day divorce
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about a get that says 'Today you are not my wife, but tomorrow you are my wife.' The Gemara considers whether this would be valid according to Rabbi Eliezer or the Rabbis, and after the inquiry, Rava resolves it.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about a conditional divorce 'Today you are not my wife, tomorrow you are my wife' — what is the law? The question applies to both Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis.
The Gemara analyzes the question for Rabbi Eliezer: perhaps he only permits a conditional divorce when the permission is permanent, but here it is temporary, or perhaps there is no difference.
The Gemara analyzes the question for the Rabbis: perhaps they only invalidate a conditional divorce when it does not completely sever the relationship, but here since it severs, it severs.
The Gemara concludes that after the question was raised, it was resolved (the resolution is not provided in the text).

items.text: Opening presumption
items.text_en: Opening presumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that it is obvious that once a husband cuts off (divorces) his wife, it is cut off, both according to Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that it is obvious that once a husband cuts off (divorces) his wife, it is cut off, both according to Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis.

items.text: First baraita and Rav Nachman's interpretation
items.text_en: First baraita and Rav Nachman's interpretation
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught about a gett conditioned on marrying a specific man. Rav Nachman initially explains that she may not marry that man due to a decree, but if she marries another, she does not leave. The Gemara objects that this would permit a married woman to remarry, so Rav Nachman revises: if she marries that man, she does not leave due to the decree.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a case of a gett conditioned on marrying a specific man, ruling that she may not marry him, but if she does, she does not leave.
Rav Nachman explains the baraita: she may not marry that man due to a decree lest people say husbands give wives as gifts, but if she marries another, she does not leave.
The Gemara objects: because of a decree we do not remove her from her husband, but we permit a married woman to remarry? That is absurd.
Rav Nachman revises: she may not marry that man due to the decree, but if she marries him, she does not leave because we do not remove her due to the decree.

items.text: Rava's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman's interpretation, arguing that if she may not marry that man, she may marry another, but she must fulfill the condition. After considering a parallel case of a vow, Rava concludes that she may not marry either: not him due to the decree, and not another because she must fulfill the condition. If she marries him, she does not leave; if she marries another, she leaves.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman's interpretation, arguing that if she may not marry that man, she may marry another, but she must fulfill the condition.
Rava considers a possible objection based on a parallel case of a vow, citing the dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman.
Rava rejects the parallel, arguing that in the vow case the person controls his own actions, but here the woman cannot control being divorced.
Rava concludes that she may not marry either: not him due to the decree, and not another because she must fulfill the condition.
Rava rules that if she marries him, she does not leave; if she marries another, she leaves.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Rava
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rava
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught that supports Rava's ruling: she may not marry either, and if she marries him she does not leave, but if she marries another she leaves.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's ruling: she may not marry either, and if she marries him she does not leave, but if she marries another she leaves.

items.text: Baraita on impossible conditions and Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima
items.text_en: Baraita on impossible conditions and Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima
items.desc_en: A baraita lists impossible conditions (e.g., ascending to heaven) and rules the gett is invalid. Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima disagrees, saying such a condition is merely rhetoric and the gett is valid. Rav Nachman cites Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports this from a mishnaic inference.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists impossible conditions (ascending to heaven, descending to the deep, swallowing a four-cubit reed, etc.) and rules the gett is invalid.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima disagrees, ruling that such a condition is merely rhetoric (מפליגה בדברים) and the gett is valid.
Rav Nachman cites Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports this ruling by inferring from a mishnaic formulation that an impossible condition renders the condition void.

items.text: Debate on eating pork as a condition
items.text_en: Debate on eating pork as a condition
items.desc_en: A question is raised about a gett conditioned on eating pork. Abaye considers it an impossible condition (like the baraita), while Rava argues it is possible (she can eat and be punished). The Gemara explains how each sage interprets the terms 'כְּלָל' and 'כָּזֶה' in the baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the validity of a gett conditioned on eating pork.
Abaye rules that this condition is identical to the impossible conditions in the baraita, making the gett invalid.
Rava argues that the condition is possible because she can eat the pork and be punished, so the gett is valid.

The Gemara explains how each sage interprets the terms 'כְּלָל' and 'כָּזֶה' in the baraita: Abaye includes pork under 'כְּלָל' (impossible conditions), while Rava excludes it via 'כָּזֶה' (possible conditions).

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about forbidden relations
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about forbidden relations
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited about a condition to be intimate with a specific man, which is valid, but not with her father or father-in-law. The Gemara challenges Rava, who explains that pork is possible (she can eat and be punished), and the case of a specific man is possible (she can bribe him), but the case of father/father-in-law is impossible because they would not sin. Rava then reinterprets 'כְּלָל' to include father/father-in-law and 'כָּזֶה' to exclude pork.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a condition to be intimate with a specific man (valid) but not with her father or father-in-law (invalid), and challenges Rava's position that impossible conditions are valid.

Rava explains that pork is possible (she can eat and be punished), and the case of a specific man is possible (she can bribe him), but the case of father/father-in-law is impossible because they would not sin.
Rava reinterprets 'כְּלָל' to include father/father-in-law and 'כָּזֶה' to exclude pork.

items.text: Abaye's interpretation of 'כָּזֶה' and 'כְּלָל'
items.text_en: Abaye's interpretation of 'כָּזֶה' and 'כְּלָל'
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the word 'כְּלָל' in the Mishnah includes pork, while 'כָּזֶה' excludes a specific person (Ploni). This sets up his view on conditions that contradict Torah law.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that 'כְּלָל' in the Mishnah includes pork, while 'כָּזֶה' excludes a specific person (Ploni).

items.text: Challenge to Abaye from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Abaye from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that lists conditions like eating pork, eating terumah, or drinking wine for a nazirite, and states that if the condition is fulfilled, the get is valid. This challenges Abaye's view, as it seems to allow conditions that contradict Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists conditions like eating pork, which seems to contradict Abaye's view.

items.text: Abaye's response: the baraita follows the Rabbis
items.text_en: Abaye's response: the baraita follows the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Abaye deflects the challenge by arguing that the baraita is not universally accepted; it reflects the view of the Rabbis, not his own. This allows him to maintain his position.

sub.desc_en: Abaye responds that the baraita is not universally accepted but follows the opinion of the Rabbis, not his own.

items.text: Objection: why not invoke the principle of 'מתנה על מה שכתוב בתורה'?
items.text_en: Objection: why not invoke the principle of 'מתנה על מה שכתוב בתורה'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even according to the Rabbis, the condition should be invalid because it contradicts Torah law. The principle 'anyone who stipulates against what is written in the Torah, his stipulation is void' should apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even according to the Rabbis, a condition contradicting Torah law should be void.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Rav Ika's distinction: the woman is the one who violates
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Ika's distinction: the woman is the one who violates
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Ika explains that the principle only applies when the husband himself uproots a Torah obligation (e.g., withholding food, clothing, or conjugal rights). Here, the woman is the one who violates the Torah by her own action, so the condition is valid.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Ika distinguishes: the rule of void conditions applies only when the husband himself uproots Torah law, but here the wife uproots it by her own choice.

items.text: Ravina's challenge: the woman only acts to fulfill his condition
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge: the woman only acts to fulfill his condition
items.desc_en: Ravina objects that the woman only violates the Torah to fulfill the husband's condition, so ultimately the husband is the one who causes the violation. This undermines Rav Adda's distinction.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects that the wife only acts to fulfill the husband's condition, so ultimately the husband is the one uprooting Torah law.

items.text: Ravina's alternative answer: the condition is not coercive
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative answer: the condition is not coercive
items.desc_en: Ravina offers a new answer: the principle applies only when the husband definitely uproots the Torah (e.g., withholding marital duties). Here, the husband does not force her to eat; he says she can choose not to eat and not be divorced. Thus, the condition is not a violation.

sub.desc_en: Ravina offers a new distinction: the rule applies only when the husband certainly uproots Torah law, but here he does not command her to eat; he says she may either eat or not be divorced.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah's ruling on taking back the get
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah's ruling on taking back the get
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah's statement 'How should he act? He should take it from her...'. Hezekiah says it is Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, while Rabbi Yochanan says it could even be Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi), because here the husband's jealousy (about the get being used to disqualify her from kehunah) is a special concern.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah's ruling about taking back the get.
Hezekiah identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, citing a baraita where he requires taking the get back and giving it again with a new statement.
Rabbi Yochanan argues the Mishnah could even follow Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi), because here the husband's jealousy about the get disqualifying her from kehunah is a special concern.

items.text: The dispute about conditions written before or after the 'to'ref'
items.text_en: The dispute about conditions written before or after the 'to'ref'
items.desc_en: Rav Safra states that the Mishnah's phrase 'wrote it inside' is explicit. The Gemara clarifies that this applies only after the to'ref; before the to'ref, even an oral condition invalidates. Rava agrees and adds that scribes should silence the husband until they write the to'ref.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra states that the Mishnah's phrase 'wrote it inside' is explicit and requires no further interpretation.

The Gemara questions why Rav Safra's statement is necessary, since the Mishnah's wording is obvious, and then clarifies that it teaches that only a written condition after the to'ref is valid, but before the to'ref even an oral condition invalidates.
Rava agrees that the Mishnah's rule applies only after the to'ref; before the to'ref, even an oral condition invalidates the get.
Rava supports his position by citing his own directive to scribes: they should silence the husband until they have written the to'ref of the get.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi and the Sages about conditions in a get
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi and the Sages about conditions in a get
items.desc_en: A baraita states that all conditions invalidate a get according to Rabbi, while the Sages distinguish between 'חוּץ' (which invalidates even orally) and 'עַל מְנָת' (which does not). Rabbi Zeira explains that the dispute applies only before the to'ref, where Rabbi fears a decree of 'עַל מְנָת' due to 'חוּץ', but the Sages do not.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi holds that all conditions invalidate a get, while the Sages distinguish between 'חוּץ' (which invalidates even orally) and 'עַל מְנָת' (which does not).
Rabbi Zeira explains that the dispute applies only before the to'ref, where Rabbi fears a decree of 'עַל מְנָת' due to 'חוּץ', but the Sages do not.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute about a get written on condition
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute about a get written on condition
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis is only after the signature of witnesses (לאחר התורף), where Rabbi invalidates due to a decree lest one do so before the signature, while the Rabbis do not decree. Before the signature, all agree it is invalid. The Mishnah's ruling that 'wrote it' outside is invalid but 'on condition' is not, is explained as referring to after the signature and according to the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces two possible interpretations of the Mishnah's ruling that a get written 'outside' is invalid but 'on condition' is not: either it refers to before the signature (לפני התורף) and follows the Rabbis, or after the signature (לאחר התורף) and is unanimous.

Rava resolves the dispute: the disagreement is only after the signature (לאחר התורף), where Rabbi invalidates due to a decree lest one do so before the signature, while the Rabbis do not decree; before the signature, all agree it is invalid.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's ruling that 'wrote it' outside is invalid but 'on condition' is not, refers to after the signature and follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Resolving a contradictory baraita about a get written on condition
items.text_en: Resolving a contradictory baraita about a get written on condition
items.desc_en: The father of Rabbi Avin taught a baraita before Rabbi Zeira stating that all agree a get written on condition is invalid. The Gemara objects that this contradicts the known dispute. It resolves by emending the baraita to say 'all agree it is valid' and explains that the tanna confused 'valid' with 'invalid' but not 'this is' with 'all agree'.

sub.text: Baraita citation (Father of Rabbi Avin before Rabbi Zeira)
sub.text_en: Baraita citation (Father of Rabbi Avin before Rabbi Zeira)
sub.desc_en: The father of Rabbi Avin taught a baraita before Rabbi Zeira stating that when a get is written on condition, all agree it is invalid.
The Gemara objects: 'All agree it is invalid?! But they explicitly dispute this!'
The Gemara resolves by emending the baraita to say 'all agree it is valid' and specifies that this refers to after the signature.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the tanna's error
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the tanna's error
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the tanna confused the word 'valid' with 'invalid' but did not confuse 'this is' with 'all agree', so he mistakenly attributed the position to all.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional clauses that permit or forbid remarriage
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional clauses that permit or forbid remarriage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists conditions that permit a woman to remarry anyone except specific individuals (e.g., father, brother, slave, gentile) and those that forbid her to marry anyone (e.g., a widow to a High Priest, a divorcee to a common priest, etc.). The distinction is whether the excluded person is one with whom she has no valid betrothal (valid) or has valid betrothal even if forbidden (invalid).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists conditions that permit a woman to remarry anyone except specific individuals with whom she has no valid betrothal.
The Mishnah lists conditions that forbid a woman to marry anyone, because the excluded person is one with whom she has valid betrothal even if forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: Generalizing the Mishnah's categories
items.text_en: Gemara: Generalizing the Mishnah's categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first clause (valid) includes other liable for karet, and the second clause (invalid) includes other liable for negative commandments, such as Ammonites, Moabites, etc.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first clause of the Mishnah includes other liable for karet, and the second clause includes other liable for negative commandments, such as Ammonites and Moabites.

items.text: Question about excluding a minor's betrothal
items.text_en: Question about excluding a minor's betrothal
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: if one says 'except for the betrothal of a minor,' is the get valid? The concern is whether we consider that currently he is not capable of betrothal, or that he will later come to be capable. Rav Nachman answers from a Mishnah that a minor girl can be divorced through her father's betrothal, showing that she comes to be capable of betrothal, so here too the get is invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether a get that excludes the betrothal of a minor is valid, questioning if we consider the minor's current incapacity for betrothal or his future potential to become capable.
Rav Nachman cites a Mishnah that a minor girl can be divorced through her father's betrothal, implying she is capable of betrothal.

The Gemara resolves the question by noting that the minor girl's divorce is based on her future capacity for betrothal (הֲוָיָה), so here too the get is invalid because the minor will later become capable of betrothal.

items.text: Question about excluding the unborn
items.text_en: Question about excluding the unborn
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one says 'except for those yet to be born,' what is the ruling? Rav Nachman answers from the Mishnah's case of a slave or gentile, who might convert, showing that potential future status is considered. The Gemara distinguishes: conversion is not common, but birth is common.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one says 'except for those yet to be born,' what is the ruling — do we consider their current non-existence or their future potential to be born?
Rav Nachman answers from the Mishnah's case of a slave or gentile, who might convert, showing that potential future status is considered.
The Gemara distinguishes: conversion is not common, but birth is common, so the analogy is rejected.

items.text: Question about excluding a sister's husband
items.text_en: Question about excluding a sister's husband
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one says 'except for my sister's husband,' what is the ruling? Rav Nachman again cites the slave/gentile case, but the Gemara distinguishes: conversion is uncommon, but death is common, so the get is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a get that excludes the sister's husband: is the exclusion valid because currently the sister's husband is forbidden to her, or invalid because the sister might die and then he becomes permitted?

Rav Nachman answers by citing the precedent of a slave or gentile, where the exclusion is valid because conversion is possible, implying that here too the exclusion is valid because the sister's death is possible.
The Gemara rejects the parallel: conversion is uncommon, but death is common, so the sister's husband case is different and the get is invalid.

items.text: Question about excluding one's adulterous partner
items.text_en: Question about excluding one's adulterous partner
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one says 'except for your paramour,' does it mean through marriage (which he did not exclude) or through intercourse? Rav Nachman cites the Mishnah's case of 'father' and 'your father,' which must refer to adultery, and there the get is valid because he excluded only those specific individuals. The Gemara objects that it might refer to marriage that was done improperly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the phrase 'except for your paramour' — whether it excludes only marriage (which is not relevant) or also sexual intercourse.
Rav Nachman cites the Mishnah's case of 'father' and 'your father,' which must refer to adultery, and there the get is valid because he excluded only those specific individuals.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's case might refer to marriage that was done improperly (with a forbidden relative), not to adultery.

items.text: Series of unresolved questions about other conditions
items.text_en: Series of unresolved questions about other conditions
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises several more questions: 'except for unnatural intercourse,' 'except for annulment of vows,' 'except for your terumah,' 'except for your inheritance,' 'except for your betrothal by document.' Each asks whether the condition refers to marriage (which he did not exclude) or to some other aspect. The Gemara concludes with 'teiku' (let it stand unresolved).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether the condition 'except for unnatural intercourse' refers to marriage (which he did not exclude) or to the act of intercourse itself, since the verse uses 'מִשְׁכְּבֵי אִשָּׁה' (the lying of a woman).

The Gemara asks whether the condition 'except for annulment of vows' refers to marriage (which he did not exclude) or to the husband's power to annul vows, since the verse says 'אִישָׁהּ יְקִימֶנּוּ וְאִישָׁהּ יְפֵרֶנּוּ' (her husband may uphold or annul).

The Gemara asks whether the condition 'except for your terumah' refers to marriage (which he did not exclude) or to the husband's right to eat her terumah, since the verse says 'קִנְיַן כַּסְפּוֹ' (the acquisition of his money).

The Gemara asks whether the condition 'except for your inheritance' refers to marriage (which he did not exclude) or to the husband's right to inherit from her, since the verses say 'לִשְׁאֵרוֹ' (to his close relative) and 'וְיָרַשׁ אוֹתָהּ' (he shall inherit her).

The Gemara asks whether the condition 'except for your betrothal by document' refers to marriage (which he did not exclude) or to the possibility of betrothal by document, since the verses 'וְיָצְאָה' (and she shall go out) and 'וְהָיְתָה' (and she shall be) link betrothal and divorce.
The Gemara concludes all these unresolved questions with 'תֵּיקוּ' (let it stand unresolved).

items.text: Mishnah: The essential text of the get
items.text_en: Mishnah: The essential text of the get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the essential text of the get is 'Behold, you are permitted to any man.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the essential text of the get is 'Behold, you are permitted to any man.'

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Formulations of a get and a bill of manumission
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Formulations of a get and a bill of manumission
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Yehuda's version of the get's essential formula and the core text of a bill of manumission: 'harei at bat chorin' or 'harei at le'atzmach'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Yehuda's version of the get's essential formula and the core text of a bill of manumission: 'harei at bat chorin' or 'harei at le'atzmach'.

items.text: Gemara's initial question: The meaning of 'harei at le'atzmach' for a woman
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question: The meaning of 'harei at le'atzmach' for a woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that saying 'harei at bat chorin' to one's wife or 'harei at muteret lechol adam' to one's slave is meaningless. It then questions whether saying 'harei at le'atzmach' to a woman is a valid divorce or merely a statement about labor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that saying 'harei at bat chorin' to one's wife or 'harei at muteret lechol adam' to one's slave is meaningless.
The Gemara questions whether saying 'harei at le'atzmach' to a woman is a valid divorce or merely a statement about labor.

items.text: Ravina's proof from the Mishnah for a woman
items.text_en: Ravina's proof from the Mishnah for a woman
items.desc_en: Ravina argues to Rav Ashi that the Mishnah's inclusion of 'harei at le'atzmach' in the bill of manumission proves it is effective for a slave, and a fortiori for a woman, since a slave acquires his own body while a woman does not.

sub.desc_en: Ravina says to Rav Ashi: come and hear, for we learned in the Mishnah that the core of a bill of manumission is 'harei at ben chorin' or 'harei at le'atzmach'; if a slave, who is acquired by his master, is freed by 'harei at le'atzmach', then a woman, who is not acquired, is certainly freed.

items.text: Ravina's second question: 'Ein li esek bach' for a slave
items.text_en: Ravina's second question: 'Ein li esek bach' for a slave
items.desc_en: Ravina asks about saying 'ein li esek bach' to a slave. Rav Chanin cites a baraita that a slave sold to a non-Jew goes free and needs a bill of manumission from the first master, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says if the master wrote 'lich'shetivrach mimeni, ein li esek bach' that is his manumission.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if a master said to his slave 'אין לי עסק בך' (I have no business with you), what is the halachic status — is it a valid act of manumission?

sub.text: Rav Chanin's citation of a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Chanin's citation of a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanin (or Rav Chanin Machozena'ah) cites a baraita: one who sells his slave to a non-Jew — the slave goes free and needs a bill of manumission from the first master; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that if the master wrote an 'ono' (condition) on him, that itself is his manumission.

Rav Sheshet explains that 'אונו' (the condition) means the master wrote to the slave: 'לכשתבח ממנו אין לי עסק בך' (when you flee from him, I have no business with you), thereby resolving that the phrase 'אין לי עסק בך' can effect manumission.

items.text: The dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda regarding 'veden'
items.text_en: The dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda regarding 'veden'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: the Rabbis hold that 'yadayim she'ein mochichot' are considered valid, so without 'veden' the get is still valid, while Rabbi Yehuda requires 'veden' to clarify that the divorce is through this document, not just speech.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yehuda's requirement that the get include the word 'veden' (and this) to clarify that the divorce is through this document.
The Gemara asks: over what principle do the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda disagree?
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis hold that 'yadayim she'ein mochichot' (inconclusive expressions) are considered valid, so even without 'veden' the get is valid.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds that 'yadayim she'ein mochichot' are not valid, so without 'veden' people would think the divorce was by speech alone and the document is merely evidence.

items.text: Abaye's scribal instructions for writing a get
items.text_en: Abaye's scribal instructions for writing a get
items.desc_en: Abaye gives detailed instructions for writing a get: write 'veden' not 'vedin', 'iggeret' not 'igeret', 'limhach' not 'limchach', and correctly spell 'ditihevyain' and 'dititzbyain' with three yods, lengthen the vav of 'teiruchin' and 'shibukin', lengthen the vav of 'dechadu', and write 'lehitnaseva' not 'leitnaseva'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye instructs that when writing a get, one should write 'veden' (וְדֵן) not 'vedin' (וְדִין).
Abaye instructs to write 'iggeret' (אִגֶּרֶת) not 'igeret' (אִיגֶּרֶת), and 'limhach' (לִמְהָךְ) not 'limchach' (לִמְחָךְ).
Abaye instructs to spell 'ditihevyain' and 'dititzbyain' with three yods each, and to lengthen the vav of 'teiruchin' and 'shibukin'.
Abaye instructs to lengthen the vav of 'dechadu' and to write 'lehitnaseva' not 'leitnaseva'.

items.text: The question of whether 'veden' is required and Rava's formula
items.text_en: The question of whether 'veden' is required and Rava's formula
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether 'veden' is required. It cites Rava's standard get formula which does not include 'veden', but the Gemara deflects that Rava's formula also omits other elements. The phrase 'miyoma denan' excludes Rabbi Yossi's view, and 'ule'alam' is also discussed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the word 'veden' is required in a get.
The Gemara cites Rava's standard get formula, which does not include 'veden', as evidence that it may not be required.
The Gemara objects that Rava's formula also omits other elements, so the absence of 'veden' does not prove it is unnecessary.
The Gemara explains that the phrase 'miyoma denan' in Rava's formula excludes Rabbi Yossi's view that the date of the document itself proves its validity.
The Gemara begins to discuss the phrase 'ule'alam' but the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening discussion on a get shichrur and a remedy for a skin condition
items.text_en: Opening discussion on a get shichrur and a remedy for a skin condition
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a tangential discussion about Rava's question to Rav Nachman regarding a conditional divorce formula, then presents the text of a get shichrur (manumission document) and a remedy for a skin condition on a slave.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tangential discussion about Rava's question to Rav Nachman regarding a conditional divorce formula.
The Gemara presents the text of a get shichrur (manumission document) and Rav Yehuda's standard formula for a slave sale document, including a warranty against skin conditions.
Abaye provides a remedy for the skin condition mentioned in the document, listing ingredients and application method.

items.text: Mishnah: Three invalid gittin
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three invalid gittin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three types of gittin that are invalid (pasul), but if the woman remarries, the child is kosher. Rabbi Eliezer adds that a get without witnesses but given in front of witnesses is valid and can collect from liened property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that three types of gittin are invalid (pasul), but if the woman remarries, the child is kosher.
The Mishnah lists the three cases: written in the husband's own hand without witnesses, has witnesses but no date, has a date but only one witness.
The Mishnah repeats that these three are invalid, but if she remarried, the child is kosher.

Rabbi Eliezer adds that a get without witnesses but given in front of witnesses is valid and can collect from liened property, because witnesses only sign for the sake of tikkun haolam (the betterment of the world).

items.text: Gemara: Why not include other invalid gittin?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why not include other invalid gittin?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists only three invalid gittin, excluding others like an old get (get yashan), a bald get (get kereach), and a get with the greeting 'shalom malchut'. It resolves each by distinguishing the severity of the invalidity (e.g., whether the child is a mamzer or the woman must leave).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists only three invalid bills of divorce, given that there is also an outdated bill of divorce (גט ישן).
The Gemara objects that the distinction works only for the opinion that here the woman must leave, but not for the opinion that she need not leave.
The Gemara answers that the distinction is that an outdated bill of divorce may be used לכתחילה (the ideal standard), while the cases in the Mishnah are only בדיעבד (after the fact).
The Gemara asks why a bare bill of divorce (גט קרח) is not listed, and answers that there the offspring is a mamzer, while here the offspring is unflawed.
The Gemara objects that the distinction works for Rabbi Meir, but not for the Rabbis who hold the offspring is not a mamzer.
The Gemara answers that the distinction is that there the woman must leave, while here she need not leave.
The Gemara objects that the distinction works for the opinion that here she need not leave, but not for the opinion that she must leave.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is not dealing with a folded and tied bill of divorce (מקושר), only an open one.
The Gemara asks why a bill of divorce with a date according to another kingdom (שלום מלכות) is not listed, and answers that there she must leave, while here she need not leave.
The Gemara objects that the distinction works for the opinion that here she need not leave, but not for the opinion that she must leave.
The Gemara answers that there the offspring is a mamzer, while here the offspring is unflawed.
The Gemara objects that the distinction works for Rabbi Meir, but not for the Rabbis who hold the offspring is not a mamzer.
The Gemara resolves that the opinion that here the woman must leave follows Rabbi Meir, so there the offspring is a mamzer and here it is unflawed.

items.text: Clarifying the exclusions of the Mishnah's count
items.text_en: Clarifying the exclusions of the Mishnah's count
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first count (three) excludes the cases already discussed, and the second count (in the Mishnah's language) excludes a case where a get from overseas was given without the declaration 'in my presence it was written and signed', which Rabbi Meir considers a mamzer but the Sages disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the first count (three) in the Mishnah serves to exclude, and what the second count serves to exclude.
The Gemara answers that the first count excludes the invalid bills of divorce already discussed in the Gemara.
The Gemara answers that the second count excludes the case of an agent who brings a get from overseas without the declaration, which Rabbi Meir says renders the offspring a mamzer.

The Sages disagree with Rabbi Meir, stating that the offspring is not a mamzer, and they prescribe a corrective procedure: the agent should take the get back and give it again in the presence of two witnesses with the proper declaration.

items.text: Rav's clarification on 'written in his own hand'
items.text_en: Rav's clarification on 'written in his own hand'
items.desc_en: Rav states that the Mishnah's phrase 'written in his own hand' refers to the first case (no witnesses). The Gemara questions which case Rav means, concluding it must be the last case (one witness), as the first is obvious and the second has witnesses.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the Mishnah's phrase 'written in his own hand' refers specifically to the case of 'written in his own hand' as taught.
The Gemara asks which case Rav's statement applies to, rejecting the first case as obvious since the Mishnah explicitly says 'written in his own hand'.
The Gemara rejects the second case because it has witnesses, and concludes that Rav's statement applies to the last case: a get with a date but only one witness.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on a get written by a scribe
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on a get written by a scribe
items.desc_en: Rav holds that only a get written by the husband's own hand and signed by one witness is valid, but if written by a scribe and signed by one witness it is invalid. Shmuel argues that even such a get is valid, citing a mishnah. Rav distinguishes between the mishnah's case (initial validity) and his case (post-facto). Shmuel resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a proficient and non-proficient scribe.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that only a get written by the husband's own hand and signed by one witness is valid, but if written by a scribe and signed by one witness it is invalid.
Shmuel argues that even a get written by a scribe and signed by one witness is valid, citing a mishnah that explicitly validates such a get.
The gemara objects that Rav's case is different from the mishnah: the mishnah deals with לכתחילה (the ideal standard), while Rav's case is בדיעבד (after the fact).
Shmuel resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a proficient scribe (מוּבְהַק) and a non-proficient scribe (לָא מוּבְהַק).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar on the same mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar on the same mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the mishnah says 'his own handwriting'. Rabbi Elazar objects that there are witnesses on it. Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that he refers to the latter clause of the mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the mishnah explicitly says 'his own handwriting'.
Rabbi Elazar objects that the document has witnesses on it, so why emphasize handwriting?
Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that his statement refers to the latter clause of the mishnah, not the first.

items.text: Rav's contradictory rulings and the challenge from Mar Zutra
items.text_en: Rav's contradictory rulings and the challenge from Mar Zutra
items.desc_en: Rav sometimes says the woman may leave (her second husband) and sometimes not. The resolution: if she has children she does not leave, if not she leaves. Mar Zutra bar Toviyah challenges this from a mishnah about doubtful divorces, which implies she may not remarry. The Gemara answers that the concern is rabbinic, so she may remarry and the yevamah may enter levirate marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav sometimes rules that the woman leaves (her second husband) and sometimes that she does not.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: if she has children she does not leave, if not she leaves.
Mar Zutra bar Toviyah challenges from a mishnah about doubtful divorces, which implies that a woman with a doubtful get may not remarry.
The Gemara infers that if she does not leave, her co-wife would come to enter levirate marriage, which is problematic.
The Gemara answers that the concern is rabbinic, so she may remarry and the yevamah may enter levirate marriage.

items.text: Levi and Rabbi Yochanan: the woman never leaves; digression on kartsit
items.text_en: Levi and Rabbi Yochanan: the woman never leaves; digression on kartsit
items.desc_en: Levi and Rabbi Yochanan rule that the woman never leaves. Rabbi Yochanan tells the sons of Rabbi Chalapta that their father said the same, and adds that a kartsit in a sheaf does not disqualify the water of purification. Abaye explains what a kartsit is. Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina challenges this from a mishnah listing birds that disqualify the water, which does not mention kartsit. The answer: a large kartsit does not disqualify, but a small one does, up to the size of an olive.

sub.desc_en: Levi rules that the woman never leaves (her husband).
Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Levi's ruling.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan to the sons of Rabbi Chalapta
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan to the sons of Rabbi Chalapta
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan tells the sons of Rabbi Chalapta that their father also ruled that the woman never leaves.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that a kartsit (a type of bird) in a sheaf does not disqualify the water of purification.
The Gemara asks what a kartsit is.
Abaye explains that a kartsit is a bee that nests between rocks.

sub.text: Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina challenges from a mishnah listing birds that disqualify the water, which does not mention kartsit.
The Gemara resolves that a large kartsit does not disqualify, but a small one does.
The Gemara asks up to what size a small kartsit disqualifies.
Rabbi Yirmeya, or alternatively Rabbi Ami, answers that a small kartsit disqualifies up to the size of an olive.

items.text: Halakha like Rabbi Elazar in gittin; multiple attestations
items.text_en: Halakha like Rabbi Elazar in gittin; multiple attestations
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says Rav ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar in gittin. Shmuel extends this to shtarot. The Gemara questions Rav's view on shtarot, and resolves that Rabbi Elazar said two things, and Rav agrees with one but disagrees with the other. Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi, Rabbi Yannai, Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina, and Rabbi Yochanan all weigh in, with some saying even the 'scent of a get' is not valid. The Gemara clarifies that they refer to the rabbis' opinion. Finally, a series of messages confirm the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar in gittin.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules the הלכה follows רבי אליעזר in גיטין, and Shmuel extends this to שטרות (documents).
The Gemara challenges whether Rav really holds that the ruling does not apply to שטרות, since the משנה teaches she collects from liened property.
The Gemara resolves that רבי אליעזר stated two rulings, and Rav agrees with one and disagrees with the other.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: רבי יעקב בר אידי citing רבי יהושע בן לוי rules the הלכה follows רבי אליעזר in גיטין, while רבי ינאי says it does not even have the scent of a גט.
The Gemara clarifies that רבי ינאי means: according to the רבנן, it does not even have the scent of a גט.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina citing Reish Lakish, and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina citing Reish Lakish, and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: רבי יוסי בר רבי חנינא citing ריש לקיש rules the הלכה follows רבי אליעזר in גיטין, while רבי יוחנן says it does not even have the scent of a גט.
The Gemara clarifies that רבי יוחנן means: according to the רבנן, it does not even have the scent of a גט.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to Marei bar Mar
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to Marei bar Mar
sub.desc_en: רבי אבא בר זבדא sends to ask רב הונא whether the הלכה follows רבי אליעזר in גיטין or not.

sub.text: Rabbah citing Rava, and Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah citing Rava, and Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: רב הונא dies before answering; רבה citing רבא, and the well-versed teachers citing רב, confirm the הלכה follows רבי אליעזר in גיטין.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: An alternative version: the colleagues and disciples citing רב, via רב חסדא citing רב חמא בר גוריא citing רב, confirm the הלכה follows רבי אליעזר in גיטין.

sub.text: Ravin citing Rabbi Elazar citing Rav
sub.text_en: Ravin citing Rabbi Elazar citing Rav
sub.desc_en: When רבין came from ארץ ישראל he reported that רבי אליעזר citing רב says the הלכה follows רבי אליעזר in גיטין.

items.text: Mishnah: two identical gittin mixed up, and five who wrote a collective get
items.text_en: Mishnah: two identical gittin mixed up, and five who wrote a collective get
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents two cases: (1) Two agents who sent two identical gittin that got mixed up: each woman receives both gittin, and if one is lost the other is void. (2) Five people who wrote a collective get listing all divorces, with witnesses at the bottom: all are valid. If he wrote a separate text for each with witnesses at the bottom, only the one whose name appears with the witnesses is valid.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah's first case: two men sent two identical גיטין (bills of divorce) that got mixed up, so each woman receives both, and if one is lost the other is void.
The mishnah's second case: five husbands who wrote a collective wording in one גט listing all the divorces, with witnesses signed below, are all valid and it is given to each wife.
The mishnah's contrasting case: if a separate טופס (formula) was written for each couple with witnesses signed below, only the one whose text the witnesses' signatures are read with is valid.

items.text: Gemara: analysis of the mishnah's author and definitions of 'klal' and 'tofes'
items.text_en: Gemara: analysis of the mishnah's author and definitions of 'klal' and 'tofes'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya says the mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Elazar, who holds that witnesses to delivery are essential, so the witnesses would not know which woman is being divorced. Abaye argues it could even be Rabbi Elazar, who requires writing for her sake but not delivery for her sake. Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish define 'klal' (one date for all) and 'tofes' (a separate date for each).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna (author) of the mishnah.

Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Elazar, because Rabbi Elazar holds that witnesses to delivery (עדי מסירה) are essential, and they would not know which woman is being divorced.
Abaye objects that the mishnah could even be in accordance with Rabbi Elazar, because Rabbi Elazar requires writing for her sake (כתיבה לשמה) but does not require delivery for her sake (נתינה לשמה).
The Gemara asks: what is the definition of 'klal' (a single date for all) and 'tofes' (a separate date for each)?
Rabbi Yochanan defines 'klal' as one date for all the women, and 'tofes' as a separate date for each woman.
Reish Lakish begins his own definition of 'klal' and 'tofes' (the continuation is in the next section).

items.text: Definition of a general formulation (כלל) according to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Definition of a general formulation (כלל) according to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that even a single date for all is still a template (טופס), so what constitutes a general formulation (כלל)? It is when the text reads: 'We, so-and-so and so-and-so, have divorced our wives, so-and-so and so-and-so.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that even a single date for all is still a template (טופס), and defines a general formulation (כלל) as the text: 'We, so-and-so and so-and-so, have divorced our wives, so-and-so and so-and-so.'

items.text: Rabbi Abba's objection and Rabbi Avahu's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's objection and Rabbi Avahu's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects to Rabbi Yochanan's view: if a single date is considered a general formulation (כלל), we should worry that witnesses signed at the end, only for the last one. The Gemara cites a precedent about witnesses signing on a greeting in a get, which is invalid. Rabbi Avahu resolves that the case is different because the text includes 'so-and-so and so-and-so and so-and-so,' analogous to the distinction between 'Sha'alu' (invalid) and 'V'Sha'alu' (valid).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects to Rabbi Yochanan: if a single date is a general formulation (כלל), we should worry that witnesses signed only for the last one, citing a baraita that witnesses signing on a greeting in a get invalidates it.

Rabbi Avahu resolves that the case is different because the text includes 'פלוני ופלוני ופלוני' (so-and-so and so-and-so and so-and-so), analogous to the distinction between 'שאלו' (invalid) and 'ושאלו' (valid).

items.text: Another objection to Rabbi Yochanan and Mar Kashisha's answer
items.text_en: Another objection to Rabbi Yochanan and Mar Kashisha's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection: according to Rabbi Yochanan, why is the problem only that it is a template (טופס)? It should also be invalid because it is 'written by day and signed at night' (since the date is for all, but the signing might be later). Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda answers in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the text includes 'on the first day of the week, on the first day of the week' for each, so the date is repeated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yochanan, why is the problem only that it is a template (טופס)? It should also be invalid because it is 'written by day and signed at night' (since the date is for all, but the signing might be later).

sub.text: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda's answer in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda's answer in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda answers Rav Ashi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the text includes 'on the first day of the week, on the first day of the week' for each, so the date is repeated.

items.text: Reish Lakish's view and the definition of כלל
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's view and the definition of כלל
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi about Reish Lakish's view: even a single date for all is a template (טופס). So what is a general formulation (כלל)? It is when the text says: 'We, so-and-so and so-and-so, have divorced our wives, so-and-so and so-and-so,' which results in two women being divorced by one get, violating 'and he writes for her' – not for her and her friend. The solution is that the text then writes each divorce separately.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: according to Reish Lakish, even a single date for all is a template (טופס), so what is a general formulation (כלל)? It is when the text says 'We, so-and-so and so-and-so, have divorced our wives, so-and-so and so-and-so,' which results in two women being divorced by one get, violating 'and he writes for her' – not for her and her friend.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's answer (implied by the continuation)
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer (implied by the continuation)
sub.desc_en: The solution is that the text then writes each divorce separately, as 'So-and-so divorced so-and-so, and so-and-so divorced so-and-so.'

items.text: Ravina's comparison to the case of two slaves
items.text_en: Ravina's comparison to the case of two slaves
items.desc_en: Ravina asks why this case is different from the baraita where one writes all his property to two slaves – they acquire and free each other. The Gemara answers that this was established as referring to two separate documents.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi why the case of two wives in one get is different from the baraita where one writes all his property to two slaves, who acquire the property and free each other.
The Gemara answers that the baraita about two slaves was established as referring to two separate documents, not a single document.

items.text: Baraitot supporting Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Baraitot supporting Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites two baraitot: one supports Rabbi Yochanan, where five people write in the get 'So-and-so divorces so-and-so' with one date and witnesses below – all are valid; but with separate dates, only the one the witnesses accompany is valid, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira adds a condition about spacing. The second supports Reish Lakish, where the general formulation is used with one date – all are valid; with separate dates and spacing, only the one the witnesses accompany is valid, and Rabbi Meir says even without spacing it is invalid because the date separates them.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the case of five people writing in the get with one date and witnesses below, ruling all are valid.

sub.text: Baraita continuation with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.text_en: Baraita continuation with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that with separate dates and witnesses below, only the one the witnesses accompany is valid, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira adds a condition about spacing.
The baraita presents the case of five people writing a general formulation with one date and witnesses below, ruling all are valid.
The baraita rules that with separate dates and spacing, only the one the witnesses accompany is valid, and Rabbi Meir says even without spacing it is invalid because the date separates them.

items.text: Reconciling Reish Lakish's view with the baraita
items.text_en: Reconciling Reish Lakish's view with the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Reish Lakish, why mention separate dates? He said even a single date is a template! The answer is that this applies when they were not mixed from the start; but here, since they were mixed from the start, if he separates them with dates – yes, it is valid; if not – no.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Reish Lakish, why does the baraita specify separate dates for each? He holds that even a single date for all is a template (טופס).

The Gemara answers: that ruling applies when the divorces were not mixed from the start; but here, since they were mixed from the start, if he separates them with dates – yes, it is valid; if not – no.

items.text: Mishnah: Two gittin side by side with mixed witnesses, and Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two gittin side by side with mixed witnesses, and Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses two gittin written side by side with two Hebrew witnesses under one and two Greek witnesses under the other – the one whose first witnesses accompany it is valid. If there is one Hebrew and one Greek witness under each, both are invalid. The Gemara questions why one cannot be validated by reading 'Reuven ben' from the first and 'Yaakov eid' from the second, or by reading 'Reuven ben' for one and 'Yaakov eid' for the other, citing a baraita that 'ben so-and-so eid' is valid. The Gemara answers that 'eid' is not written, or alternatively, we know that the signature is not Yaakov's.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of two gittin written side by side with mixed witnesses, ruling that the one whose first witnesses accompany it is valid, but if each has one Hebrew and one Greek witness, both are invalid.
The Gemara asks why the first get cannot be validated by reading 'Reuven ben' from the first and 'Yaakov eid' from the second, citing a baraita that 'ben so-and-so eid' is valid.
The Gemara alternatively asks why the first get cannot be validated by reading 'Reuven ben' for one and 'Yaakov eid' for the other, citing a baraita that 'ish ploni eid' is valid.
The Gemara answers that the word 'eid' is not written, or alternatively, we know that the signature is not Yaakov's.

items.text: Rejecting the possibility that the father's name is a signature or a mark
items.text_en: Rejecting the possibility that the father's name is a signature or a mark
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the father's name might be the actual signature or a distinguishing mark, but concludes that a person would not be so brazen as to use his father's name as a mere mark.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the father's name might be the actual signature, but immediately rejects this because a person does not abandon his own name to sign his father's name.
The Gemara alternatively suggests that the father's name might be a distinguishing mark, citing examples of rabbis who used personal marks like a fish, a palm branch, a samekh, an ayin, or a wound.
The Gemara rejects this possibility, concluding that a person would not be so brazen as to use his father's name as a mere distinguishing mark.

items.text: Proposing and rejecting the use of two sets of witnesses
items.text_en: Proposing and rejecting the use of two sets of witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that each get could be validated by two Hebrew and two Greek witnesses, citing a Mishnah that allows mixed scripts. It then raises the issue of a gap between lines, but Ze'eri's teaching resolves that both are valid; the Tanna's concern is that a single signature might be a 'gundalit' (a single line of signatures).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that each get could be validated by two Hebrew and two Greek witnesses, citing a Mishnah that permits mixed scripts.
The Gemara raises the objection that a gap between lines might invalidate the get, but cites Chizkiyah's teaching that filling the gap with relatives is valid.
Ze'eri resolves that both gets are valid, and the Tanna's concern is that a single line of signatures (גונדלית) might be written, with all witnesses signing on one line.

items.text: Proposing and rejecting one Hebrew and one Greek witness for each get
items.text_en: Proposing and rejecting one Hebrew and one Greek witness for each get
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that each get could be validated by one Hebrew and one Greek witness, citing a Mishnah that allows such a pair. Ze'eri's teaching again resolves that both are valid, but the Tanna's concern is that a single signature might be a 'gundalit', with three witnesses on one get and one on the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that each get could be validated by one Hebrew and one Greek witness, citing the Mishnah that such a pair is valid.
Ze'eri's teaching resolves that both gets are valid, but the Tanna's concern is that a single signature might be a 'gundalit'.
The Tanna's concern is that a single signature might be a 'gundalit', with three witnesses on one get and one on the other.

items.text: Mishnah: Rules for witness placement on a get
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rules for witness placement on a get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents various scenarios of where witnesses sign relative to the text of a get, ruling on validity based on whether the witnesses are read with the text.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that if one left part of the get and wrote it on a second page with witnesses below, it is valid, but if witnesses signed at the top, side, or back of a simple get, it is invalid.
The Mishnah continues with cases of two documents placed head-to-head, foot-to-foot, or head-to-foot, ruling on validity based on whether the witnesses are read with the text.

items.text: Mishnah: Additional valid witness formats
items.text_en: Mishnah: Additional valid witness formats
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues with cases where the get and witnesses are in different scripts, or where the witness writes his name without the word 'witness', all of which are valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists additional valid witness formats: a get written in Hebrew with Greek witnesses, Greek with Hebrew witnesses, one Hebrew and one Greek witness, a scribe writing as a witness, and various witness signature styles without the word 'witness'.

items.text: Gemara's concern about two separate gittin and Rabbi Abba's solution
items.text_en: Gemara's concern about two separate gittin and Rabbi Abba's solution
items.desc_en: The Gemara worries that the two signatures might come from two different gittin, with the date from one and witnesses from the other. Rabbi Abba quoting Rav resolves this by requiring space below the text, though the Gemara questions whether the later date could have been cut off, and Rav's answer reiterates the need for space.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that the two signatures might come from two different gittin, with the date from one and witnesses from the other, and that the later date and earlier witnesses might have been cut off.
Rabbi Abba quoting Rav resolves the concern by requiring that there be space (ריוח) below the text, ensuring the signatures belong to the same get.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the later date was cut off, undermining the solution.
The Gemara resolves the objection by reiterating Rav's requirement of space below the text, which prevents the possibility of cutting off the later date.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the two-column get issue
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the two-column get issue
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case of a get written on a paper with two columns is when there is space above the text, so the witnesses can sign there. It then raises a concern that the husband might have consulted and written a second get, but dismisses it because the formula 'you are permitted' is written above, and we do not worry about such a remote possibility.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the two-column get issue by stating that the case is when there is space above the text for witnesses to sign.
The Gemara raises the objection that the husband might have consulted and written a second get.
The Gemara dismisses the concern because the formula 'you are permitted' is written above, and we do not worry about such a remote possibility.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi offers a different explanation: the case is where the bottom of the parchment is known, meaning the witnesses sign at the bottom of the document.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi offers an alternative explanation: the case is where the bottom of the parchment is known, meaning the witnesses sign at the bottom of the document.

items.text: Discussion of witnesses signing at the top of the page
items.text_en: Discussion of witnesses signing at the top of the page
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that witnesses who sign at the top of the page are valid, citing Rav who signed on the side. It resolves that Rav's case was when the witnesses' signatures were opposite the writing. Then it raises a contradiction from a baraita about two documents with witnesses in the middle, and resolves that the baraita deals with a case where the witnesses' signatures are written like a beam, making it impossible to tell which document they belong to. Finally, it explains that Rav signed on disks (separate sheets).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that witnesses signing at the top of the page are valid, citing that Rav signed on the side.
The Gemara answers that Rav's case was when the witnesses' signatures were opposite the writing.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about two documents with witnesses in the middle, arguing that one could see which document the witnesses face.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita deals with a case where the witnesses' signatures are written like a beam, making it impossible to tell which document they belong to.
The Gemara concludes that Rav signed on disks (separate sheets), resolving the original question.

items.text: The scribe may sign as a witness
items.text_en: The scribe may sign as a witness
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a scribe wrote the get and one witness signed, it is valid. Rabbi Yirmeya clarifies that the Mishnah says 'the scribe signed' (i.e., he was one of the witnesses). Rav Chisda identifies this as the opinion of Rabbi Yosi. A story is told about a ketubah that came before Rabbi Avahu, where he was about to validate it based on knowing the scribe's handwriting, but Rabbi Yirmeya stopped him, citing the rule that only the scribe's signature as a witness counts.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: a גט (bill of divorce) written by a scribe and signed by one witness is valid.
רבי ירמיה (Rabbi Yirmeya) clarifies that the Mishnah means the scribe himself signed as a witness, not merely that his handwriting appears in the text.
רב חסדא (Rav Chisda) identifies the Mishnah's ruling as following the opinion of רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei).
A case is related: a marriage contract came before רבי אבהו (Rabbi Avahu), where the scribe's handwriting and one witness's signature were recognized, and he thought to validate it.
רבי ירמיה (Rabbi Yirmeya) rejects Rabbi Avahu's intended validation, citing that the Mishnah requires the scribe to have signed as a witness.

items.text: Writing the family nickname in a get
items.text_en: Writing the family nickname in a get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one wrote his or her family nickname, the get is valid. The Tanna Kamma says that using the father's nickname is valid up to ten generations, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar limits it to three generations. Rabbi Chanina's ruling that it is valid up to three generations follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. Rav Huna cites a verse: 'For you will bear children and children's children and you will become old in the land.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one wrote his or her family nickname, the get is valid.
The Tanna Kamma rules that using the father's nickname is valid up to ten generations.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar limits the validity of the father's nickname to three generations.
The Gemara asks whose opinion Rabbi Chanina's ruling follows.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chanina's ruling follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
Rav Huna cites the verse 'For you will bear children and children's children and you will become old in the land' as the scriptural basis for the three-generation limit.

items.text: Aggadic discussion about the exile
items.text_en: Aggadic discussion about the exile
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi lists seven idolatrous courts that caused the destruction of Israel. Rav Ami cites a verse about bearing children and grandchildren. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi question why Hoshea ben Elah is included, since he was relatively good. Rav explains that Hoshea removed the guards Jeroboam had placed on the roads to prevent pilgrimage, but the people still did not go up, so God exiled them. Marimar explains a verse about God's righteousness in bringing evil, and Ulla says that God advanced the exile by two years before the time of 'you will become old.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi lists seven idolatrous courts that caused the destruction of Israel, citing a verse.
Rav Ami cites the verse 'כִּי תוֹלִיד בָּנִים וּבְנֵי בָנִים' (when you bear children and grandchildren) as a prooftext for the exile.
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi question Rav why Hoshea ben Elah is included in the list, since he was relatively good and the verse says 'only not like the kings of Israel'.
Rav explains that Hoshea removed the guards Jeroboam had placed on the roads to prevent pilgrimage, but the people still did not go up, so God exiled them.

sub.text: Marimar (via Rav Chisda / Mar Ukva / Rabbi Yirmeya)
sub.text_en: Marimar (via Rav Chisda / Mar Ukva / Rabbi Yirmeya)
sub.desc_en: Marimar questions the verse 'וַיִּשְׁקוֹד ה׳ עַל הָרָעָה וַיְבִיאֶהָ עָלֵינוּ, כִּי צַדִּיק ה׳' — how can bringing evil be an act of righteousness?
Marimar resolves that God acted righteously by exiling Zedekiah's generation while Jeconiah's exile still existed, explaining the terms 'חָרָשׁ' and 'מַסְגֵּר'.
Ulla says that God advanced the exile by two years before the time of 'וְנוֹשַׁנְתֶּם' (you will become old).

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's calculation of 'meheirah'
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's calculation of 'meheirah'
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov infers from the word 'meheirah' in the previous Mishnah that it refers to 852 years, a numerical calculation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov infers from the word 'meheirah' in the previous Mishnah that it refers to 852 years.

items.text: Mishnah: Coerced get by Jews vs. gentiles
items.text_en: Mishnah: Coerced get by Jews vs. gentiles
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a coerced get (me'useh) performed by a Jewish court is valid, but by gentiles it is invalid; gentiles beat the husband and tell him to do what the Jew says.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: a coerced get (גט מעושה) from a Jewish court is valid, but from gentiles it is invalid; gentiles beat the husband and tell him to do what the Jew says, and it is valid.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Nachman and Rav Mesharshiya on coerced get by gentiles
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Nachman and Rav Mesharshiya on coerced get by gentiles
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel distinguishes between a get done properly (kadin) and improperly (she'lo kadin) by Jews and gentiles. Rav Mesharshiya suggests that by Torah law a coerced get by gentiles is valid, but the Sages invalidated it to prevent women from attaching themselves to gentiles. The Gemara rejects this as fabricated, explaining the real reason is to avoid confusion with Jewish practice.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel rules that a coerced get (גֵּט מְעוּשֶּׂה) by a Jew is valid if done properly (כַּדִּין) and invalid if done improperly (שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין), while by gentiles it is invalid even properly and has no validity at all if done improperly.
The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman's ruling: if gentiles are capable of effecting divorce, the get should be valid even improperly; if not, it should not invalidate at all.
Rav Mesharshiya explains that by Torah law a coerced get by gentiles is valid, but the Sages invalidated it to prevent women from attaching themselves to a gentile and escaping their husband.
The Gemara objects: if Rav Mesharshiya's reason is correct, then an improperly done get by gentiles should at least invalidate like a Jewish get, not be completely void.
The Gemara rejects Rav Mesharshiya's explanation as fabricated (בְּדוּתָא).

The Gemara provides the real reason: a properly done get by gentiles is invalid because it might be confused with a properly done Jewish get, while an improperly done one is not confused and thus completely void.

items.text: Abaye and Rav Yosef on acting as agents for gentile courts
items.text_en: Abaye and Rav Yosef on acting as agents for gentile courts
items.desc_en: Abaye finds Rav Yosef writing gittin for gentile courts and challenges him based on a baraita of Rabbi Tarfon that one may not appear before gentile courts. Rav Yosef responds that they act as agents of the Jewish litigants, and Abaye limits this to common matters, not uncommon ones like theft and assault.

sub.desc_en: Abaye finds Rav Yosef writing gittin for gentile courts and challenges him, citing Rabbi Tarfon's baraita that one may not appear before gentile courts, based on the verse 'וְאֵלֶּה הַמִּשְׁפָּטִים אֲשֶׁר תָּשִׂים לִפְנֵיהֶם' — before them, not before gentiles or laymen.
Rav Yosef responds that they act as agents of the Jewish litigants, in matters that are common like admissions and loans.
Abaye objects that if so, they should also act as agents for theft and assault cases, and then limits the principle: they act as agents only for common matters, not uncommon ones.

items.text: Mishnah: Rumors of betrothal or divorce
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rumors of betrothal or divorce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a rumor spreads in town that a woman is betrothed or divorced, she is considered so, provided there is no plausible alternative explanation (amatla). Examples of amatla include conditional divorce or uncertain proximity of kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if a rumor spreads in town that a woman is betrothed, she is considered betrothed.
The Mishnah adds that if the rumor is that she is divorced, she is considered divorced.
The Mishnah conditions the ruling on the absence of a plausible alternative explanation (amatla).

items.text: Gemara: Concern for rumors after marriage
items.text_en: Gemara: Concern for rumors after marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we forbid a woman to her husband based on a rumor, citing Rav Ashi that we do not worry about rumors after marriage. It clarifies that the Mishnah means if a rumor of betrothal or divorce spreads, she is considered betrothed or divorced.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah forbids a woman to her husband based on a rumor, citing Rav Ashi's principle that we do not worry about rumors after marriage.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah does not forbid her to her husband; rather, it means that if a rumor of betrothal or divorce spreads, she is considered betrothed or divorced for other purposes.

items.text: Opening statement: the case of a rumor with a document
items.text_en: Opening statement: the case of a rumor with a document
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement that if a rumor says a woman is divorced, she is considered divorced, because the rumor is accompanied by a document (the get). This establishes the basic principle that a rumor alone is not enough; it must be supported by evidence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a woman is considered divorced based on a rumor, because the rumor is accompanied by a document (the get).

items.text: Rava's ruling: rumor of promiscuity is not feared
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: rumor of promiscuity is not feared
items.desc_en: Rava states that if a rumor spreads that a woman is promiscuous, we do not suspect her, because it is merely a matter of licentiousness that people saw. This distinguishes between a rumor of a legal act (like divorce) and a rumor of behavior.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that if a rumor of adultery circulates about a woman, we do not suspect her, because it is merely a rumor of promiscuity.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: behavior in the marketplace
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: behavior in the marketplace
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Tannaitic dispute about a woman who eats, nibbles, or nurses in the marketplace. Rabbi Meir says she must leave her husband, while Rabbi Akiva says only if people gossip about her. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri objects, arguing that this would leave no daughter of Abraham living with her husband, and cites the Torah requirement of a clear matter (דבר ברור) as in the case of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Meir rules that a woman who eats, nibbles, or nurses in the marketplace must leave her husband, while Rabbi Akiva requires that people gossip about her.

Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri objects, arguing that such a strict standard would leave no daughter of Abraham living with her husband, and cites the Torah requirement of a clear matter (דבר ברור) as in the case of witnesses.

items.text: Baraita: cases where we do not suspect a rumor
items.text_en: Baraita: cases where we do not suspect a rumor
items.desc_en: A Baraita lists various cases where a rumor is not feared: for a woman who is a virgin, married, betrothed, or not designated to a specific man, or in another city; also for a rumor of mamzerut, slavery, or dedication of property. This establishes that rumors are only feared in specific contexts.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists various rumors (e.g., about a woman being married, betrothed, or a mamzeret) for which we do not suspect the woman, as well as rumors about property dedication.
The Baraita continues with additional cases where a rumor is not feared: a rumor of mamzerut (illegitimacy) or slavery.
The Baraita concludes with cases of dedication or declaration of ownerless property, where a rumor is also not feared.

items.text: Ulla's and Levi's definitions of a credible rumor
items.text_en: Ulla's and Levi's definitions of a credible rumor
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that a credible rumor is not one where people heard a voice, but where there are visible signs like lit candles and prepared beds, and people say 'Plonit is being betrothed today.' The Gemara corrects the wording to 'was betrothed' to avoid uncertainty. Levi's version adds women spinning by candlelight and rejoicing, and Rav Pappa corrects the wording similarly.

sub.desc_en: Ulla defines a credible rumor as visible signs (lit candles, prepared beds, people coming and going) and people saying 'Plonit is being betrothed today,' not just hearing a vague voice.
The Gemara objects that the phrase 'is being betrothed' (present tense) is uncertain, as the betrothal might not have actually occurred.
The Gemara corrects the wording to 'Plonit was betrothed today' (past tense) to remove uncertainty.
Levi's version adds women spinning by candlelight and rejoicing, with the same present-tense phrase.
The Gemara again objects to the present-tense wording in Levi's version.
Rav Pappa corrects Levi's version to the past tense 'Plonit was betrothed today.'

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's definition: speech vs. silence
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's definition: speech vs. silence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan defines a credible rumor as one where people are talking about it (they said something), while silence indicates it is a mere rumor (אמתלא). The Gemara clarifies that this excludes the view of Rabbah bar Rav Huna, who held that an אמתלא can be up to ten days later; here, if they didn't speak, it is an אמתלא, but if they did, it is not.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports Rabbi Yochanan's definition: a credible rumor is when people speak about the event, while silence indicates an אמתלא (excuse).
The Gemara objects: if they said nothing, that is meaningless — how can silence be a valid אמתלא?

The Gemara clarifies: Rabbi Yochanan's statement excludes the view of Rabbah bar Rav Huna, who held that an אמתלא can be offered up to ten days later; here, if they did not speak, it is an אמתלא, but if they did speak, it is not.

items.text: Rav's definition: tracing the rumor to a clear source
items.text_en: Rav's definition: tracing the rumor to a clear source
items.desc_en: Rav initially defines a credible rumor as one where people can trace the source from person to person until reaching a clear matter. The Gemara objects that a clear matter is valid testimony. The corrected version from Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda says that the rumor is credible if the chain of speakers goes to people who have gone overseas, so they cannot be cross-examined.

sub.text: Rav (via Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna)
sub.text_en: Rav (via Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna)
sub.desc_en: Rav defines a credible rumor as one that can be traced from person to person until reaching a clear matter (דבר ברור).
