The Gemara objects that a clear matter (דבר ברור) constitutes valid testimony, not mere rumor.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda (correcting Rav's statement)
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda (correcting Rav's statement)
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda corrects the tradition: the rumor is credible only if the chain of speakers ends with people who have gone overseas, so they cannot be cross-examined.

items.text: Abaye and Rav Yosef: can a rumor be nullified?
items.text_en: Abaye and Rav Yosef: can a rumor be nullified?
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether a rumor can be nullified. Rav Yosef infers from Rav Chisda that it can, because the rumor must come from kosher witnesses. Abaye counters from Rav Sheshet that even from women it is a rumor, implying it cannot be nullified. Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by noting different local customs: in Sura they nullify rumors, in Nehardea they do not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether a rumor (קול) about a woman's betrothal can be nullified.
Rav Yosef infers from Rav Chisda's statement that a rumor must come from kosher witnesses, implying it can be nullified.
Abaye counters from Rav Sheshet that even a rumor from women is considered a rumor, implying it cannot be nullified.
Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by noting different local customs: in Sura they nullify rumors, in Nehardea they do not.

items.text: Two practical cases: conditional betrothal and invalid betrothal
items.text_en: Two practical cases: conditional betrothal and invalid betrothal
items.desc_en: Two cases are brought: one where a rumor spread that a woman was betrothed to a scholar's son, but the father said it was conditional and the condition was violated. Rav Chama ruled that since at the time of the rumor there was no אמתלא, the father cannot later claim it was an אמתלא. The second case involves a betrothal with a date pit in a defective place; Rav Idi bar Avin asked Abaye, who ruled that even those who do not nullify rumors would nullify this one, because the Sages examined the betrothal and found it lacked a perutah's worth.

sub.desc_en: A rumor spread that a woman was betrothed to a scholar's son; Rav Chama asked the father, who said the betrothal was conditional on the son not going to Bei Chozai, and he went.
Rav Chama ruled that since at the time of the rumor there was no אמתלא (plausible explanation), the father cannot later claim it as an אמתלא.
A rumor spread that a woman was betrothed with a date pit in a defective place; Rav Idi bar Avin sent a query to Abaye asking about this case.
Abaye answered that even those who do not nullify rumors would nullify this one, because the Sages examined the betrothal and found it lacked a perutah's worth.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a rumor of betrothal
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a rumor of betrothal
items.desc_en: Rava states that even according to the opinion that we do not nullify a rumor, in this case we do nullify it, because the Sages investigated the betrothals and they were minor betrothals.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that even according to the opinion that we do not nullify a rumor, in this case we nullify it because the Sages investigated and found the betrothals were minor betrothals.

items.text: Case of a rumor about a minor appearing as an adult
items.text_en: Case of a rumor about a minor appearing as an adult
items.desc_en: A case occurred where a rumor spread that a woman was betrothed to a minor who appeared as an adult. Rav Mordechai told Rav Ashi that the Sages said the minor had not yet reached the age of 'divisions of Reuven', as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts a case where a rumor spread that a woman was betrothed to a minor appearing as an adult, and Rav Mordechai told Rav Ashi that the Sages said the minor had not yet reached the age of 'divisions of Reuven' as per the verse.

items.text: The condition of no counter-rumor (אמתלא)
items.text_en: The condition of no counter-rumor (אמתלא)
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the rumor is only considered if there is no counter-rumor. Rabba bar Rav Huna says a counter-rumor can be up to ten days later. Rav Zevid says in a place of a counter-rumor, we are concerned. Rav Pappa objects from the Mishnah, and Rav Zevid clarifies that the Mishnah refers to a place of a counter-rumor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the condition that a rumor is only considered if there is no counter-rumor (אמתלא).
Rabba bar Rav Huna rules that a counter-rumor (אמתלא) can be effective even up to ten days after the rumor.
Rav Zevid states that in a place where a counter-rumor exists, we are concerned about it.
Rav Pappa objects to Rav Zevid by citing the Mishnah's condition that there must be no counter-rumor, implying that if there is one, we are not concerned.
Rav Zevid clarifies that the Mishnah's condition refers to a place where there is a counter-rumor, meaning the Mishnah itself is discussing such a case.

items.text: Rav Kahana's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav Pappa from a Mishnah where a woman who was betrothed and then her husband came is permitted to return, implying we assume the betrothal was conditional. The Gemara distinguishes: there the husband comes and protests. If she married, she is penalized; if only betrothed, she is not.

sub.text: Rav Kahana's question to Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's question to Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges Rav Pappa from a Mishnah where a woman who was betrothed and then her husband came is permitted to return, implying we assume the betrothal was conditional.
The Gemara distinguishes: there the husband comes and protests, so the case is different.
The Gemara resolves: if she married, she is penalized (קונסין); if only betrothed, she is not penalized.

items.text: Rav Ashi's principles about rumors
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's principles about rumors
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that any rumor not confirmed in court is not a rumor. He adds that a rumor after marriage is not considered, but one after betrothal is. Rav Chaviva says even after betrothal it is not considered, and the halacha follows that we are not concerned.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that any rumor not confirmed in court is not considered a valid rumor.
Rav Ashi adds that a rumor arising after marriage is not concerning, but one after betrothal is concerning.
Rav Chaviva argues that even a rumor after betrothal is not concerning.
The halacha (הלכה) is ruled that we are not concerned about any such rumor.

items.text: Inquiry to Shmuel about a rumor and subsequent betrothal
items.text_en: Inquiry to Shmuel about a rumor and subsequent betrothal
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba reports that the house of Rav sent to Shmuel: if a rumor went out about a first man, and another betrothed her with a proper betrothal, what is the law? Shmuel replied: she must leave, and investigate the matter. The Gemara explains that this means if the first betrothal is invalid, we nullify the rumor; but since Shmuel's place does not nullify rumors, it means if the first betrothal is valid, she needs a get from the second.

sub.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba (reporting the house of Rav's inquiry)
sub.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba (reporting the house of Rav's inquiry)
sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba reports that the house of Rav sent to Shmuel: if a rumor went out about a first man, and another betrothed her with a proper betrothal (קידושי תורה), what is the law? Shmuel replied: she must leave, and investigate the matter and inform him.

The Gemara explains Shmuel's ambiguous response: it cannot mean that if the first betrothal is invalid we nullify the rumor, because Shmuel's place (Nehardea) does not nullify rumors; rather, it means that if the first betrothal is valid, she needs a get (גט) from the second.

items.text: Dispute with Rav Huna and Rav Hamnuna's principle
items.text_en: Dispute with Rav Huna and Rav Hamnuna's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Shmuel's ruling disagrees with Rav Huna, who says a married woman who accepted betrothal from another is betrothed, based on Rav Hamnuna's principle that a woman is believed to say 'you divorced me' because she would not be brazen. The Gemara distinguishes: Rav Hamnuna's principle applies only in his presence; not in his presence she is brazen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Shmuel's ruling disagrees with Rav Huna, who holds that a married woman who accepted betrothal from another is betrothed.
The Gemara cites Rav Hamnuna's principle that a woman is believed to say 'you divorced me' because she would not be brazen in her husband's presence.
The Gemara distinguishes: Rav Hamnuna's principle applies only in his presence; not in his presence she is brazen.

items.text: When the matter is not clarified
items.text_en: When the matter is not clarified
items.desc_en: If the matter is not clarified, Rav Huna says the first divorces and the second marries, but not the reverse, lest people say he takes back his divorcée from betrothal. Rav Shinana bar Rav Idi says even the second divorces and the first marries, because the Sages investigated and it was a mistaken betrothal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the matter is not clarified, what is the ruling?
Rav Huna rules: the first divorces and the second marries, but not the reverse, lest people say he takes back his divorcée from betrothal.

sub.text: Rav Shinana bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shinana bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shinana bar Rav Idi rules: even the second divorces and the first marries, because the Sages investigated and it was a mistaken betrothal.

items.text: Rumor from both men
items.text_en: Rumor from both men
items.desc_en: If a rumor went out about her from both this one and that one, Rav Pappa says she divorces the first and marries the second. Amemar says she is permitted to both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a rumor went out about her from this one and from that one (i.e., two men), what is the law?
Rav Pappa rules: even this woman divorces the first and marries the second.
Ameimar says: she is permitted to both of them.

items.text: Halakhic ruling on the previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling on the previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the final halakha that a woman who was divorced due to a suspicion of adultery is permitted to marry both her original husband and the suspected paramour.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that a woman divorced due to suspicion of adultery is permitted to marry both her original husband and the suspected paramour.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute over grounds for divorce
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute over grounds for divorce
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai holds that a man may divorce his wife only if he finds a matter of sexual immorality (ervah), citing the verse. Beit Hillel permits divorce even if she spoiled his cooking, citing the same verse. Rabbi Akiva permits divorce even if he finds another woman more attractive, citing a different verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute: Beit Shammai rules that a man may divorce his wife only if he finds a matter of ערווה (sexual immorality) in her, citing the verse.
Beit Hillel states that a man may divorce even if she burned his cooking, citing the same verse.
Rabbi Akiva adds that a man may divorce even if he finds a more beautiful woman, citing a different verse.

items.text: Gemara: Debate between Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai on the verse
items.text_en: Gemara: Debate between Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai on the verse
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel argues that the verse includes both 'ervah' and 'davar', so a minor flaw suffices. Beit Shammai counters that 'davar' is used elsewhere to require two witnesses. The Gemara explains that Beit Hillel reads 'ervat davar' as encompassing both meanings.

sub.text: Beit Hillel's objection to Beit Shammai
sub.text_en: Beit Hillel's objection to Beit Shammai
sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel objects that the verse already says 'דבר' (matter), implying a broader ground; Beit Shammai retorts that it also says 'ערוות' (sexual immorality).
Beit Hillel explains that both words are necessary: 'ערוות' alone would permit divorce only for immorality, and 'דבר' alone would permit remarriage after divorce for any reason, so both are written.
The Gemara asks how Beit Shammai interprets the word 'דבר', and answers that they derive a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the verse about witnesses, requiring two witnesses for divorce.
Beit Hillel objects that the verse does not say 'ערווה בדבר' (immorality in a matter), and Beit Shammai retorts that it does not say 'או ערווה או דבר' (either immorality or a matter).
Beit Hillel resolves that the phrase 'ערוות דבר' is written to imply both meanings simultaneously.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Akiva's position via Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Akiva's position via Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Beit Shammai and Rabbi Akiva using Resh Lakish's principle that the word 'ki' has four meanings. Beit Shammai reads 'ki matza bah ervat davar' as 'indeed he found', while Rabbi Akiva reads it as 'or perhaps he found', allowing divorce even without ervah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva and Beit Shammai disagree about, and introduces Resh Lakish's principle that the word 'כי' has four meanings.
Beit Shammai interprets 'כי' as 'דהא' (since), limiting divorce to cases of immorality, while Rabbi Akiva interprets it as 'אי נמי' (or also), allowing divorce for any reason.
The Gemara resolves that Beit Shammai read 'כִּי' as 'דְּהָא' (indeed), limiting divorce to ervah, while Rabbi Akiva read it as 'אִי נָמֵי' (or perhaps), allowing divorce even without ervah.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question: divorce without any cause
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question: divorce without any cause
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rava about a case where a man divorces his wife without any cause. Rava answers that since the Torah explicitly forbids sending away a raped woman, by implication other divorces are valid, and the divorce is effective.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rava: if a man divorces his wife without any cause at all, what is the halakhic status of the divorce?
Rava answers that unlike the case of rape where the Torah explicitly forbids divorce, here the divorce is valid retroactively (מאי דעבד עבד).

items.text: Rav Mesharshiya's question: divorcing while she serves him
items.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya's question: divorcing while she serves him
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya asks Rava about a man who intends to divorce his wife while she is still living with him and serving him. Rava cites the verse 'Do not plot harm against your neighbor who dwells trustingly with you' to condemn such behavior.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya asks Rava: if a man intends to divorce his wife but she continues to serve him, what is the ethical status? Rava cites the verse 'do not plot harm against your neighbor who dwells securely with you.'
Rava cites the verse 'Do not plot harm against your neighbor who dwells trustingly with you' to condemn such behavior.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's analogy: attitudes toward food and women
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's analogy: attitudes toward food and women
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir compares different attitudes toward women to attitudes toward food: some are fastidious (like Papus ben Yehuda who locks his wife in), some are tolerant (like most men who allow their wives to speak with relatives), and some are degraded (like a bad man who tolerates his wife going out with uncovered hair).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir compares attitudes toward women to attitudes toward food: some men, like Papus ben Yehuda, lock their wives in and leave, analogous to one who throws away a cup with a fly in it.
Rabbi Meir describes the second type: a man who removes the fly and drinks, analogous to the common man who allows his wife to speak with relatives and leaves her.
Rabbi Meir describes the third type: a man who sucks the fly off the dish and eats it, analogous to the evil man who tolerates his wife going out with uncovered head and spinning in the market.

items.text: Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's phrase 'with men'
items.text_en: Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's phrase 'with men'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah stated that an improper woman bathes 'with men.' The Gemara objects that this literal reading is impossible, and explains it means she bathes in a place where men bathe.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the woman wears a torn garment and bathes 'with men.'
The Gemara objects that a literal reading of 'with men' is impossible.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah means she bathes in a place where men bathe, not with them directly.

items.text: Derashot on the fate of a divorced woman and her second husband
items.text_en: Derashot on the fate of a divorced woman and her second husband
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a man who finds indecency in his wife has a Torah commandment to divorce her. The second husband is called 'other' because he is not a suitable match for the first; if he is righteous, he too will divorce her, but if not, she may ultimately bury him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that it is a Torah commandment to divorce a wife who has been found to have indecency, citing the verse.
The Gemara explains that the second husband is called 'other' to indicate he is not a peer of the first, as the first expelled wickedness and the second brought it in.
The Gemara explains that if the second husband is righteous, he will divorce her; if not, she will bury him, as he deserves death for bringing wickedness into his house.

items.text: Dispute on 'For He hates divorce' and its resolution
items.text_en: Dispute on 'For He hates divorce' and its resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan offer contrasting interpretations of the verse 'For He hates divorce.' The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda refers to a first marriage and Rabbi Yochanan to a second marriage, so they do not actually disagree.

sub.desc_en: רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) reads the verse 'כי שנא שלח' as a directive: if you hate your wife, send her away.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) reads the same verse as a condemnation: one who sends his wife away is hated by God.
The Gemara resolves that they do not disagree: רבי יהודה speaks of a second marriage, while רבי יוחנן speaks of a first marriage.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar on the divine sorrow caused by divorcing a first wife
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar on the divine sorrow caused by divorcing a first wife
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that a man who divorces his first wife even causes the altar to weep, as the prophet Malachi condemns treachery against the wife of one's youth.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that a man who divorces his first wife causes even the altar to weep, citing Malachi's condemnation of treachery against the wife of one's youth.
